papers.title: Construction and Commissioning of the Warwick TPC Platform
papers.abstract: Active-target gas time projection chambers (TPCs) could provide the ultimate measurements of neutrino interactions needed for future neutrino oscillation measurements. Their development requires optimisation of the gas mixture, pressure, electric fields, and readout configuration. Warwick TPC (WarTPC) is an R\&D platform for investigating in these directions for neutrino physics and beyond. It can operate at pressures up to approximately 10 bar and features a combination of thick gas electron multipliers and a Timepix3 camera for optical readout. In this paper, we present the construction and commissioning of the WarTPC platform, describing the design and integration of its subsystems, and report the first measurements of its optical response under different operating conditions, demonstrating a stable and functioning R&D platform.

papers.intro:
Neutrino oscillation measurements in the GeV regime require precise knowledge of neutrino interactions to reconstruct the neutrino flux and energy. This is complicated by the underlying interaction dynamics and intranuclear medium effects. Gas time projection chambers (TPCs) can be used as active-target detectors for neutrinos. They offer low detection thresholds and a 4π\pi angular acceptance that are crucial for understanding these effects. Their immediate drawback—limited target mass—can be compensated by using a large detector volume with pressured gas in an intense neutrino beam. At a pressure of 10 bar, a gas medium still performs better in tracking than solid or liquid [1]. TPC can operate with a range of gas mixtures; hydrogen-rich ones could enable direct measurements of neutrino interactions on hydrogen and hence neutrino energy reconstruction free of nuclear effects [2, 1].

This is complicated by the underlying interaction dynamics and intranuclear medium effects. Gas time projection chambers (TPCs) can be used as active-target detectors for neutrinos. They offer low detection thresholds and a 4π\pi angular acceptance that are crucial for understanding these effects. Their immediate drawback—limited target mass—can be compensated by using a large detector volume with pressured gas in an intense neutrino beam. At a pressure of 10 bar, a gas medium still performs better in tracking than solid or liquid [1]. TPC can operate with a range of gas mixtures; hydrogen-rich ones could enable direct measurements of neutrino interactions on hydrogen and hence neutrino energy reconstruction free of nuclear effects [2, 1].

A sufficient target mass in an active-target TPC for neutrinos requires a large detector volume and a capable readout system. Conventional charge readout can be costly as the number of channels increases with the readout area. Optical readout offers a potentially scalable alternative, with a small sensor imaging a much larger area while providing fine spatial granularity and good timing resolution [3]. In noble gases such as argon and xenon, ionisation electrons can produce secondary scintillation, or electroluminescence [4]. The corresponding optical tracking signal can be imaged by cameras.

Conventional charge readout can be costly as the number of channels increases with the readout area. Optical readout offers a potentially scalable alternative, with a small sensor imaging a much larger area while providing fine spatial granularity and good timing resolution [3]. In noble gases such as argon and xenon, ionisation electrons can produce secondary scintillation, or electroluminescence [4]. The corresponding optical tracking signal can be imaged by cameras.

The electron-transport properties and light yield that determine TPC performance rely on the gas composition, pressure, and drift and amplification fields. It may not be possible to achieve suitable electron-transport properties and sufficient light yield simultaneously in hydrogen-rich mixtures at high pressure within practical limitations such as high voltage and drift length. In particular, methane can suppress noble-gas scintillation [5], while increasing pressure can reduce the light yield [4]. It is therefore important to verify such expected limitations in situ and identify suitable combinations of gas mixture, pressure, electric fields, and readout configuration. Hence, an R&D platform is required. Such a platform may also reveal further opportunities for active-target, or general tracking, TPCs through a systematic exploration of operating conditions, including, for example, at low pressures or with charge readout.

Warwick TPC (WarTPC) is such a platform for investigating novel TPC technologies for neutrino physics and beyond. Construction began in August 2022, and commissioning has been concluded with the observation of alpha-particle tracks from a 241Am source and cosmic-ray tracks. This paper presents an overview of the construction and commissioning of WarTPC, describing the design and integration of its subsystems and the first optical signal observations under different operating conditions. More details can be found in Ref. [6]. This paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes WarTPC and its subsystems. Section 3 describes the commissioning measurements, followed by the conclusions in Section 4.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Enhancing deep-learning models: the impact of image processing and training data selection for strong-lens detection
papers.abstract: Euclid is expected to discover ~$10^5$ galaxy-galaxy strong gravitational lenses across ~14,000deg$^2$, requiring automated searches with high completeness and low false-positive rates. Despite advances in deep learning, the effects of training-set composition, image representation, and preprocessing on survey-scale detection remain poorly understood. We present an ablation study of the convolutional neural network used in the ECLIPSE strong-lens detection pipeline, evaluating different training configurations on a fixed test set. Using simulated and real Euclid data, we compare VIS-only and pseudo-RGB representations, FITS and JPEG formats, training-set composition, hard-negative selection, and multi-stage training. We also assess ensembling on ~67 million DR1 cutouts. Training-set composition and strategy strongly affect high-Recall performance. Omitting simulation based pre-training reduces high-Recall weighted average Precision by 83.7% for VIS-only and 74.5% for pseudo-RGB models. Negative-sample selection also substantially affects performance, while FITS yields modest gains over JPEG at high Recall (~2-5%). On DR1, the logit-mean ensemble improves average Precision by 28.0% and 39.9% over the individual VIS-only and pseudo-RGB models. Among ~70,000 candidates selected for visual inspection, it recovers 11,256 unique grade A (secure) and B (probable) lenses, compared with 9650 and 10,395 for the individual models. The branches show complementary ranking preferences, particularly for lenses benefiting from near-infrared information. Careful training-set design, realistic negatives, and multi-band ensembling improve survey-scale searches. Our final ensemble achieves ~80% Recall at the operational selection threshold, outperforming ablation models with higher global classification metrics and highlighting the need to optimise performance for realistic survey conditions.[Abridged]

papers.intro:
Strong gravitational lensing provides a unique probe of the distribution of matter in the Universe across a wide range of scales. Galaxy-scale strong lenses enable detailed measurements of the total mass profiles of galaxies and constraints on the nature and distribution of dark matter (Treu et al. 2010; Auger et al. 2010), studies of highly magnified high-redshift sources (Pettini et al. 2000; Quider et al. 2009), and independent cosmological measurements through lensing statistics and time-delay analyses (Oguri and Marshall 2010; Suyu et al. 2017; Sonnenfeld 2021). The scientific return of strong-lens samples therefore scales directly with the number, diversity, and completeness of the systems that can be identified.

The scientific return of strong-lens samples therefore scales directly with the number, diversity, and completeness of the systems that can be identified.

The advent of large-area imaging surveys has transformed the search for strong gravitational lenses from a targeted observational effort into a large-scale data mining problem. Surveys such as CFHTLS, DES, HSC, and KiDS have motivated the development of increasingly automated lens-finding techniques capable of processing millions of galaxies (Jacobs et al. 2019; Petrillo et al. 2019b; Huang et al. 2021). Among these approaches, deep-learning (DL) methods have emerged as one of the most effective solutions, consistently achieving state-of-the-art performance in lens-identification tasks (Lanusse et al. 2018; Petrillo et al. 2019a; Cañameras et al. 2021).

Euclid (Laureijs et al. 2011; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) represents the next major step in this progression. The survey is expected to image approximately 14 00014\,000 deg2 of the extragalactic sky with unprecedented combinations of area, depth, and angular resolution. Simulations predict that Euclid will discover of order 10510^{5} galaxy–galaxy strong lenses, increasing the currently known population by an order of magnitude (Collett 2015). However, realising this scientific potential requires highly efficient automated search strategies. Even a classifier with excellent overall accuracy must operate at extremely low false-positive rates when applied to hundreds of millions of galaxies, while simultaneously maintaining high completeness to avoid losing rare lens systems.

After Q1, the Euclid strong-lens search has now been extended to the first major public data release (DR1; Euclid Collaboration: Aussel and others 2026), covering approximately 20002000 deg2 of extragalactic sky. At this scale, exhaustive visual inspection is no longer feasible, and candidate selection relies on automated ranking pipelines capable of processing tens of millions of galaxies. To construct the ECLIPSE strong-lens catalogue (Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026b), multiple independently developed ML models were applied to the full survey footprint, followed by citizen science and expert visual-inspection stages (Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al. 2026a). This effort yielded a catalogue containing more than 15 00015\,000 strong-lens candidates, complete with lensing-model fits (Euclid Collaboration: Nightingale et al. 2026) and photometric redshifts (Euclid Collaboration: Nersesian et al. 2026), increasing the number of known candidates by more than an order of magnitude relative to the Q1 release.

The network presented in this work formed one of the ML components used in the DR1 ECLIPSE pipeline (described in Euclid Collaboration: Vincken et al. in prep.), achieving the highest single performance overall. While the operational performance of the DR1 pipeline demonstrates the effectiveness of DL approaches for large-scale lens discovery, it also raises a number of important methodological questions. For this reason, we investigated which aspects of the training strategy contribute most strongly to performance, how much information is lost when astronomical images are compressed or reformatted for ML applications, to what extent does the selection of positive and negative training examples influence the final candidate rankings, and how can complementary representations of the same astronomical scene be combined to maximise completeness while maintaining manageable candidate volumes. Addressing these aspects is particularly relevant for Euclid observations. The survey simultaneously provides high-resolution VIS imaging (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025) and multi-band NIR photometry (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025), enabling multiple strategies for constructing ML inputs. Furthermore, the rarity of galaxy-scale strong lenses (approximately 1 lens every 10 00010\,000 ML-scored images) means that the dominant challenge is not distinguishing lenses from random galaxies, but from visually similar non-lenses that populate the high-score tail of candidate rankings. As a result, the selection of realistic hard negatives and the preservation of subtle lensing signatures may be as important as the choice of network architecture itself.

papers.title: AmbiSteer: Selectively Eliciting Ambiguity-Aware Responses in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often exhibit overconfidence, providing firm answers even when visual evidence is insufficient. A prominent case is referential ambiguity in Visual Question Answering (VQA), where multiple entities in an image are plausible referents of a question. Addressing such cases requires recognizing when ambiguity is present: ambiguous questions can be handled by asking for clarification or enumerating plausible referents, while unambiguous questions should receive a direct answer. Current VLMs struggle with this distinction, often defaulting to a single interpretation. To investigate whether activation steering can serve as an inference-time mechanism to elicit such behaviors, we introduce AmbiSteer, a lightweight framework to selectively elicit ambiguity-aware behavior. Across three VLMs, we find that steering alone has limited and model-dependent effects, while prompting is generally more effective. Combining prompting and steering substantially increases clarification and enumeration behaviors, but also elicits them on unambiguous cases. AmbiSteer addresses this using a linear classifier to predict input ambiguity and condition the steering direction accordingly, increasing the proportion of inputs handled appropriately from 59.0% to 77.0% on average across models. Our work sets the ground for lightweight approaches to reduce model overconfidence in uncertain multimodal settings.

papers.intro:
Visual Question Answering (VQA) requires models to interpret natural-language questions in visual context (Antol et al., 2015). This often involves resolving which entity in the image a question refers to. However, visual context does not always uniquely identify the intended referent. For example, in Figure 1, the question “What is the man holding?” is referentially ambiguous because multiple people in the image are equally plausible referents. Motivated by Testoni et al. (2025), we focus on two ambiguity-aware strategies observed in human responses to referential ambiguity: asking which referent is intended (clarification) and providing answers for multiple plausible referents (enumeration). Yet, their analysis shows that current VLMs often overcommit to a single arbitrary interpretation without acknowledging ambiguity.

(2025), we focus on two ambiguity-aware strategies observed in human responses to referential ambiguity: asking which referent is intended (clarification) and providing answers for multiple plausible referents (enumeration). Yet, their analysis shows that current VLMs often overcommit to a single arbitrary interpretation without acknowledging ambiguity.

Crucially, clarification and enumeration should not be elicited unconditionally. Figure 1 also illustrates the complementary case: when the referent is clear, a direct answer is most appropriate, while clarification or enumeration would be unnecessary and violate Grice’s maxim of quantity by providing more information than required (Grice, 1975). Effective ambiguity handling is therefore inherently selective: ambiguity-aware responses are appropriate when the referent is unresolved, but not when the intended referent is already clear.

We investigate activation steering as a lightweight inference-time control mechanism that leaves the VLM’s weights unchanged. By modifying internal representations during generation, activation steering offers a way to selectively promote or suppress target behaviors without fine-tuning.

To this end, we introduce AmbiSteer, a framework for selective ambiguity handling in VQA. Using ClearVQA and AQuA to study clarification and enumeration behaviors, respectively, we derive steering vectors from contrastive pairs consisting of an ambiguity-aware response and a response that commits to a single interpretation. Because effective ambiguity handling requires knowing both how to respond and when to intervene, AmbiSteer combines activation steering with classifier-gated ambiguity prediction. A linear classifier over VLM representations predicts whether each image-question pair is ambiguous, and its prediction determines the steering direction, encouraging ambiguity-aware behavior for ambiguous inputs and suppressing it otherwise.

papers.title: In the Eye of the Beholder: Human Label Variation in Textual and Visual Entailment
papers.abstract: Human Label Variation (HLV) is increasingly recognised as an informative signal that reflects meaningful differences in how people interpret the same input. While HLV has been studied extensively in Natural Language Inference (NLI), much less is known about HLV in Visual Entailment (VE; Xie et al., 2019), where the textual premise is replaced by an image, keeping the hypothesis and label space fixed. We introduce VariNLI-VE, a dataset for studying how HLV changes between paired NLI and VE instances. We re-annotate a subset of originally neutral SNLI (Bowman et al., 2015) instances and their visual counterparts, with the same annotators evaluating both the textual and visual versions. Each annotation includes a label, confidence score, and explanation, yielding 2,250 annotations. Labels and explanations are collected jointly, providing ecologically valid explanations. Because the image may reveal information not stated in the text, one might expect disagreement to decrease in VE. Instead, we find no clear overall reduction: disagreement decreases for some instances while it increases for others. Explanations reveal further variation, as annotators can retain the same label while changing their rationale. When evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on the paired data, we find lower accuracy, weaker alignment with human label distributions, and generally higher uncertainty in VE than in NLI.

papers.intro:
Many Natural Language Processing tasks assume that each input is associated with a single correct label. In practice, however, annotators often disagree, giving rise to Human Label Variation (HLV; Plank, 2022). Rather than being noise, such variation can reflect ambiguity, different interpretations, and multiple valid readings (Aroyo and Welty, 2015; Uma et al., 2022). While substantial prior work has studied variation and disagreement in the Natural Language Inference (NLI) task (Pavlick and Kwiatkowski, 2019; Nie et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2023, inter alia), human inference is not restricted to textual evidence. In the Visual Entailment (VE) task (Xie et al., 2019), the premise is presented as an image rather than text, while the hypothesis and label space remain unchanged. However, HLV in VE remains underexplored. We therefore use VE as a test bed to study how HLV changes from NLI to VE when the same annotators judge the same hypothesis under textual and visual premises.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Control of Magnetoconvective Flows via Differentiable Simulation
papers.abstract: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) fluid flows are central to demanding engineering applications, most prominently fusion blanket cooling, where flow control is a promising tool to optimize key properties such as heat transfer. While active flow control (AFC) has recently advanced through machine learning, its application to MHD flows remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present $\phi$-PICT, a novel differentiable GPU-accelerated MHD solver targeted at AFC. We validate $\phi$-PICT against MHD benchmarks and demonstrate its high computational efficiency. Integrated into FluidGym, $\phi$-PICT enables sample-efficient gradient-based algorithms to improve heat transfer by $>25$% and allows optimizers to achieve $10^3\times$ higher accuracy in inverse design than black-box methods. $\phi$-PICT is publicly available at https://github.com/upb-sciml/phiPICT.

papers.intro:
Control of large-scale physical systems governed by high-dimensional, non-linear partial differential equations (PDEs) remains a fundamental challenge at the intersection of machine learning, physics, and control theory (Brunton et al., 2020). Among such systems, magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) introduces distinct control challenges driven by the interaction between an electrically conducting fluid and external magnetic field. papers.title: Two correlation scales in homogeneous density-matrix functionals: the M\"uller logarithm and the sharp Cs\'anyi--Arias asymptotics
papers.abstract:
We resolve the exact high-density correlation scales and coefficients of the three-dimensional translation-invariant, spin-symmetric M\"uller and Cs\'anyi--Arias corrected Hartree--Fock (CHF) functionals, settling long-standing numerical observations of M\"uller overcorrelation and apparently vanishing CHF correlation. In Hartree units, for fixed spin multiplicity $q$ and Fermi momentum $k=(6\pi^2\rho/q)^{1/3}$, their gains per particle over the filled Fermi sea satisfy \[
  D_{\rm M}(k)=\frac{3}{4\pi^2}\log k+O(1),\qquad
  D_{\rm CHF}(k)=12e^{-1/2-\pi^2/8}
  k^2e^{-\pi^{3/2}\sqrt{k}}(1+o(1)). \] The M\"uller proof retains the occupation cap and identifies the factor-of-two cancellation between exchange defect and energy gain. For periodic M\"uller jellium, convexity and translation--spin averaging allow a global minimizer to be chosen invariant and identify the unrestricted thermodynamic energy with the homogeneous spin-symmetric value. The CHF upper bound follows from a deterministic comparison built from the explicit Hartree--Fock dispersion, combining a full Birman--Schwinger bound with one-sided norms and completion of the square; a number-preserving trial state provides the matching lower bound, and the retained remainder yields weighted $L^2$ convergence of the occupation defect without analyzing the self-consistent gap. We also prove existence for both functionals and uniqueness of the CHF minimizer. Relative to the unpolarized quantum high-density benchmark, M\"uller has a larger logarithmic coefficient, providing quantitative evidence for the conjectured M\"uller lower-bound property, whereas CHF misses the logarithmic scale altogether. The quantum benchmark is not used in either functional proof.

papers.title: Deep Bundle Adjustment
papers.abstract: We present \textbf{DeepBA} (\textbf{Deep} \textbf{B}undle \textbf{A}djustment), a graph neural network (GNN) that recovers camera poses, intrinsics, and scene structure from 2D matches across an arbitrary number of views. Rather than solving a non-linear least-squares problem per scene, DeepBA amortizes bundle adjustment into a learned graph network that iteratively refines its estimate from geometric residuals. Where classical SfM computes its updates analytically and needs careful initialization, DeepBA learns them and converges from a cold start. It is trained with scale-invariant supervision (ground-truth rotation, translation direction, and intrinsics, plus reprojection self-consistency), so datasets with arbitrary metric units can be mixed without per-scene normalization. DeepBA is decoupled from the matcher. At 2.04M parameters, it outperforms prior learned SfM from matches on scene reconstruction and on most pose metrics, is competitive with classical SfM at moderate accuracy thresholds and overtakes it in wall time as the view count grows, and approaches monolithic image-to-geometry transformers such as VGGT ($\sim$1.2B parameters) with greater modularity. Project~page: https://cphjsn.github.io/deep-ba/

papers.intro:
Recovering camera poses and scene geometry from a set of images is a foundational problem in 3D computer vision, addressed by structure-from-motion (SfM) [40] and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) [34]. Most modern SfM pipelines and keyframe-based SLAM systems rely on the same classical solver, bundle adjustment (BA) [52, 14], which jointly refines cameras and 3D points by minimizing reprojection residuals via non-linear least squares. Bundle adjustment is near-optimal given a good initialization, but its non-convex landscape is fragile. Incremental SfM obtains such an initialization through heuristics and per-scene tuning [40], yet these heuristics break down on weak baselines or planar structure [51]. Meanwhile, learning-based semi-dense [45] and dense [8, 9] matchers have made matches far more reliable than SIFT-style keypoints [32], shifting the bottleneck from matching to the solver. However, feeding them into a COLMAP-style pipeline does not automatically help, as its rigid track building is overwhelmed by the volume and its initialization stays brittle. This mismatch motivated a line of feed-forward 3D networks (DUSt3R [58], MASt3R [24], and VGGT [57]) that regress geometry directly from images, trading the classical pipeline’s modularity for robustness. There is a missing middle: a learned solver that amortizes bundle adjustment itself, while leaving the matcher decoupled and solving any number of views at once. Classical bundle adjustment already operates on a graph of cameras and their 2D matches, so a graph neural network is the natural architecture for that structure.

We introduce DeepBA (Deep Bundle Adjustment, Fig. 1), a GNN that takes 2D matches from an off-the-shelf matcher and jointly infers absolute camera poses, intrinsics, and 3D points. DeepBA replaces the per-scene non-linear least-squares solver with a learned Markovian iterative refinement. Each iteration recomputes geometric features from the current state and predicts an updated state via shared GNN weights. The number of iterations is a free choice at test time, independent of the training schedule: accuracy rises with the iteration count until it saturates, mirroring an iterative classical solver. It operates directly on pairwise matches, with no separate track-building stage. Our contributions are: • Amortized cold-start bundle adjustment via a GNN. We formulate bundle adjustment as a learned iterative refinement over the view graph of any number of views, with a Markovian update that lets the user trade runtime for accuracy at test time. It requires no initial poses or intrinsics and converges from a cold start, where classical BA fails. • Scale-invariant, anchor-free, multi-dataset supervision. Chordal rotation, direction-only translation, intrinsics, self-consistent reprojection and 3D losses train DeepBA on datasets with arbitrary metric units without per-scene normalization. Because DeepBA predicts state updates rather than geometry, it needs no anchor camera, unlike VGGT [57], which uses the first camera as its reference frame. • Robustness across matcher families. DeepBA sees only 2D matches, so a trained network can run from sparse to dense matching without retraining. We demonstrate this extensively, across every matcher family. • Competitive accuracy at a fraction of the size. With 2.042.04M parameters (∼71×{\sim}71\times fewer than the strongest prior match-based network, GASfM [2] at 145145M), DeepBA outperforms learned SfM from matches on most metrics and is competitive with classical SfM at moderate thresholds, approaching image-to-geometry transformers such as VGGT (∼1.2{\sim}1.2B parameters).

papers.title: High-Transmission Cryogenic Fiber-Optic U-Bench Filter for Ultra-Low-Background Single-Photon Detection in Superconducting Devices
papers.abstract: We report on our progress in implementing a cryogenic fiber-optic U-bench hosting an ultra-narrow bandpass filter, designed to mitigate the dominant fiber-coupled 300 K black-body background observed for superconducting single-photon detectors. While U-benches can be routinely aligned at room temperature to achieve minor optical losses, cooling them down results in substantial misalignment due to thermal contraction of their components. To mitigate the resulting losses, we have integrated cryo-compatible piezo stepper motors to the U-bench, enabling its in situ realignment while cold. In particular, this allows us to shift the temperature dependent transmission window of the used filter by rotating it with respect to the beam axis. First results show that our U-bench filter reaches a transmission coefficient of 38% (4.2 dB loss) at 40 K temperature. We project that the U-bench filter can reduce the black-body background down to $10^{-8}$ Hz and $10^{-3}$ Hz ranges for 1064 nm and 1550 nm wavelengths, respectively. With the expected background rates and the herein reported transmission coefficient, applying the U-bench filter in series with a transition edge sensor shows great potential in increasing the sensitivity of dedicated rare-event searches. We project that the noise-equivalent power for 1550 nm wavelength could be reduced down to $10^{-20}$ W Hz$^{-1/2}$ range if intrinsic background sources can be sufficiently mitigated.

papers.intro:
Superconducting single-photon detectors (SSPDs) form a broad class of devices characterized by high detection efficiencies and low background (dark count) rates [1, 2, 3]. Energy resolving transition edge sensors (TESs) [4] are arguably one of the best performing class of SSPDs operating in the optical and near-infrared range. As their main advantage, the energy sensitive detection enables the effective mitigation of dark counts induced by intrinsic background sources, such as radioactive decays and cosmic rays [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Subsequently, the extrinsic background dominated by fiber-coupled room temperature black-body radiation has been concluded as the limiting background source [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 10]. The rate of the black-body background in the region of interest for a mono-energetic source is ultimately set by the energy resolution of the TES, determining its signal-to-noise ratio.

We then provide a technical description of our prototype (Section III) and present first performance tests regarding mitigation of thermal contraction induced optical losses (Section IV).

papers.title: RAZeR: Representation Aware Zonotope Reduction
papers.abstract: Reachability analysis is a popular technique for verifying the safety of a dynamical system under uncertainty, where the uncertainty is often represented by zonotopes. As the size of the zonotope representation typically grows as the reachability analysis progresses, it must be repeatedly reduced at the cost of additional conservatism. While various methods exist to reduce the size of the representation, combined advantages are not fully leveraged as only a single reduction method is typically used throughout the analysis. In this work, we show how dynamically choosing which method to use can yield significantly tighter results, thereby easing verification. This is realized by introducing a heuristic, derived from model predictive control, that accounts for upcoming propagation of the current zonotope. We argue that order reduction is not merely a post-processing step after propagation but also a pre-processing step that shapes how the zonotope evolves under the system dynamics. We evaluate our approach, RAZeR, on nonlinear benchmarks taken from the ARCH-COMP, where we demonstrate that RAZeR produces tighter zonotopes at a negligible performance overhead.

A zonotope (Girard, 2005) is a convex, centrally symmetric, continuous set that can be represented with only a few parameters even in high-dimensional spaces. They are a crucial element in reachability analysis of dynamical systems (Girard, 2005; Althoff, 2010), neural network verification (Singh et al., 2018), and runtime monitoring under uncertainty (Finkbeiner et al., 2026; Finkbeiner et al., 2024), as the required operations are efficient to compute for zonotopes.

In these applications, the representation of a zonotope usually grows in size, i.e., the number of generators that span the zonotope grows. To remain computationally efficient, zonotope reduction methods try to find another zonotope that encloses the original zonotope with fewer generators, where a more aggressive reduction usually leads to greater conservatism in the overarching goal of verifying a safety-critical system.

papers.title: Natural Swing-Up of an Underpowered Double Pendulum
papers.abstract: Robots with weak motors must ride their natural dynamics rather than fight them. We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6\,\% of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint. The constraint uses the model-based rate of the error, so no stabilizing feedback gain is needed. Experiments in hardware show swing-ups along both modes and compare the allocation with summing-and-clipping and with prioritized stabilization.

papers.intro:
We want robots whose wanted motions are natural motions of their dynamics, and nonlinear normal modes (NNMs) are one way to embed them: control uses what is already there instead of forcing new dynamics onto the system. Our control approach holds for nn joints and their nn modes; we show it on two, whose modes are easy to understand and to visualize.

We want robots whose wanted motions are natural motions of their dynamics, and nonlinear normal modes (NNMs) are one way to embed them: control uses what is already there instead of forcing new dynamics onto the system. Our control approach holds for nn joints and their nn modes; we show it on two, whose modes are easy to understand and to visualize.

Swinging up a robot whose motors cannot even hold its arm horizontal is a matter of timing, not of force. The direct-drive motors of the planar two-link robot of Fig. 1 deliver only 1.11.1 Nm, about 6 % of the gravity torque in the first joint with the arm held horizontally. With full torque in both joints, link 2 tilts by 16.3∘16.3^{\circ} and link 1 stays hanging, because the reaction of the elbow torque cancels the shoulder torque (Fig. 1b). Neither a joint PD controller nor a controller that tracks a direct path to the upright pose (Fig. 5a) can get there; the robot has to collect the energy over many swings. A single pendulum is swung up by energy control, which puts it on the homoclinic orbit that ends upright [1]. The double pendulum is chaotic [2], so energy control alone most likely ends in chaotic motion, and energy-based swing-ups of double pendulums pass through intermediate equilibria [3, 4]. We instead guide the swing-up along the NNMs of the robot [5, 6, 7], families of periodic orbits of the free dynamics, one per energy. On one mode the robot behaves much like a single pendulum: there is no chaos, and the modes connect the hanging equilibrium to a homoclinic orbit at the upright one [8]. Pumping energy along a mode thus carries the robot from rest to almost upright, where a short precomputed trajectory catches it in a handstand.

Like earlier work, we ride a mode with two control loops, one that keeps the state on the mode and one that changes the energy. Both share the same limited motor torques, a box of admissible torques with one bound per joint, which we call the box constraint. Prior work sums the two loops [9, 10], gives priority to stabilization [8], or solves a nonlinear MPC in simulation [11]. The loops interfere: a torque that corrects the error with respect to the mode generally does work and changes the energy. On a non-strict mode, one whose orbits do not all run along the same path in configuration space, no bounded torque can change the energy while keeping the state on the mode [12, Thm. 1], and the modes of our robot are non-strict (Sec. II-D). Power-neutral steering is known from gyroscopic forces [13], power-continuous curve tracking [14] and geometric fabrics [15], and pumping along the momentum stays on a strict mode [16]. What is not known is how to allocate the two under a box constraint on a non-strict mode, where pumping leaves the mode and steering must undo it.

Like earlier work, we ride a mode with two control loops, one that keeps the state on the mode and one that changes the energy. Both share the same limited motor torques, a box of admissible torques with one bound per joint, which we call the box constraint. Prior work sums the two loops [9, 10], gives priority to stabilization [8], or solves a nonlinear MPC in simulation [11]. The loops interfere: a torque that corrects the error with respect to the mode generally does work and changes the energy. On a non-strict mode, one whose orbits do not all run along the same path in configuration space, no bounded torque can change the energy while keeping the state on the mode [12, Thm. 1], and the modes of our robot are non-strict (Sec. II-D). Power-neutral steering is known from gyroscopic forces [13], power-continuous curve tracking [14] and geometric fabrics [15], and pumping along the momentum stays on a strict mode [16]. What is not known is how to allocate the two under a box constraint on a non-strict mode, where pumping leaves the mode and steering must undo it.

We split the input torque by its power into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: pump as hard as the box allows, subject to one control-Lyapunov function (CLF) constraint [17] that makes a transverse error measure decay. Unlike classical control allocation [18], there is no actuator redundancy; we allocate the torque box between two tasks. No feedback gains are designed; the transverse instability of the orbits sets the decay rate. The PD stabilizers of earlier mode-based swing-ups [9, 10, 8] and transverse feedback linearization of orbits [19, 20] need gains tuned against the pumping, and optimal orbit stabilization [21] handles a single orbit with unbounded inputs, not a family under a tight box constraint.

papers.title: Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.

papers.intro:
Multimodal agentic coding requires agents to interleave code generation with visual reasoning to analyze inputs and verify rendered artifacts. Current frameworks predominantly follow the Thinking-with-Images paradigm [13, 9, 19], where coding agents rely on their own intrinsic vision to inspect images, whether directly or through basic image-manipulation operations such as cropping and zooming. However, tightly coupling visual perception with the coding agent introduces two fundamental limitations. First, for multimodal coding agents, output quality remains strictly bounded by their intrinsic perception. Even when recent studies design task-specific workflows [26, 24, 10] for iterative code refinement, they fail to break this intrinsic perceptual bound while sacrificing generalizability across diverse coding tasks. Second, text-only coding agents are entirely excluded from this paradigm due to the lack of native perception; while prior works attempt to equip them with fixed visual modules such as captioners and layout detectors [25, 20], or perception pipelines tailored exclusively for visual question answering [30, 11], such designs cannot support the closed-loop refinement required by agentic coding.

However, tightly coupling visual perception with the coding agent introduces two fundamental limitations. First, for multimodal coding agents, output quality remains strictly bounded by their intrinsic perception. Even when recent studies design task-specific workflows [26, 24, 10] for iterative code refinement, they fail to break this intrinsic perceptual bound while sacrificing generalizability across diverse coding tasks. Second, text-only coding agents are entirely excluded from this paradigm due to the lack of native perception; while prior works attempt to equip them with fixed visual modules such as captioners and layout detectors [25, 20], or perception pipelines tailored exclusively for visual question answering [30, 11], such designs cannot support the closed-loop refinement required by agentic coding.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm for multimodal agentic coding (Figure 1). Rather than relying on the agent’s intrinsic vision or fixed task-specific perception designs, VaaT reframes an external MLLM as general-purpose visual utilities through a unified interface. Within this paradigm, the coding agent autonomously invokes these utilities during execution to obtain perceptual feedback that guides code generation and refinement. By decoupling visual perception from code generation, VaaT allows text-only coding agents to offload visual perception entirely to external visual utilities, while enabling multimodal coding agents to dynamically augment their intrinsic vision on demand.

Within this paradigm, the coding agent autonomously invokes these utilities during execution to obtain perceptual feedback that guides code generation and refinement. By decoupling visual perception from code generation, VaaT allows text-only coding agents to offload visual perception entirely to external visual utilities, while enabling multimodal coding agents to dynamically augment their intrinsic vision on demand.

To instantiate this paradigm, we develop VHarness, a unified framework organized around five intuitive atomic actions that expose visual utilities to the coding agent. Just as software engineering relies on general-purpose shell utilities such as grep for searching text and diff for comparing files, VHarness extends this philosophy to the visual domain: transcribe for holistic structure extraction, grep for visual element localization, inspect for fine-grained attribute querying, align for visual assertion checking, and diff for image-to-image comparison between target and rendered artifacts. This compact interface seamlessly adapts across diverse tasks without task-specific workflow engineering.

To rigorously and quantitatively evaluate the VaaT paradigm, we focus on vision-to-code generation tasks where rendered outputs can be directly verified against ground-truth visual inputs. Specifically, we evaluate VHarness across three diverse domains, spanning webpage reconstruction in Image-to-HTML, vector graphics generation in Image-to-SVG, and procedural modeling in Image-to-3D [7]. Our experiments verify the effectiveness of VHarness across two categories of coding agents. First, VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across multimodal coding agents, including GPT-5.5 [15], GPT-5.6-sol [14], Claude Opus 4.8 [1], and GLM-5.3-Flash [28]. Together, these results demonstrate that modularizing visual perception into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for multimodal agentic coding.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): The MERge processing
papers.abstract: The ESA satellite mission \Euclid was launched in July 2023 and started its regular observing mode in February 2024. The data from the \Euclid instruments Visible Camera (VIS) and the Near IR Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) are complemented by ground-based imaging data in the $u$, $g$ $r$, $i$, and $z$ bands to enable the determination of photometric redshifts and other galaxy properties. This paper describes the MERge processing function (MER PF) that has been developed and run for the Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). The aim of the MER PF is to detect objects in the \Euclid imaging data, measure their properties, and combine them into a single multi-wavelength catalogue. In this paper we illustrate the design of the MER PF and introduce the different photometric methods applied to the data, which are Kron total flux, aperture photometry on Point Spread Functions (PSF) -matched images, template fitting photometry, and S\'ersic fitting photometry. We also present the various morphological measurements and quality flags that improve the scientific content of the output catalogues and better characterize the detected sources. We illustrate the processing and measurements that help to validate the MER PF results, which is an essential step to qualify the output for the public DR1 release. We discuss the global assessment of the photometric homogeneity and provide an internal comparison of our processing results. In addition, we give an extensive overview of the DR1 output data and the various processing scenarios

papers.intro:
The cosmology and fundamental physics mission Euclid (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) was successfully launched in July 2023. Euclid aims at collecting data in the 14 000​deg214\,000\,\text{deg}^{2} large Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and the approximately 63​deg263\,\text{deg}^{2} large Euclid Deep Survey (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022, EDS;). In additon to the VIS and NIR data directly from Euclid, the project also includes data from ground-based photometric surveys such as DES (Abbott et al. 2021), CFIS (Ibata et al. 2017), Pan-STARRS (Magnier et al. 2020), WHIGS and WHISHES (Aihara et al. 2018, see) to enable photometric redshift determination and determine the SED of the PSF to be used for the shape measurements (Eriksen and Hoekstra 2018).

In additon to the VIS and NIR data directly from Euclid, the project also includes data from ground-based photometric surveys such as DES (Abbott et al. 2021), CFIS (Ibata et al. 2017), Pan-STARRS (Magnier et al. 2020), WHIGS and WHISHES (Aihara et al. 2018, see) to enable photometric redshift determination and determine the SED of the PSF to be used for the shape measurements (Eriksen and Hoekstra 2018).

The processing of the very large volume of Euclid data is, in the context of the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), organized into a set of processing functions (PFs), with each PF developed and maintained by a corresponding Organisation Unit (OU). The Euclid Consortium (EC) is committed to release fully processed data at pre-defined dates, and this paper describes the MERge PF that contributed to the core products of Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). A full description of the area selection, processing organization, and processing details of Euclid DR1 are provided in Euclid Collaboration: Aussel and others (2026). After Euclid Quick Release Q1 (Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026) DR1 now comprises ∼1900​deg2\sim 1900\,{\rm deg}^{2} of EWS and EDS in all three sub-fields down to different depth.

The main output products of the MER PF are coadded images and a final catalogue with the photometric and morphological properties of all detected sources. As input, the MER PF needs VIS and NISP calibrated frames, processed by OU-VIS (Euclid Collaboration: McCracken et al. 2026) and OU-NIR (Euclid Collaboration: Polenta et al. 2026), respectively, and stacked frames from selected external surveys as processed by OU-EXT (Euclid Collaboration: Corcho-Caballero et al. 2026), together with related ancillary data and PSF models. Object detection is done on both the VIS and NIR (stacking the three NISP bands JEJ_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, HEH_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, and YEY_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}) imaging data. A multi-wavelength flux determination is performed on detected objects with different photometric techniques. The final product of the MER PF is a catalogue of sources with unique identification numbers, multi-wavelength photometric measurements, and ancillary information (morphological estimates, quality flags, etc.).

Within the Euclid SGS the output of the MER PF is fed to the pipelines for photometric redshift computation (Euclid Collaboration: Hartley et al. 2026) and spectra extraction (Euclid Collaboration: Scodeggio et al. 2026). The object catalogues are used as an input for the shear estimation which is performed by OU-SHE and the subsequent OU-LE3 work on cosmology, which constitutes the core science of Euclid.

This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the MER pipeline and the processing elements (PEs) that were implemented and utilized for the Euclid DR1 processing. In Sect. 3 we discuss the data validation, Sect. 3.7.2 shows a method to assess the homogeneity of the MER photometry, Sect. 4 discusses the treatment of the PSF models, and Sect. 5 shows a comparison of the properties of the objects measured on EWS and EDS. Section 6 contains an overview of the MER EWS and EDS data released in DR1. We close the paper with an outlook in Sect. 7.

papers.title: OrbitWeaver: LLM Agent Planning with Simulation Feedback for Optically Interconnected Orbital GPU Clusters
papers.abstract: Space-based data-center designs increasingly consider GPU computing formations connected by inter-satellite optical links. With limited neighboring connections, jobs assigned disjoint GPUs can still contend on shared relay paths. Rank placement and communication priorities jointly affect this contention and the readiness of downstream computation. We present OrbitWeaver, an offline large language model (LLM) agent planner that jointly optimizes rank placement and communication order. Guided by communication structure, execution dependencies, and simulation feedback, the agent constructs and refines plans that coordinate shared-link access with computation progress. This coordination reduces contention and dependency blocking, shortening mean job completion time (JCT). Simulation experiments on optically interconnected orbital GPU clusters show that OrbitWeaver reduces aggregate mean JCT by 6.2-33.5% relative to the state-of-the-art baselines CASSINI, Crux, and Symphony. These results demonstrate the value of LLM-guided planning for efficient concurrent computing in orbital GPU clusters.
papers.intro:
The growing computational and energy demands of artificial intelligence (AI) have motivated interest in space-based data centers. One proposed architecture distributes accelerators across satellites flying in close formation and connects them through optical inter-satellite links, as explored in Google’s SunCatcher study [1]. Fig. 1(a) illustrates such an orbital GPU cluster. A distributed job comprises logical processes, or ranks, that run on different GPUs, execute computation, and exchange data through collective communication [2]. When multiple jobs run concurrently, these exchanges share the optical interconnect even if the jobs have separate GPU allocations.

The growing computational and energy demands of artificial intelligence (AI) have motivated interest in space-based data centers. One proposed architecture distributes accelerators across satellites flying in close formation and connects them through optical inter-satellite links, as explored in Google’s SunCatcher study [1]. Fig. 1(a) illustrates such an orbital GPU cluster. A distributed job comprises logical processes, or ranks, that run on different GPUs, execute computation, and exchange data through collective communication [2]. When multiple jobs run concurrently, these exchanges share the optical interconnect even if the jobs have separate GPU allocations.

Payload and power budgets, together with formation design, constrain the number and capacity of optical connections [1]. When each satellite has a limited number of neighboring connections, communication between remote nodes traverses relay paths. In Fig. 1(b), jobs assigned disjoint GPUs still contend for shared links, and the resulting waits can delay downstream computation and job completion. Placement affects communication paths and costs [3], while communication order affects computation–communication overlap [4, 5]. These decisions are coupled: remapping ranks can reduce one group’s path overlap while creating another, and prioritizing a short collective may not advance the dependencies that determine job completion. Efficient execution therefore requires joint planning of rank placement and communication order, accounting for workload structure, job arrivals, and link capacity.

Job placement, communication scheduling, and workload-oriented interconnect design offer ways to coordinate distributed GPU execution [6, 7, 8, 9]. Their execution outcomes depend on when communications become ready and how resource waits propagate through computation dependencies, as well as on traffic volume and path length [10, 11]. Static traffic summaries can identify heavily used links, yet they do not by themselves indicate which placement and communication order will minimize job completion time. Joint planning thus calls for a process that connects workload analysis to candidate construction and uses complete-execution feedback to decide which changes to explore next.

Large language model (LLM) agents combine reasoning with tool use and can adapt subsequent actions to returned observations [12]. Studies of LLM-driven optimization and GPU kernel generation further demonstrate how candidate scores and execution diagnostics can guide iterative revision [13, 14]. These capabilities suggest a way to address joint planning in orbital GPU clusters: an agent could examine job dependencies and path conflicts, form hypotheses about placement and communication order, and use simulation feedback to select or revise candidates. Execution-graph analysis and complete-job simulation provide observations for this process [10, 15]. With job graphs available in advance, these interactions can take place offline to produce a validated placement and scheduling plan for subsequent execution.

To support this form of joint planning, we present OrbitWeaver, an offline LLM agent planner that uses simulation feedback to jointly optimize rank placement and communication order for optically interconnected orbital GPU clusters. It operates on job execution graphs available in advance under fixed GPU allocations and interconnect conditions. Structured tools expose communication membership, path overlap, and execution dependencies to guide candidate construction. Fast simulation supports candidate exploration, while reference simulation provides completion times and diagnostics for revision and validation. Planning concludes with a reference-validated joint plan. Fig. 2 illustrates the intended effect: coordinating rank placement and communication order can reduce blocking on shared paths and allow dependent computation to begin earlier.

Our main contributions are as follows. • We formulate an execution model for orbital GPU jobs on optical interconnects with limited neighboring connections. The model connects rank mapping, shared relay paths, communication admission, and computational dependencies, yielding a joint planning problem for within-job placement and cross-job communication order that minimizes mean job completion time (JCT). • We develop OrbitWeaver, an LLM agent planner driven by simulation feedback. Structured tools expose communication subgroups, path conflicts, and dependency waits. The agent uses these observations to construct placement–priority combinations and uses candidate execution results to guide subsequent exploration, producing executable joint plans tailored to each workload. • We evaluate OrbitWeaver using three measured GPU execution traces over 16–64 GPUs and four operating conditions. OrbitWeaver achieves the lowest aggregate mean JCT for all three workloads. Ablations further support jointly planning rank placement and communication order to improve concurrent execution.

The agent uses these observations to construct placement–priority combinations and uses candidate execution results to guide subsequent exploration, producing executable joint plans tailored to each workload.

We evaluate OrbitWeaver using three measured GPU execution traces over 16–64 GPUs and four operating conditions. OrbitWeaver achieves the lowest aggregate mean JCT for all three workloads. papers.title: Protection-Oriented Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Fault Detection in Power Systems
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based fault detectors are increasingly proposed for power system protection, yet aggregate metrics can obscure the consequences of false and missed trips. We present a protection-oriented assessment of three ML detectors and a sequence-current reference on PROTECT-90, comprising 9,022 simulated fault episodes on a 90 kV double-circuit line. The assessment combines five window conditions, causal window-end labelling, episode-grouped cross-validation, and operating-point selection under a fixed security budget. It reports security, dependability, detection timing, decision margins, and episode-level nuisance assertions. Gradient-boosted trees, a convolutional neural network, and logistic regression achieve AUC-ROC values above 0.999, yet at a security budget of $10^{-3}$ their developed-fault missed-trip rates range from 0.007% to 1.99%. Post-clearing false-trip rates of approximately 0.12-0.16% per window coexist with nuisance assertions in 11.3-19.1% of episodes. Among the analysed physical descriptors, missed trips are most consistently associated with higher fault resistance within the sampled range. An analytical current proxy suggests a fault-current gradient only partly reproduced by waveform-derived current (rank correlation 0.62). No single topology state or faulted phase consistently dominates within the sampled domain. Because PROTECT-90 contains fault episodes only, security is assessed on pre-fault and post-clearing windows rather than independent non-fault disturbances.

papers.title: Hierarchical Bayesian physics-augmented neural networks for populations of hyperelastic laws: specimen variability and uncertainty from scarce, noisy data
papers.abstract: The hyperelastic law of a material such as soft tissue differs between specimens, and often only a few specimens can be tested. Physics-augmented neural networks (PANNs) learn such laws from data without a prescribed functional form while keeping them physically admissible, and Bayesian versions of related models quantify the uncertainty of the law of one specimen or of a pooled group of specimens. A pooled fit, however, attributes the differences between specimens to measurement noise or to uncertainty about a mean law, and neither describes a new specimen. We first develop a Bayesian PANN for one specimen, whose priors keep the learned law plausible for few, noisy data. We then extend it to a hierarchical Bayesian PANN, a nonlinear mixed-effects model in which all specimens share learned polyconvex features and each specimen is a draw from a population of laws. Features, specimens, and population are inferred jointly by variational inference, with a separate model of the measurement noise, so that the variability between specimens is not mistaken for noise, the population carries its own uncertainty, and every specimen drawn from it is polyconvex. The population predicts the response of new specimens with credible intervals, without data or from a partial test, and assigns them to cohorts with quantified uncertainty, all without a prescribed form of the law. On synthetic populations, it recovers the population from few specimens and predicts new specimens more reliably than three published methods. On Treloar's rubber and on healthy and aneurysmal aortas, it reaches the accuracy of a deterministic PANN and assigns no aorta specimen to the wrong cohort with confidence, although it underestimates the uncertainty of untested curves.

papers.intro:
To choose an adequate treatment for an aortic aneurysm, physicians have to tell diseased from healthy vessel wall, and the mechanics of the tissue, which differ markedly between the two, can help to do so [1]. The reuse of recycled plastics raises the same kind of question: a component made from a recyclate can only be designed if its deformation under load can be predicted, and a recyclate is a mixture of material streams in varying proportions [2]. Both questions depend on the same quantity, the constitutive law of the material, which relates how the material is deformed to the stresses it carries. In both examples the law cannot be looked up, since seemingly similar materials, such as two batches of a recyclate or the tissue of two patients, have different laws, which may differ even in the qualitative shape of their stress–stretch curves. We call these differences between specimens of one material specimen variability. The standard remedy is to test the material and to infer its law from the measurements, which is known as constitutive model discovery. We first review how the law is inferred, and return to specimen variability afterwards.

We call these differences between specimens of one material specimen variability. The standard remedy is to test the material and to infer its law from the measurements, which is known as constitutive model discovery. We first review how the law is inferred, and return to specimen variability afterwards.

Approaches to constitutive-model discovery can be ordered by how strongly they restrict the form of the law in advance, which in turn sets how much data they need. At one end, an expert selects a closed-form law, such as the Neo-Hookean, Ogden or Holzapfel-type models [3]. If the choice is right, few parameters have to be inferred, the law satisfies the physical requirements, and a single test may suffice to determine it. If the choice is wrong, the result suffers from a model-form error, i.e. a discrepancy between the chosen law and the true one, and no amount of data repairs it [4]. For the materials above, the right choice is not known. At the other end, a neural network [5] or a Gaussian process [6] maps strains directly to stresses with no restriction beyond generic smoothness. It can approximate any response, but it needs data that cover many deformation modes, and nothing guarantees that its predictions of unseen responses are physically meaningful. The approaches discussed next lie between these two ends.

For the materials above, the right choice is not known. At the other end, a neural network [5] or a Gaussian process [6] maps strains directly to stresses with no restriction beyond generic smoothness. It can approximate any response, but it needs data that cover many deformation modes, and nothing guarantees that its predictions of unseen responses are physically meaningful. The approaches discussed next lie between these two ends.

We focus on hyperelastic materials, such as soft tissue under non-destructive, quasi-static loading. Such constitutive laws are physically admissible if the energy density is objective and respects the material symmetry, the reference state is stress-free, and boundary value problems with it have solutions, for which polyconvexity is the most widely used sufficient condition [7]. The approaches between the two ends of the spectrum differ in how they ensure these conditions. A hand-selected law satisfies them by design. Library-based methods ensure them term by term, by letting the data choose a non-negative combination of admissible candidate terms: EUCLID finds a sparse combination of invariant-based terms from full-field data [8], similar to variational system identification [9], constitutive artificial neural networks (CANNs) learn the weights of terms of fixed form, e.g. powers or exponentials of invariants [10], and Material Fingerprinting matches the measured response against a database of candidate laws [11, 12, 13]. The result is a sparse, interpretable formula, but only within the library: a law outside its span, e.g. one that couples invariants multiplicatively, cannot be found. Symbolic regression [14], agents built on large language models [15] and spline interpolants of the energy [16] remove the library, but in general also the guarantee. Physics-augmented neural networks (PANNs) [17, 18] ensure admissibility by their architecture: invariants as inputs give objectivity and material symmetry, an input convex neural network (ICNN) [19] with non-negative weights gives polyconvexity, and correction terms give a stress-free reference state. Within these constraints, the network learns the terms itself and can combine invariants. A model-form error nevertheless remains possible if the chosen invariants do not describe the material or the true law lies outside the class of the ICNN, e.g. because it is not polyconvex or not a convex, non-decreasing function of the invariants. The PANN thus avoids the choice of a law and still guarantees a polyconvex one, which in our view makes it a good balance for the materials above.

The flexibility of the PANN, however, leaves more to the data, and finite, noisy data do not single out one law. Different parameters can produce the same response, already because of symmetries such as the permutation of hidden units, the non-convex loss makes the result depend on the initialisation, which the original CANN and PANN works handle by selecting the best of several restarts [10, 18], and a flexible model can fit the measurement noise instead of the law. A single fit hides this ambiguity. Bayesian approaches quantify it instead: the posterior assigns a probability to every set of parameters compatible with the data, and thereby a distribution over the responses of the material. Bayesian-EUCLID [20] does so with a sparsity-promoting prior on the coefficients of its library, the Bayesian CANN [21] with a variational posterior on the weights of its network, and a sparsified input convex network has been combined with Stein variational gradient descent [22]. What these works estimate, however, is a mean law of the material with its uncertainty, for one specimen or for a group of specimens.

A group of specimens is commonly pooled, i.e. all measurements are treated as repeated measurements of one law. This answers the question of the mean law, but its uncertainty is easily mistaken for specimen variability, which we call the pooling trap. A pooled fit attributes the differences between specimens either to parameter uncertainty, which shrinks as measurements are added while the differences do not, or to measurement noise, which perturbs each point independently, whereas a specimen deviates from the mean law coherently along its whole curve and across load cases (Figure 1). The Bayesian CANN [21] pools the specimens of a tissue group, and its authors note that their differences are absorbed by the noise and the weight uncertainty, consistent with its aim of a mean law per group. Yi et al. [23] and Anton et al. [24] likewise merge the scatter between samples with the measurement noise into one pointwise error term.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). AstroVink-TREX: Automated strong gravitational lens segmentation as input for mass modelling pipelines
papers.abstract: Strong gravitational lens modelling requires the lens light, lensed source light, and contaminants to be separated in each image before mass modelling codes can fit the system. Within Euclid this separation has so far been done by hand, which does not scale to the more than 15,000 candidates in the Euclid Lens Identification Pipeline and Scientific Exploration (ECLIPSE) catalogue of Data Release 1 (DR1). We present AstroVink-TREX , a neural network that performs this separation automatically and predicts three flux maps, in a standard format directly usable by mass-modelling pipelines. The network uses a hybrid architecture, pairing a vision transformer encoder reused from the lens detection network with a parallel convolutional branch. A custom loss function penalises both flux and structural error, while allowing independent weighting per component. From the network's predictions we also derive the modelling centre, fitting region, conjugate points, and binary maps, providing all the inputs that a modelling pipeline needs to run without manual setup. We evaluate the efficiency of the network on DR1 systems against existing fits and through expert validation. Across approximately 3000 inspected systems, taking 75% agreement between inspectors, just 39 lens models fail because of a segmentation error. Following this validation, the network provides the component separation and modelling setup for every system modelled in DR1. With automated segmentation, lens modelling is no longer limited by manual preprocessing and can now operate at the same scale as lens discovery.

papers.intro:
The Euclid Space Telescope (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) is transforming the landscape of strong gravitational lens science through its combination of wide-area coverage, high spatial resolution, and depth. The Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) Strong Lensing Discovery Engine (SLDE) catalogue contains over 500 high-confidence strong lens candidates (Euclid Collaboration: Walmsley et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. 2026), and for DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1 2026) the ECLIPSE catalogue contains over 15 000 candidates (Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026).

The Euclid Space Telescope (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) is transforming the landscape of strong gravitational lens science through its combination of wide-area coverage, high spatial resolution, and depth. The Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) Strong Lensing Discovery Engine (SLDE) catalogue contains over 500 high-confidence strong lens candidates (Euclid Collaboration: Walmsley et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. 2026), and for DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1 2026) the ECLIPSE catalogue contains over 15 000 candidates (Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026).

Modelling these systems at scale requires automated mass modelling pipelines such as PyAutoLens (Nightingale et al. 2018; Nightingale et al. 2021; Euclid Collaboration: Nightingale et al. 2026), Lenstronomy (Birrer and Amara 2018; Birrer et al. 2021), GLEE (Suyu and Halkola 2010; Suyu et al. 2012), Herculens (Galan et al. 2022), GIGA-Lens (Gu et al. 2022), and pronto (Vegetti and Koopmans 2009; Rybak et al. 2015; Rizzo et al. 2018; Powell et al. 2021; Ndiritu et al. 2025). These models provide constraints on the mass distribution of the lens (Gavazzi et al. 2007; Nightingale et al. 2019; Shajib et al. 2024, e.g.,), allow observations of magnified distant sources (Welch et al. 2022, e.g.,), and measure cosmological parameters including the Hubble constant (Wong et al. 2020; TDCOSMO Collaboration: Birrer et al. 2025, e.g.,) and properties of dark matter (Vegetti et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024, e.g.,).

Before any of these codes can model a system, the lens and source light must be identified in the image, and contaminants such as line-of-sight galaxies and imaging artefacts must be masked out. Automated solutions for this exist outside of Euclid, such as DOLPHIN (Shajib et al. 2025), which uses a neural network (NN) for component recognition as part of its forward modelling pipeline with Lenstronomy applied to Hubble Space Telescope (HST) data. Object detection tools such as SExtractor (Bertin and Arnouts 1996) and SourceXtractor++ (Bertin et al. 2020; Kümmel et al. 2022) detect and catalogue objects in survey images but are not built for decomposing a lens system into its components. Within Euclid, identifying and masking the different components of strong lens systems has so far been done entirely by hand: an expert maps contaminants and outlines the lens and source regions for each system, one at a time. This is slow, difficult to reproduce, and dependent on individual judgement. With the volume of lens candidates in our catalogue, this manual approach is no longer an option.

In this work we present AstroVink-TREX (Transformer for Ring Extraction), a NN that automates strong lens component separation. The outputs of the network are used for the full ECLIPSE catalogue, providing automated setup for all systems modelled in DR1 (Euclid Collaboration: Nightingale et al. 2026).

In this work we present AstroVink-TREX (Transformer for Ring Extraction), a NN that automates strong lens component separation. The outputs of the network are used for the full ECLIPSE catalogue, providing automated setup for all systems modelled in DR1 (Euclid Collaboration: Nightingale et al. 2026).

The network builds on AstroVink, a vision transformer (ViT) based strong lens detection network applied to Euclid Q1 and DR1 data (Euclid Collaboration: Vincken et al. 2026a). AstroVink-TREX reuses this pre-trained network and adds components that predict three continuous flux maps: one each for the lens, one for the lensed source, and a third one for nearby contaminants that should be masked before modelling. Additionally, from these flux maps, we automatically determine the relevant modelling region and centre, identify conjugate points, and create binary maps for each component. All segmentation outputs of the network are provided in standard Flexible Image Transport System (FITS) format that many mass modelling codes can use directly.

The network builds on AstroVink, a vision transformer (ViT) based strong lens detection network applied to Euclid Q1 and DR1 data (Euclid Collaboration: Vincken et al. 2026a). AstroVink-TREX reuses this pre-trained network and adds components that predict three continuous flux maps: one each for the lens, one for the lensed source, and a third one for nearby contaminants that should be masked before modelling. Additionally, from these flux maps, we automatically determine the relevant modelling region and centre, identify conjugate points, and create binary maps for each component. All segmentation outputs of the network are provided in standard Flexible Image Transport System (FITS) format that many mass modelling codes can use directly.

Segmentation requires training data in which each of the components is labelled separately, and no such data exists within Euclid. We construct a custom training set by deriving targets from systems that have already been successfully modelled with PyAutoLens, which limits us to just a few hundred systems. A set this small would normally be far too limited to train a deep NN from scratch. However, by using AstroVink, we already have a network that recognises lens and source structure from its training for detection. The labelled set only has to teach it to separate that structure into distinct maps, rather than identify lensing features from scratch.

A set this small would normally be far too limited to train a deep NN from scratch. We evaluate the network on new strong lens candidates from DR1. Standard segmentation metrics measure how closely the predicted maps match the lens and source light from existing PyAutoLens models, which partly reflects their suitability for modelling but does not fully capture it. We therefore also feed the automated maps into the PyAutoLens pipeline and assess the resulting model fits, supported by visual inspection from strong lens modelling experts.

Results on performance validation are given in Sect. 4, including the expert inspection campaign. Finally, Sect. 5 concludes and discusses the application.

papers.title: The speed of convergence for propagation of chaos in the mean-field Ising model
papers.abstract:
We derive sharp relative-entropy asymptotics for increasing propagation of chaos in the Curie--Weiss model at zero external field. For every fixed inverse temperature $0<\beta<1$, the relative entropy of a $k$-spin marginal with respect to the symmetric product measure is $$ \frac{\beta^2}{4(1-\beta)^2}\frac{k(k-1)}{N^2}+o\left(\frac{k^2}{N^2}\right),\qquad k=o(N). $$ At the critical inverse temperature $\beta=1$, the rate changes to $\alpha_{\mathrm c}^2 k(k-1)/(4N)+o(k^2/N)$ in the regime $k=o(\sqrt N)$, where $\alpha_{\mathrm c}$ is the second moment of the limiting quartic law of the rescaled magnetization. We also obtain asymptotics for sequences $\beta_N\uparrow1$ that interpolate between these two regimes.
  Crucially, the proof reveals that the pair correlations determine the leading correction to the likelihood ratio, providing precise control of both the chi-square divergence and relative entropy.

papers.title: Numerical experiments on sunspot penumbral flows
papers.abstract: We present 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations of sunspots with a self-consistently generated penumbra. We analyze the impact of resolution, surrounding opposite-polarity fields and subsurface large-scale flows on the structure and stability of the simulated penumbra. Extended penumbral filaments are obtained for a subset of the simulations. These were run at 25 km (15 km) horizontal (vertical) resolution and with initial conditions favoring fields with strong horizontal components in the penumbral region. The surface velocities in these simulations are consistent with observations of Evershed flow. The main driving mechanism remains the same as illustrated previously in Rempel (2012). The most successful simulations produce extended penumbrae using a potential magnetic field top boundary, in contrast to previous simulations of extended penumbra with an artificial enhancement of horizontal magnetic field at the top boundary.
