papers.title: Finite-Larmor-radius vortex interaction from {\delta}f to full-f gyrofluid dynamics
papers.abstract: We study finite-size electrostatic gyrofluid vortex pairs in a two-dimensional isothermal model, focusing on finite-Larmor-radius effects and the transition from local perturbative to finite-amplitude full-distribution dynamics. An effective response kernel based on Pad\'e ion gyroaveraging regularizes the short-range Euler interaction on the Larmor-radius scale while preserving its logarithmic far field, yielding a finite- core prediction for the orbital frequency. Local-model scans show that increasing the ion temperature relative to the electron temperature enhances gyrospinning and filamentation and drives a separation-dependent transition from merger to long-lived co-rotation. Long-wavelength simulations reproduce the predicted finite-Larmor- radius-induced dip in orbital angular frequency, corresponding to a pronounced slowdown of the vortex-pair rotation. For the full-distribution regime, we introduce a quasi-neutrality-consistent initialization that reconstructs the ion gyrocenter density from prescribed electron density and electrostatic potential. It recovers the local limit at small amplitude, whereas finite-amplitude simulations reveal additional mean-density polarization vorticity, delayed or arrested merger, and a loss of density- vorticity sign symmetry already in the cold-ion full-f system. An independent sign scan of density and vorticity then shows how this nonlinear NOB asymmetry combines with the local warm-ion FLR symmetry breaking identified in earlier {\delta}f vortex studies; for warm ions, Pad\'e-based arbitrary-wavelength NOB and NOB+LWL polarization additionally produce distinct morphologies and trajectories. These results demonstrate that nonlinear density-dependent polarization and FLR physics form separate but coupled mechanisms that can qualitatively alter elementary vortex interactions in two-dimensional gyrofluid dynamics.

papers.intro:
Isolated vortices are among the most persistent coherent structures of nonlinear fluid motion and provide a particularly transparent route to the elementary dynamics underlying two-dimensional turbulence. In an ideal two-dimensional fluid, kinetic energy and enstrophy are simultaneously conserved, producing the familiar dual-cascade phenomenology in which energy is transferred towards larger scales while enstrophy is transported towards smaller scales [1, 2]. The dynamics of this transfer is not exhausted by spectral arguments: it is realized through the formation, deformation, merger and filamentation of coherent vortices. Numerical and experimental studies have linked the inverse cascade to the elongation and thinning of small vortices by large-scale strain, while filamentary structures are central to the forward transfer of enstrophy [3, 4]. At the level of a vortex pair, mutual rotation, co-advection, merger and the generation of vorticity sheets already reproduce many of the basic nonlinear ingredients of a turbulent vortex population [5, 6, 7, 8]. Such deliberately reduced configurations are therefore valuable not because an isolated vortex pair is expected to occur unmodified in a magnetized plasma, but because they isolate the interaction law that is otherwise embedded in a much more complicated turbulent state.

The neutral-fluid analogy becomes incomplete when perpendicular scales approach the ion gyroradius. A charged ion does not sample the electrostatic potential only at its instantaneous gyrocenter position, but experiences an orbit-averaged field over its Larmor motion. At k⟂​ρi∼1k_{\perp}\rho_{i}\sim 1, finite-Larmor-radius (FLR) effects therefore modify both the gyrocenter advection and the polarization relation connecting the particle and gyrocenter densities to the electric potential. Gyrokinetic theory provides the systematic low-frequency reduction in which the fast gyrophase is removed while the relevant orbit-width, kinetic and polarization effects are retained [14, 15, 16]. Gyrofluid models proceed by taking velocity-space moments of the gyrokinetic distribution and closing the resulting hierarchy, retaining gyroaveraging and polarization physics at a substantially reduced computational cost [17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. In this description the evolved densities are gyrocenter rather than particle densities, and the electrostatic field is obtained from quasi-neutrality together with the polarization response. The underlying role of polarization in guiding-center and gyrocenter reductions has a long theoretical history [23, 24]. This distinction is essential here: in the cold-ion, long-wavelength limit the gyrofluid polarization reduces to a Poisson equation and the vorticity dynamics approaches the two-dimensional Euler equation, whereas at finite ion temperature the gyroaveraging operators alter the connection between density, potential and vorticity.

FLR effects on coherent plasma structures have been observed in several related settings. Knorr et al. already showed that finite-Larmor-radius corrections can qualitatively alter a vortex-merger calculation [17]. In interchange-driven filament dynamics, FLR corrections break poloidal symmetry and generate sheared or spinning flows around the structures [25]. For finite-amplitude blobs, ion-temperature effects can alter coherence, morphology and propagation, while nonlinear polarization introduces amplitude-dependent inertia and blob–hole asymmetries [26, 27, 28]. More generally, rotational dynamics of plasma blobs can be important for their stability and propagation [29]. These results establish that ion gyro-orbit physics cannot in general be treated as a perturbative correction to otherwise Euler-like motion: it can modify the effective velocity field, the redistribution of vorticity, and the lifetime of coherent structures.

The direct conceptual predecessor of the present work is the gyrofluid vortex-interaction study [30]. That work reduced the problem to two-dimensional, isothermal, electrostatic δ​f\delta f gyrofluid dynamics and showed explicitly how the classical vortex-pair picture is reorganized by FLR polarization. In the cold-ion limit, co-rotating vortices undergo the expected parity-related Euler-like merger, while counter-rotating vortices co-advect in the familiar dipolar fashion. For warm ions, however, the evolution is no longer determined by the initial vorticity profile alone. The relative distribution of electron and ion gyrocenter densities fixes the FLR contribution to polarization, so two states with identical initial vorticity can evolve differently. Spatial asymmetry between density and vorticity contours generates gyrospinning: spiral arms form around the vortex cores, vorticity is wound into thin sheets, and the resulting structures can either accelerate merger or drive separation depending on the underlying gyrocenter-density configuration [30]. The same mechanism also modifies counter-rotating co-advection and was shown to persist in many-vortex drift-wave turbulence modelled with the Hasegawa–Wakatani system, where FLR effects enhance vorticity filamentation and alter the small-scale structure of the flow [30, 31].

papers.title: Regularized Neural Quantum States for Heisenberg Magnets
papers.abstract: We introduce an approach to solving locally ordered quantum spin systems using neural network quantum states. First, our approach rests on choosing a spin basis constructed from the magnetic texture of a classical or quantum reference state. Second, the method improves convergence and suppresses parameter-space drift through a regularized Riemannian gradient descent adapted to the quantum state geometry of the variational state manifold. Combining these techniques enables stable ground-state calculations for two- and three-dimensional chiral spin systems with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions. The resulting variational ground-state energies are competitive with those of high-fidelity density matrix renormalization group calculations and, for periodic and layered geometries, provide significantly tighter upper bounds on the ground-state energy.

papers.title: Projection of massive and interacting conformal theories to the future null infinity
papers.abstract: On a four-dimensional, globally hyperbolic and asymptotically flat spacetime, we consider a real, linear, massive scalar field. Within the framework of perturbative algebraic quantum field theory and inspired by the principle of perturbative agreement, we regard the mass term in the underlying Lagrangian as an interaction potential. This allows us to construct the algebra of observables of the massive theory and, using a M{\o}ller map, to represent its elements as formal power series in the squared mass, with coefficients in the algebra of observables of a massless, conformally coupled scalar field. Following [DMP06], we use the bulk-to-boundary correspondence for the massless theory to project each coefficient to future null infinity $\mathscr{I}^+$.In four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime, we prove convergence of the projected series in the presence of an infrared cut-off and show that the global adiabatic limit exists but is trivial. We circumvent this obstruction by exploiting the time-slice axiom, which allows us to restrict our attention to observables localized in a causally convex neighbourhood containing a Cauchy hypersurface. Removing the cut-off locally yields a non-trivial limit and hence a bulk-to-boundary correspondence for the massive theory. We then extend our procedure to a self-interacting real scalar field. We represent interacting observables as formal power series in the coupling constant, with coefficients in the algebra of observables of a massless, conformally coupled scalar field. Each coefficient in the domain of the bulk-to-boundary map can thus be projected to future null infinity. As a concrete example, we apply this method to the stress-energy tensor of a massless scalar field with a quartic self-interaction, computing its projection up to first order in perturbation theory.

papers.intro:
The aim of this work is to investigate the extent to which the bulk-to-boundary correspondence for a massless, conformally coupled scalar field can be generalized to massive and self-interacting theories. More precisely, we consider a four-dimensional, globally hyperbolic and asymptotically flat spacetime (M,g)(M,g) with future null infinity ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+}, using the formulation of [Fri86a, Fri86b]. Starting from the algebraic description of quantum fields on ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+}, see, e.g., [DMP17], we address two related questions. We investigate, on the one hand, whether observables of a massive Klein–Gordon field admit a non-trivial realization at the null, conformal boundary, while, on the other hand, we discuss whether the same procedure can be implemented for observables of a perturbatively interacting theory. The two problems require different analytic tools and they lead to distinct notions of convergence.

Future null infinity plays a distinguished role in the study of asymptotically flat spacetimes. Within Penrose’s conformal framework, ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+} is the endpoint of future-directed null geodesics and it provides the natural, covariant, geometric setting for describing outgoing radiation data. Most notably, its intrinsic geometric structure is universal. It does not depend on the details of the bulk metric, up to a conformal freedom. Its group of asymptotic symmetries is the infinite dimensional Bondi–Metzner–Sachs (BMS) group [BBM62, Sac62]. These properties make ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+} a natural candidate for encoding field-theoretic information associated with the bulk, an idea which has been investigated within the algebraic approach to quantum field theory in [DMP06, Mor06, DMP17].

The relevance of such boundary description is not confined to quantum field theory on curved spacetimes. In gravitational theories, asymptotic symmetries and the associated charges enter the infrared structure of scattering, including their relation with soft theorems and memory effects, see, e.g., [Str18]. In addition, the degenerate geometry induced on null hypersurfaces has a natural interpretation in terms of Carrollian geometry, which has become a prominent ingredient in Carrollian formulations of asymptotically flat gravity and in approaches to flat-space holography [Ruz26]. We mention these developments to emphasize the broader interest in field theories at null infinity. The correspondence studied in the present work is, however, an algebraic construction for scalar quantum fields on a prescribed background. It is not our goal neither to assume nor to establish a duality for gravitational degrees of freedom.

For a massless, conformally coupled, real scalar field, the construction is well-understood. Under suitable hypotheses on the conformal completion, the rescaled solutions of the Klein–Gordon equation admit a restriction to ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+}, yielding an injective symplectic map from the space of bulk observables into a boundary counterpart. Upon quantization, this induces an injective ∗*-homomorphism between the corresponding field algebras [DMP06, DMP17]. On the boundary, the universal BMS structure allows one to single out a quasifree state, which is unique in its folium. Its pullback to the bulk satisfies the Hadamard condition, thereby providing a geometrically motivated selection of a physically admissible state even in the absence of a preferred bulk vacuum [Mor06, DMP17]. The usefulness of this perspective is not limited to the construction of Hadamard states since it has also been exploited in the analysis of modular Hamiltonians, relative entropy and energy inequalities on suitable asymptotically flat backgrounds [DMM+25].

The situation changes considerably when a non-vanishing mass is introduced. The mass term breaks conformal covariance and the rescaled massive Klein–Gordon equation develops a singular coefficient at the conformal boundary. In particular, ordinary radiation data on ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+} cannot be expected to retain the information carried by a massive field, whose asymptotic propagation is associated instead with timelike infinity. This obstruction does not exclude other procedures for representing massive data at null infinity. In [Dap08], for example, harmonic analysis on the mass hyperboloid and global estimates for the wave equation were used to associate boundary data with norm-finite massive solutions on Minkowski spacetime. A different, recent development is [Mol26], where microlocal scattering methods yield distinguished incoming and outgoing Hadamard states for massive Klein–Gordon fields on non-trapping asymptotically flat spacetimes. The latter approach concerns asymptotic positive- and negative-frequency data and scattering, with particular attention to timelike infinity. Neither construction amounts to restricting the massive field itself to the ordinary massless radiation space at ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+}.

This gives a formal boundary expansion on general backgrounds satisfying our standing hypotheses. To address its convergence and the removal of the infrared cut-off, we then specialize to four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime 𝕄4\mathbb{M}^{4}.

papers.title: Digitally-alloyed magnetic topological insulator nanostructures grown via stencil mask molecular beam epitaxy
papers.abstract: Magnetic topological insulator nanostructures are a promising platform for the realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation. For this, such nanostructures need to be embedded into the necessary superconducting architectures. In this study, we demonstrate a method for the growth of magnetic topological insulator nanostructures via molecular beam epitaxy, utilising digital alloying and defining their shapes in-situ by stencil mask technology. Cr-doped (Bi$_y$Sb$_{1-y}$)$_2$Te$_3$ micro- and nanometer-sized Hall bars are fabricated and the magneto-transport properties for various Cr doping amounts and different Hall bar dimensions are investigated at low temperatures. We find indications that the Fermi energy is located inside the bulk band gap, while disorder and charge puddles affect the transport behaviour. Furthermore, we investigate the magnetic properties and discuss the transition from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic behaviour.

papers.intro:
Magnetic topological insulators (MTIs) are a promising material platform for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation utilizing Majorana zero modes [1, 2, 3]. To achieve this, the chiral edge channels of an MTI nanoribbon need to be proximitized with an s-wave superconductor [4, 5]. There are already some reported cases where superconducting correlations are present in antiferromagnetic [6, 7] and ferromagnetic MTIs [8, 9], but theoretical studies motivate to explore lower magnetic doping for superconducting applications [10, 5, 11, 4]. A prominent material is Cr-doped (BiySb1-y)2Te3. Previously, it has been studied how the ferromagnetic and magneto-transport properties of this type of MTI change as a result of varying the Cr content [12, 13, 14]. Therefore, in a previous work we investigated low Cr-doped magnetic topological insulator thin films grown via molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and showed that even for weak internal magnetization, a pronounced anomalous Hall effect is observed [1]. This means that we are able to tune the MTI into a regime that is very promising for superconducting applications [4, 5]. A challenge of embedding MTI nanoribbons in superconducting architectures is the need for very clean interfaces. For regular topological insulator nanostructures grown via MBE, a complete in-situ process has proven to be superior to ex-situ processes [16]. It also has been reported that electron beam lithography as a tool to create nanostructures can cause damage to the MTI material [17, 18, 19].

In order to tackle both problems at once, we developed a fully in-situ process scheme to fabricate MTI nanostructures by using MBE and stencil-masks. In order to demonstrate the feasibility of this processing scheme, Hall bars are fabricated in varying dimensions ranging from micro- to nanometer-sized devices. Furthermore, we investigate how Cr content affects the magnetic and electric properties at low temperatures, and discuss how narrowing down the width of the Hall bars changes these properties. papers.title: Space-based Zero-trust Architecture for Securing the Direct-to-Cell Paradigm
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of Direct-to-Cell (D2C) technology has emerged as a pivotal enabler for ubiquitous 6G global coverage, seamlessly connecting massive numbers of User Equipment (UEs) in remote and underserved areas. However, by bypassing traditional terrestrial satellite access gateways, the D2C paradigm inadvertently renders conventional front-end security perimeters obsolete. Consequently, malicious UEs can directly expose satellites and their core networks to severe security vulnerabilities. To address these critical threats, this article proposes a Space-based Zero-Trust Architecture (SZTA) empowered by on-board satellite computing. Specifically, the proposed SZTA consists of three core components: radio frequency (RF) fingerprint-based authentication, distributed identity management, and behavior-driven dynamic access control. This architecture enables continuous, real-time verification of UE identity authenticity and behavioral legitimacy, effectively mitigating the inherent network-layer security risks of D2C networks. Simulation results demonstrate the robustness, effectiveness, and efficiency of the proposed SZTA. Finally, to facilitate the practical deployment of {the SZTA}, we discuss key technical challenges, propose corresponding solutions, and outline open research issues to guide future investigations.

papers.intro:
In September 2023, China Telecom initiated the world’s first commercial direct-to-cell (D2C) deployment, enabling satellite calls and messaging on the mass-market Huawei Mate 60 Pro. By March 2026, SpaceX had deployed 650 D2C satellites, authorized by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to provide text messaging over T-Mobile’s mobile spectrum [1]. The D2C paradigm is thus rapidly moving satellite mobile communications from an industry-specific domain toward the mass-consumer market.

The D2C paradigm is thus rapidly moving satellite mobile communications from an industry-specific domain toward the mass-consumer market.

D2C offers global coverage, strong anti-jamming capability, and independence from terrestrial infrastructure, making it particularly attractive where ground networks are absent. Unlike terrestrial cellular systems, D2C—also known as satellite direct-to-device (D2D)—employs satellites as relay nodes to serve mobile user equipments (UEs) directly, without altering user habits or requiring cross-network protocol conversion, and is thus expected to underpin the ubiquitous connectivity envisioned for 6G.

papers.title: Evaluating Polling Schemes for OFDMA Uplink Scheduling in Time-Sensitive Wi-Fi Networks
papers.abstract: IEEE 802.11ax introduced orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA) to improve channel utilization through concurrent multi-user transmissions. For effective uplink (UL) scheduling, the access point (AP) requires timely knowledge of buffered traffic at the stations (STAs). Explicit buffer-status polling provides this, yet each polling round can query only as many STAs as there are resource units (RUs). Scheduled-access, random-access, activity-based, and learning-based schemes address this buffer-status acquisition problem differently and have generally been evaluated in isolation under different conditions, so it remains unclear how they compare across time-sensitive workloads. We evaluate common schemes from the Wi-Fi standard and literature under three time-sensitive environments: a large-scale teleconferencing session, an industrial IoT deployment, and an extended reality (XR) service. The relative performance of the schemes depends strongly on traffic characteristics and offered load. In conferencing, activity-based and learning-based polling perform best, while conventional contention-based access remains competitive under light load. In the industrial scenario, scheduled-access most effectively delivers time-sensitive packets within their deadlines under heavy load, whereas contention-based access performs best under lighter load. In XR, OFDMA-based schemes achieve high video throughput that contention-based access cannot sustain; among them, activity-based polling achieves the lowest deadline-miss ratios for uplink head-tracking traffic, at the expense of longer video delay tails. These findings highlight the importance of selecting channel access and scheduling schemes according to traffic requirements and operating conditions.

papers.intro:
Enhanced distributed channel access (EDCA)is the default contention-based channel access mechanism in Wi-Fi. Each station (STA)contends independently for the medium, and the winner transmits over the full channel bandwidth. This requires no per-transmission coordination from the access point (AP), but scales poorly. As the network becomes denser, collisions and back-off consume an increasing share of the airtime, degrading the latency of time-sensitive applications such as industrial automation and extended reality (XR) [1]. The IEEE 802.11ax amendment introduced orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA)to improve channel utilization under such conditions. The channel is partitioned into resource units (RUs), allowing the APto serve several STAsin one transmission by assigning each its own RU [21].

In the uplink (UL), OFDMAshifts access control to the AP, which coordinates transmissions using trigger frames (TFs)to assign RUsto individual STAs. The standard also allows contention-based EDCAaccess to be suppressed at the STAs. Efficient scheduling requires timely knowledge of buffered traffic, which the APcan obtain implicitly from the QoS Control field of transmitted frames or explicitly by polling STAs. However, implicit reporting cannot reveal newly buffered traffic at STAsthat have not recently transmitted, while explicit polling is limited by the number of available RUs. Consequently, polling a STAwith an empty buffer may delay the discovery of another with queued traffic. The polling policy therefore determines how quickly the APcan identify STAsrequiring ULresources [4].

Within each environment, all schemes are evaluated under the same traffic and channel conditions, with their configurations tuned to achieve the best performance among the evaluated settings.

papers.title: CHARMING: Parallel Edge AI Acceleration Across Tensor Processing and In-Memory Computation
papers.abstract:
Edge AI increasingly relies on specialized accelerators for low-latency inference under tight resource and energy constraints, yet their efficiency remains limited by data movement. Prior work, CHARM, mitigates this overhead by overlapping data movement with computation. We observe that in-memory computing can further supplement tensor processing as a parallel accelerator while eliminating certain data movements entirely.
  We present CHARMING, a heterogeneous edge AI architecture that uses accuracy- and quantization-aware partitioning to distribute and concurrently execute inference workloads across tensor processing and in-memory computation. CHARMING partitions attention heads between an AIE array and an in-DRAM compute unit, balancing execution according to model architecture, sequence length, and precision while selecting heads to minimize accuracy degradation. CHARMING also integrates quantization into the AIE projection stage to further reduce data movement. We validate CHARMING end-to-end in hardware on AMD Versal VCK5000 and Alveo U200 platforms and evaluate LLM and video-generation models across multiple precisions using measured hardware results and simulation of the latest in-memory compute hardware.
  CHARMING improves prefill performance by up to 23.6 percent and decode performance by up to 44 percent over AIE-only acceleration. With int4 x int4 fixed-point in-memory computation, CHARMING reduces per-layer energy by up to 7.6 percent and improves energy-delay product by up to 24.7 percent, while maintaining accuracy similar to a 32-bit floating-point baseline.

papers.intro:
The growing computational demands of artificial intelligence have motivated a broad range of specialized hardware. Graphics processing units (GPUs) remain the dominant platform for deep learning because their massive thread-level parallelism provides substantially higher throughput than general-purpose CPUs on data-parallel workloads (Brodtkorb et al., 2013; Dally et al., 2021). Recent GPUs further improve efficiency through dedicated matrix engines, such as Tensor Cores, and reduced-precision arithmetic (Markidis et al., 2018; Choquette et al., 2021). Nevertheless, deploying these accelerators at the edge remains challenging under tight memory, energy, and computational resource budgets.

Nevertheless, deploying these accelerators at the edge remains challenging under tight memory, energy, and computational resource budgets.

Edge devices increasingly execute inference locally to reduce communication latency and cloud-computing costs, preserve data privacy, and operate without continuous network connectivity (Qu et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2024). At the same time, edge workloads are evolving from compact convolutional networks to transformer-based language and multimodal models whose storage, computation, and memory-bandwidth requirements can exceed device capabilities (Zheng et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024). Dense self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, while autoregressive decoding repeatedly accesses model weights and a growing key–value cache. Low-bit quantization and model optimization reduce these demands (Zandieh et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025; Nielsen and Schneider-Kamp, 2024), but substantial latency and energy are still spent moving weights, activations, and intermediate results between memory and compute (Wolters et al., 2024). Consequently, efficient edge inference depends not only on computational throughput, but also on how efficiently data can be moved, and where computation is performed.

Consequently, efficient edge inference depends not only on computational throughput, but also on how efficiently data can be moved, and where computation is performed.

Heterogeneous reconfigurable platforms, such as AMD Versal ACAP, combine arrays of AI Engine (AIE) tiles with programmable logic and embedded processors, providing both high-throughput matrix computation and configurable data movement (Dong et al., 2024; Zhuang et al., 2023a; Zhuang et al., 2025; Zhuang et al., 2024; Zhuang et al., 2023b). Prior work, CHARM, demonstrated that optimizing this data movement is critical to achieving high performance on AIE-based accelerators. By coordinating computation and communication across the programmable logic and AIE array, CHARM overlaps operand movement with matrix computation to reduce its impact on execution time (Zhuang et al., 2023a; Zhuang et al., 2024). Reconfigurable platforms provide a second opportunity: FPGA-based memory controllers can expose fine-grained control over DRAM commands and timing, enabling computation directly within the memory system. Prior work has demonstrated bulk-bitwise and arithmetic operations using commodity or minimally modified DRAM (Oliveira et al., 2024; Hajinazar et al., 2021; Seshadri et al., 2017), while recent in-DRAM designs extend these mechanisms to matrix computation (de Lima et al., 2026).

In this paper, we present CHARMING (CHARM with In-memory computiNG), a heterogeneous edge-AI architecture that combines AIE-based tensor processing with in-memory computation to reduce data movement and improve inference performance. As illustrated in Figure 1, CHARMING integrates the CHARM (Zhuang et al., 2023a; Zhuang et al., 2024) compilation framework with a new in-memory computing backend to coordinate an AIE Compute Unit (ACU) and an In-Memory Compute Unit (IMCU) based on state-of-the-art DRAM PIM (de Lima et al., 2026). Starting from a PyTorch model, the CHARMING frontend feeds a CHARMING partitioner that distributes transformer inference workloads across the two compute units. Offline accuracy profiling evaluates the effects of quantization and head selection on model accuracy, identifying computations suitable for reduced-precision in-memory execution. Subject to these accuracy constraints, analytical performance models determine the ACU–IMCU partition for both prefill and decode to maximize performance and improve energy efficiency through concurrent execution. The resulting partitions are passed to the existing CHARM(ACU) backend and the new CHARMING PIM backend. CHARMING jointly orchestrates these backends, integrating CHARM’s existing coordination of programmable logic and host processing with the corresponding control, data movement, and synchronization required for in-memory computation. This unified execution flow enables the ACU and IMCU to operate concurrently while exploiting their complementary computational capabilities to improve performance and energy efficiency.

papers.title: DIRT: Depth-completed Image-based Rendering using Two-band Blending for Live Novel-view Synthesis
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art novel-view synthesis (NVS) methods commonly require per-scene optimization before rendering, limiting their applicability in live settings. Live or ad-hoc NVS, however, demands low-latency rendering during capture and strong generalization to new scenes. Some previous work tried to address this task by adapting training- and optimization-based methods, trading quality for low latency. We introduce a live NVS approach following traditional image-based rendering that operates on a posed set of depth sensor observations and images. Our method leverages explicit, sparse point-based geometry obtained from active sensors, resulting in a sparsely filled depth buffer that is completed in the (novel) target view's screen-space. Using this proxy, a posed set of images is projected into the target frame before fusing the resulting observations through a frequency-aware two-band blending strategy. The pipeline is entirely non-neural and optimization-free, requiring no training data or scene-specific optimization. As a result, our approach reduces the delay between capture and novel-view rendering and does not rely on favorable network generalization. We validate the method's applicability to heterogeneous sensor setups - including handheld RGB-D cameras, automotive LiDAR, and thermal cameras - as well as challenging scenarios, such as low light captures. Our experiments demonstrate that the approach outperforms prior methods in live reconstruction scenarios, while maintaining competitive performance in conventional NVS benchmarks.

papers.intro:
Recent advances in novel-view synthesis (NVS) have demonstrated stunning visual quality, enabling photorealistic rendering of scenes from previously unseen viewpoints [FRFS24, BMV*22, KKLD23]. These approaches typically utilize a dataset comprising multiple images as input to optimize a detailed intermediate scene representation that is subsequently leveraged to render the scene from novel viewpoints. High visual quality, however, is often achieved at the expense of lengthy scene-specific optimization procedures, significantly extending the time between scene capture and re-rendering. To overcome this constraint, generalizable neural rendering networks are explored which amortize per-scene optimization, enabling immediate, high-quality view synthesis [HFF*23, RK21, SESM22]. These networks, however, are contingent on favorable generalization to new datasets. Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] has been applied in an on-the-fly manner by [MSL*25]: 3D Gaussians are predicted online and optimized concurrently while rendering novel views. Given the real-time constraints, their initial rendering starts out commendable, but the ongoing optimization process is still noticeable, and image quality and optimization duration remain tightly linked. In contrast, our work omits iterative optimization as well as neural components within the NVS pipeline, thereby enabling more efficient resource allocation. We target scenarios involving simultaneous acquisition and re-rendering, a process that enables an observer to commence exploration of a scene while capture is still ongoing. Instead of solely focusing on RGB-only camera setups, we demonstrate how multi-sensor configurations enhance visual fidelity by leveraging data from different modalities. Therefore, we specifically target scenarios where multiple cameras, in addition to depth sensors (e.g., LiDAR sensors) are operating simultaneously.

papers.title: Symmetry induced spin splitting of topological surface states at equal carrier density
papers.abstract: Surface states are among the most striking consequences of band inversion in topological materials. In magnetotransport of three-dimensional topological insulators, the typical signature of surface state transport is a quantized Hall conductance with nontrivial sequences of integer filling factors, varying with the total carrier density. For two independent Dirac carriers, one expects Hall plateaus only at odd-integer filling factors. In this work, we report the observation of symmetry induced spin splitting in magnetotransport experiments on a dual-gate three-dimensional topological insulator device based on HgTe. In the topological surface state regime, we observe Hall plateaus at both odd and even integers when we gate the device symmetrically, i.e., with equal density at the top and bottom. This phenomenon originates in structural inversion symmetry, which remarkably induces a spin splitting and forces the eigenstates to be symmetric and antisymmetric linear combinations of the top and bottom surface states. This is in contrast with two-dimensional systems, where spin splitting is caused by absence of inversion symmetry. We interpret the experimental observations with a perturbative model using isoparity eigenstates, the conserved quantum number associated with structural inversion. The result demonstrates that the picture where the top and bottom states are treated as independent Dirac carriers is not valid when the carrier density is symmetric.

papers.intro:
Surface-state transport is a key feature of three-dimensional topological insulators (3D TIs) [1, 2, 3, 4]. As originally predicted in 1985 [5, 6], the band inversion occuring at the interface between a band inverted and normal material leads to two-dimensional Dirac-type surface states at the interface. Magnetotransport experiments of 3D TI devices have confirmed the existence of these surface states through observation of the quantum Hall effect. These experiments typically exhibit clear signatures of multi-carrier behavior, such as the absence of certain Hall plateaus [7, 8, 4], caused by the presence of at least two types of carriers, namely the surface states at top and bottom interface. In some configurations, the presence of further carrier types, such as massive Volkov-Pankratov states, can be observed [9, 10].

Thus, gating generally affects the carrier population asymmetrically, breaking structural inversion symmetry. For two-dimensional devices, structural inversion asymmetry generally manifests itself as Rashba spin-orbit coupling, and this also holds for two-dimensional topological insulator (2D TI) materials [12, 13, 14, 15, 16].

We have performed magnetotransport experiments on a 70​nm70\,\mathrm{nm} thick layer of HgTe, a three-dimensional topological insulator, equipped with gates on top and bottom, and fabricated into a Hall bar geometry. In order to theoretically interpret these features, we perform in-depth analysis of the Landau levels by means of 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory [21, 22, 23]. Based on these results, we propose a perturbative effective model involving one pair of Landau levels, in a basis of isoparity ±1\pm 1 eigenstates, acting as two pseudospin states. (Total angular momentum JzJ_{z} and proper spin SzS_{z} are not suitable for this purpose, because they are not conserved.) The model involves two perturbative terms that lift the degeneracy, one symmetric and one antisymmetric in isoparity, which model the magnetic field [19] and electric field [20], respectively. The perturbative model fits accurately to the experimental conductance map, establishing the following physical picture: The magnetic field induces a Zeeman-like splitting between the two states with the same Landau index (see Fig. 3(a)). For symmetric gating (i.e., a symmetric charge carrier distribution) the splitting is purely Zeeman-like and there is no Rashba effect. Only a sufficiently strong asymmetry in the electrostatic potential can overcome the Zeeman splitting and force the eigenstates to the top and bottom surfaces. Our perturbative model with competing terms explains both limits: On the one hand, the splitting in the symmetric case (i.e., for equal carrier density at top and bottom) leads to the even-and-odd filling-factor Hall plateaus. On the other hand, no splitting occurs between the plateau transitions in the asymmetric-density regime, because states with unequal Landau indices do not mix. The observed spin splitting at equal density is thus the result of a protected symmetry, i.e., structural inversion asymmetry, with isoparity as its conserved quantum number.

papers.title: Talk to Act: A Synthetic Multi-Turn Dialogue Benchmark for Human Intent Extraction and Action Planning in Robotics
papers.abstract:
Multi-turn conversational human-robot interaction (HRI) continues to be a challenging problem in robotics, as many existing systems rely on rigid, command-driven interfaces that can be unintuitive for users. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a promising direction, given their ability to process natural language, generate structured outputs, and support tool-based reasoning, all of which are relevant for interpreting user intent in robotic settings. However, progress in this area is constrained by the limited availability of datasets and benchmarks that capture the nuances of real-world human communication, such as multi-turn dialogue, ambiguity, and context-dependent requests.
  In this work, we present a synthetically generated multi-turn dialogue dataset for HRI, annotated with action intents, object references, and task plans across a range of scenarios and user personas. Our primary focus is on evaluating the capability of small, open-weight language models for robotic tasks, particularly in settings where local deployment and efficiency are important. To this end, we frame intent extraction as a tool-calling problem where each predicted action corresponds to a structured function call with arguments grounded in the dialogue and benchmark models ranging from 270M to 8B parameters on their ability to perform intent extraction and action planning without task-specific fine-tuning.
  Our results show that these models can achieve reasonable performance on the task even at relatively small scales and without any task-specific fine-tuning. This suggests that compact, locally deployable models already provide a useful baseline for conversational robotic systems. We expect that task-specific fine-tuning and more realistic training data will enhance performance further and make such models increasingly suitable for real-world robotic applications.

As robots move from controlled industrial cells into homes, care environments, and shared workspaces, communication becomes a core capability rather than a peripheral interface.

In recent years, substantial progress has been made in robotics, particularly in perception and control. Large embodied datasets and generalist robot policies have advanced robotic performance. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have demonstrated the effectiveness of web-scale pretraining in enhancing semantic generalization in robotic control. However, interaction between humans and robots is still unnatural. A robot that is capable of perceiving objects and executing movements with precision may still struggle when a user makes an underspecified, multistep, or revised request in everyday language.

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have demonstrated the effectiveness of web-scale pretraining in enhancing semantic generalization in robotic control. However, interaction between humans and robots is still unnatural. A robot that is capable of perceiving objects and executing movements with precision may still struggle when a user makes an underspecified, multistep, or revised request in everyday language.

Nevertheless, natural language is the most intuitive communication medium for people. Previous studies have contrasted natural language with complex graphical interfaces, structured command languages, and formal abstractions, which require training before a user can effectively control a robot. For robots in homes, assistive scenarios, or shared human environments, it is often unrealistic to expect the human to learn a rigid interaction protocol. A more realistic objective is for robots to be able to interpret natural, unconstrained, and potentially messy human language as it is actually spoken. However, unrestricted language is challenging because human requests are often context-dependent, incomplete, and ambiguous.

Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have introduced new opportunities for integrating natural language into robotic tasks. Models such as GPT-5, Claude and Gemini demonstrate strong capabilities in common sense reasoning, following instructions, and tool calling — properties that are directly relevant to interpreting user intent and translating it into structured robot actions. LLMs ability to handle compositional instructions and generate structured outputs makes LLMs a promising foundation for the interaction layer. Furthermore, LLMs offer a promising approach to generating synthetic data, enabling the creation of extensive and diverse dialogue corpora that would otherwise be too costly to collect through human annotation.

papers.title: Implicit discretization of PID-like sliding-mode control with third-order output accuracy
papers.abstract: A digital PID-like sliding-mode controller is proposed for a double integrator with a Lipschitz matched disturbance. A proper implicit discretization, matched to the exact sampled dynamics of the plant, attains the accuracy of the continuous-time controller without discretization chattering. Global finite-step convergence to a discrete-time sliding mode is established for two gain designs and every sampling time, using an implicit Lyapunov function and a computer-assisted certificate in exact arithmetic. The resulting controller provides third-order output accuracy, second-order accuracy for its derivative, and exact finite-time rejection of constant matched disturbances. These accuracy orders are proved to be optimal among deterministic causal controllers using the same sampled information.
papers.intro:
Conventional sliding-mode control achieves robustness against matched disturbances through discontinuous control action, which generates chattering in the presence of parasitic dynamics and excites unmodeled actuator dynamics. The development of continuous higher-order sliding-mode controllers was motivated by the possibility of eliminating the discontinuity of the control signal while simultaneously increasing the sliding order and the corresponding accuracy (Fridman et al., 2015).

The development of continuous higher-order sliding-mode controllers was motivated by the possibility of eliminating the discontinuity of the control signal while simultaneously increasing the sliding order and the corresponding accuracy (Fridman et al., 2015).

In particular, the continuous terminal sliding-mode controller proposed by Kamal et al. (2016) and the continuous twisting algorithm developed by Torres-González et al. (2017) demonstrated that third-order sliding modes can be achieved for uncertain second-order systems using only direct measurements of the output and its first derivative. Thus, no additional measurements are required compared with conventional sliding-mode control of second-order systems. The extended closed-loop dynamics of these algorithms are homogeneous of degree −1-1 with weights (3,2,1)(3,2,1), corresponding to third-order sliding accuracy with respect to the output (Levant, 2005).

The stability of both designs was established using homogeneous Lyapunov functions.

papers.title: Scan-specific k-space interpolation using deep Koopman autoencoders
papers.abstract:
Purpose: To develop a scan-specific, interpretable k-space interpolation technique for the reconstruction of accelerated MRI data.
  Methods: A deep Koopman autoencoder for nonlinear k-space interpolation was developed consisting of an encoder, a linear layer for interpolation and a decoder. The resulting network is implemented using mean square error loss function on k-space neighbourhoods derived from the autocalibration signals (ACS), combining a prediction loss and an autoencoding loss. The approach was compared to GRAPPA and RAKI in 281 retrospectively undersampled brain datasets, using quantitative reconstruction metrics. In a subset of 52 randomly selected images, a clinical reader study compared the proposed approach and RAKI in a forced choice scenario and using a five-point ordinal scoring, assessing sharpness, SNR, aliasing and overall image quality. Additionally, the effect of varying parameters such as the number of autocalibration signals, the contribution of the autoencoding loss, the kernel size, and the latent space dimension for the proposed technique was studied.
  Results: The proposed approach showed improved quantitative metrics compared to GRAPPA and RAKI. Visually, the method showed higher resilience to noise amplification and improved preservation of sharp details. In the clinical reader study, the proposed approach was preferred overall to RAKI and yielded higher scores than GRAPPA and RAKI. The proposed method showed robustness to parameter variations.
  Conclusion: Deep Learning based k-space interpolation can be achieved using a Koopman autoencoder for k-space neighbourhoods.
  Keywords: Parallel imaging, Koopman autoencoder, nonlinear mapping, k-space interpolation, deep learning reconstruction

papers.intro:
MRI enables non-invasive in-vivo visualisation and assessment of anatomy and function with excellent soft tissue contrast. However, MRI has relatively long acquisition times, which can be a significant limitation in clinical practice. To address this challenge, undersampling strategies combined with tailored reconstruction algorithms [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] are used to reduce scan time. Parallel imaging [3, 4] is a widely used acceleration technique. Taking multi-channels phased array coils, each receiver channel has a different sensitivity profile, and this multichannel information can be used for reconstruction of undersampled data either in image space (e.g. SENSE [3]) or in the k-space domain (e.g. GRAPPA [4]). GRAPPA reconstructs unacquired k-space lines by performing a weighted combination of neighbouring lines across all channels, with weights learned from a fully-sampled autocalibration region. Although it is widely employed in clinical imaging, GRAPPA can suffer from a decrease of SNR or aliasing artifacts, especially for high acceleration factors [8, 9, 10, 11]. This is because the estimated GRAPPA coefficients can greatly amplify the noise inherently present in the acquired MRI signals [8, 9, 10, 11] when the GRAPPA inverse problem is ill-conditioned.

Regularisation approaches [12, 13] to the GRAPPA least-square problem have been proposed to reduce noise amplification, but at the cost of introducing aliasing artifacts. Previous studies [8, 9, 10, 14] have shown that GRAPPA coefficients exhibit a bias that can become significant with high noise level or high acceleration factors, compared to the derived coefficients if the scan was noise-free, leading to a nonlinear error in the reconstruction [14]. Nonlinearities are also present due a truncation effect due to the use of a GRAPPA kernel with limited support [15].

To reduce the nonlinear errors in GRAPPA, nonlinear GRAPPA techniques [14, 15, 16, 17] use a kernel method inspired by classical machine learning. The kernel function maps nonlinearly the data into a higher dimensional space for a robust nonlinear estimation. However, choosing the optimal kernel is not trivial and is done in a heuristic manner [14, 18, 19, 20]. In addition, the reconstruction can still present blurring or aliasing artifacts depending on mapping complexity [14].

More recently, deep learning methods [21] have gathered interest as they capture complex patterns and can learn representations and nonlinear relationships in a scan-specific manner. For example, RAKI [22] performs a nonlinear estimation of missing k-space lines using a three-layer convolutional neural network (CNN) and autocalibration signals (ACS). Recent work has focused on reducing RAKI’s reconstruction time with an optimized GPU implementation [23] or pre-trained models [24], and on improving the reconstruction quality with residual networks [25], iterative reconstruction [26], increasing model size and initialising the reconstruction with GRAPPA reconstruction as input (residual estimation found in SPARK [27]) or using a convolutional recurrent neural network (LORAKI [28]) to propose a deep learning approach to AC-LORAKS [29] iterative reconstruction. However, in addition to limited interpretability, RAKI suffers from blurring and artifacts due to the network design, since the ReLU activation function can be interpreted as an element-wise multiplication with a mask in k-space, so a convolution in image space [30]. Additionally, both techniques have potentially higher computational cost and limited interpretability.

papers.title: Agentic induction of common data elements and information extraction from sarcoma case report abstracts
papers.abstract: Common data elements (CDEs) support clinical data comparability but are usually defined manually. We investigated whether large language model agents could derive a CDE schema from sarcoma case report abstracts and apply it at scale. An agent proposed 72,909 candidate CDEs from 24,588 PubMed abstracts; agentic consolidation yielded 1,570 CDEs. We retained 53 supported by at least 50 abstracts and attempted evidence-linked extraction across the corpus. Processing succeeded for all retained CDEs in 79.2% of abstracts, including responses indicating non-mention. Two human reviewers approved 83.0% of retained CDEs for relevance, 67.9% for clarity, and 56.6% for correctness. In 100 sampled abstracts, exact agreement with the value extracted by the LLM was 94.9% among 1,116 pairs with a non-empty answer (abstract-level bootstrap 95% CI, 93.0-96.4%). Errors concentrated in anatomical and temporal fields. These findings support agent-assisted schema drafting followed by expert curation before large-scale extraction.

papers.intro:
Sarcomas are a rare and heterogeneous group of malignancies differing in histology, anatomic origin, molecular alterations, treatment, and clinical course Sbaraglia and Dei Tos (2019). They account for about 5.6 new cases per 100,000 persons per year in Europe Stiller et al. (2013). A case report is a detailed description of the presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and outcome of an individual patient Nissen and Wynn (2014). Case reports and case series contribute to the recognition of new diseases and the course of rare medical scenarios Vandenbroucke (2001). Their value as a collective resource is limited by narrative presentation, inconsistent terminology, and uneven reporting. The CAse REport (CARE) guidelines support more complete and transparent case reporting, but inconsistent and unstandardised reporting remains common in case reports Gagnier et al. (2014); Yang et al. (2022).

Common data elements (CDEs) were introduced within the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) to standardise data collection in clinical trials National Library of Medicine (). Each CDE combines a clearly defined concept or question with a specified response format, including the data type, permissible values, and units where applicable, enabling consistent recording and reuse across studies Sheehan et al. (2016). Beyond clinical trials, CDEs are used for real-world applications, because they define directly usable data Huser and Amos (2018). Examples include the oncology-specific mCODE standard Osterman et al. (2020) and LLM-assisted mapping of local variables onto NIH CDEs Wang and others (2025).

In conventional CDE definition workflows, domain experts usually define a set of CDEs, also known as a CDE schema, before reviewing the entire input corpus. This provides control over the data elements and their meaning, but requires substantial domain understanding and can overlook concepts that emerge only when a diverse corpus is examined. As a result, a (semi-)automated system for deriving CDE schemas directly from an input corpus would be very valuable. Outside the CDE context, large language models (LLMs) are being used to populate a user-supplied knowledge schema Caufield et al. (2024), to learn ontological structure Babaei Giglou et al. (2023), or to induce and canonicalise a schema from text for knowledge-graph construction Zhang and Soh (2024); Bai et al. (2026). For CDEs specifically, embeddings and clustering have been used to group existing elements Krishnamurthy et al. (2025), but not to derive new ones from a literature corpus.

(2022); Deng et al. (2026), a task commonly referred to as (biomedical) information extraction (IE) Jurafsky and Martin (2026). For example, Zhang et al. investigated LLM-based extraction of clinical information from case reports on inborn errors of metabolism and introduced CaseReportBench, an expert-annotated benchmark comprising 138 reports with information organised into 14 predefined clinical categories Zhang et al. (2025). In our earlier study, an LLM classified radiotherapy case report abstracts using 23 predefined boolean CDEs with the model gpt-oss-120b achieving an overall F1 score of 93.64% Dennstädt et al. (2026a). While these studies demonstrate successful data extraction using LLMs based on investigator-specified data schemas, they do not establish whether an LLM can also construct a useful CDE schema from an input corpus of biomedical literature. This study aimed to assess whether LLM agents can derive a clinically useful CDE schema from sarcoma case report abstracts and whether the resulting schema can support accurate information extraction at scale. papers.title: The directions of science: How we search the unknown
papers.abstract: Science is producing knowledge at unprecedented scale, while artificial intelligence promises to accelerate the generation of hypotheses, analyses, and scientific outputs further. Yet increasing the volume of research does not necessarily expand the range of directions science effectively explores. We argue that science can be understood as a collective search process in which finite resources are allocated across an evolving space of possible research trajectories. Careers, funding, organization, publication, attention, and technology act as interacting selection mechanisms that shape this allocation. This Perspective distinguishes the visible diversity of scientific activity from its effective diversity: apparently different researchers, institutions, or projects need not provide genuinely different routes of exploration or evaluation. Our principal contribution is to introduce cross-stage dependence, which occurs when selection processes operating at different stages of science are not fully independent in the grounds through which they favour scientific trajectories. We hypothesize that, under uncertainty, repeated filtering through overlapping criteria, information, prior selections, or technological infrastructure can reduce the capacity of science to maintain plausible alternatives and redirect effort when evidence changes their relative promise. Artificial intelligence makes this problem increasingly consequential because it can simultaneously expand scientific search capacity and participate across multiple stages of production and selection. The challenge is therefore not simply to produce more knowledge, but to preserve sufficiently distinct routes of exploration, verification and correction while retaining the ability to change direction.

papers.title: Photogrammetric 3D Model-Based Animal Behavior Classification
papers.abstract: Video-based behavior estimation is often implemented end-to-end from image sequences. We advocate a two-stage alternative: reconstruct 3D body and object geometry before classifying behavior. This makes ambiguities of the ill-posed 2D-to-3D inverse problem explicit and potentially correctable. We demonstrate the strategy with simulated interacting mice and extend it to real video.

papers.intro:
Behavior is a higher-level construct inferred from measurable movement patterns. In a semantic network, video features may connect directly to movement, whereas behavior is inferred indirectly through movement [1]. Because video provides only 2D projections and cannot capture all causal subtleties of living behavior, behavior is not directly observable; inferring it from video is therefore an ill-posed inverse problem. We therefore propose a fully three-dimensional (3D) simulation and reconstruction framework: 3D body kinematics are reconstructed from video first, and behavioral states are inferred afterward rather than directly from raw frames.

Reconstruction also uses prior 3D models: deformable animal bodies, static cage geometry, and kinematic enrichment devices such as lock-boxes. These provide structural and motion constraints. We illustrate the concept with simulated interactions between two mice and real multi-view video of a mouse solving a lock-box task.

papers.title: Learning Word-Level Explanations of Text Reuse in Latin Literature with Little Annotation
papers.abstract: Detecting an intertextual reference is only the first step; philologists also need to know how a later author reworked the source. We explain a reuse pair word by word: each word of the reusing passage is first aligned to its source word, then labeled with the operation that transformed it, such as a copy, a change of inflection, or a substitution. Such word-level operations are expensive to annotate, and only a few corpora annotated at this level exist for text reuse in Latin literature. We describe a procedure that needs only a limited number of annotations: synthetic pairs, built by applying known operations to Latin text, train a first model, and active learning chooses the pairs an annotator corrects. Among several architectures, a model that links and labels together performs best: a pointer network that, for every reuse word, chooses a source word and names the operation in the same step. We show that with active learning, 200 pairs chosen by uncertainty are enough for the model to match one trained on every annotated pair of the 1,490 references of the Loci Similes benchmark. We release our code, word-level predictions for all references, and an interactive demo.

papers.intro:
Identifying intertextual references is a central task in classical philology: it shows how later works engage with the texts they inherit, what inspired them, and which works their authors knew. Recent work on Latin literature has established sentence-pair baselines that frame the problem as a three-way classification of a (query, candidate) pair into no reference, verbatim reference (cit.), or allusion (cf.) (Schelb et al., 2026). The two reference types follow the convention of critical editions and quotation indices (Revellio, 2022; Schropp et al., 2024b), but they divide reuse only coarsely, and scholars draw the line between them differently. More importantly, such a label indicates only whether two passages are related; it does not explain how the later author reworked the source.

Figure 1 illustrates this with Virgil and its reuse in Valerius Flaccus. In Virgil, Aeneas presses his care down in his heart; Valerius Flaccus reuses the expression for Aeson, who holds down his fears. He keeps corde (heart), the word that makes the reference recognizable; he turns the verb premebat (he pressed) into the participle prementem (pressing) to fit his own sentence; and he replaces the object curam (care) with metus (fears), a word of similar meaning. Together, the three operations show that the expression of an emotion pressed down in the heart survives intact, while its grammar and one of its words are adapted: Valerius Flaccus alludes to Virgil rather than quoting him verbatim. Such an explanation makes the boundary between cit. and cf. measurable, allows comparison of how different authors handle their sources, and shows at a glance which words were copied and which were changed.

We therefore explain a reuse pair at the level at which philologists describe it: the word. Each word of the reusing passage is linked to the source word it corresponds to, or to none, and each link is labeled with the operation that relates the two words: a copy, a change of inflection, or a substitution. We call the result an edit script. For a verbatim reference, a script shows which words were copied and whether their order changed; for an allusion, it shows which words survive and which were replaced. Producing such a script resembles word alignment between a source and a reuse passage, with two differences. First, each link carries a label that names the operation the later author applied. Second, unlike alignment in translation or other multilingual settings, most words of a reusing passage have no counterpart in the source, so deciding that a word has no source is most of the task.

Second, unlike alignment in translation or other multilingual settings, most words of a reusing passage have no counterpart in the source, so deciding that a word has no source is most of the task.

Training a model to produce such scripts requires labeled data. For Latin, such data exists only for 100 Bible reuses (Moritz et al., 2016). Extending it by hand is slow, since an annotator must decide a link and an operation for every word of both passages. We therefore combine two ways to reduce the number of annotations required. The first is synthetic data. In the spirit of Trinh et al. (2024), we build pairs by applying known operations to clean Latin text, so their scripts are correct by construction. A model trained on these pairs learns what a script looks like before any pair is annotated. The second is active learning (Settles and Craven, 2008). The model pre-annotates the corpus and selects the pairs it is least sure of. An annotator corrects these pairs, and the model trains again. Together, the two turn annotation into correction, starting from zero annotated pairs. We simulate this procedure on the 1,490 references of the Loci Similes benchmark (Schelb et al., 2026) and find that with 200 corrected pairs, the model matches one trained on every annotated pair.

papers.title: Balancing-based model reduction for output-constrained optimal control of switched linear systems
papers.abstract: We develop a balanced-truncation (BT) framework for model-order reduction of optimal control problems governed by switched linear systems, with quadratic tracking costs, convex input constraints, and Moreau--Yosida-regularized output constraints. For general Petrov--Galerkin reduced models, we derive an a posteriori bound for the error in the optimal value function, and combine it with BT-based estimates of the dynamical-system reduction error. We show that BT preserves the duality structure underlying the first-order optimality conditions, making first-reduce-then-optimize and first-optimize-then-reduce equivalent. Consequently, reducing the forward system also reduces the associated optimality system, leading to a certified, online-efficient, and online-adaptive approximation of the parameterized solution operator. The reduced model can therefore be reused across different regularization parameters, constraint sets, switching signals, and reference trajectories.

papers.title: Performance-Portable Exact Gaussian Process Regression in Python via SYCL and oneMath
papers.abstract: Modern multi-vendor GPU environments force a choice between portable code and native performance. GPRat is an open-source Python library for exact Gaussian process regression built on the HPX asynchronous many-task runtime, tiled algorithms, and CPU/CUDA BLAS backends. We contribute a UXL Foundation oneMath backend with a hybrid HPX/SYCL design, extending GPRat to AMD and Intel GPUs. The new SYCL backend comes within 3% of native CUDA on an NVIDIA A30 at the largest problem size and outperforms the GPflow and GPyTorch libraries by up to 1.75x and 2.17x on the A30 and up to 1.79x and 4.62x on an AMD Instinct MI210. On an Intel Arc B580, a consumer-class card with FP64 throughput below our CPUs, the unmodified SYCL backend trails GPRat's CPU backend. Overall, oneMath's dispatch to vendor-native BLAS lets a single SYCL codebase match CUDA on NVIDIA and outperform established Python GP frameworks on AMD, without vendor-specific code.

papers.intro:
More than half of the systems on the TOP500 list of the world’s fastest supercomputers use accelerators, predominantly manufactured by NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel [1]. Yet the dominant GPU programming models remain vendor-specific. Writing and maintaining a separate native-code path per vendor is costly, so a single portable implementation is attractive, provided its performance overhead relative to native code is small and well quantified. SYCL [2], backed by vendor-native math libraries through oneMath [3], is a candidate for closing this portability gap, and measuring the resulting portability overhead is a central concern of this work.

We study this portability question in the setting of Gaussian processes (GPs). GPs are a non-parametric alternative to the parametric models, such as neural networks, for various machine learning (ML) applications [4]. Unlike neural network models, a GP naturally provides uncertainty estimates for its predictions and allows the direct integration of prior knowledge, such as periodicity [5]. GPs are applied, inter alia, in control theory [5], geostatistics [6, 7], Artificial Intelligence (AI) [8], scientific computing [9], big data [10], chemistry [11], and psychology [12].

Established Gaussian process regression (GPR) Python libraries largely inherit their portability from a general-purpose backend. As native Python implementations struggle to harness modern high-performance computing (HPC) devices [13], many libraries write their core logic in C or C++ and expose it through Python bindings. Popular examples in the context of ML include PyTorch [14] and TensorFlow [15]. GPyTorch [16] and GPflow [17] are two notable GPR implementations built on top of these general-purpose libraries. Both focus on a broad feature set and delegate performance, scalability, and hardware portability to their respective backends, which can be a limitation when targeting heterogeneous hardware. Moreover, on less common hardware, installing GPyTorch and, especially, GPflow can be complicated due to strict and sprawling dependencies.

Moreover, on less common hardware, installing GPyTorch and, especially, GPflow can be complicated due to strict and sprawling dependencies.

To address these challenges, we developed the GPRat [18] library. It provides a Python interface via pybind11 [19] and, under the hood, leverages asynchronous, task-based parallelization via the HPX [20] runtime. Its entire dependency tree is available via Spack [21], which contributes to a mature installation pipeline. Portability is a core design goal of GPRat, demonstrated across x86, ARM, and RISC-V CPUs [22] and across NVIDIA accelerators [23]. Performance and portability across accelerators from both AMD and Intel remained unclear.

papers.title: Differentially Private Federated Class-Incremental Learning for EEG Mental State Classification
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) under differential privacy (DP) is typically evaluated on large client cohorts, where subsampling and cross-client averaging amplify privacy and smooth injected noise. Personal biosignal applications such as wearable EEG instead involve small federations of a handful of subjects, a regime whose interaction with formal client-level DP is largely uncharacterized. We study differentially private federated class-incremental learning in this small-cohort regime, combining a public EEG dataset with a custom four-channel MUSE 2 recording set into a K=5-client federation, and give a masked per-class training protocol that avoids degenerate gradients and missing negative supervision under class-incremental streaming. We propose FedEEG, combining Synaptic-Intelligence consolidation with a lagged adaptive FedProx term, and show it reduces catastrophic forgetting relative to FedAvg, FedProx, and a federated Learning-without-Forgetting baseline; on-device balanced-batch replay reduces mean forgetting by a further 56.7%. A class-scoping diagnosis yields $50.5\%\pm3.6\%$ accuracy with 6 seeds and 2.02 times chance. We also introduce head-scoped client-level DP, which protects the classification head and alone reduces the achievable $\varepsilon$ by 200 times at a matched round budget; combined with fewer communication rounds it reaches $\varepsilon\!\approx\!10.4$ with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training.

papers.title: Controllability-Informed Distributed Electric Propulsion Aircraft Design Using Probabilistic Attainable Moment Sets
papers.abstract: Integrated aircraft design combines models of aerodynamics, propulsion, mass, and mission performance in one design loop, so that the disciplines can be traded against each other from the earliest stage. For configurations with distributed electric propulsion (DEP), part of the control authority comes from the propulsion system itself, which directly affects the required size of the tail and should therefore be known while the aircraft is being sized. This paper presents a controllability measure that is evaluated for every design in the loop and returned to it as a design signal. The attainable moment set of each candidate design is computed from the surrugate models of the loop and it is compared with a required moment set. Since the low-fidelity surrugate models are uncertain, the comparison is formulated with probabilistic attainable moment sets: the uncertainty is propagated to the boundary of the set, which yields a margin for every direction in the moment space and the probability of violating the requirement. The design loop thereby informed whether a configuration provides sufficient control authority, on which axes it falls short, and how this changes with the design variables. The approach is demonstrated on a DEP regional aircraft, where the signal is used to assess the size of the vertical tail.

papers.intro:
Distributed electric propulsion (DEP) replaces a few large propulsion units by many smaller ones that are distributed over the airframe. The propulsion system can be integrated closely with the wing, which increases the maximum lift coefficient, permits a smaller wing that is better matched to cruise, and adds redundancy [1].. The same propulsion units can also generate moments: differential thrust acts as an additional control effector, in particular about the yaw axis, where it has been studied as a means of yaw control and of reducing the vertical tail [2, 3]. These effects do not belong to a single discipline. A smaller wing changes mass and trim, the propulsion layout changes the available control authority, and a smaller tail changes drag, mass, and balance, so that the configuration has to be evaluated as a whole. This is the purpose of integrated aircraft design loops, in which models of aerodynamics, propulsion, mass, and mission performance are iterated until the aircraft is consistent, and which have been extended to hybrid-electric and fuel-cell electric configurations with distributed propulsion [4, 5]. In the collaborative research center SynTrac, such a loop is the common platform to which the individual disciplines contribute models and surrogates in order to exploit the synergies between them. Controllability is not yet represented in it: the loop has no information on whether a design provides sufficient control authority, although for a DEP aircraft this authority depends on the very quantities that the loop is sizing.

A DEP aircraft is overactuated: its propulsion units and aerodynamic control surfaces together provide more effectors than the three rotational axes to be controlled. Control allocation decides how a commanded moment is distributed among these effectors, but it can only deliver moments that the effectors are able to produce within their limits. The set of these moments is fixed by the sizing and placement of the effectors, that is, by aircraft design, and it bounds everything that allocation and the control laws can achieve in flight. To assess controllability, the attainable moment set (AMS) was introduced by Durham in the context of constrained control allocation as the set of moments that a redundant suite of effectors can generate within its position limits [6, 7, 8]. For a linear effectiveness model it is a convex polytope whose geometry and computation are well understood [9, 10]. Beyond allocation, the AMS has become a tool to visualize and quantify control authority during vehicle design [11]. Its size alone, however, does not state whether the available authority is sufficient. Söpper et al. [12] therefore introduced the required moment set (RMS), which is assembled from the aerodynamic disturbances over the flight envelope and the maneuver accelerations demanded by the mission, and assessed controllability through the margins between the two sets along a common grid of query directions. Zhang et al. [13] turned these margins into a cost function and optimized the propeller installation angles of an eVTOL such that its AMS covers the RMS. Both works are deterministic, and the need to include model uncertainty in order to obtain probabilistic controllability statements was already noted in [12]. Tsagkaris et al. [14] recently addressed it with the probabilistic attainable moment set (PAMS), which propagates parametric uncertainty of the effector model to the boundary of the set through a first-order expansion along fixed rays and uses the probability of violating the requirement as the objective for optimizing multirotor tilt angles.
