papers.title: PoliMop: Policy-in-the-Loop Motion Planning in 3D Spaces for Mobile Robots
papers.abstract: Reaching a goal state in a complex environment often requires a robot to overcome challenging terrain and obstacles. Which routes are accessible depends on the robot's physical design, the control policy it uses, and how it modifies its surroundings. We present a kinodynamic rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) planner that uses physics simulation to exploit skills encoded in the control policy, which allows it to find a path in the scene with respect to the robot's capabilities. The planner samples states from a reduced state space in 3D around the scene and expands the RRT toward each sample using policy rollouts. We guide sampling with a preplanned path for a simple mass-point model to focus exploration on promising regions leading toward the goal state, reducing planning time by up to 63%. Simulation experiments with quadrupeds, humanoids, and wheeled robots demonstrate that our approach supports drop-in integration of various robots and control policies, exploiting their physical and policy capabilities without modifying the underlying planning algorithm. Predefined environmental modifications, such as placing a plank across a gap to build a bridge, will automatically be picked up by the planner as the robot's reachable space expands.
papers.intro:
Motion planning is typically treated as the problem of finding a feasible path through a fixed environment. For robots operating in complex terrain, however, reachability depends not only on the scene geometry but also on the robot’s body and brain, i.e., its mechanical design and control policies. A path that is feasible for a quadruped equipped with a parkour control policy (e.g., [1]) may be infeasible for a wheeled robot or for the same quadruped using a simpler locomotion policy. Moreover, a robot can intentionally change the scene by manipulating objects to actively extend its reachable space. For example, a robot may place a plank across a gap to create a bridge to make a final platform reachable. Thus, reachability is not a fixed property of the scene: it emerges from the combination of the robot, the selected policy, and the current environment state. Ultimately, our vision is to enable robots not only to exploit the capabilities of their control policies to traverse challenging terrain but also to deliberately modify their environment to reach a goal or complete a task. In this work, we take a step toward this goal by asking: how can a motion planner find paths in environments whose reachable regions change through prescribed manipulation actions and policy selections?

Many conventional motion-planning approaches use explicit representations of traversable terrain, such as 2.5D elevation maps combined with robot-specific traversability estimates [2, 3]. A single-layer elevation map stores one terrain height per horizontal location and therefore cannot perform motion planning on vertically overlapping surfaces (Fig. 1, right). Additionally, the planner should automatically exploit the robot’s capabilities encoded in its control policy. To achieve both, our planner samples target positions throughout the 3D scene and uses a physics simulator as a state-transition mechanism to roll out motions generated by the control policy. This enables us to plan through multi-level structures, as illustrated in Fig. 1, while accounting for the selected robot–policy pair’s capabilities without the requirement of an explicit parameterization of the reachable space that the planner needs to sample from.

papers.title: The Complexity of Traffic Engineering in Segment Routing Networks
papers.abstract:
Segment routing is a modern variant of source routing which has recently become popular in the Internet. It allows operators to equip network packets with an additional header which specifies segments: a list of waypoints the packet needs to traverse on its way to the destination. This is reminiscent of Valiant routing in parallel computing and introduces an additional degree of freedom in traffic engineering. This flexibility can be exploited to minimize congestion in the network.
  This paper sheds light on the computational complexity of traffic engineering in segment routing networks. We consider two problem variants: a fixed-length variant where link weights are given and only waypoints can be chosen, and a variable-length variant where additionally the network operator can also choose the link weights, which then define the shortest paths taken between the waypoints. We prove that the first variant is NP-hard even if the network graph is planar and if all demands and link weights are 1. We also show that the second variant is NP-hard already for planar network graphs with all demands being 1. On the positive side, we present a compact and general mixed integer linear program to compute exact solutions for the first variant.
papers.intro:
To make best use of their infrastructure and to provide good performance to their customers, Internet Service Providers (ISPs) employ traffic engineering (TE) to select paths for their communication traffic that minimize congestion. Segment routing (SR) has recently emerged as a powerful approach to perform TE, which received much attention in industry and standardization bodies (the IETF). Traditionally, packets are restricted to follow shortest paths which are indirectly defined by the link weights which can be set by network operators. In SR networks, there is an additional degree of freedom: packets can be equipped with a packet header defining a list of waypoints: nodes (essentially IPv6 addresses) which the packet needs to traverse on its way to the destination.11 1 Technically and more generally, segments are instructions (e.g., forwarding to an interface) that are executed on subsequent nodes in the network. Between each pair of waypoints as well as from the source to the first waypoint and from the last waypoint to the destination (called segments), a packet takes a shortest path, defined as usual, based on link weights. If there are multiple shortest paths, traffic is split across them on a per-flow granularity (to minimize packet reordering). Segment routing can hence be seen as a modern variant of source routing and is inspired by Valiant routing known in parallel computing [28]. Empirical studies show that such a redirection, already with a single waypoint, can significantly improve TE performance in practice [6, 29].

Segment routing networks introduce a novel graph-theoretical optimization problem: how to select waypoints in order to minimize congestion? This problem is interesting already in scenarios where link weights are given, and we will refer to this problem version as the fixed-length variant in the following (interpreting weights as distances). Here, we also consider settings which support splitting ratios [10]: scenarios where network operators can decide to assign different amounts of traffic to different shortest paths. The problem version where in addition to the waypoints, also the link weights can be chosen, is referred to as the variable-length variant.

This problem is interesting already in scenarios where link weights are given, and we will refer to this problem version as the fixed-length variant in the following (interpreting weights as distances). Here, we also consider settings which support splitting ratios [10]: scenarios where network operators can decide to assign different amounts of traffic to different shortest paths. The problem version where in addition to the waypoints, also the link weights can be chosen, is referred to as the variable-length variant.

This paper is concerned with these algorithmic problems underlying segment routing. Specifically, we investigate the case of a single waypoint per demand. Given the high interest of industry in the topic, surprisingly little is known today about the graph-theoretical challenges of traffic engineering with waypoints. Parham et al. [24] showed that a joint optimization of link weights and waypoints can in principle significantly improve traffic engineering compared to scenarios where link weights and waypoints are optimized separately. Amiri et al. [2, 3, 4] initiated the study of the parametrized complexity of routing through waypoints in a related problem in which the task is to find a shortest walk visiting a given set of waypoints and respecting edge capacities; they presented exact polynomial-time algorithms for graphs of bounded treewidth or restricted problems where the number of waypoints is logarithmically bounded. Recently, Bazgan et al. [7] showed that the fixed-length segment routing problem is NP-hard even for graphs with constant treewidth and when only one waypoint per demand is allowed. In our work, we complement these results, among others (see below), by showing that both the fixed-length variant (for which we also consider splitting ratios which Bazgan et al. did not) and the variable-length variant are NP-hard even on the practically relevant class of planar graphs (many ISP topologies are planar [25]).

Our main contributions concern the computational complexity of traffic engineering in segment routing networks. We first rigorously prove that even the fixed-length problem variant (where link weights are given and traffic can be distributed across paths according to operator-defined splitting ratios) is NP-hard already if the network graph is planar and if all demands and link weights are 1. We further show that the variable-length problem variant is also NP-hard already for planar network graphs, even with all demands being 1. Complementing these negative results, we present a compact and general mixed integer linear program to compute exact solutions. We next present the high-level idea of our two hardness results.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning for Null-Space Exploitation in Pseudo-Inverse Control Allocation
papers.abstract: Pseudo-inverse methods are widely used to solve control allocation problems for overactuated aircraft with redundant control effectors. These methods reliably satisfy the primary command tracking objective, while the remaining null-space degrees of freedom are in principle available for secondary objectives such as drag reduction or actuator wear balancing. However, exploiting this freedom in practice requires hand-tuned weighting matrices or a priori preferred deflections that are difficult to specify across a wide flight envelope with nonlinear, state-dependent dynamics. This paper presents a hybrid architecture in which a reinforcement learning agent operates exclusively within the null space of the control effectiveness matrix, learning secondary objective strategies directly from interaction with the flight dynamics. The null-space projector guarantees by construction that primary command tracking remains invariant regardless of the agent output, providing a principled separation between certified primary control and adaptive secondary optimization. The approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear six-degree-of-freedom distributed electric propulsion aircraft model with aero-propulsive effects across diverse mission scenarios, achieving measurable drag reduction compared to the baseline allocation while preserving tracking integrity and respecting actuator constraints. The proposed architecture forms a foundation for future extensions toward multi-objective, mission-conditioned policies.

Modern engineered systems are increasingly designed with more control effectors than independent degrees of freedom to be controlled, resulting in overactuated configurations. Examples range from autonomous robots with several effectors to satellites equipped with clusters of reaction wheels and fighter aircraft with redundant aerodynamic surfaces [1, 2]. When the actuator set is redundant, the allocation problem admits infinitely many solutions, and the surplus degrees of freedom can in principle be directed toward secondary objectives such as minimizing drag, reducing power consumption, limiting actuator wear, or preserving a low radar cross-section. Classical methods including pseudoinverse-based allocation [3], null-space augmentation, and iterative redistribution strategies [5] reliably solve the primary task, but secondary objective optimization remains dependent on fixed weighting schemes or manual tuning that do not generalize across flight conditions and mission requirements. When multiple competing objectives must be balanced under nonlinear, state dependent dynamics, a learning based approach that discovers effective allocation strategies directly from interaction with the flight dynamics becomes attractive.

The decomposition of the control allocation solution into a pseudo-inverse particular solution and a null-space component was first formalized by Bordignon and Durham [6, 7], who introduced the null-space intersection method for constrained allocation of overactuated aircraft. Durham et al. [8] subsequently exploited this freedom for drag minimization by projecting cost gradients into the null space of the control effectiveness matrix. The comprehensive treatment by Durham, Bordignon, and Beck [3] established the geometric theory relating the null-space structure to the Attainable Moment Set.

Several authors have applied null-space methods to specific secondary objectives in flight control. Stolk and de Visser [9] developed minimum-drag control allocation for the Innovative Control Effector (ICE) tailless fighter, combining weighted pseudo-inverse prioritization with gradient descent in the null space toward minimum-drag deflections. Pfeifle and Fichter [10] derived a closed-form null-space increment for minimum propeller shaft power in over-actuated transition aircraft. Pollack and van Kampen [11] extended incremental control allocation for secondary objectives using the null-space degrees of freedom.

Data-driven methods have been increasingly applied to control allocation, with neural networks trained to approximate or replace classical allocators. Kang et al. [12] train a neural allocator for a tailless aircraft that replicates a dynamic allocation scheme while avoiding heavy online optimization. Madruga et al. [13] use offline-trained networks to substitute the fixed allocation matrix on a quadrotor, compensating for aerodynamic effects without explicit inflow models. Chen et al. [14] combine an adaptive neural attitude controller with a constrained allocation layer to handle uncertainties and time-varying disturbances. Reinforcement learning extends this direction by learning allocation policies directly from interaction with the environment: de Visser et al. [15] apply RL to distribute control commands across 13 effectors for longitudinal control without a preidentified effectiveness matrix. However, these approaches are fundamentally black-box function approximators in which the mapping from state to actuator command is not transparent. Secondary objectives and constraints are enforced indirectly through reward or loss shaping, behavior under distribution shift is difficult to bound, and failure diagnosis is hindered by limited interpretability. In safety-critical applications such as flight control, these limitations present significant barriers to verification and certification that often outweigh empirical performance gains.

While the present work was in preparation, Isci and Koyuncu [16] recently proposed a hybrid allocation scheme for the ICE aircraft in which a reinforcement-learning agent adjusts the effector weights of an incremental quadratic programming allocator. Since a weight change only redistributes effort among solutions that satisfy the demanded moment, primary tracking is preserved while the actuator constraints remain inactive, and the agent is trained to reduce allocation error. The present work differs in the nature of the secondary objective. In their scheme the objective is internal to the allocator, the allocation error itself, whereas the secondary objectives considered here are external and mission-dependent, such as energy, actuator wear, and acoustic noise, which are nonlinear functions of the operating point rather than quantities the allocator already represents. The two directions are therefore complementary: their weight adaptation refines the allocator’s internal behavior, while the present approach exploits the null space to optimize external, mission-level objectives.

papers.title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.

papers.title: PyVesta: A new Versatile Echelle Spectra exTraction and Analysis pipeline
papers.abstract: We present PyVesta, an automatic data reduction software for fiber fed echelle spectrographs. PyVesta is designed to be used with different instruments, both high resolution spectrographs such as HARPS or FEROS as well as inexpensive off-the-shelf spectrographs like the Shelyak eShel II. Special additions were implemented to improve the stability and resolution of inexpensive instruments especially. PyVesta provides tools for all extraction steps from raw CCD images to continuum normalized spectra, e.g., CCD image corrections, spectra extraction, wavelength calibration, and continuum normalization. Our software is based on the software package CERES and was ported to Python 3, revised, and supplemented.

papers.intro:
Echelle spectrographs offer high resolution spectra combined with large spectral coverage. That makes them ideal for many use cases, such as spectral classification of stars or the determination of companions via the radial velocity method. Most dedicated exoplanet searching instruments such as HARPS or CARMENES are echelle spectrographs [20, 29].

Echelle spectrographs offer high resolution spectra combined with large spectral coverage. That makes them ideal for many use cases, such as spectral classification of stars or the determination of companions via the radial velocity method. Most dedicated exoplanet searching instruments such as HARPS or CARMENES are echelle spectrographs [20, 29].

The main disadvantage of echelle spectrographs in comparison to single order spectrographs is the complexity of data reduction for those instruments. Echelle spectra feature multiple diffraction orders, which are shifted relative to each other on the detector chip. These orders are also often curved, which requires precise tracking. Many spectrographs feature multiple fibers, e.g. for calibration spectra, and image slicers, which complicates the extraction even more. In addition, less expensive spectrographs in particular exhibit optical errors in their images, which must be taken into account during extraction.

Many data processing routines were developed especially for high resolution spectrographs. For example, [31] developed a software package to extract the data from ESPRESSO and also from HARPS and HARPS-N. In the past, ESO‘s MIDAS package [3] was used to extract echelle spectra from most of the ESO spectrographs such as HARPS, UVES and XSHOOTER [2]. IRAF/PyRAF [35, 30] is an old but powerful software package for analyzing data from various instruments, but it is now practically out of use as well. PyReduce [26] is a port of the REDUCE software [25] to Python, while PypeIt [28, 27] provides a modern and modular data reduction pipeline. PyReduce and PypeIt are both well established, (Py)Reduce is used with fiber-fed and slit echelle spectrographs (e.g. [18, 16]), PypeIt with a wide range of slit and multi-object instruments (e.g. [34, 8]). Many instruments also come with extraction software that has been specifically developed for that particular instrument, e.g., [5, 9, 12]. In addition to these large instruments, there is also software for smaller instruments, e.g., the Audela11 1 https://audela.org/dokuwiki/doku.php/en/start package.

PyReduce [26] is a port of the REDUCE software [25] to Python, while PypeIt [28, 27] provides a modern and modular data reduction pipeline. PyReduce and PypeIt are both well established, (Py)Reduce is used with fiber-fed and slit echelle spectrographs (e.g. [18, 16]), PypeIt with a wide range of slit and multi-object instruments (e.g. [34, 8]). Many instruments also come with extraction software that has been specifically developed for that particular instrument, e.g., [5, 9, 12]. In addition to these large instruments, there is also software for smaller instruments, e.g., the Audela11 1 https://audela.org/dokuwiki/doku.php/en/start package.

The various software packages differ in many details such as spectrum extraction or wavelength calibration. Using different packages in projects that require data from multiple instruments can lead to systematic errors, especially for high resolution radial velocity analysis. For this reason, MIDAS supports several ESO instruments, but cannot be used for other instruments. These packages are usually written in very specific programming languages and/or development environments, which makes it difficult to adapt them to other instruments. An approach to analyzing data from a number of instruments using only one pipeline was presented by [6] with the CERES software package. This package provides the possibility to work with different instruments , e.g. CORALIE, FEROS and HARPS. However, this software was originally written in Python 2, which reached its end of life in 2020. Also new extraction and wavelength calibration routines were published in the meantime by PyReduce [26] and xwavecal [7, 11], respectively. Therefore, we developed PyVesta, the spiritual successor to CERES. This new software package is written in Python 3 completely, so that adjustments can be done much easier compared to some older or less common programming languages. In addition, PyVesta was specifically designed to extract data from off-the-shelf spectrographs. These spectrographs are generally much less well characterized than high-resolution instruments, which means they benefit significantly from PyVesta’s more flexible data reduction. A uniform data reduction using PyVesta also allows data from off-the-shelf and high-resolution spectrographs to be combined more effectively.

papers.title: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors
papers.abstract: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\gamma}\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.

Many domain experts have a computer program clearly in mind that encodes certain rule-based behavior, but they cannot easily write it down themselves. For instance, a spreadsheet user often knows how they would like the column of names to be reformatted, but cannot write the regex. Similarly, a linguist knows how a sentence in their native language should be segmented, but cannot program the tokenizer. Inductive programming, also known as programming by example (Summers, 1977; Lieberman, 2001; Gulwani et al., 2012; Gulwani et al., 2017), aims to bridge this gap by recovering the program from input–output examples. The paradigm has been deployed at scale for specific applications, most prominently in Microsoft Excel’s FlashFill (Gulwani, 2011).

Li & Ellis (2024) report a substantial gap to hand-engineered systems on programming-by-example, and Wei et al. (2025) report limited success of LLM agents doing autonomous program induction in Python with oracle feedback.

papers.title: AI-aided Decision-Making in Education - Uncertainty, Explainability, and Human Responsibility
papers.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based systems have become increasingly integrated into various aspects of everyday life, including education, understanding how these systems make decisions is of paramount importance. AI holds significant potential to enhance educational practices through the facilitation of personalized and adaptive learning, automation of assessment procedures, and assistance with administrative tasks. However, the opacity of AI-based decision-making in education (especially with deep learning and generative AI models) can hamper decision-making, especially when outcomes appear unjustified or incorrect. In this chapter, we argue that three key principles (uncertainty, explainability, and human responsibility) are essential for the legitimate use of AI in educational settings. Acknowledging the inherent uncertainties in AI-based decisions, analogous to those in human decision-making, is fundamental. Explainability is critical for ensuring that the functioning and outcomes of AI applications are transparent and comprehensible to both educators and learners. Furthermore, human responsibility is crucial, particularly in human decision-making, which remains indispensable across all stages of AI development and deployment. By examining these three principles, this chapter provides a comprehensive guide for stakeholders seeking to integrate AI thoughtfully and effectively into the educational system.

papers.title: Pressure-driven evolution of crystal and molecular structures reshapes excited-state competition in coronene
papers.abstract: Molecular nanocarbons exhibit unique optoelectronic properties and considered as promising candidates for organic device applications, however, understanding how molecular geometry and crystal packing jointly govern physical properties remains a fundamental challenge in {\pi}-conjugated molecular materials. Here, we demonstrate how these structural factors modulate the photoluminescence of coronene under high pressure. Combining high-pressure single-crystal X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, optical spectroscopy, and density functional theory calculations, we establish a relationship between distinct structural changes and the evolution of competing emissive states. Our results reveal that crystal polymorphism modifies the balance between free-exciton (FE) and self-trapped-exciton (STE) emission, while pressure-induced molecular bending is associated with a nonmonotonic evolution of STE emission. As intermolecular distances shorten, enhanced intermolecular electronic interactions give rise to excimer-related emission, introducing an additional emissive pathway. Although pressure-dependent optical properties of coronene have been linked to changes in crystal packing, our findings highlight that the optical response of a molecular solid is not governed by molecular deformation or crystal packing alone, but emerges from their interplay with intermolecular electronic coupling. By directly resolving molecular bending alongside changes in excited-state emission, this work provides insight into how distinct structural degrees of freedom can reshape the photophysical behavior of {\pi}-conjugated molecular solids.

papers.title: A Machine-learning-aided Workflow for Sampling Small Polaron Dynamics in Energy Materials
papers.abstract:
One of the defining characteristics of most energy materials, used as e.g.~battery electrodes, photovoltaics, or photocatalysts, is their ability conduct charges such as electrons and holes. The exact mechanism of this conductivity depends on the material, but is often dominated by the existence of mobile small polarons, i.e.~electrons or holes strongly localised through the polarisation of their environment. Computationally, small polarons can be treated with reasonably accuracy through the use of self-interaction corrected or hybrid density functional theory (DFT) together with local geometry optimisation. Similar approaches can be employed to determine the energy barriers to movement of the polarons through hopping. Unfortunately, realistic energy materials tend have very large numbers of symmetry inequivalent polaronic configurations and correspondingly large numbers of hopping barriers, making them hard to tackle explicitly.
  In this work we therefore extend the computational reach of DFT calculations with machine-learned (ML) surrogate models, which then feed into a kinetic model to quantitatively estimate the conductivity of a battery anode material (Li$_4$Ti$_5$O$_12$ or LTO) at realistic, defected conditions. We calculate the conductivity at room temperature to be 6.7 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ S/cm which lies well in the experimental range. To this end, we only needed a total of 154 polaron barrier calculations, out of 3649 symmetry inequivalent ones, achieving an over 20-fold increase of computational efficiency. Overall, our work demonstrates how DFT-trained ML surrogates can be used to quantitatively and efficiently sample the dynamics of small polarons in energy materials.

In this work, we utilize a similar approach to predict dynamical properties of polarons. Combining electronic density functional theory (DFT), ML, and a kinetic Monte Carlo (kMC) dynamics approach, we are able to calculate the conductivity of LTO to a high degree of accuracy. Given a specific supercell of LTO, we first grouped similar polaron configurations together, resulting in seven distinct clusters. We then randomly selected 161 configurations from these clusters for DFT calculations. With this, we ensured a diverse training dataset, which is crucial for small data learning. To predict the macroscopic properties, we performed kMC simulations using the trained GBDT model as a barrier calculator for the kMC simulations. The calculated conductivity was found to be in good agreement with the experimental study performed on Ta-doped reduced LTO. We showed that any more approximate calculation of the barriers, such as, e.g. taking only the mean barrier height of the test set, would result in a much different conductivity.

papers.title: The QBF Gallery 2026
papers.abstract:
The QBF Gallery 2026 is the latest evaluation event of (dependency) quantified Boolean formula (QBF) solving technology. Its goal is to assess the current state-of-the-art, enable the evaluation of novel solvers on newly curated benchmark instances and present the progress made since the previous competition. This report discusses the solvers, instances and tools submitted by the community and introduces new benchmark collections for evaluation. We evaluate solvers in three tracks, reflecting most common input formats in (dependency) QBF solving. In addition to those main evaluations, we investigate effects of preprocessing and include a track of new crafted benchmark families.
  The results are analyzed using various metrics and complementary statistics on solver similarities, different memory limitations and performance across formula families. Finally, the dedicated benchmarks for each track are made available as an artifact to support future research and reproducible evaluation.
papers.intro:
Quantified Boolean formulas (QBFs) arise in numerous practical applications including synthesis, bounded model checking and planning [63]. The corresponding decision problem is widely regarded as the canonical PSPACE-complete problem [66]. To assess the state-of-the-art in QBF solving, regular events such as the QBFEval and the QBF Gallery have been organized. This tradition began in 2003 and had its latest entry 2023, with numerous editions in between [4, 5, 33, 34, 43, 46, 49, 54, 53]. This paper reports on the organization and results of the QBF Gallery 2026.

To assess the state-of-the-art in QBF solving, regular events such as the QBFEval and the QBF Gallery have been organized. This tradition began in 2003 and had its latest entry 2023, with numerous editions in between [4, 5, 33, 34, 43, 46, 49, 54, 53]. This paper reports on the organization and results of the QBF Gallery 2026.

The event itself was conducted virtually with the evaluations performed on a local compute cluster. The results were presented at the Federated Logic Conference (FLoC) 2026, as part of the FLoC Olympics, affiliated with the International Conference on Theory and Applications of Satisfiability Testing [59]. In addition to solvers and preprocessors, participants were invited to submit novel problem instances to different tracks covering different QBF formalisms and input formats. The results are analyzed not only to determine a winner for each track but also to identify the practical challenges currently faced by the field. By including instances and solvers from previous competitions, we aim to show the progress made over the last iterations. This paper is structured as follows: First, we describe the organizational aspects of the Gallery including the experimental setup and the individual tracks. We then present the benchmarks and solvers newly submitted and further the selected participants of this Gallery. Finally, we evaluate the results on their different performance metrics and provide a deeper analysis of the collected data.

The results are analyzed not only to determine a winner for each track but also to identify the practical challenges currently faced by the field. By including instances and solvers from previous competitions, we aim to show the progress made over the last iterations. This paper is structured as follows: First, we describe the organizational aspects of the Gallery including the experimental setup and the individual tracks. We then present the benchmarks and solvers newly submitted and further the selected participants of this Gallery. Finally, we evaluate the results on their different performance metrics and provide a deeper analysis of the collected data.

papers.title: HOL in HOL: mechanized soundness, completeness and consistency, with and without infinity
papers.abstract: What can a logic certify about a copy of itself? For Church's simple theory of types, formalized as a deep embedding in Isabelle/HOL with Henkin semantics and a natural-deduction calculus, the answer has two tiers. On the first tier, plain Isabelle/HOL certifies the logic without an axiom of infinity, by a standard model with one individual. On the second tier, the logic with a Dedekind-style axiom of infinity is certified only in Isabelle/HOL extended by a large enough set-theoretic universe. Both tiers appear in Harrison's self-verification of HOL Light. What the present formalization adds is Henkin completeness, and with it a semantics that matches the calculus exactly, compactness and model existence on the first tier, and the boundary between the tiers. Comparing two ways of adding infinity to the object logic shows where the boundary lies. One is an infinite domain of individuals, expressed by the first-order sentences "there are at least $n$ individuals", each of which has a finite model; the other is the Dedekind axiom, a single sentence with no finite model, and there the first tier ends. In the calculus the axiom is strictly stronger than the sentences together: it derives each of them, but they do not derive it. The witness is a countable Henkin model in which every sentence holds and the axiom fails, because its function domain is too sparse for an injective, non-surjective self-map. On the second tier, the universe serves one purpose only: to prove the Dedekind axiom consistent. Everything that follows, completeness and even the countable Henkin model of the axiom, is obtained in plain Isabelle/HOL. The universe axiom is Harrison-style, realized in Paulson's ZFC_in_HOL with the domain of every type in $V_{\omega+\omega}$; with it, full classical higher-order logic with infinity and relational choice is consistent relative to set theory.

papers.intro:
A theory that interprets arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency; this is Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem. Yet proof assistants are routinely trusted with the verification of their own logical cores. Harrison proved the kernel of HOL Light sound and consistent twice: for the kernel without its axiom of infinity inside full HOL Light, and for the kernel with it inside HOL Light extended by one axiom postulating a large universe [19]. Kumar, Arthan, Myreen and Owens, and later the Candle project, extended the soundness result to HOL’s definitional mechanisms, with the set-theoretic universe as an explicit assumption of the soundness theorem rather than an axiom [25, 1]. Between Gödel’s limit and these results lies a question that this paper answers by machine-checked theorems, for Church’s simple theory of types [14]: what exactly can a copy of the logic certify about the logic, and at what point does the certifying side have to become stronger than the certified one? Harrison’s two results fix the two tiers of the answer for standard semantics and soundness. This paper transfers his division to a deep embedding with Henkin semantics, where a completeness theorem is available, and completeness has three consequences here. First, the calculus acquires a semantics that matches it exactly: NK\mathrm{NK} proves exactly what holds in all Henkin models, so every statement about derivability below is also a statement about all Henkin models. Second, compactness and model existence belong to the first tier: both are theorems of plain Isabelle/HOL, and even the countable Henkin model of the Dedekind axiom of infinity is built there, from its consistency alone. Third, both sides of the boundary become visible: finite models show where the first tier ends, and the Henkin model built by the completeness proof shows that the two familiar ways of adding infinity, an infinite domain of individuals and a Dedekind-style axiom, differ there.

papers.title: Thermally Activated Magnetic Switching in Antiferromagnetic Van der Waals Trilayers Resolved by Single-Spin Diamond Magnetometry
papers.abstract: Van der Waals magnets provide a versatile platform for exploring magnetic phenomena that emerge from reduced dimensionality, including layer-dependent magnetic ordering. Here, we use scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond magnetometry to measure the magnetization of a trilayer of the A-type antiferromagnet CrPS$_4$, resolving its zero-field bistability between the up-down-up ($\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow$) and down-up-down ($\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow$) layer magnetization configurations. The coercive field decreases approximately linearly with temperature, consistent with the N\'eel--Arrhenius model. Density Functional Theory calculations capture the temperature dependence of the magnetization and determine the coercive field in the coherent-rotation case. The measured coercive fields are lower, identifying thermally activated domain nucleation as the reversal mechanism. Spatial magnetic imaging supports this picture, revealing independently switching regions likely pinned by structural inhomogeneities. Our results highlight the power of scanning NV magnetometry for the quantitative investigation of magnetization reversal in two-dimensional magnets, unraveling the magnetic phenomenology that emerges in low-dimensional systems.

papers.intro:
Van der Waals magnets provide a unique platform for investigating low-dimensional magnetism and tailoring magnetic functionality at the atomic scale, bridging fundamental studies of correlated spin phenomena with emerging spintronic and magnonic applications [58, 59, 60, 61]. Thinning down van der Waals magnets to the two-dimensional (2D) limit can profoundly alter their magnetic properties, giving rise to phenomena such as layer-dependent magnetic ordering [62], thickness-dependent magnon spectra [63] or lateral exchange bias [64, 65].

A paradigmatic manifestation of reduced dimensionality occurs in antiferromagnetic magnetization reversal, which is governed by the competition between magneto-crystalline anisotropy, exchange, demagnetization and Zeeman energies [66]. The interplay between these energies determines the stabilization and dynamics of spin textures such as domain walls, vortices and coherently rotating states, and governs switching processes driven by magnetic fields, electrical currents, and ultrafast optical excitations [67]. Magnetization reversal in antiferromagnets is of particular interest due to its implications for ultrafast and densely integrated spintronic technologies such as information storage [68].

In layered antiferromagnets, the interlayer exchange coupling and its evolution with thickness govern both the magnetic ground state and its switching [69, 70, 71]. A-type antiferromagnets such as CrPS4 combine ferromagnetic intralayer order with antiferromagnetic interlayer coupling (fig. 1a), so their magnetic properties depend strongly on layer number and, in particular, on its parity [64, 71]. In atomically thin odd-layer stacks, the Zeeman energy of the uncompensated layer can overcome the anisotropy barrier of the entire stack, whose magnitude grows with the number of layers [64]. This enables reversal of the entire stack (from ↓↑↓\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow to ↑↓↑\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow, where the arrows indicate the layer’s magnetization) at fields well below the spin-flop transition. This process, however, is inaccessible in bulk, where the spin-flop occurs first [72, 73].

By using an out-of-plane NV tip, we are able to characterize the flake’s magnetization in out-of-plane bias fields that reach up to 0.8 T0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{T}, which are large fields for NV magnetometry experiments [79], without loss of imaging quality. We resolve the two bistable magnetic states of the trilayer at zero field: ↓↑↓\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow and ↑↓↑\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow. Magnetic imaging confirms this picture by directly visualizing independently switching domains. papers.title: Electrocardiographic Imaging via Posterior Sampling under Operator Discrepancy
papers.abstract: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface potentials, an ill-posed inverse problem. Diffusion posterior samplers combine a learned prior with an explicit forward operator that they assume to be accurate. In ECGI this operator is only an estimate, because the body changes with respiration and posture, and body composition such as subcutaneous fat is rarely known for an individual patient. The resulting operator discrepancy is structured and depends on the heart signal. We introduce OpDis-PS, a diffusion posterior sampler that models this discrepancy instead of treating it as signal-independent noise. OpDis-PS learns how the discrepancy depends on the signal, folds this into a corrected forward operator, and reconstructs with a fixed prior across all operator conditions. We study two realistic sources of discrepancy, changing lung conductivity and an added subcutaneous-fat layer. Across both, OpDis-PS reconstructs more accurately than classical regularization and learned predictors, with its largest gains on held-out cardiac pathologies.

papers.intro:
Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of mortality worldwide, accounting for an estimated 19.8 million deaths in 2022 [26]. The diagnosis and treatment of arrhythmias and conduction disorders often rely on identifying where abnormal ventricular activation originates and how it propagates. Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) reconstructs heart-surface potentials (HSPs), defined here on the outer surface of the ventricles, from body-surface potentials (BSPs) measured on the torso [38]. These spatio-temporal signals reveal ventricular activation and recovery without requiring electrodes on the cardiac surface and can support the analysis and treatment of arrhythmias [11]. However, the torso attenuates and spatially smooths the cardiac field [35], rendering ECGI an ill-conditioned inverse problem that amplifies measurement and model errors.

However, the torso attenuates and spatially smooths the cardiac field [35], rendering ECGI an ill-conditioned inverse problem that amplifies measurement and model errors.

Traditional ECGI methods stabilize the inversion using Tikhonov penalties, spatio-temporal constraints, or total variation [27, 7, 37]. While these regularizers improve stability, their generic smoothness assumptions capture only limited physiological structure and can attenuate localized activation patterns. Learning-based methods can capture complex cardiac dynamics directly from data, with approaches ranging from discriminative predictors that estimate HSPs directly from BSPs to conditional generative models that learn the distribution of HSPs given BSP observations [2, 17]. The latter are particularly suited to representing uncertainty and ambiguity in the inverse solution. Despite this advantage, both approaches encode the observation process in their parameterization and do not permit substituting an explicit case-specific forward operator at inference.

An alternative is to learn a generative prior over cardiac signals independently of the observation model and combine the two only during inference. Diffusion posterior samplers such as Denoising Diffusion Restoration Models (DDRM) and Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) realize this separation by coupling a learned diffusion prior with an explicit measurement-consistency model [21, 10]. Originally introduced for vision tasks, both methods assume that the supplied forward operator accurately represents the measurement process. In ECGI, however, the nominal operator used for reconstruction is only an estimate derived from an anatomical model and assumed tissue conductivities. The recording operator, which represents the actual volume conductor at measurement time, can differ from this nominal operator because of respiration, posture, electrode placement, or body composition. The resulting operator discrepancy produces a structured error that depends on the underlying cardiac signal. Because ECGI is ill-conditioned, even a modest operator discrepancy can cause substantial reconstruction errors.

papers.title: Menu Design Meets Market Design: Strategic Simplicity vs. Choice Complexity
papers.abstract: Strategic simplicity removes the incentive to misreport preferences, but it does not ensure that participants can identify what they prefer. We study this distinction in a laboratory experiment on serial dictatorships, where optimal play only requires choosing one's favorite bundle of real-effort tasks. Participants make fifteen incentivized choices among bundles that vary in how many tasks they combine. They choose either from a large menu or through a series of binary choices. Having made all choices, they unexpectedly reconsider each assignment against a previously rejected alternative. We find that roughly one in six choices is reversed and almost one in five involves an objectively dominated bundle. Simplifying the choice architecture does not help. Binary decomposition even raises reversal rates among low-ability participants and further inflates their confidence about their choices.

papers.intro:
Centralized allocation mechanisms ask participants to report what they want. Whether they can do so reliably, and how the answer depends on the complexity of what they are asked, is a central concern of market design. The canonical response has been to simplify incentives: under a strategy-proof mechanism, truthful reporting is optimal regardless of what others do, and behavioral refinements such as (strong) obvious strategy-proofness (Li, 2017; Pycia and Troyan, 2023) make this optimality straightforward to recognize. Accordingly, when participants deviate from optimal play, the standard diagnosis is incentive complexity: they fail to see that honesty is best. In contrast, we consider a setting in which truthful play is obvious, allowing us to focus on the complexity of the choice process itself: whether individuals can reliably identify their preferred options.

In this vein, our paper cautions against hastily attributing puzzling behavior to strategic mistakes. For instance, in New York City’s strategy-proof high-school match, about 7 percent of families file a reapplication after learning their assignment, and more than 70 percent of these reapplicants reverse rankings they themselves submitted months earlier, requesting a school they had ranked below, or omitted from, their original list (Narita, 2018). In this paper, we use a controlled experiment to study a prominent and appealingly simple remedy: binary decomposition replaces a single choice from a large menu with a sequence of binary comparisons to improve choice consistency.

In our experiment, subjects are assigned real-effort tasks in a five-person sequential serial dictatorship, i.e., they make choices in a specified order and are assigned the task they select among the remaining options upon their turn. We isolate the choice architecture through two treatment conditions: Subjects in condition Menu SD select from the entire menu of remaining options, whereas the subjects in condition Binary SD face a series of binary choices. Each participant makes fifteen choices across three complexity blocks. In each block, the five participants cycle through each priority position, and, by construction, face smaller menus in later positions. Across blocks, the complexity of the bundles increases: bundles contain one task in the first block, two tasks in the second, and three tasks in the third block. That is, we compare choice architecture across subjects, but choice complexity (bundle and menu size) within subject.

Therefore, we have real-effort tasks that are experienced, and choices are incentivized not because of induced values, but because a successful completion of an assignment yields a bonus payment. Preferences over such bundles are real and our data suggest that participants report them inconsistently.

Our central result contradicts our predictions. Binary decomposition does not help on average, and it harms those it is meant to help. Flip rates, dominance violations, and payoffs are on average indistinguishable across the two mechanisms after multiple-testing corrections. However, this average hides effects of opposite signs for low- and high-ability participants, defined as those who perform below and above the median in the tasks, respectively. Among low-ability participants, Binary SD raises the flip rate from 17.2 to 23.5 percent, an increase of more than a third over their Menu SD baseline. In contrast, high-ability participants benefit modestly, and only when bundle complexity is low. Decomposing a choice into simpler steps is therefore not a general-purpose remedy: its effect depends on who is choosing.

papers.title: Vestiges of magnon fractionalization in the quasi-two-dimensional quantum magnet rouaite Cu$_2$(NO$_3$)(OH)$_3$ with alternating ferro- and antiferromagnetic $S=\frac{1}{2}$ chains
papers.abstract: Ferro- and antiferromagnetic quantum spin chains host qualitatively distinct elementary excitations --- magnons ($S=1$, bosonic quasiparticles) and spinons ($S=\frac{1}{2}$, fractionalized quasiparticles), respectively. Weakly coupled networks of both chain types therefore provide an ideal platform for exploring spinon-magnon coupling and the hybridization of sharp magnon modes with spinon continua. Here we investigate the spin-excitation spectrum of the frustrated quantum magnet rouaite, Cu$_2$(NO$_3$)(OH)$_3$ --- a model realization of weakly coupled ferro- and antiferromagnetic Cu$^{2+}$ spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ chains. The frustrated interchain interactions, while weaker than the dominant intrachain exchange, are sufficient to stabilize a long-range-ordered state that is not reproduced by classical calculations. Neutron spectroscopy reveals a spectrum of well-defined spin waves associated with both types of chains, with clear signatures of hybridization but no observable spinon continuum. Certain magnon branches resulting from this hybridization exhibit substantial broadening near the zone center. We attribute this to vestiges of spinon fractionalization persisting partway through the dimensional crossover from isolated quantum spin chains to a 2D network of frustrated spins.

papers.title: Charge-tunable acoustic surface plasmons in topological nodal-line semimetals
papers.abstract: Topological nodal-line semimetals host drumhead surface states, carrying a large surface density of states. We show that these states support an acoustic surface plasmon, whose velocity is strongly enhanced by the Coulomb interaction. At sufficiently small wavevectors, the mode lies above the surface particle-hole continuum and below both mixed surface-bulk absorption thresholds, leaving bulk particle-hole creation as the leading damping channel. Near drumhead depletion, the dispersion is highly sensitive to the surface charge, which suggests applications of plasmon spectroscopy of nodal-line semimetals to sensing technologies.

papers.title: Characterisation of the DQsym Framework Against Harmonic State-Space and Dynamic Phasor Models for Modular Multilevel Converters
papers.abstract: Modern power systems rely on power converters that exhibit multifrequency periodic dynamics, such as modular multilevel converters (MMCs). Such converters are commonly analysed using harmonic state-space (HSS) and dynamic phasor (DP) representations. Both approaches rely on building state matrices based on the system topology, whose size grows with the number of harmonics retained in the model. This paper shows that a symmetrical direct-quadrature (dq) dynamic phasor formulation for time-domain simulation, named DQsym, has a smaller solver state matrix than HSS and DP, and whose size is independent of the truncation order K. This reduction results from evaluating harmonic coupling outside the state matrix, in the nonlinear signal blocks. The open-loop MMC model used in this paper is derived in three harmonic-domain (HD) formulations and validated against a three-phase time-domain reference model. The models are compared in terms of state-space size and sparsity, harmonic content, steady-state accuracy and eigenvalues. For truncation at K = 4, the DQsym solver has 45 states against 135 for HSS and DP, stays within about 4% of the reference, and, once closed with its coupling blocks, yields eigenvalues identical to those of HSS and DP.

papers.title: TetraCoder: Adaptive Tetrahedral Encoding for Neural Fields
papers.abstract: Implicit and explicit representations of geometry are central in computer graphics applications and come with their pros and cons. With surface sampling being faster on explicit representations and spatial queries being faster on implicit representations, finding efficient conversions between them is a highly desirable property. We present TetraCoder, a single resolution hash-free adaptive tetrahedral encoding that links an explicit tetrahedral spatial encoder with an underlying implicit signed distance field (SDF). The resulting hybrid implicit-explicit space is continuous piecewise affine (CPWA) by design, allowing to obtain an exact correspondence between the implicit SDF and the explicit analytic mesh. TetraCoder's design comes with additional perks, in particular: (a) it scales better than multi-resolution encoding methods due to its single resolution optimizable grid, (b) unlike hash-based methods, it is not affected by collisions, (c) it enables fast tetrahedral ray-tracing, geometry and appearance editing, directly through its adaptive tetrahedral scaffold. We demonstrate the versatility of TetraCoder by showing an improvement over state-of-the-art methods on multiple tasks: 2D/3D fitting from images and point clouds, 3D novel view synthesis, 3D reconstruction, and geometry/appearance editing.

Neural fields support learning continuous geometry and view-dependent appearance from observations (Mildenhall et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023). However, the usage of these reconstructions for geometric processing, simulation, and editing also benefits from explicit surfaces. For an SDF, the surface is defined by its zero-level set. Sampling-based mesh retrieval approximates this surface, with accuracy depending on the sampling resolution (Lorensen and Cline, 1987). Continuous piecewise-affine (CPWA) fields enable analytic retrieval of the learned surface (Lei and Jia, 2020; Oh et al., 2026), establishing a direct correspondence between implicit and explicit geometry with no sampling errors. The spatial encoding therefore influences not only fitting accuracy but also how the learned surface can be extracted and edited.

Existing encodings come with different compromises. Multiresolution hash grids capture detail efficiently (Müller et al., 2022), but hash collisions can couple distant regions, and trilinear interpolation does not preserve piecewise-affine structure. Tetrahedral encodings enable analytic mesh retrieval provided that the downstream decoders don’t introduce nonlinearities, yet overlapping grid levels require costly geometric intersections (Oh et al., 2026). Fixed tetrahedral encodings (Kulhanek and Sattler, 2023) cannot adapt their spatial domains during training, while mesh-based encodings (Yang et al., 2022; Bao et al., 2025) depend on reconstructed surfaces.

papers.title: A systematic comparison of physics-informed neural networks and mechanistic models for epidemic modeling and forecasting
papers.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently been applied to epidemic modeling and forecasting with promising results. These methods integrate mechanistic knowledge with data-driven learning. Yet, their comparative performance against well-established, and simpler epidemic models is underexplored. Here, we conduct a systematic comparison of a PINN-based framework and a stochastic mechanistic model. Both approaches share the same age-structured SEIRD core and rolling-window forecasting pipeline, in a deliberately minimal setting. We evaluate their retrospective fits and probabilistic forecasts in two synthetic scenarios and the first COVID-19 wave in London. Interestingly, while PINNs underperform in synthetic scenarios, they achieve better performance on real data. Furthermore, PINNs provide narrower uncertainty intervals and sharper estimation of parameters in synthetic scenarios. Our findings confirm PINNs as a promising tool in epidemiology. At the same time, the results reaffirm the value of simpler approaches such as traditional compartmental models, and promote additional benchmarking studies.

papers.title: Pose-based Neural Clothing for Animated Characters
papers.abstract: Traditional garment simulation for animated characters is a time-consuming bottleneck for artists due to slow simulations and tedious parameter tunings.Recent data-driven methods offer a powerful alternative, capable of learning from a dataset of simulated data to generate high-quality deformations. A lightweight network design allows data-driven systems to achieve a real-time inference speed. This significantly improves the artist workflow, as they can interactively pose a character and see high-quality folds and wrinkles at animation time, thereby allowing to make creative decisions ahead of time. However, existing neural clothing methods have presented appealing results on datasets based on realistic human models (\eg SMPL), but when trained on animated character datasets, they struggle to generalize to unseen poses. In this paper, we aim at designing neural networks and training strategies to generalize better to unseen poses in real-time to enable the interactive posing applications. We focus on a production-oriented setting where the model is trained for a single garment in a quasi-static setup. Technically, we leverage a smooth, expressive latent space by first training a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). We then progressively train the VAE encoder to transition from reconstruction to pose-driven prediction. To guide this prediction, we condition the network on both low-dimensional pose parameters and character body surface displacements. Finally, we introduce a novel local gradient histogram loss that mitigates the over-smoothing effect of reconstruction losses. Extensive evaluations on production-level assets and public datasets demonstrate that our method produces sharp, realistic wrinkles, smooth large-scale drape, and temporal coherence in real-time, offering a robust and easily integrable solution for interactive posing workflows.

papers.intro:
Cloth deformation plays a central role in conveying both realism and style in digital characters. In production settings such as film, interactive media, virtual try-on, and web-based character customization, interactive posing is essential in artistic decisions: artists expect immediate visual feedback when posing a character, including how garments fold and wrinkle. Standard physically-based cloth simulation is therefore often unsuitable for interactive use, due to its dynamic formulation and computational cost, even though it produces highly realistic results. Moreover, production cloth is rarely “off-the-shelf”: studios rely on highly specialized solvers and carefully tuned pipelines refined over the years of show-specific expertise. It is not uncommon for artists to perform manual interventions on certain frames to resolve difficult cases: persistent body inter-penetrations, unstable contacts causing popping or jitter, loss of volume in layered folds, or solver artifacts such as cloth snagging and sticking in extreme poses are some examples. As a result, even though deploying a faster GPU-based simulator [WWYW20, WWW22, GWL∗25] can potentially reach interactive rates, they are often insufficient to reproduce the final production-approved look. These constraints motivate a data-driven alternative: a supervised neural deformer trained directly on production-generated targets, capturing both the solver’s tuned behavior and the artist-approved outcomes.

A vast literature [PLPM20, SOC22, STOC21, BME22, GBH23, ZL24, BME21] has explored learning-based approaches to improve the performance–realism trade-off of cloth simulation, typically by approximating full simulations using neural networks that operate over time or leverage simplified dynamics. While these learning-based methods present appealing results on datasets featuring realistic human models (e.g., SMPL [LMR∗15]), our experiments in Section 4 reveal that they struggle when trained on animated characters, often producing inaccurate details and visual artifacts. Furthermore, these approaches often assume access to simulation states or poses in previous frames, which are typically unavailable during interactive character posing. Additionally, while many existing methods train their models to generalize across multiple body shapes and garment materials [PLPM20, GBH23], we intentionally focus on a single-mesh paradigm. This targeted approach allows us to train a lightweight network that faithfully preserves the unique style avoiding the loss of detail often caused by generic priors and guarantees real-time inference. Finally, although some works incorporate physically-based unsupervised [BME21, BME22, SOC22, LKL23, GBH23, GBB∗24] terms to improve visual quality, production-level garment deformations are hard to reproduce with simple energy terms, compelling us to adhere to a strictly supervised setting to ensure our results faithfully replicate targeted artistic intent.

We aim to train real-time neural deformers that predict cloth deformations from character poses. Additionally, we target a single garment simulated using a quasi-static setup for a single character. The design space, the input representations, and training strategies of our network are extensively explored in the paper. We start with a popular architecture, employing spiral convolutions for mesh-aware computations [CMM∗20], which outperforms simpler options such as variants of global and local MLPs [BODO18, PLPM20]. Our first insight decouples the task of predicting pose-dependent deformations from the generation of plausible, high-frequency wrinkle patterns: before training the deformer, we first train a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) to reconstruct a modest set of deformations to create a smooth, concise, and expressive latent space. Our second insight is to progressively train the VAE encoder to transition from reconstruction to deformation prediction from body poses, thus simplifying the task. We find that this progressive strategy significantly improves the visual quality while maintaining architectural complexity and keeping inference times at interactive rate. In addition to conditioning the re-purposed encoder on low-dimensional pose parameters, we splat body surface displacements onto the garment mesh using linear blend skinning weights to provide deformation guidance on the mesh level. Finally, we leverage a novel local gradient histogram loss over surface neighborhoods to preserve high-frequency wrinkles and mitigate the over-smoothing that is commonly associated with reconstruction-based losses.

papers.title: Hierarchical Interactions in Mobility Networks: A Model-Free Feedback Approach
papers.abstract: Urban mobility systems are large-scale networked systems whose performance emerges from hierarchically coupled decisions of public authorities, competing mobility operators, and travelers. Existing approaches to policy design either collapse one of these levels or assume that the authority can model and differentiate through the equilibrium responses of operators and travelers. In this paper, we model policy design as a tri-level game on a multimodal network, in which a municipality sets taxes, licenses, and integration subsidies, a public transport and a taxi operator compete on prices and service supply, and heterogeneous travelers reach a stochastic user equilibrium. We prove that the traveler equilibrium is unique and continuously differentiable in the operator strategies, that the variational inequality characterizing operator equilibria admits a solution for every policy, and that the resulting tri-level game admits a Stackelberg equilibrium. Building on this structure, we design a model-free hierarchical controller in which the municipality and the operators update their decisions from zeroth-order evaluations of observed equilibrium outcomes. On the Zurich multimodal network, operator equilibria computed from different initializations differ by a median of 0.3% in the municipal objective. On a grid of 3,125 policies, only those that subsidize transfers between public transport and taxis benefit both operators, and 24 of them also lower travel costs without degrading the municipal objective. Finally, the controller matches the best policies of three black-box optimizers and terminates at the most consistent policies across runs.

papers.intro:
Urban mobility systems are large-scale socio-technical systems whose performance emerges from the interactions of self-interested stakeholders. Travelers choose routes and modes according to private preferences, mobility operators set prices, capacities, and frequencies to pursue their own objectives, and public authorities are increasingly called upon to steer the resulting system toward societal goals, such as the European Union’s target of a 90% reduction in transport-related greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 [1]. Authorities, however, cannot dictate behavior. They can only reshape incentives through taxes, subsidies, and licensing constraints, whose effect depends on how operators and travelers respond. Designing such instruments is difficult for at least three reasons. First, the interactions are both horizontal and vertical. Horizontally, heterogeneous travelers reach a multimodal user equilibrium under congestion, while operators compete in prices, capacities, and frequencies. Vertically, municipal policy shapes the incentives under which both make their choices. Second, the resulting equilibrium maps are nested and implicit. Operator payoffs depend on the traveler equilibrium, the societal objective depends on both, and neither map is available in closed form. Moreover, the operator game is nonconvex, so classical existence results do not apply and equilibria need not be unique. Third, the authority rarely knows the operators’ costs or the travelers’ preferences, and observes only aggregate outcomes, such as ridership, revenues, and emissions, after the system has re-equilibrated. Taken together, these obstacles call for design methods that treat the nested game as a plant, rely only on its observed equilibrium responses, and rest on structural properties that make the design problem well posed. This raises the central question of this paper: How can a public authority iteratively optimize its policy, using only observed equilibrium responses, to steer a hierarchical strategic mobility system toward societal objectives?

Our work lies at the intersection of transportation research and the control of strategic multi-agent systems.

Our work lies at the intersection of transportation research and the control of strategic multi-agent systems.

Multimodal mobility systems couple three strategic levels, namely municipal policy, operator interaction, and traveler routing under congestion, but existing work mostly models only one or two of them. At the traveler level, congestion games are the standard lower-level model in mobility control problems such as congestion pricing and tolling [2, 3] and autonomous-vehicle routing [4, 5]. At the operator level, game-theoretic formulations capture competition and cooperation among self-interested providers [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. Representative settings include mobility-on-demand operators competing with public transit, where fleet-wide pricing can cannibalize transit ridership [8], competitive vehicle sharing and fleet routing [12, 13], and cooperative benefit allocation in multi-regional network design [14]. These works capture horizontal interactions but hold the regulatory environment fixed, although taxes, fleet-size licenses, and integration subsidies can reshape the strategic interaction itself [15, 16].

A recent line of work places a public authority above the operators, yielding a tri-level problem [17, 18, 19, 20, 16]. Gu et al. [17] retain competition among profit-maximizing road operators below a public agency in a static, deterministic, single-mode network, and Xi et al. [18] regulate a two-sided Mobility-as-a-Service market as a single-leader multi-follower game. Both compute exact solutions through a mathematical program with equilibrium constraints, which requires explicit models of all followers. Dandl et al. [19] couple a welfare-maximizing regulator, a profit-maximizing provider, and an agent-based traveler simulator, using Bayesian optimization at the upper two levels, but their operator level is monopolistic. Yao et al. [20] collapse a multi-leader–multi-follower Mobility-as-a-Service game into a single-level variational inequality, in which the top-level agent has full model knowledge and a differentiable follower response and tunes a single wholesale price.

Our approach differs from these works in two key ways. First, it retains strategic interaction at every level, with competing operators coupled through intermodal transfers above a congested traveler equilibrium that is neither collapsed into a single level nor available in closed form. Second, the municipality needs no model of the lower levels and updates its policy from observed equilibrium outcomes only, while the properties established in Section III guarantee that the design problem is well posed.

Settings in which a leader acts before a population of followers are commonly modeled as Stackelberg or bilevel problems [21]. When the followers play a non-cooperative game, the leader faces a nonconvex and nonsmooth mathematical program with equilibrium constraints, which has motivated specialized solution methods [22, 9]. A parallel literature studies equilibrium seeking in network games, with convergence guarantees under mild assumptions on utilities and information [23, 24].

Most closely related is feedback optimization, where a controller optimizes the steady state of a dynamical system from output measurements, without an explicit model of the input-output map [25, 26], including its interconnection with equilibrium-seeking dynamics in games [27]. We adopt the same framework, but our plant is a nested game whose equilibrium maps are unavailable in closed form and may be set-valued or non-differentiable. Existing approaches handle such maps by requiring the followers’ exact cost functions [22], limiting lower-level action spaces [28], or considering a single follower rather than competing ones [29]. By contrast, we use zeroth-order feedback updates at both the municipal and the operator level, which require no explicit equilibrium model.

papers.title: Observation of Non-Equilibrium Phonon Loss Across a Solid-Superfluid Interface
papers.abstract: We measure the performance of an athermal phonon calorimeter in vacuum and in thermal contact with superfluid $^4$He. Using a cryogenic photon calibration system, we show that the superfluid suppresses the collection of the phonon signal by over 99\%. We conclude that submerged sensors will not benefit TESSERACT's superfluid helium dark matter target, but that superfluid helium may be useful to superconducting qubits as a sink for athermal phonons generated by radiation and other spontaneous sources. Our measurement is the first probe of solid-to-superfluid phonon transmission at energies higher than those stably supportable by the superfluid. We discuss thermal flow inside the calorimeter, as well as systematics from an alternative calibration scheme.

papers.intro:
The search for low-mass dark matter induced nuclear recoils in terrestrial experiments requires the development of new technologies to overcome poor kinematic matching and low recoil energies when compared with more massive dark matter models such as the WIMP [9]. Recently, superfluid 4He has gained interest as a potential dark matter recoil target due to its low nuclear mass, interesting signal channels, ease of chemical purification, and intrinsic scalability [19, 40, 4, 39]. We have operated a detector that uses un-wetted athermal phonon calorimeters to detect recoils in a superfluid 4He bath sitting below [4]. An additional array of submerged sensors would improve signal reconstruction by enhancing collection of prompt scintillation photons or triplet excimer decays [12].

We have developed calorimeters with energy resolutions as low as 253 meV [6, 11]. The extreme sensitivity of these low-threshold athermal phonon detectors has provided a window into non-equilibrium energy transport in solids, which is also an important consideration for superconducting quantum circuits [3, 13]. In superconducting qubits, the same non-equilibrium processes contribute to excess quasiparticle densities in superconducting films, leading to premature decoherence of the qubit state. Band-gap engineering [42, 33, 30] and large-area normal metal films [21] have been successfully deployed to reduce the impact of non-equilibrium energy in superconducting qubit circuits; however, further improvements are still required. The unique properties of superfluid helium motivate exploring its potential as an additional channel for removing non-equilibrium energy from superconducting circuits. Understanding energy transport across the solid–helium interface is therefore essential.

Key to evaluating this possibility, and to the performance of submerged calorimeters, is the behavior of athermal phonons at the solid–helium interface. Phonon transmission at solid–superfluid interfaces has long been of interest to the condensed matter community due to anomalously high transmission probabilities despite severe acoustic mismatch [43]. Historically, interest has gone towards the study of conduction via the stable quasiparticles present in the superfluid below 1.49 meV (phonons and rotons) [38, 24, 14, 2, 7, 49, 10]. Notably, solid materials can support phonons with energies of 𝒪⁡(100)\mathcal{O}(100) meV. Until now, no observation of the transmission of athermal phonons with energies greater than 1.491.49 meV has been made.
