Microbes thrive throughout the biosphere, from the atmosphere to deep oceans and subsurface rocks [1, 2, 3]. Many of their habitats are spatially heterogeneous and mechanically confined, including soils [4, 5, 6], depleted gas reservoirs [7, 8], host tissues and mucus-rich environments [9, 10, 11, 12], and marine snow and biologically-active sediments [13, 14, 15, 16]. In such environments, bacterial cells experience combinations of compression, adhesion, steric restriction, and crowding, all of which can influence microbial growth and survival [17, 18]. Understanding how single cells respond to these mechanical constraints is therefore essential for connecting microbial ecology with quantitative biophysics.

In such environments, bacterial cells experience combinations of compression, adhesion, steric restriction, and crowding, all of which can influence microbial growth and survival [17, 18]. Understanding how single cells respond to these mechanical constraints is therefore essential for connecting microbial ecology with quantitative biophysics.

Bacteria can sense and respond to mechanical cues across scales, from changes in single-cell physiology to the collective organization of growing populations. At the single-cell level, surface attachment and external mechanical stress—such as hydrostatic pressure and soft-matter confinement—can alter cell metabolism [19, 20, 21], change envelope mechanics [22], suppress cell elongation [23, 24], and initiate biofilm formation [25]. Intense mechanical constraints can further disrupt cell morphology and division [26, 27, 28, 29, 30], leading to irregular cell shapes [31, 32], delayed division, and in extreme cases, cell death [33, 26]. Beyond these single-cell responses, mechanical forces, confinement, and crowding can shape colony organization, spatial structure, topology, and collective behavior in growing microbial populations. However, majority of previous studies have characterized cells after they have already adapted to a sustained stressed or confined state, leaving the dynamics of the initial acclimation process largely unresolved.

Under steady growth conditions, E. coli and Bacillus subtilis exhibit robust size control in both microfluidic and agarose-pad assays [43, 44, 45, 46, 47]. Bacterial size homeostasis relies on tight coupling between growth and division across generations. Single-cell measurements have shown that this coordination is often well described by the adder principle, in which cells add an approximately constant size between birth and division, largely independent of their birth size [45, 46]. Recent mechanistic studies have further suggested that division control can emerge from threshold accumulation of key division proteins, such as FtsZ, through balanced biosynthesis [48, 49]. These studies have focused primarily on cell-size control under steady-state growth. How this coordination is reshaped across generations following an abrupt switch in the mechanical environment remains poorly understood.

Here, we use single-cell time-lapse microscopy to track E. coli across successive generations after the onset of mechanical confinement. We quantify elongation rates, division timing, and birth-size distributions and use generation-resolved correlations to characterize size control. We further develop a minimal stochastic model to compare the observed dynamics with idealized adder-, sizer-, and timer-like reference behaviors. Our results show that confinement induces not only an immediate slowdown in growth, but also a transient transformation of canonical adder-like growth–division coupling.

papers.title: Demonstrating CBM Capabilities through $\Lambda$ Reconstruction with mCBM
papers.abstract:
The Compressed Baryonic Matter (CBM) experiment at the upcoming Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) is a high-rate fixed-target experiment designed to investigate nuclear matter at extreme baryon densities in relativistic nucleus-nucleus collisions. To enable high-statistics measurements of rare probes, CBM is designed to operate at event rates up to 10 MHz. This necessitates the development of fast and radiation-tolerant detectors, self-triggered front-end electronics, a free-streaming data acquisition architecture, and real-time event reconstruction capabilities. Prototype versions and pre-series productions of the CBM detector systems have been deployed in the mini-CBM demonstrator setup mCBM - an experimental precursor comprising sub-components of all major CBM systems, installed at the SIS18 facility of GSI/FAIR within the FAIR Phase-0 program.
  In 2024, Ni+Ni collisions at a kinetic beam energy of 1.93 AGeV and an average interaction rate of about 500 kHz were successfully recorded. This dataset enables a detailed evaluation of the operational performance of the detector systems as well as the complete CBM data chain, while the reconstruction of $\Lambda$ baryons, which constitute a relatively rare signal within the limited geometrical acceptance of mCBM, serves as a natural benchmark. This paper presents the first results on $\Lambda$ baryon reconstruction with the mCBM experiment, demonstrating the functionality of the detector technologies and the data chain for the upcoming full-scale CBM experiment.

The primary aim of these proceedings is to demonstrate the operation of the mCBM experiment as a full-system precursor of the CBM experiment, encompassing detector integration, free-streaming data transport, and particle reconstruction using the CBM data-acquisition and reconstruction framework. papers.title: Effect of galaxy-informed merger timescales on massive black hole binaries in LISA
papers.abstract: Over a decade of direct N-body simulations tell us that massive black hole binary (MBHB) merger timescales are strongly dependent on the structural and kinematic properties of the host galaxy merger remnant. The physical stages of stellar scattering and gravitational wave (GW) emission of MBH coalescence occur below the resolution limit of most cosmological simulations, requiring post-processing to achieve accurate merging times. We apply a recently developed galaxy-informed merger timescale for MBHBs to the Romulus25 simulation and compare with current MBH merger rate and event rate estimates for the upcoming Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). We find a median stellar scattering time of ~ 10^8.2 yr^-1, roughly an order of magnitude faster than those produced by timescales that rely on extrapolations of the stellar density profile. We predict a merger rate of ~ 11.5 yr^-1 corresponding to 46 merger events over a 4-year LISA mission. We also investigate the importance of the relative orbital inclination of the MBHB with respect to the host galaxy and of nuclear star cluster (NSC) modeling, finding that the quickest merger events correspond to MBHBs that counterrotate and galaxies assigned to host NSCs, which may be important for host galaxy identification in the multi-messenger era.

papers.intro:
Galaxies can grow by merging together, which offers opportunities in turn to form massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) (Begelman et al., 1980). The journey of the two MBHs toward pairing and coalescence is typically categorized into phases depending on the mechanism dominating the energy loss of the binary. In the canonical picture for MBHBs (104​M⊙≲Mtot≲107​M⊙10^{4}M_{\odot}\lesssim M_{\text{tot}}\lesssim 10^{7}M_{\odot}), dynamical friction dominates on ∼\sim kpc scales, driving the MBHs towards the center of their newly-shared host (Chandrasekhar, 1943; Binney and Tremaine, 1987). Stellar scattering effects become important on ∼10−1\sim 10-1 pc scales, hardening the binary further (provided there is a sufficient supply of stars) (Milosavljević and Merritt, 2003). The presence of an accretion disk on ∼\sim sub-pc scales in gas-rich nuclei may also aid the hardening of the binary (Mayer et al., 2007; Cuadra et al., 2009; Haiman et al., 2009; Siwek et al., 2023). Once ∼\sim mpc separations are reached, the decay is dominated by the emission of gravitational waves (GWs) until coalescence (Peters and Mathews, 1963).

Stellar scattering effects become important on ∼10−1\sim 10-1 pc scales, hardening the binary further (provided there is a sufficient supply of stars) (Milosavljević and Merritt, 2003). The presence of an accretion disk on ∼\sim sub-pc scales in gas-rich nuclei may also aid the hardening of the binary (Mayer et al., 2007; Cuadra et al., 2009; Haiman et al., 2009; Siwek et al., 2023). Once ∼\sim mpc separations are reached, the decay is dominated by the emission of gravitational waves (GWs) until coalescence (Peters and Mathews, 1963).

The timescale governing each of these phases is complicated, however, and is highly dependent on the properties of the host galaxy. Dynamical friction is enhanced when MBHs are encased in a dense nuclear star cluster (NSC), increasing the effective mass and invoking tidal distortion that sinks the MBHs quickly (Ogiya et al., 2020; Mukherjee et al., 2025). Spikes from self-interacting dark matter may also aid the efficiency of sinking (Alonso-Álvarez et al., 2024). In contrast, MBHs can fail to sink for a multitude of reasons, including (but not limited to) getting trapped in galactic bar-induced resonances (Bortolas et al., 2022; Herrero et al., 2025), encountering star-forming clumps in non-relaxed systems, as would be common at high redshift (Ma et al., 2021), or being stripped of their associated stellar systems in minor mergers, leaving them “wandering" for longer than the age of the Universe (Bellovary et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2025).

At scales where the hardening is dominated by stellar scattering, NN-body simulations and analytic estimates alike show that non-spherical galactic potentials are required to overcome the “final parsec problem" (Yu, 2002; Berczik et al., 2006; Khan et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015; Gualandris et al., 2017). Additionally, any degree of rotation of the stellar component (Holley-Bockelmann and Khan, 2015; Varisco et al., 2021), inclination of the MBHB with respect to the host (Mirza et al., 2017), and the presence of a nuclear star cluster (NSC) (Khan and Holley-Bockelmann, 2021; Khan et al., 2026) also encourage efficient hardening. When embedded in a gaseous accretion disk, the orbital evolution of the binary depends on both binary properties, like mass ratio and initial eccentricity (Siwek et al., 2023), as well as the disk structure and thermodynamic properties (Tiede et al., 2020; D’Orazio and Duffell, 2021; Dittmann et al., 2026; Clyburn and Zrake, 2026). Simulations in the thin disk regime (which is expected for astrophysical disks surrounding MBHs in gas rich nuclei) do not yet agree on the sign of the imparted torque on the binary within the full range of possible parameter space (Duffell et al., 2024; Derdzinski et al., 2025). All of these effects combine in highly nonlinear ways, requiring expensive detailed modeling to achieve self-consistent predictions, albeit only for a few galaxy types at a time.

With their rich variety of host galaxy properties and ancestries, cosmological simulations offer a promising way to investigate the broader possible range of MBH coalescence times. A large challenge with these models, however, is that many of the aforementioned physical processes occur below the resolution limit of the simulation, which can be as large as ∼\sim few kpc. Instead, to prolong the lifetime of the MBHB, simulations either invoke sub-grid models, which operate on-the-fly, or post-processing models, which can be performed on simulation outputs. Both of these methods require analytical estimates for MBH merger timescales since the dynamics are not resolved outright.

papers.title: Selective coupling and spectral evolution of topological domain-wall states under local perturbations
papers.abstract: In this work we investigate the spectral evolution of topological domain-wall states in a one-dimensional structure described by the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model. We show that a local potential applied to the domain wall induces a selective coupling between a topological state and specific bulk states. Moreover, by increasing the gate potential, we observe that the domain wall state energies asymptotically reach a bulk band, whereas new domain wall states appear on the opposite side of the band. As a consequence, the domain-wall-state spectrum evolves through a sequence of localized states that remain separated from the bulk continuum. These effects are also reflected in transport calculations, where the conductance peaks follow the evolution of the energy spectrum. To experimentally verify these phenomena, we realize an RLC topo-electrical circuit and perform impedance spectroscopy measurements. We find that the impedance matches the local density of states, exhibiting resonances at frequencies associated with the bulk energies that selectively couple to the domain wall topological state.
papers.intro:
Topological invariants have been extensively studied in the last decades as a new paradigm to identify non-equivalent phases in condensed matter systems[11]. A key feature of these non-conventional phases is the bulk-boundary correspondence. This principle establishes that a system with a non-trivial topological invariant hosts edge states that depend solely on the value of the invariant and are robust against adiabatic perturbations [7]. Topological edge states (TES) are localized near the physical borders of the system as well as near boundaries between two non-equivalent topological phases, which we refer to as domain walls (DWs). These robust states have been proposed for promising applications such as dissipationless current pathways in low-dimensional circuits [33, 34, 16], qubit formation [19, 3, 27], quantum information transfer [35, 21, 18] and adiabatic charge pumping [31, 25].

Topological edge states in 1D materials are particularly relevant for quantum computing applications. For instance, Zurita et al. proposed a quantum information transfer protocol based on a time-dependent Hamiltonian that varies adiabatically [35]. In their scheme, an electron is transferred between the edges of a 1D structure exclusively through topological states localized in DWs. Since only few states participate in quantum transport, the protocol is expected to reduce decoherence and enhance fidelity. This idea builds on previous efforts to re-scale systems by forming DW lattices which, within a tight-binding (TB) framework, can be described through re-scaled hopping parameters and on-site energies relative to the underlying lattice [26].

A key aspect of electron localization in topological DWs is that TES localized in neighboring domains are close to each other and might couple. This phenomenon has been studied using atomic-like effective models, which show that as TES approach to each other they form bonding-antibonding pairs with energies that differ from the original uncoupled TES [13]. This effective model successfully explains why the number of edge states in a DW between Chern insulators with Chern numbers C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} is exactly |C2−C1||C_{2}-C_{1}|. More recently, it has been shown that coupling between TES in infinite DWs in graphene nanoribbons within the quantum Hall regime produces a deformation of the Landau level flat bands, enabling phenomena such as anti-chirality, anomalous bulk-like dispersion and valley-specific current pathways [6]. These results demonstrate that TES couple when they are close to each other both spatially and energetically, which naturally raises the question if TES can couple with bulk states when brought into energetic proximity by a local potential. More generally, it is unclear how the energy spectrum evolves when a localized topological state approaches a bulk band, and whether this process can induce measurable rearrangements of the bulk spectrum itself.

These results demonstrate that TES couple when they are close to each other both spatially and energetically, which naturally raises the question if TES can couple with bulk states when brought into energetic proximity by a local potential. More generally, it is unclear how the energy spectrum evolves when a localized topological state approaches a bulk band, and whether this process can induce measurable rearrangements of the bulk spectrum itself.

Theoretical models of topological insulators (TIs) include the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) [30], Haldane [12] or Kane-Mele models [17]. However, these models are often difficult to apply in real materials or require complex and expensive synthesis processes and experimental setups [20, 10, 14]. Meta-material realizations such as cold atoms in optical lattices [1, 22], phononic [34] and photonic [4] crystals or topo-electrical circuits [23] are therefore powerful alternatives to observe or even utilize TES. Among these options, topo-electrical circuits provide a versatile and usually low-cost option for modelling topological systems. A simple way to emulate a 1D topological structure such as an SSH chain is by forming a lattice of RLC resonators with capacitive or inductive coupling [24, 8]. In this case, the circuit Laplacian is analogous to a TB Hamiltonian with a one-on-one relationship between frequency and energy, allowing to identify eigen-energies of the Hamiltonian as the frequencies for which there is a local maximum of impedance. These ideas were recently harnessed to develop a low-cost topoelectrical circuit that allows to simulate 1D topological insulators with a DW, gathering information of the energy spectrum through voltage measurements [8].

papers.title: Asteroseismology of blue straggler stars in $\omega$ Centauri. Stellar collisions as a possible formation scenario
papers.abstract:
Context. Blue stragglers are intriguing stars that appear more massive and younger than expected from single-star evolution, yet their evolutionary histories remain elusive because of the multiple possible formation channels. A promising and poorly explored avenue for addressing this problem is asteroseismology, which provides the most stringent constraints on internal structure and evolution.
  Aims. We investigate five SX Phoenicis stars from the core of the globular cluster \omega Centauri that pulsate in two radial modes and occupy the blue-straggler region of the colour-magnitude diagram. Seismic models are constructed assuming a collisional origin and compared with our previous seismic studies based on single-star evolution. For comparison, we also explore a binary-evolution scenario involving mass transfer for one of the stars.
  Methods. The evolution of the parent stars is computed with MESA. The collision is then modelled with the MMAMS code, which reconstructs the merger remnant using an entropic variable. The subsequent evolution is followed with MESA up to the current age of the cluster. Finally, we construct seismic models reproducing the observed frequencies of the two radial modes.
  Results. We present the first seismic modelling of SX Phe stars (blue stragglers) based on the collision-formation scenario. Convective-core overshooting is essential for rejuvenation and for obtaining seismic models in the main-sequence phase of evolution, but it is not always sufficient. Whether a merger remnant undergoes rejuvenation depends in a complex way on the masses of the parent stars, metallicity, and collision time. We identify three evolutionary behaviours: no, delayed, and immediate rejuvenation. The collisional seismic models imply younger ages and higher masses than the seismic models based on single-star evolution.

Blue straggler stars (BSSs) are among the most challenging astrophysical objects for the theory of stellar formation and evolution. This is because BSSs are more massive and much younger than the population they belong to and in which they formed (Sandage, 1953). These facts contradict the single-star evolution, and blue stragglers appear to lag behind in their evolution. BSSs can be easily identified in stellar clusters as their position on the colour-magnitude diagram (CMD) is well defined, i.e., they are bluer and brighter than stars at the main sequence (MS) turn-off (Sandage, 1953).

BSSs can be formed in more than one way, i.e., via mass transfer (MT) in binary systems (McCrea, 1964; Ivanova, 2015, e.g.,), coalescence in primordial binaries (Nelson & Eggleton, 2001; Chen & Han, 2008, e.g.,) or direct collisions of stars in dense cluster regions (Benz & Hills, 1987; Sills et al., 2002, e.g.,). Although the proposed formation scenarios are physically plausible and justified, distinguishing between them using available observables remains a major challenge and does not usually lead to a unique solution. For example, Ferraro et al. (2009) identified two sequences of BSSs on the CMD in the globular cluster M 30, suggesting the existence of two distinct sub-populations. They proposed that the bluer sequence arose from direct collisions and the redder one arose from mass transfer and mergers in close binaries. This interpretation was further supported by Portegies Zwart (2019), who modelled stellar mergers formed either through direct collisions or during an unstable phase of mass transfer in binary systems. However, the most recent studies by Kumawat et al. (2026) of 56 Milky Way globular clusters (including M 30) showed no statistical evidence for double BSS sequences.

In this paper, we assume a collision-formation scenario and, for one star, also consider binary evolution.

papers.title: COPASI Skills: Agent Skills for COPASI analyses through Basico
papers.abstract: Biochemical models represent biological systems as networks of reactions that describe the production, consumption, and transformation of molecular species over time. These models provide a quantitative framework for analyzing system dynamics and enable computational experiments that complement traditional wet-lab approaches, helping researchers gain mechanistic insight and make predictive assessments of biological behavior. COPASI is a widely used program for simulating and analyzing those models. These tasks are made availabe to Python through Basico. COPASI Skills is a set of instruction files that tell an assistant how to drive Basico for one analysis at a time. Each skill is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` file. A short description at the top tells the assistant when the skill applies, and the rest of the file states which calls to make, which files to write, and which potential neighboring skill to choose additionally. A researcher can ask for example, in ordinary language, for a time course, a fit, or a published model. The assistant follows the matching skill and leaves tables or a report next to the model. The collection is released under a two-clause BSD license from [https://github.com/fbergmann/copasi-skills](https://github.com/fbergmann/copasi-skills).

papers.title: When Copying Is Hard to Beat: A Negative Result in Clinical Assessment Forecasting
papers.abstract: We report a negative result in next-day clinical assessment forecasting: the evaluated models show no consistent advantage over strong persistence-based baselines. Clinicians can view the previous day's questionnaire answers, a plausible source of documentation persistence. Predicting 45 items on 29,715 ICU day-pairs with patient-disjoint splits, a physiology-informed gated model improves item-macro-F1 over a one-line clinical rule by +0.0019 [+0.0006,+0.0031], while losing accuracy. No macro-F1 advantage is established when the physiology window ends at the previous form's reference time (+0.0001 [-0.0006,+0.0008]), or when scoring excludes the 68.5% of cells derived from parent answers; combining both changes yields a small disadvantage. Four checkpoints across three families underperform persistence, and a fine-tuned one differs from it on only two cells. A categorical read-out raises changed-cell accuracy eightfold, but a state-only read-out scores higher overall than forecast-only decoding and matches a transition matrix. This negative result highlights how the documentation process, input cutoff, observation mask and decoding rule shape conclusions about forecasting recorded assessments.

We report a negative result: the evaluated predictors do not consistently improve on strong simple baselines for next-day clinical assessment forecasting. Clinicians completing the questionnaire can view the previous day’s answers, making persistence directly relevant to the documentation workflow. Access to prior answers could contribute to label stability alongside genuine clinical stability; the data cannot separate these effects. We therefore evaluate forecasts of recorded assessments, whose temporal consistency may partly reflect how they are collected.

papers.title: Which Model, For Which Variable? Per-Variable Forecast Combination in Sparse ICU Time Series
papers.abstract: Clinical forecasting papers typically report a single best architecture. We show that on multivariate ICU physiology this question conceals variable-specific differences: no architecture is best on every variable, and which model wins changes from variable to variable. Across five ICU databases (MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, eICU, HiRID, and UMM (University Medicine Mannheim), a German single-center ICU) we forecast 94 channels over a 24-hour horizon with a pool of 14 models, and combine them with weights fitted per variable. On test, the combination beats the best single model on all five databases by 6.1-11.0% mean squared error (mean 8.7%). The gain is concentrated where clinical data is thinnest: the sparsest third of channels improves by 11.9% and laboratory values by 7.5%, against 3.1% for the densest third. Rank-based harmonic weighting of the best five models per variable, with no fitted weights at all, recovers about four-fifths of the gain. Extending the pool afterwards with a per-channel gradient-boosted tree, ARIMA and ETS makes the tree the validation-selected best single model on all five databases; per-variable combination still improves on it by 2.9-5.9% (significant on four of five), while equal weighting of the same members does not. As on univariate benchmarks, learned combination beats simple averaging - but only once the weights are constrained. We also report which model to prefer when, and show that the ordering changes with database size.

papers.intro:
A clinical time-series forecasting paper typically ends with a table in which one architecture has the lowest error, and that architecture is described as the best model for the task. This paper argues that on multivariate ICU physiology the single-best-model framing is suboptimal. The target is not one series but a 94-channel state vector mixing daily laboratory values, continuously sampled vital signs, medications that are administered, not measured, and derived scores. The observation process is extremely sparse — 8.8–18.6 % of (variable, hour) cells carry a measurement — and the sparsity is itself informative, because sicker patients are sampled more often. Furthermore, the channels are heterogeneous in a way univariate benchmarks are not: a creatinine trajectory and a noradrenaline infusion rate have almost nothing in common as forecasting problems. Asking which architecture is best therefore assumes one inductive bias dominates the whole panel. We show that fitting combination weights separately for each variable — a per-variable stacked generalization — recovers a consistent 6.1–11.0 % error reduction over the best single model on every database we examine, on a test set spent exactly once.

We formulate stacking with variable-specific weights, shared across windows and forecast horizons rather than tied to a series, and give an efficient estimator that makes the full combiner ladder a seven-minute CPU job over cached predictions. 2. A five-database held-out confirmation. Per-variable forecast combination improves over the best single model on all five databases (6.1–11.0 %), with the combiner chosen on validation before test was touched. 3. Sparse channels gain most. Improvement tracks channel sparsity: averaged over the five databases the sparsest third of channels gains 11.9 % against 3.1 % for the densest. We also show that the metric conventionally used for such panels is dominated by near-unobserved channels, and report it with a minimum-support filter. 4. Adding a gradient-boosted tree changes the picture: it wins most cells on every database (Section 5.3), and per-variable combination still improves on it.

papers.title: MR-ToF-assisted In-Source Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy at IGISOL
papers.abstract: Multi-Reflection Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometer (MR-ToF-MS) assisted in-source laser resonance ionization spectroscopy (RIS) has been implemented at the Ion Guide Isotope Separator On-Line (IGISOL) facility, University of Jyv\"askyl\"a. Exotic nuclei, produced via fusion-evaporation reactions, are stopped and neutralized in a hot-cavity catcher, and selectively laser-ionized through a multi-step resonance ionization scheme before being transported to the MR-ToF-MS device. This combination of techniques is aimed at optically probing the very exotic N=Z nuclei in the immediate vicinity of $^{100}$Sn. The laser system, hot-cavity ion source, isobaric purification and detection stages are described. A representative hyperfine-structure spectrum of the proton-rich silver isotope $^{101}$Ag is presented as a case example.

Reaching the most exotic cases is however an experimental challenge: towards the NN = ZZ line, production rates fall below one ion per second, half-lives decrease to hundreds or tens of milliseconds, and isobaric contamination from competing fusion-evaporation channels often overwhelms the ions of interest [6, 7]. In-source resonance ionization spectroscopy (RIS), performed inside a heated ion-source cavity, combines the efficiency and selectivity needed to reach such cases, although at the cost of a spectroscopic resolution limited to several GHz by a combination of Doppler broadening and laser bandwidth [8, 9]. When combined with fast and precise mass filters, the effects of isobaric contamination can be mitigated [6, 10], enabling optical measurements with rates as low as an ion every few minutes.

papers.title: Radiation in relativistic plasmas via particle simulations
papers.abstract: We investigate radiation in relativistic electron-proton isotropic plasmas using molecular dynamics, with velocity-dependent inertia, retarded interactions, and quantum-corrected pair potentials. Radiation spectra from the Li\'enard-Wiechert fields agree with analytical models. Successive scattering events suppress bremsstrahlung even at weak coupling, while jitter radiation becomes comparable at higher coupling for all resolved frequencies. This first-principles framework will help develop radiation models for suppression and field effects that are inaccessible in typical particle-in-cell methods.

papers.title: High-resolution Observations of Physical Properties of Dynamic Fibrils Around a Sunspot
papers.abstract: Understanding the formation and evolution of dynamic fibrils (DFs) in active regions is essential for uncovering the physical processes operating in the highly structured and magnetized solar atmosphere. High-resolution chromospheric observations from the New Vacuum Solar Telescope (NVST) show DFs with periodic up-and-down motions. We carry out a statistical analysis of 176 DFs around a sunspot. The mean values of deceleration, maximum velocity, maximum length, and duration of the DFs are $120 \boldsymbol{\pm 43}~\mathrm{m~s^{-2}}$, $15.9 \boldsymbol{\pm 4.5}~\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$, $1.13 \boldsymbol{\pm 0.48}~\mathrm{Mm}$, and $270 \boldsymbol{\pm 63}~\mathrm{s}$, respectively. Several pairs of parameters exhibit correlations, most notably a clear positive correlation between deceleration and maximum velocity. The consistency between the periodicities of DFs and running penumbral waves is first identified. We further find that DFs in regions with more vertical magnetic fields exhibit larger decelerations and shorter periods, whereas those in regions with more horizontal magnetic fields exhibit the opposite behavior. These results, together with the presence of running penumbral waves, support the interpretation that DFs are driven by slow magnetoacoustic waves. Furthermore, the multiwavelength signatures of DFs from the chromosphere to the corona imply a potential contribution to energy transport and heating in the solar atmosphere.

papers.intro:
Dynamic fibrils (DFs) are elongated, jet-like chromospheric features observed in solar active regions, characterized by their periodic up-and-down motions (see reviews by 46 and 4). In recent years, a series of detailed studies of DFs has emerged from advances in high-resolution observations and numerical simulations (e.g., 14, 10, 7, 27, 28, 41, 45). Extensive evidence suggests that DFs are the active region counterparts of spicules observed at the solar limb and mottles observed on the solar disk, with similar morphologies and characteristics. Such small-scale dynamic phenomena are therefore crucial to understanding the dynamics of the solar atmosphere.

In recent years, a series of detailed studies of DFs has emerged from advances in high-resolution observations and numerical simulations (e.g., 14, 10, 7, 27, 28, 41, 45). Such small-scale dynamic phenomena are therefore crucial to understanding the dynamics of the solar atmosphere.

A widely accepted explanation for DFs is that they are driven by magnetoacoustic shocks [14]. One-dimensional MHD simulations by De Pontieu et al. [9] show that photospheric oscillations leak into the chromosphere along inclined magnetic flux tubes, where they steepen into shocks that drive jet-like motions. Hansteen et al. [14] and De Pontieu et al. [7] compared the properties of DFs derived from observations and numerical simulations, finding excellent agreement that supports the shock-driven mechanism. In this scenario, chromospheric plasma experiences an impulsive acceleration followed by a nearly constant deceleration as the shock propagates, naturally producing the observed parabolic motions of DFs.

Understanding the origin of these shocks lies in the generation and propagation of slow magnetoacoustic waves in the solar atmosphere. Numerical simulations show that convective motions in and around magnetic flux concentrations can excite slow magnetoacoustic waves [24, 23]. As slow magnetoacoustic waves propagate upward in the stratified atmosphere, their amplitudes rapidly increase with decreasing density, eventually steepening into shocks [5]. The propagation of slow magnetoacoustic waves is constrained by the acoustic cutoff frequency, which varies with height due to changes in the local plasma conditions [1, 12]. In addition, advanced numerical simulations show that long-period waves preferentially propagate in regions with strong, inclined magnetic fields, whereas short-period waves dominate in regions with weaker or more vertical magnetic fields [17, 18]. This result provides a natural explanation for the observed regional differences in the properties of DFs, which are driven by waves with different periods [7, 45].

papers.title: BeST: Beta splatted tomography for direct reconstruction from coherent imaging measurements
papers.abstract: Conventional coherent X-ray tomography requires the phase of each projection to be reconstructed with high fidelity. However, individual reconstructed projections might be flawed, e.g. due to positioning errors, yielding inconsistent tomographic reconstructions. By directly coupling phase retrieval and tomography, consistency is enforced through a common object volume. But reconstructing a full volume demands substantial computational resources. To reduce this demand, we introduce Beta Splatted Tomography (BeST), which represents the common object volume using compactly supported beta primitives with closed-form analytical projections, enabling efficient reconstruction directly from coherent scattering images. This representation substantially reduces the number of optimizable parameters compared to a voxel grid. We demonstrate BeST on experimental datasets from hard X-ray near-field holography and far-field ptychography measurements. In both cases, the joint technique improves reconstruction quality compared to two-step methods.

Understanding the internal structure of samples is essential to solving questions in biology and material science. Imaging techniques, particularly X-ray tomography, reveal this structure, providing insights into pathological processes [1] and informing the optimization of functional materials, including catalysts [2]. Multimodal imaging enriches this structural information with complementary measurements, such as elemental distributions [3]. Hard x rays from synchrotron radiation sources are particularly suited to these investigations because their coherent and spectral properties enable access to the interior of specimens at the nanoscale.

Many specimens investigated at nanometer resolution absorb hard x rays only weakly and therefore provide little attenuation contrast. The phase shifts they induce, however, provide a substantially stronger contrast mechanism. Coherent imaging techniques exploit this effect by encoding phase variations into measurable intensity patterns. Because the detector records only intensity, the phase information must be recovered computationally through a process known as phase retrieval [4, 5, 6].

X-ray tomography based on coherent imaging methods acquires projections over a range of rotation angles, which are combined to reconstruct the 3D object. In this work, we consider near-field holotomography and far-field ptychotomography. Near-field holotomography is a full-field method that combines phase retrieval with tomography to recover 3D information [4]. X-ray ptychography is a scanning far-field method that exploits overlapping illuminated regions for phase retrieval [6, 7]. Combined with tomography it enables three-dimensional nanoscale imaging [8], including 3D reconstructions of integrated circuits [9, 10]. These two methods typically use a similar reconstruction scheme: projections are reconstructed independently and subsequently combined into a volume [11]. This approach does not enforce consistency with a 3D object during phase retrieval, allowing discrepancies between projections to propagate into the tomographic reconstruction. Joint reconstruction instead couples the measurements through a common object representation, enforcing tomographic consistency and providing additional constraints that can stabilize phase retrieval under measurement uncertainties.

Joint reconstruction instead couples the measurements through a common object representation, enforcing tomographic consistency and providing additional constraints that can stabilize phase retrieval under measurement uncertainties.

Previous work has formulated ptychographic phase retrieval and tomography as a joint inverse problem, using direct gradient-based optimization or alternating schemes that couple ptychographic and tomographic subproblems [12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. Kahnt et al. demonstrated that coupling ptychographic and tomographic reconstruction improves spatial resolution in experimental ptychotomographic data [17]. In near-field holography, Ruhlandt and colleagues coupled phase retrieval and algebraic tomography through iterative reprojection [18] and subsequently introduced a 3D propagation scheme under the weak-object approximation [19]. Automatic-differentiation frameworks have enabled optimization of 3D object models from near- and far-field intensity measurements, including multislice propagation to account for wave propagation within the specimen when the projection approximation is insufficient [20, 21].

A major computational challenge for joint reconstruction is the number of optimizable parameters when the object is represented on a dense voxel grid. For the ptychographic application considered here, a grid covering the reconstructed field of view (FOV) at the chosen sampling would contain approximately 4800×4800×7004800\times 4800\times 700 voxels. Independently optimizing both components of the complex refractive index in a voxel representation would introduce more than 3.2×10103.2\times 10^{10} scalar unknowns. Storing these arrays, their gradients, and optimizer states, together with repeatedly evaluating the forward model, places substantial demands on memory and computation.

Continuous representations offer alternatives to optimizing an independent value at every voxel. Zha et al. represent the attenuation coefficient as a continuous function of spatial coordinates parameterized by a neural network, whose parameters are optimized against measured projections [22]. An alternative uses Gaussian primitives whose analytical projections permit efficient forward projection [23]. Recently, implicit neural representations (INR) have also enabled joint reconstruction directly from inline holographic measurements [24]. INRs provide a compact object parameterization, but evaluating their projections can still require many network queries along integration paths. Combining a compact representation with analytical projection is therefore an attractive route to reducing the computational cost of joint phase retrieval and tomography.

Here, we introduce Beta Splatted Tomography (BeST), a method for joint phase retrieval and tomography using a continuous complex refractive-index representation built from compactly supported beta primitives. Following Liu et al. [25], we adopt a beta kernel with an optimizable shape parameter that adjusts its radial profile in addition to the spatial extent and orientation controlled by the primitive scales and rotation. Building on their inverse Abel construction, we derive an explicit closed-form volumetric kernel to represent and evaluate the 3D refractive-index fields. We incorporate analytical line-integral projections of these primitives into differentiable forward models for near-field inline holography and far-field ptychography. The projected refractive-index contrast determines the complex transmissivity, which is propagated to predict the measured intensities and optimize the 3D object.

papers.title: Precise Deep-Learning Reconstruction of Galaxy Cluster Mass Maps and Substructures from Optical Observations
papers.abstract: Accurately mapping the total mass distribution within galaxy clusters, including dark matter, is fundamental to understanding structure formation and constraining cosmological parameters. Conventional mass-mapping techniques rely predominantly on gravitational lensing and often produce smooth mass distributions based on analytical profiles, potentially missing important internal substructures. We introduce a complementary, simulation-based inference approach to reconstruct detailed galaxy cluster mass maps and resolve their internal substructures directly from optical imaging. We trained deep learning models on realistic hydrodynamical simulations of galaxy clusters to infer their mass distributions from optical observations. We subsequently applied this framework to observations of real galaxy clusters obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) as part of the Cluster Lensing And Supernova survey with Hubble (CLASH) programme. The reconstructed mass maps successfully reproduce the overall shapes and radial mass profiles of the CLASH clusters, showing strong agreement with independent gravitational lensing measurements. Furthermore, the subhalo mass functions derived from the reconstructed maps exhibit power-law behaviour broadly consistent with predictions from numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that combining optical imaging with deep learning provides a scalable and physically meaningful approach to mapping galaxy cluster mass distributions. This framework opens a new avenue for exploiting upcoming wide-field imaging surveys to systematically investigate dark matter substructures across large cluster samples, complementing traditional gravitational lensing techniques. Moreover, the model is inherently flexible and can incorporate multi-wavelength observations, including X-ray and Sunyaev--Zel'dovich data, to further improve total mass predictions.

papers.intro:
Galaxy clusters, which represent the final stage of hierarchical structure formation, are primarily composed of dark matter, contributing ∼85%\sim 85\% of their total mass, while ordinary baryonic matter (i.e., gas and stars) accounts for only the remaining 15%(White et al. 1993; Fukugita et al. 1998). The dominant dark matter component cannot be directly observed; its presence must be inferred from its gravitational influence on ordinary matter. Therefore, estimating the total mass of clusters (including both dark and baryonic matter) is challenging. However, this is crucial for many astrophysics and cosmology studies. For example, the abundance of galaxy clusters as a function of mass and redshift is highly sensitive to the fundamental cosmological parameters such as the matter density parameter Ωm\Omega_{m} and the mass fluctuation amplitude σ8\sigma_{8} on a scale of 8 h−1h^{-1} Mpc. As such, cluster masses can serve as a powerful tool for constraining cosmological parameters (Vikhlinin et al. 2009; Mehrtens et al. 2012; Ade et al. 2016). Hence, it is essential to improve the accuracy of total mass estimates in galaxy clusters (for an extensive review see Pratt et al. 2019).

The global masses of galaxy clusters are commonly inferred from X-ray (Vikhlinin et al. 2006; Kravtsov & Borgani 2012; Ettori et al. 2013) and Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (SZ) observations (Planck Collaboration et al. 2016; Adam et al. 2015; Eckert et al. 2022) of the intracluster medium, or from the kinematics of member galaxies (Aguado-Barahona et al. 2022; Biviano & Girardi 2003; Saro et al. 2013). These approaches rely on assumptions of hydrostatic or dynamical equilibrium, which are sensitive to non-thermal gas motions, substructure, projection effects, and contamination by interlopers, leading to systematic biases—most notably the hydrostatic mass bias—that can underestimate the true cluster mass (Rasia et al. 2004; Meneghetti et al. 2010; Biffi et al. 2016; Old et al. 2018; Gianfagna et al. 2021). Cosmological simulations play a key role in robustly quantifying the systematics and biases (Piffaretti & Valdarnini 2008; Bahé et al. 2012; Ferragamo et al. 2020; Muñoz-Echeverría et al. 2024). Nevertheless, these methods are limited to determining total cluster masses within only a few characteristic radii. As such, they cannot recover detailed mass distributions or characterize the subhalo population within galaxy clusters.

Recent deep learning (DL)–based mass inference methods trained on cosmologically based hydrodynamical simulations have attracted significant attention. This enables a more direct data-driven modeling approach that is independent of these conventional theoretical assumptions discussed above. DL models trained on simulated X-ray, Sunyaev-Zel’dovich, galaxy kinematics, and weak-lensing data have been shown to recover cluster masses with high fidelity (Ntampaka et al. 2019; Ferragamo et al. 2023; Kodi Ramanah et al. 2020; Hong et al. 2021). By applying the DL method to the observed Planck SZ cluster images, de Andres et al. (2022) showed that it can recover cluster masses without a bias. More recently, DL techniques have been shown to successfully reconstruct projected total mass maps of galaxy clusters from multi-wavelength images generated by hydrodynamic simulations, providing far richer information than scalar mass estimates alone (de Andres et al. 2024; Hsu et al. 2025). However, that approach has so far been tested only on simulations and has not yet been applied to real observations.

papers.title: Between Obligations and Evidence: A Participatory Study of Translating the EU AI Act into Technical Requirements
papers.abstract: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. We investigate these challenges through a participatory workshop involving 32 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners from different disciplines, using realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment, and public transport to examine how regulatory obligations are interpreted, translated into technical requirements, and evaluated in practice. Through a thematic analysis of workshop data, we identify recurring tensions between how regulatory obligations are translated into measurable system properties, how responsibility and human oversight are exercised in practice, and how the validity of compliance evidence is affected by changing operational conditions and system uses. For example, participants highlighted how fairness metrics could conceal discrimination in recruitment, how time pressure and limited information could undermine human oversight in public transport, and how changes in patient populations could invalidate previously established evidence of system performance. Our findings suggest that technical, organizational, and evidentiary challenges are interdependent, and that establishing and maintaining compliance requires attention not only to technical assessments but also to how AI systems are used, governed, and monitored over time. We discuss implications for supporting context-sensitive and ongoing compliance.

papers.intro:
The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) [4] is a horizontal regulatory framework that governs AI systems through a risk-based logic. Systems classified as high-risk are subject to a package of technical and governance obligations, including risk management, documentation, oversight, and lifecycle monitoring. In addition, a parallel classifier for general-purpose AI models identifies a systemic risk threshold that imposes additional obligations. In this sense, the Act shifts AI governance from voluntary ethics-by-design toward compliance-by-design: providers and deployers must produce evidence that obligations are met, not merely state design principles.

The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) [4] is a horizontal regulatory framework that governs AI systems through a risk-based logic. Systems classified as high-risk are subject to a package of technical and governance obligations, including risk management, documentation, oversight, and lifecycle monitoring. In addition, a parallel classifier for general-purpose AI models identifies a systemic risk threshold that imposes additional obligations. In this sense, the Act shifts AI governance from voluntary ethics-by-design toward compliance-by-design: providers and deployers must produce evidence that obligations are met, not merely state design principles.

A central challenge is translating these legal obligations into concrete technical requirements. Provisions concerning data governance (Art. 10), transparency (Art. 13), human oversight (Art. 14), and accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity (Art. 15) do not directly specify which system properties engineers should implement, which metrics or tests they should use, or what evidence should demonstrate that a requirement has been satisfied. The AI Act anticipates parts of this implementation problem to be solved through instruments intended to support compliance. For example, harmonized standards (Art. 40), common specifications (Art. 41), and codes of practice (Art. 56) [4, 19]. However, these instruments do not eliminate the need to interpret legal requirements within specific technical and organizational contexts [27]. These decisions cannot be made by developers alone. They depend on how AI systems are integrated into organizational workflows, how responsibilities are distributed, and how people affected by these systems are considered in design and evaluation.

A central challenge is translating these legal obligations into concrete technical requirements. Provisions concerning data governance (Art. 10), transparency (Art. 13), human oversight (Art. 14), and accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity (Art. 15) do not directly specify which system properties engineers should implement, which metrics or tests they should use, or what evidence should demonstrate that a requirement has been satisfied. The challenge extends beyond specifying technical requirements. An AI system may satisfy predefined performance criteria without adequately supporting the decisions for which it is used. Similarly, providing human oversight mechanisms does not guarantee that people have the information, competence, or authority to intervene effectively. Compliance also depends on organizational arrangements and operating conditions that may change after deployment [64]. These challenges raise questions about whether technical evidence alone can adequately demonstrate that regulatory obligations are being met, and how such evidence should be interpreted and maintained across different contexts of use.

papers.title: Stochastic Nonlocal Conservation Laws with L\'evy Noise: Stability, BV Estimates, and Vanishing Viscosity
papers.abstract: We study one-dimensional stochastic nonlocal conservation laws with a convolution-type interaction field, driven by multiplicative Brownian noise and compensated Poisson random measures. The nonlocal operator modifies the classical entropy structure, while the jump noise produces nonlinear correction terms in the entropy inequality. We introduce a notion of stochastic entropy solution and establish an $L^1$-stability estimate using spatial doubling of variables and the It\^o--L\'evy formula. This yields uniqueness in the vanishing-viscosity class and, under additional bounds, a localized Cauchy estimate of order $\sqrt{\varepsilon+\varepsilon'}$. Existence is obtained by vanishing viscosity: we construct the viscous solutions through a Faedo--Galerkin scheme and derive viscosity-uniform $L^1$ and localized $BV$ estimates, which allow us to pass to the limit and obtain a spatially $BV$ stochastic entropy solution.

papers.title: Near-wall sedimentation of short cylinders at low Reynolds numbers: Translational and angular velocity models and experimental validation
papers.abstract: The sedimentation of short cylinders near rigid walls involves coupled translational and rotational motion, for which readily applicable kinematic descriptions remain limited. In this study, theoretical expressions for the translational and angular velocities were derived by combining slender-body theory, semi-empirical finite-aspect-ratio corrections, and hydrodynamic descriptions of fluid inertia and wall effects. The resulting expressions were assessed through time-resolved sedimentation experiments with rigid cylinders of mean aspect ratios $\bar{\chi}\approx3.8$--$5.8$ in a rectangular duct at particle Reynolds numbers of $Re_{\mathrm P}\approx O(10^{-1})$. The experiments revealed distinct near-wall trajectories, including non-contact glancing motion and contact-induced flipping. For glancing trajectories, the predicted translational and angular velocities reproduced the principal features of the measured kinematics, with good qualitative and, over substantial parts of the trajectories, quantitative agreement. The comparisons also identified different ranges of applicability for the investigated wall corrections and showed that wall-induced effects dominated the angular velocity under the conditions studied. The resulting, experimentally validated expressions provide readily applicable estimates of the instantaneous translational and angular velocities of short cylinders near rigid walls and a reference for investigating additional influences on their sedimentation dynamics, including lower Reynolds numbers and particle or wall elasticity.

papers.title: Polarization Lifetime as a Design Axis for Task-Adaptive Photonic Reservoir Computing
papers.abstract: Photonic time-delayed reservoir computing (TDRC) based on conventional Class B lasers is limited by fragile external cavity mode (ECM) locking dynamics. Here, we show that engineering the polarization lifetime (T$_2$) with the carrier lifetime ($T$) reshapes the topology and stability of TDRC. Comparing four laser classes (Class A, Class B, Class C$_A$, and Class C$_B$), a finite polarization lifetime acts as an intrinsic dynamic filter, dissolving discrete ECM chaos grids into continuous, phase-tolerant operational basins. Information processing capacity (IPC) decomposition further exposes distinct computational profiles: matched Class C$_A$ achieves the highest nonlinear capacity (16.28) and the highest total capacity (19.29), whereas Class A exhibits the highest linear capacity (4.70). A task-dependent reversal governs hardware design: Class A and Class C$_A$ achieve comparable, and the lowest, NRMSE on short-horizon Mackey--Glass prediction (0.0103 and 0.0105, within one standard deviation), while the time-scale-matched Class C$_A$ dominates the higher-dimensional Lorenz (0.0506) and the experimental Santa Fe (0.4251) tasks. Linear-IPC ranking matches Mackey-Glass accuracy; nonlinear-IPC ranking matches the Lorenz exactly and Santa Fe within the mask-to-mask uncertainty. Under realistic quantum noise, resilience is dictated mainly by $T$, not T$_2$: Class A retains the lowest NRMSE (0.47) even at spontaneous emission factor $\beta$ = $10^{-1}$, whereas the long-carrier Class B degrades (0.98). A residual T$_2$-mediated benefit of 20$\%$ persists in the slow-carrier Class C$_B$ (0.78 vs. 0.98). Time-scale engineering thus offers a nuanced design paradigm for optical computing, where optimal hardware is set by the task's time-scale hierarchy rather than a universal figure of merit.

papers.intro:
The exponential growth of artificial intelligence, particularly in time-series forecasting and real-time control, has created an urgent demand for neuromorphic hardware capable of processing temporal data streams with ultrahigh throughput and minimal energy consumption [1, 29]. Photonic reservoir computing (RC) has emerged as a promising paradigm to meet these demands [40]. By harnessing the transient, high-bandwidth dynamics of optical systems to project input signals into a high-dimensional state space, photonic RC circumvents the computationally expensive iterative training of recurrent neural network weights [2, 31]. In the widely adopted time-delayed RC (TDRC) architecture, the spatial complexity of a conventional network is elegantly replaced by the temporal multiplexing of a single physical nonlinear node subject to delayed optical feedback [14, 13, 25]. Consequently, the computational capacity, memory depth, and noise resilience of the entire system are dictated entirely by the intrinsic physical dynamics of this single node.

Consequently, the computational capacity, memory depth, and noise resilience of the entire system are dictated entirely by the intrinsic physical dynamics of this single node.

To date, the vast majority of photonic TDRC implementations have relied on semiconductor lasers as the nonlinear node [9, 35, 18, 36, 2, 5, 8]. Experimentally, photonic TDRC has achieved high-throughput processing at multi-gigabit rates using transients in delayed feedback systems [5]. Theoretically, the rich dynamics of semiconductor lasers subject to optical feedback have been extensively modeled using delay differential equations to design optimal reservoir states [8]. The dynamics of such lasers are universally modeled by Class B rate equations, a simplified mathematical framework that assumes the macroscopic medium polarization decays infinitely fast compared to the cavity photon lifetime and the carrier inversion lifetime TT [32, 27]. By adiabatically eliminating the polarization dynamics, Class B models reduce the system to a two-dimensional phase space dominated by relaxation oscillations [38, 22]. While these lasers have been successfully applied to benchmark tasks, their pronounced, carrier-induced relaxation oscillations (which are typically underdamped in conventional semiconductor quantum-well lasers) impose fundamental constraints on the accessible dynamical responses. Most critically, the high-dimensional dynamics close to the edge of stability in Class B lasers are accessible only within narrow windows of a highly structured parameter space, where stable and chaotic dynamics alternate frequently owing to the complex locking of external cavity modes (ECMs). This operational intricacy implies that even minute thermal drifts or fabrication imperfections can push the system out of its optimal computational window, leading to a catastrophic collapse in performance. These fragilities stem from an inherent mismatch between the ultra-fast polarization and slow carrier relaxation timescales.

A promising route is to systematically engineer the laser’s intrinsic timescales, deliberately retaining a finite polarization lifetime (T2) that acts as a dynamical filter and a topological smoother. The adiabatic elimination of the polarization lifetime in Class B models completely discards a rich dynamical resource that could fundamentally alter this picture. This omission has been shown to be particularly significant in the context of the modulation response of nanolasers, where standard rate-equation approaches miss essential dynamical features [4]. When the polarization lifetime (T2T_{2}) becomes comparable to or longer than the cavity photon lifetime, the laser enters the coherent Class C regime, where polarization evolves as an independent dynamic variable [38]. Moreover, by decoupling T2T_{2} from the carrier lifetime TT, one obtains a distinct Class CB regime, where a long T2T_{2} acts as a natural low-pass filter, imposing a smoothing effect on the complex dynamics of conventional Class B lasers. The role of such slow polarization dynamics as an intrinsic spectral filter has been previously discussed in the context of delay-coupled laser systems [21]. This raises a pressing and previously unanswered question: can the deliberate reintroduction of macroscopic polarization and its interplay with carrier lifetimes fundamentally transform the computational landscape of photonic TDRC? Specifically, can a finite polarization lifetime dissolve the rigid phase-matching constraints that render Class B reservoirs fragile, endow the system with intrinsic adaptability to diverse task timescales, and generate high-dimensional nonlinear mappings that are genuinely robust to spontaneous emission noise?

In this work, we answer this by conducting a systematic comparative study of four representative laser classes: Class A (fast T2T_{2}, fast TT), Class B (fast T2T_{2}, slow TT), Class CA (finite T2T_{2}, finite TT), and Class CB (finite T2T_{2}, slow TT). We perform comprehensive sweeps across feedback strength κ\kappa, detuning δ​ω\delta\omega, and phase ϕ\phi to map the operational phase diagrams for each class, revealing that Class CB lasers benefit from polarization-induced filtering that significantly broadens their stable regions compared to the fragile locking grids of Class B, namely the strictly phase-matched stable continuous-wave (CW) operation locked onto external cavity modes (ECMs) [21]. papers.title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs
papers.abstract: Research in the domain of Physics-Informed Neural Networks applied to PDE modelling has advanced significantly in recent years, providing a wide ecosystem of novel methods. However, one frequent limitation is the inability of PINNs to scale out on High-Performance Computing architectures to address more ambitious challenges, particularly non-linear physics models with turbulent dynamics in large spatial domains. Typical studies restrain demonstrations to toy models with simple physics equations, few variables, and rarely any complex non-linear dynamics evolved over long timescales. Part of the AI community has even adopted the idea that "PINNs don't scale". This work proves otherwise. We present a mathematically robust formulation of Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN) implemented into a comprehensive, modular framework: Fuse-PINN. This formulation provides the basis for a sclable parallelisation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks on GPU-based HPC systems. Furthermore, an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser is implemented to allow high-precision convergence. Fuse-PINN is demonstrated on physics models relevant to Magnetic Confinement Fusion, including non-linear convective models with fine-scale dynamics. Near-perfect scaling is achieved on multi-GPU runs with increasing problem size.

papers.intro:
The numerical modelling of non-linear systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) is used in research and industrial applications across scientific and engineering challenges. From aerospace to automotive, from weather to climate predictions, from solar to fusion energy, numerical solvers are a core component of engineering design and technological advances. Predicting the non-linear evolution of complex physical systems typically relies on conventional numerical methods, which are constantly being developed and improved, both for academic scientific research ([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) as well as industrial tools ([6, 7, 8]). In recent years, a particular branch of Machine Learning has brought a promising alternative to these conventional approaches: Physics-Informed Neural Networks [9]. Three practical barriers continue to limit the use of PINNs for challenging scientific simulations. First, high-accuracy training remains difficult because the loss landscape is often poorly conditioned, with competing domain, initial and boundary residual terms that can converge different rates. Second, many physically relevant non-linear PDE systems contain multiple length and time scales, with sharp gradients, transport-dominated dynamics, and long time evolution, all of which expose the spectral bias and optimisation fragility of standard neural-network approximations. Third, although conventional simulation codes routinely exploit distributed-memory HPC systems, many PINN methods remain confined to single-GPU implementations, limiting the size of the domain, the number of collocation points, and the complexity of the physics that can be treated in practice.

We propose Fuse-PINN [10]: a scalable framework for Physics Informed Neural Networks that combines finite-element residual assembly with a physics-based high-precision optimiser, demonstrated on High-Performance Computing (HPC) architectures. The implementation is designed for multi-node, multi-GPU execution, with a domain decomposition embedded directly into the FEM-NN formulation. We demonstrate the approach on nonlinear models relevant to fusion energy, including convective systems with fine-scale dynamics, as a step towards PINN methods that can operate beyond the limits of single-device PINN workflows.

Complex Physics Models: PINNs have been applied to a wide range of non-linear PDEs, including Burgers-type systems, diffusion equations, Navier-Stokes flows and wave propagation [9, 12]. These studies have demonstrated the conceptual flexibility of physics-informed learning: the same framework can incorporate governing equations, initial and boundary conditions, sparse measurements, unknown parameters, and differentiable surrogate quantities. However, most PINN demonstrations remain concentrated on relatively low-dimensional benchmarks, simplified geometries, or short-time dynamics, with some notable exceptions, such as 3D turbulence simulations [12] (and references therein, like PirateNets [13]). The physics models relevant to fusion research can be most challenging: transport, instability, and turbulence models involve stiff non-linear couplings, scale separation, anisotropic dynamics, high-order derivatives, while requiring long integration windows. For instance, the MHD equations involve 8 variables (3D velocity and magnetic fields, plus density and temperature), while gyrokinetic turbulence evolve a density distribution in 5D.

High-Precision Optimisers: Among several novel methods in high-precision PINN optimisation is the recent work of [14]. Standard optimisers like Adam and L-BFGS can provide useful approximations, but they typically fail to reach the level of precision expected from mature numerical solvers, particularly for stiff or non-linear PDEs due to the ill-conditioning of PINNs [15, 16]. Müller & Zeinhofer’s Energy Natural Gradient Descent method (ENGD) addresses this limitation by defining the optimisation step in function space using a physics-based preconditioner, so that the update direction approximates a Newton step projected onto the tangent space of the neural-network manifold. This method achieves errors orders of magnitude lower than standard optimisers on representative benchmark problems. Notable extensions of ENGD as well as other high-precision approaches include [17, 18, 19].

Domain Decomposition: Domain decomposition has emerged as one of the most natural routes for improving both the trainability and scalability of PINNs. Conservative PINNs (cPINNs) and extended PINNs (XPINNs) decompose the physical domain into subdomains, assigning separate neural networks to each region and enforcing interface consistency through additional constraints [20, 21]. XPINNs generalise this idea to flexible decompositions in space and time, enabling different architectures, sampling densities, and optimisation settings in different subdomains [21]. Finite Basis PINNs (FBPINNs) provide a related construction inspired by finite-element methods, in which compactly supported neural components are combined over overlapping subdomains, reducing spectral-bias effects through local input normalisation and smaller subdomain networks [22]. These approaches show that locality is beneficial, but they also reveal an open question: how to combine domain decomposition with a high-precision optimiser and a finite-element residual formulation in a way that maps cleanly onto modern distributed GPU systems. The works by [23] and [24] also propose FEM-NN ideas, but these are conceptually different from the nodal NN formulation we present here. Likewise, hp-VPINN [25] combines Galerkin discretisation with a single PINN network, but it does not provide a recipe for parallelisation. Finally, TensorGalerkin [26] augments a standard Galerkin/FEM discretisation with differentiable assembly and neural-operator learning, but it does not provide a parallelisation recipe for pure PINNs.

papers.title: Parity conservation of the isotropic galaxy 4PCF in redshift space
papers.abstract: Recent observational investigation of cosmological Parity Violation (PV) through the galaxy Four-point Correlation Function (4PCF) has motivated a careful theoretical examination of potential systematic contributions. In this work, we demonstrate that parity-odd contributions to the isotropic 4PCF estimator induced by Redshift Space Distortion (RSD), up to the leading order $\mathcal{H}/k$ of general relativistic corrections, vanish upon averaging over all the Line-of-Sight (LOS). We analyse the perturbative relativistic galaxy number density, combining the biased tracer expansion and the dark matter gravitational dynamics within the framework of Standard Eulerian Perturbation Theory (EPT) to third order in the density perturbation. Building on prior studies of the parity-odd mode of the trispectrum (the Fourier-space counterpart of the 4PCF), we extend existing results in three directions: incorporating the wide-angle effect by adopting a local LOS definition for each galaxy in the 4PCF, accounting for tidal bias in the galaxy population, and generalising the assessment to an arbitrary cosmological background. Expanding the 4PCF in spherical harmonics, we show that angular momentum selection rules, encoded in the Wigner 3-j symbols, enforce that only parity-even contributions survive the integration over all LOS orientations, both in the plane-parallel approximation and in the full wide-angle case. This result is crucial for large-scale statistical analyses using isotropic estimators. It supports interpreting possible PV detections as a signal not due to a systematic RSD artefact. We conclude with a discussion of the caveats of our results and identify potential sources of PV.

papers.intro:
The research on Parity Violation (PV) in the galaxy distribution, as a Large-Scale Structure (LSS) probe, was proposed by Cahn et al. (2023), who introduced the Four-point Galaxy Correlation Function (4PCF) as a statistical tool to test parity symmetry on cosmological scales. Subsequently, the same group reported up to 7​σ7\sigma-detection of a non-zero parity-odd mode in the observed 4PCF of the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) galaxy catalogue of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Hou et al. (2023). In the same year, Philcox (2022) also performed an independent analysis on the same dataset and reported a 2.9​σ2.9\sigma-detection. Such intriguing claims spurred further studies, and the subsequent analyses did not support evidence for parity violation in LSS Philcox and Ereza (2025); Krolewski et al. (2024); Adari and Slosar (2024). On the other hand, using a sample of the Luminous Red Galaxies (LRGs) from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the authors of Slepian et al. (2025) recently found a potential 4−10​σ4{-}10\sigma detection. Taken together, these results constitute a promising step for LSS analyses of possible parity-violating signatures on cosmological scales, and they motivate theoretical investigations of inflationary mechanisms that can generate such signals. Since GR conserves parity, any such mechanism must involve physics beyond GR. The simplest and most studied example is Chern-Simons gravity Lue et al. (1999); Jackiw and Pi (2003) (see Salvarese (2022) for the first attempt), where a parity-violating term coupled to a scalar field is added to the GR Lagrangian (see also Bartolo and Orlando (2017) and references therein). In a broader landscape, Bartolo et al. (2021); Moretti et al. (2025) (see also references therein) study chirality in more general scalar-tensor models, which include parity-violating operators with higher derivatives of the inflaton field. Beyond modified gravity theories, parity-odd correlation functions can also be generated within the Effective Field Theory (EFT) of inflation, where the no-go theorems and yes-go examples are derived in Cabass et al. (2023). In addition, Shiraishi (2016); Liu et al. (2020); Niu et al. (2023); Fujita et al. (2024); Reinhard et al. (2024) compute the parity-odd trispectrum arising from the matter sector of Axion inflation (see also, e.g., Coulton et al. (2024) and Cabass et al. (2023), for the discussion of other possibilities).

(2025) develops a model for the 4PCF with RSD effects in the plane-parallel limit, using perturbative solutions for dark matter in the Einstein-de Sitter (EdS) universe and a power-law biased tracer expansion. papers.title: A trap-based platform for cooling and laser spectroscopy of fast ions toward radioactive-ion applications
papers.abstract: We report on the first experiments with the Stopping and Trapping of Radioactive Isotopes for Precision Experiments (STRIPE) segmented linear Paul trap. The intent for this apparatus is to serve as an efficient capture and laser-cooling trap for radioactive isotopes produced at radioactive ion beam facilities. We demonstrate the deceleration of 10 keV ion beams and their trapping and laser cooling into Coulomb crystals. As an initial spectroscopic benchmark, the dipole-forbidden $5s$ $^2S_{1/2}$ $\rightarrow$ $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ transition in $^{88}$Sr$^+$ was driven, partially resolving the Zeeman structure and yielding a Gaussian linewidth of 14.5(8) MHz, with the residual width attributed to the ions' micromotion. The lifetime of the metastable $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ state was measured to be 0.325(5)$_{\mathrm{stat}}$(4)$_{\mathrm{sys}}$ s, uncorrected for collisional quenching. Several measurements to quantify the cooling timescale, the detection rate of the photon collection region and the trap storage lifetime were also performed. The developed technique will allow radioactive ion beams to be decelerated and cooled for precision spectroscopy measurements.

papers.intro:
Laser spectroscopy (LS) gives nuclear-model-independent access to four complementary nuclear observables: the spin II, the magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole moments μ\mu and QsQ_{s} [1], and the mean-square charge radius ⟨r2⟩\langle r^{2}\rangle [2]. For radioactive isotopes it is typically performed on fast beams in the collinear geometry [3, 4, 5], where the microsecond-scale ion–laser interaction time restricts it mostly to dipole-allowed transitions with natural linewidths of tens of MHz\mathrm{MHz}. Confining the ions in a Paul trap extends the interaction time by many orders of magnitude and makes narrow dipole-forbidden and RF transitions accessible [6]. These enable both a higher precision on the above observables and access to higher-order ones, such as the magnetic octupole moment, an additional probe of the distribution of nuclear magnetization [7], and isotope shifts precise enough for King-plot searches for physics beyond the Standard Model [8]. Applying this to radioactive isotopes requires injecting externally produced ions, delivered as a beam from a radioactive ion beam (RIB) facility, into a trap and laser-cooling them [9].

To date, transition frequencies of stable, laser-cooled ions in Paul traps have been measured with sub-hertz uncertainty by several groups, for example in Sr+88{}^{88}\mathrm{Sr}^{+} and Yb+171{}^{171}\mathrm{Yb}^{+} [10]. Isotope shifts have reached hertz-level precision along the even Yb+ chain [11], and uncertainties below 100 mHz100\text{\,}\mathrm{mHz} along the even Ca+ chain [12] and between 86,88Sr+ [13]. However, the application of such measurements to radioactive cases has been limited. Typical examples include the work on Ra+224{}^{224}\mathrm{Ra}^{+} and Ba+133{}^{133}\mathrm{Ba}^{+} [14, 15], where the radioactive samples were placed close to the linear Paul trap and ion loading was performed by photoionization. Ra+ has also been decelerated and captured from keV\mathrm{keV} energies using buffer gas [16], where collisions leading to thermalization at room temperature limited the precision to the GHz\mathrm{GHz} level. A similar approach was used for Be+11{}^{11}\mathrm{Be}^{+} [17], where the buffer gas was removed from the trap prior to measurement. This improved the precision to the kHz\mathrm{kHz} level, at the expense of a delay of several seconds before each measurement. Avoiding buffer gas altogether would extend in-trap LS to reactive species, for which molecule formation can prevent spectroscopy, and to highly charged ions, which would otherwise rapidly undergo charge exchange. Within this context, capture and cooling of keV\mathrm{keV} beams without buffer gas has been demonstrated by Sels et al. [18] for Mg+, K+ and O+2{}_{2}^{+}, using Doppler and sympathetic cooling.
