This paper is structured as follows. Section II gives an overview of the Stopping and Trapping of Radioactive Isotopes for Precision Experiments (STRIPE) beamline, as well as new details on the two laser–trap configurations investigated in this work, together with the laser system, the photon collection region (PCR) and the RF amplifier. Section III presents the results of this work: Doppler cooling and Coulomb-crystal formation (Section III.1), the detection rate of the PCR (Section III.2) and the trap storage lifetime (Section III.3), followed by spectroscopy of the 5​s2​S1/2→4​d2​D5/25s\,^{2}S_{1/2}\to 4d\,^{2}D_{5/2} clock transition in the between-electrodes and within-electrode configurations, from which the residual broadening mechanisms and the metastable 4​d2​D5/24d\,^{2}D_{5/2}-state lifetime are extracted (Section III.4). papers.title: Learning monotone game-theoretic linear MPC
papers.abstract: We propose a method to learn a game-theoretic model predictive control (GT-MPC) law by imitation from input and output data of a running multi-agent system. By interpreting the recorded inputs as the first moves of the equilibria of a game played by the agents, we learn the GT-MPC weights under hard input constraints and soft output constraints, without requiring the agents to reveal their objectives. We also impose that the resulting generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problem is strongly monotone, which ensures the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium and, hence, that the learned GT-MPC law is well defined and can be evaluated efficiently online by variational GNE-seeking algorithms for linear-quadratic games. Moreover, strong monotonicity implies that the equilibrium is almost everywhere differentiable with respect to the references and the weights, which enables automatic differentiation for gradient-based optimization. In addition, we promote closed-loop stability of the unconstrained equilibrium feedback by incorporating a penalty that involves a jointly learned quadratic Lyapunov function. Learning a GT-MPC formulation enables us to explain the agents' objectives, reproduce their behavior in simulation in new scenarios, optimize their set-points, design mechanisms, and enforce additional constraints. A numerical example illustrates the approach.

In game-theoretic model predictive control (GT-MPC), several agents act on a common dynamical system, each optimizing a personal objective that depends on the other agents’ moves under local and shared constraints, and applying the first move of the resulting generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) at every time step [26, 18, 19, 8, 17, 13]. Each GT-MPC problem is a finite-horizon dynamic game; see [16, 21, 23] for solution algorithms and multi-vehicle applications. Modeling the agents’ costs is often difficult: the agents may be unwilling to disclose their objectives and strategies for privacy reasons, and in many applications the plant is even operated without explicit objectives to minimize, e.g., by standard decentralized control loops or even manually. A natural goal is then to learn, from the observed actions only, a GT-MPC law that reproduces them, so that the agents do not have to reveal their strategies, and that adds the main benefit of MPC, namely, handling input and output constraints. Moreover, once a game representation of agents’ behavior is available, it can be used for higher-level tasks, such as optimization of the set-point signals that enter the game at each step. It also allows reproducing the agents’ behavior in closed-loop simulation, e.g., on a digital twin of the plant, to evaluate what-if scenarios that have not been observed yet.

We restrict our attention to strongly monotone linear-quadratic (LQ) games. papers.title: Super-Analysis for Aggressive yet Scalable Compiler Optimization
papers.abstract:
Aggressive compiler optimization today occupies two distant extremes. Conventional optimizers run in milliseconds but reason through ad-hoc heuristics that miss opportunities; superoptimizers synthesize faster code but take hours, confining them to small kernels and offline use. We introduce solver-based super-analysis, a middle ground that uses expensive SMT-based analysis while transformations remain conventional, avoiding program synthesis entirely. The key argument for super-analysis is that conventional compilers have rich transformation rules, but proving them to be safe requires complex reasoning: proving a safety check dead often needs facts from three independent LLVM analyses simultaneously, a conjunctive entailment problem suited to an SMT solver, not to any single dataflow pass.
  We instantiate super-analysis in ODeSSy, an LLVM pass that proves sanitizer traps and native-language safety checks unreachable and removes them. One mechanism serves four frontend languages and yields speedups in each, including a 3.78x speedup for a GEMM implemented in Julia. A further solver-based optimization, guard synthesis, handles checks that are not dead for every input: the solver synthesizes a cheap invariant safety guard under which a fast check-free loop is cloned, speeding up a Swift Base64 encoder by 1.44x and a Julia LZ77 compressor by 4.01x. Compared with Souper, the synthesizing superoptimizer for LLVM, ODeSSy removes more safety checks in significantly less time, making it viable as an online compiler pass.

papers.intro:
Optimizing compilers decide how fast software runs. Every program in a compiled language, from operating systems to an artificial intelligence training kernel, passes through compiler optimization at an intermediate representation (IR) level. A compiler infrastructure such as LLVM (Lattner and Adve, 2004) serves many input languages at once, including C and C++, Swift, Rust, and Julia, all compiled to its IR and aggressively optimized through it. Almost all software nowadays goes through such optimization pipelines, so the effectiveness of optimizers heavily influences the performance of the software we use.

Almost all software nowadays goes through such optimization pipelines, so the effectiveness of optimizers heavily influences the performance of the software we use.

Aggressive compiler optimization currently falls into two general classes. Conventional optimizers, such as LLVM’s -O3 pipeline, apply a fixed sequence of analyses and rewrites. They are fast: they make millions of decisions in milliseconds, each justified by a heuristic or a lightweight analysis that reasons locally and gives up early. They are perfect for online use in the programmer’s develop-and-test loop. Superoptimizers (Massalin, 1987; Schkufza et al., 2013; Sasnauskas et al., 2017) are the extreme alternatives. They aggressively search for faster replacement code and use a solver to prove each candidate correct. Correctness consists of checking if the candidate and the original piece of code are equivalent, usually offloaded to an SMT solver. Superoptimizers find more optimal code as they conduct an exhaustive search, in contrast with the conventional rule-based transformations.

Each class pays for its strength and has critical weaknesses. Conventional optimizers are fast, but they miss optimizations whose safety needs deeper reasoning. Their lightweight conventional heuristics give up and are unable to provide sufficient analysis for many cases (Taneja et al., 2020). Superoptimizers are more aggressive in optimization as they find code heuristics cannot, but their search is expensive and coupled with the solver’s expensive check, as each candidate code found should be verified correct. Because of this, superoptimizers take up to hours to run, so they are confined to small code windows and run offline, outside the everyday development and testing loops.

SMT-based compiler analysis is more precise than native lightweight compiler analysis. Our central empirical finding is that the missed opportunities require complex reasoning over multiple domains and from different fact sources to prove safe. Proving one bounds check dead in a real SHA-256 kernel (Figure 2) requires the return-value range of one function, a scalar-evolution loop bound, a value-range fact on a third value, and two dominating branch conditions from the program’s prefix — simultaneously. Each fact lives in a different LLVM analysis; no single pass computes their conjunction, and the phase-ordering problem poses an obstacle for a sequence of analyses to be successful. Deciding satisfiability of a complex conjunction is, in principle, an entailment problem — exactly what an SMT solver decides. We inspect the unsat core of every proof, so this claim is not an intuition but a measurement: the cores name the contributing analyses, and they usually draw on several sources at once.

We instantiate super-analysis in ODeSSy11 1 On-Demand SMT System., an LLVM module pass targeting one of the most consequential classes of provably-dead code in modern software: safety checks. Sanitizers such as UBSan (LLVM Project, 2026) and the native checks of memory-safe languages (Swift bounds and overflow checks, Rust panics, Julia bounds errors) compile to trap-guarded branches (Figure 2) whose hot-path cost is the standing tax of memory safety — we measure it at up to 1.069×1.069\times on the zstd library under signed-overflow checks and up to 4.15×4.15\times on a native-language kernel (Julia GEMM). Today the only recourse to avoid this performance tax is to turn checks off wholesale (-Ounchecked, --check-bounds=no), trading away the safety guarantee entirely. ODeSSy offers the sound alternative: delete exactly the checks that are provably redundant with the guards, contracts, and invariants already present in the program, and keep every check that is not. ODeSSy is able to recover up to 3.78×3.78\times of performance by removing redundant safety checks and enabling a cascade of further optimizations.

papers.title: Tracing Actual Causes with Counterfactual Witness Maps
papers.abstract: Halpernian actual causation, the formal study of which events in a specific situation caused a specific outcome in acyclic structural causal models, underpins legal responsibility, moral blame, and the assessment of causal harm. Despite the rich logical framework, no prior sound and complete enumeration procedure is known for finding all actual causes in a given setting, blocking downstream tasks such as responsibility attribution, blame assessment, and causal-harm grading that aggregate over the full cause set. We close this gap by introducing witness targets: sets of joint configurations containing every counterfactual witness. In combination with an ancestor intervention grammar we derive a finite directed acyclic witness map. We prove that for every actual cause there exists a contingency set such that the joint intervention set appears as a node of this map, and present an algorithm for Tracing Actual Causes (TrAC) that is sound and complete for enumerating all actual causes of any target event. We compare TrAC empirically with existing single-cause baselines on random Boolean structural causal models, demonstrating practical feasibility for graphs of up to 15 nodes.

papers.intro:
What actually caused a specific outcome, such as a patient’s death after medication, an accident, or a software failure? Actual causation [17] answers this question for singular, context-dependent cases, grounding legal responsibility [25], moral blame [11], and algorithmic accountability [10]. Downstream tasks that aggregate over the full cause set, notably responsibility and blame scores [10] and the grading of causal harm [3], are blocked without an efficient enumeration procedure. The dominant framework [15, 17] formalises actual causation in acyclic structural causal models (SCMs) [27] via three conditions (AC1)–(AC3) on a candidate variable assignment, requiring its actual co-occurrence with the effect, a contingency set of variables held at actual values exposing counterfactual dependence, and subset-minimality (formal definitions in Sec. 3). We adopt the modified HP definition [16, 17], one of several proposals in the literature, for its conceptual clarity and favourable complexity profile: verifying a single candidate is 𝖣1P\mathsf{D}_{1}^{P}-complete [1, 16], vs. Σ2P\Sigma_{2}^{P}-complete in general under the original [12]. The modified definition is also the natural fit for our construction: holding contingencies at their actual values is exactly the membership constraint of Corollary 2, so condition AC2 collapses to a single query against a precomputed target set, whereas the original definition’s additional universal clause over contingency subsets admits no such collapse in general.

We present the first constructive, sound-and-complete algorithm for enumerating all actual causes of an event in an acyclic SCM. Rather than iterating over alternative values forward, we propagate the complement of the target event backward through the structural equations, yielding the witness targets: for each candidate intervention set, the exact set of joint variable configurations compatible with that complement. This converts the existential search in AC2 into a single set-membership query, eliminating the dependence on alternative-value cardinality from the per-candidate verification cost. Rather than iterating over alternative values forward, we propagate the complement of the target event backward through the structural equations, yielding the witness targets: for each candidate intervention set, the exact set of joint variable configurations compatible with that complement. This converts the existential search in AC2 into a single set-membership query, eliminating the dependence on alternative-value cardinality from the per-candidate verification cost. A finite witness map over structurally admissible ancestor subsets then enumerates all candidate intervention sets; its worst-case cost remains exponential (Section 4.3), which pruning substantially reduces in practice. First, witness targets (Section 4.1) provide an exact backward-propagation criterion for counterfactual satisfaction, converting AC2 into a set-membership query (Definitions 1–3, Theorem 1, Corollary 2). Second, the witness map (Section 4.2) builds on the ancestor intervention grammar and ancestral map to enumerate all structurally admissible candidate intervention sets (Definitions 4–6, Propositions 3–4). Third, the Tracing Actual Causes (TrAC) algorithm (Section 4.3, Algorithm 1) combines both with soundness and completeness guarantees (Theorem 7) and an explicit complexity analysis (Appendix E).

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent
papers.abstract: Can you trust a finance agent you did not build? We take the reference agent shipped with the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2, leave it untuned, and ask four questions a leaderboard score does not answer. Is the score stable? Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, and the bill varies by up to 17%. When the agent fails, who owns the fix? We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data. Can that diagnosis be trusted? Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%). Can a change be trusted? An optimization loop reads the traces, makes one targeted change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold. Under a cost objective its final configuration costs 0.34x the baseline on the held-out questions (95% CI [0.22, 0.58]) at accuracy within noise. Under an accuracy objective it gains 14 points on the development questions and 1.5 on the held-out ones (CI [-5.3, +7.2]). Judged against the measured run-to-run noise, under a rule written before the test was opened, the first is a real saving and the second is not. This is a case study of one agent and nine test questions, not a general result.

A financial research agent is in production. It has a leaderboard score. A compliance officer asks what it does when it is wrong. The score does not answer: it was computed once, on questions the officer has never seen, by a grader the institution does not control, and it says nothing about where the wrong answers came from or who in the building should fix them.

Benchmarks of financial agents have multiplied since 2025. The Vals Finance Agent Benchmark (Bigeard et al., 2025) scores answers to expert-written research questions against rubric criteria; BigFinanceBench (Wang et al., 2026) grades the visible derivation step by step. Both measure how much of the answer, or of its derivation, is right. Neither says why a wrong answer was wrong, and neither names the layer of the system that owns the remedy. The processes diverge; the benchmark establishes it and stops there.

papers.title: A Parametric Active-Set Algorithm for Solving Monotone Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problems
papers.abstract: We present a fast active-set algorithm for the solution of monotone linear-quadratic generalized Nash equilibrium problems (GNEPs) with shared affine inequality and equality constraints. The algorithm, which we call gPAQ, is an adaptation of the parametric active-set method proposed by Best (1996) and extended in qpOASES by Ferreau et al. (2014) to solve convex quadratic programs. Under strong monotonicity, we show that the same active-set strategy applies. We handle the case of merely monotone problems by using gPAQ as the inner solver within proximal-point iterations. To solve strongly monotone convex nonlinear GNEPs, we propose a Newton-type iterative scheme, which we call gPAN, which iteratively linearizes the nonlinear problem and solves the resulting LQ-GNEP subproblems using gPAQ. We show in numerical examples that the proposed algorithms are significantly faster than existing methods.

papers.title: Making Experiment Results Comparable through Sitewide Impact Estimation
papers.abstract: Roblox spans many product surfaces-discovery, the virtual economy, creator tools-that differ sharply in reach and in how much the affected population contributes to any sitewide metric. A randomized experiment shows whether a treatment works for the users in its sample, but this experiment lift is not comparable across surfaces, because surfaces differ in reach and in their contribution to sitewide metrics. The quantity a strategic decision needs is a counterfactual-how much an aggregated sitewide metric (e.g., total platform play time) would move if the treatment reached 100% of its target population, which may be only part of the sitewide population, during the measurement period. We call this sitewide impact. Its scaling factor, which we call the coverage factor, combines the reach and the target population's contribution to the sitewide metric under no treatment. Hence a low-reach surface whose users carry much of the metric could outrank a high-reach surface whose users carry little. We develop two estimators under this framing: one for difference-in-means metrics and one for variant-level ratio metrics (a metric defined as a ratio of two population aggregates). Empirically, experiment lift is a poor proxy for sitewide impact-across 139 experiments that are statistically significant on time spent, the Spearman rank correlation between the two is 0.20, and 5 of the 10 largest experiment lifts are among the 10 largest sitewide impacts. We validate the estimator with A/A tests and against a long-term holdout, and apply it to cross-domain prioritization and attributing year-over-year growth to shipped innovations.

papers.title: Higher derived limits, Kurepa families and Chang's Conjecture
papers.abstract:
We investigate the interplay between homological algebra and combinatorial set theory, specifically focusing on the (non)vanishing of higher derived limits of certain inverse systems of abelian groups, denoted $\mathbf C_{[\kappa]^\lambda}$, indexed by the ordered sets $([\kappa]^{\lambda},\subseteq)$, where $\lambda < \kappa$ are infinite cardinals.
  Our first main result is a general structural theorem which provides a generalisation of Goblot's theorem to the setting of locally small directed sets. We then present the first systematic study of generalised cofinal Kurepa families. We establish their existence in the constructible universe $L$ and under specific cardinal arithmetic hypotheses. Then, we apply our structural result to show that $\mathrm{lim}^{n+2} \mathbf{C}_{[\kappa]^{\aleph_n}} = 0$ in environments where the appropriate cofinal Kurepa families exist.
  In contrast, we explore conditions that force these derived limits to be nonzero. In particular, we prove that certain instances of Chang's conjecture (CC), together with the existence of suitable $\diamondsuit$ sequences, imply that $\mathrm{lim}^{n+2} \mathbf{C}_{[\kappa]^{\aleph_n}} \neq 0$ for appropriate values of $\kappa$. Adapting forcing techniques from Eskew and Hayut, we construct models of these instances of CC together with the required $\diamondsuit$ sequences, establishing the consistency, for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, of $\mathrm{lim}^{n+2} \mathbf{C}_{[\aleph_{\omega_n}]^{\aleph_n}} \neq 0$.

papers.title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
papers.abstract: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.

papers.intro:
Ensemble methods are a well-established class of machine learning techniques that improve generalization by aggregating the predictions of multiple models. Their effectiveness is typically attributed to two complementary factors: the performance of the individual members and the diversity among them (Krogh and Vedelsby, 1994; Wood et al., 2023). Improving individual members lowers their individual error, while diversity promotes error de-correlation, allowing aggregation to cancel out model-specific mistakes.

Ensemble methods are a well-established class of machine learning techniques that improve generalization by aggregating the predictions of multiple models. Their effectiveness is typically attributed to two complementary factors: the performance of the individual members and the diversity among them (Krogh and Vedelsby, 1994; Wood et al., 2023). Improving individual members lowers their individual error, while diversity promotes error de-correlation, allowing aggregation to cancel out model-specific mistakes.

Classical ensemble methods induce diversity implicitly via bagging (Breiman, 1996), as in random forests (Breiman, 2001), where members are trained on different subsets of the data, whereas boosting methods, such as gradient boosting (Friedman, 2001), construct members sequentially to focus on errors made by earlier models. In deep learning, diversity can be encouraged explicitly through mechanisms such as negative-correlation learning (Chen and Yao, 2009), extended to deep ensembles by Buschjäger et al. (2020), or expert orthogonalization (Liu et al., 2024). However, Fort et al. (2019) showed that, in many cases, initializing ensemble members with different random weights is sufficient to induce substantial diversity. Later, it was shown that explicitly maximizing expert diversity can be harmful to overall ensemble performance (Wood et al., 2023).

Mixture-of-experts models combine several experts with input-dependent weights produced by a learned router (gating network) (Jacobs et al., 1991). Sparse variants, in which only a subset of experts is active for a given input, have gained prominence because of their computational advantages in large-scale language modeling. In the most prominent setting, each expert, or subset of experts, is responsible for a particular region of the input domain, allowing the ensemble to approximate the capacity of a larger model while retaining the computational cost of a smaller one. Existing variants balance computation and model capacity in different ways: selecting the top-kk experts for each input (Shazeer et al., 2017), maximizing cost reduction by routing each input to a single expert (Fedus et al., 2022), or allocating a dynamic number of experts per input (Wang et al., 2025). Routing-based methods decompose prediction into two coupled subproblems: a routing problem, handled by a router, and a prediction problem, handled by the experts.

This motivates studying whether increasing the number of routers improves the allocation of unseen samples to experts and, consequently, the overall performance of the ensemble. Recent methods combine multiple routers (Zhang et al., 2025; Ran et al., 2025) and tune their number as a hyperparameter. However, to our knowledge, there is no systematic analysis of router ensembles through the lens of ensemble theory. papers.title: Lower bounds on ranks of universal quadratic forms through geometry-of-numbers
papers.abstract: We obtain lower bounds for the ranks of universal forms over totally real cubic fields using techniques from geometry-of-numbers and the parametrisation of cubic rings by binary cubics due to Delone--Faddeev. Additionally, our methods give lower bounds for totally real primitive fields of any degree with codifferent generated by a totally positive element.

The study of quadratic forms and the integers they represent has a long history, dating back essentially to the origins of mathematics itself. In this article, we will focus on positive definite universal forms, that is, positive definite quadratic forms that represent all positive integers. Over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, Lagrange proved that every positive integer can be represented by the sum of four squares, or in other words that the form x2+y2+z2+w2x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+w^{2} is universal.

papers.title: Density fluctuations in pseudo-streamer and helmet streamer: Generation, propagation and comparison with Metis observations
papers.abstract: Recent white-light observations from the Metis coronagraph on board Solar Orbiter have shown the presence of propagating density fluctuations with a period of $\sim5$ minutes, particularly in the observationally bright regions of helmet streamers and pseudo-streamers. These density fluctuations have been shown to originate from magnetohydrodynamic wave modes -- slow and fast modes can directly compress the plasma, whereas Alfv\'en waves generate density fluctuations via a non-linear coupling with the slow and fast modes. In general, in low plasma $\beta$ regions, slow modes contribute more towards the generation of density fluctuations, whereas in high $\beta$ regions, there are significant contributions from both slow and fast waves. In this work, we investigate the propagation of (non-linear) Alfv\'en waves and the associated density fluctuations using a 2.5D axisymmetric global solar wind model that includes two distinct magnetic field topologies -- a helmet streamer and a pseudo-streamer. Key differences in these magnetic configurations give rise to differences in the wave behaviour due to, for example, the presence of a current sheet in the helmet streamer and an X-type null point in the pseudo-streamer, and the structure of the $\beta = 1$ layer in both magnetic field configurations. This leads to the possible creation of prominent interference patterns along the helmet streamer axis, which do not appear along the pseudo-streamer axis. Unlike in the streamer region, we also find that along the pseudo-streamer axis, the contribution to the density fluctuations is due to the fast waves only, despite being in a low $\beta$ plasma.

papers.intro:
The solar atmosphere is filled with magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves, which are expected to play an important role in the transport of energy. While there are three decoupled fundamental MHD wave modes in a homogeneous medium – Alfvén, and slow and fast magnetoacoustic modes – a direct observation of the fundamental wave modes is less likely due to the complex plasma distribution in the solar atmosphere. Instead, a combination of the fundamental modes or effects due to them are routinely observed (e.g. Cirtain et al., 2007; De Pontieu et al., 2007; Banerjee et al., 2009; Banerjee et al., 2021; Jess et al., 2023, and references therein). Furthermore, the presence of periodic (or quasi-periodic) fluctuations/inhomogeneities in the solar atmosphere suggests their wave origin. Some examples of these fluctuations/inhomogeneities are provided below.

While Alfvén waves are difficult to observe directly as they require simultaneous measurements of velocity and magnetic field fluctuations, Kumar et al. (2026) recently showed that through non-linear effects, they could be associated with density perturbations, observed as white-light intensity fluctuations. For example, recent white-light observations by the Metis coronagraph on board Solar Orbiter have revealed the presence of propagating 5-minute oscillations in helmet streamers as well as pseudo-streamers, extending as far as up to ∼2.3​R⊙\sim 2.3\,R_{\odot} in the middle corona (Andretta et al., 2025). In this study, the authors detected fluctuations of the order of ∼0.1%\sim 0.1\% of the background density in the corona, propagating with speeds ranging in 150−450​km​s−1150-450\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} measured along different paths in the Metis field of view.

The 5-minute periodicity (3​mHz3\,\mathrm{mHz} frequency) associated with the density fluctuations in Andretta et al. (2025) corresponds to the dominant periodicity of the global internal pressure waves (p-modes) of the Sun. Hence, these authors suggest that the observed density fluctuations are due to the p-modes. On the global scale, gravitational stratification imposes an acoustic cutoff such that frequencies lower than 3​mHz3\,\mathrm{mHz} are filtered out and only higher frequencies can propagate through the upper layers of the solar atmosphere (e.g. Felipe and Sangeetha, 2020, and references therein). However, the acoustic cutoff can vary if the magnetic field strength and its inclination with respect to the direction of wave propagation are changed (Jefferies et al., 2006; Stangalini et al., 2011). As the purely acoustic p-mode waves reach upper layers of the atmosphere, they can mode convert into Alfvén and slow magnetoacoustic wave modes (e.g. Schunker and Cally, 2006; Cally and Goossens, 2008; Khomenko and Cally, 2012, and references therein) that can produce wave-like fluctuations with a corresponding period.

While Alfvén waves remain challenging to detect from remote observations, previous studies have linked such oscillations with the injection of Alfvénic waves in the corona (Morton et al., 2019). Recent observations from the Cryo-NIRSP on board the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) have also shown the presence of high frequency (>10​mHz>10\,\mathrm{mHz}) Alfvénic waves as well as the presence of small amplitude torsional Alfvén waves (Morton et al., 2025b; Morton et al., 2025a). In the solar wind, Parker Solar Probe (PSP) observations of Alfvénic wave trains with periods around 55 minutes at ∼9.9​R⊙\sim 9.9\,R_{\odot} have also been reported (Huang et al., 2026). Furthermore, p-modes can also modulate magnetic reconnection to generate short period periodic density structures in the heliosphere (Viall et al., 2008; Kepko et al., 2024, e.g.).

(2025). Density fluctuations can be generated directly from the slow and fast magnetoacoustic modes, or indirectly from Alfvén waves undergoing mode conversion to the compressive slow and fast modes. Alfvén waves can mode convert via non-linear ponderomotive effects (Hollweg et al., 1982; Verwichte et al., 1999), non-linear phase mixing (Heyvaerts and Priest, 1983; Nakariakov et al., 1997; Botha et al., 2000; Thurgood and McLaughlin, 2013), or a combination of both. Using both Alfvén and magnetoacoustic waves in their simulations, Kumar et al. (2026) demonstrated that the dynamical behaviour of the resulting density fluctuations is similar in both cases, with slow modes predominantly contributing to the generation of density fluctuations in a low β\beta regime, and significant contributions from both slow and fast modes in the high β\beta regime. A helmet streamer consists of a single system of coronal loops that extend outwards to form a current sheet that separates opposite polarity magnetic field lines. In contrast, a pseudo-streamer consists of two adjacent coronal arcades that open into the same magnetic polarity, with the open field lines separated by a separatrix. As such, there is no current sheet associated with a pseudo-streamer, but there is instead an X-type null point (in two-dimensions) above the closed loops.

papers.title: No free lattice contains an infinite ascending chain of copies of FL(3)
papers.abstract:
No free lattice contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of sublattices isomorphic to FL(3), the free lattice on three generators; this answers a question that R. A. Dean asked and the second author's 1997 notes on the problem left open. Every such chain would yield, inside FL(3), a coherent chain of proper self-embeddings $\Theta_0, \Theta_1, \Theta_2, \dots$ with $\Theta_k \circ \Theta_j = \Theta_j$ for $j < k$, so that each later embedding fixes the image of each earlier one pointwise. Every proper self-embedding of FL(3) whose fixed sublattice contains a free generating triple fixes one of the three generators, say $z$, because a power of it or of its dual lies above the identity, and a self-embedding that moves every generator and lies above the identity fixes at most eleven elements. Up to duality, a proper self-embedding fixing the image of such a $\Theta_1$ pointwise fixes only elements above $z \wedge (x \vee y)$, where no free generating triple containing $z$ can lie. We also verify the one-step example of the 1997 notes, prove that no step toward such a chain is self-similar, and show that the configuration the argument rules out at length three does occur at length two.
  Without freeness the answer reverses: FL(3) contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of 3-generated sublattices, so the lattice analogue of Takahasi's chain condition for free groups fails. The theorem itself is checked by the Agda proof assistant under its safe flags, for free lattices over generators with decidable equality, and its formal proof uses no classical principle: finite searches and an induction on a finite set replace the infinite pigeonhole principle by which a chain yields a coherent chain.

papers.title: Pseudo-profiles for vectorial Allen-Cahn systems
papers.abstract: The purpose of the present paper is to present a new type of solutions to the elliptic vectorial Allen-Cahn system of equations. Its main feature is that in the classical rescaling its asymptotics do not follow the rule of balance of energies, which is crucial in the analysis of the asymptotics for the scalar problem.

papers.title: Analytical treatment of reentrant localization via Lyapunov branch structure
papers.abstract: In reentrant localization, states become localized under a growing quasiperiodic potential partly become extended again before localizing once more. So far this has been demonstrated only numerically. Here we prove it in a chain of weakly coupled dimers in which we vary only the overall strength of a fixed onsite potential. As the strength increases, the lower orbital of each dimer shifts its weight between the two sites. At a particular strength, the quasiperiodic potential it feels cancels, while the hopping between dimers stays finite. When the energy scales are well separated, we prove that, over a finite range of potential strengths, all states in a central part of the lower band, one third of its states, have a vanishing Lyapunov exponent that is stable against small changes of phase, the certification of extended states. On both sides of this range, all states are localized. Numerical calculations confirm that the recovery covers the whole lower band, while the upper band stays localized.

papers.intro:
Anderson localization shows how in a disordered medium, interference can confine waves and suppress diffusion [5]. In one dimension, uncorrelated onsite disorder produces localization even at weak disorder [2]. Quasiperiodic potentials provide a different setting: their deterministic correlations allow localization transitions at finite modulation strength. The Aubry-André (AA) model [6, 20, 25] is the standard example, with a self-dual transition criteria, the potential amplitude equals twice the hopping [29]. Localization in such models is most often characterized through the Lyapunov exponent, or equivalently the localization length, and through participation ratios and the multifractal structure of eigenstates [30, 14]. Beyond these probes, localization in AA-type models has also been studied through bulk polarization and geometric Binder cumulants [24, 23].

Extensions of the AA model reveal a richer spectral structure. Longer-range hopping and changes in the onsite potential can produce mobility edges, separating localized and extended states at different energies [9, 33, 15, 34, 57, 64, 19, 56, 26]. Non-Hermitian models extend these questions to asymmetric hopping and complex onsite potentials, where localization is connected to changes in the complex spectrum and, in some models, symmetry breaking [21, 36, 55, 65, 27, 32, 22, 53, 37, 35]. The AA model and its generalizations have also been studied on ladders [42, 52], two-dimensional lattices [48, 13], diamond chains [3], and helical structures [61, 62]. These examples show that localization depends on both the strength and the structure of the modulation.

Quasiperiodic localization has been observed with ultracold atoms in optical lattices [41] and light in photonic waveguide arrays [31]. In atomic systems, interactions can be tuned while keeping the spatial potential fixed. This connects quasiperiodic localization to many-body localization, where an isolated interacting system can retain local memory and fail to thermalize [8, 1]. Experiments with interacting fermions in a quasiperiodic optical lattice have observed a density imbalance that persists over the accessible times [46]. Related studies of interacting localization have used trapped-ion simulators [47] and superconducting circuits [43].

Reentrant localization changes this sequence. A further increase in an onsite control can restore spatial extent in part of the spectrum, followed by localization again at larger coupling. Such behavior has been reported in dimerized quasiperiodic chains [45, 44, 4, 60, 63], models with an additional staggered potential [39, 58, 11], lattices with longer-range hopping [18, 10, 50], helical systems [17, 16], and non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattices [40, 59, 28, 51].

Here we study this question in a nearest-neighbor chain of weakly coupled dimers. All hoppings and the spatial onsite profile remain fixed while one overall potential amplitude is varied. This amplitude changes both the local detuning and the quasiperiodic modulation. The resulting redistribution of dimer weights cancels the first-order potential in the lower band while leaving its hopping finite. The upper band has no such cancellation, so the recovery is band selective. Wang et al. [54] identified orbital-weight cancellation numerically in a trimer ladder; here we establish its consequences for the full dimer chain, beyond the projection. We place the weak hopping between the residual modulation scale near cancellation and the larger modulation away from it.

This bound limits the complexified Lyapunov exponent on the strip. Since its slopes are quantized by Avila’s global theory [7], the exponent must be flat near the real axis, and a flat positive exponent is excluded on the spectrum. papers.title: Game-Theoretic Analysis of RIS-Assisted Challenge-Response PLA - Part II: Partial Channel Knowledge
papers.abstract: We consider a physical layer authentication scenario in which a legitimate user (Alice) communicates with an authenticator (Bob) through a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), controlled by Bob. An attacker (Trudy) aims to impersonate Alice by suitably precoding her messages and still transmitting them through the RIS. This two-part study analyzes this attack-defense interaction between Bob and Trudy under perfect (Part I) and partial (Part II) channel knowledge by all the agents. Part I formulates the joint RIS selection and precoder design under perfect channel knowledge as a finite zero-sum game, establishing exact channel subspace conditions for attack indistinguishability alongside equilibrium mixed strategies. Part II extends the defense to incomplete channel information, where each agent observes only its own channel, by formulating a finite-action Bayesian game and characterizing the resulting Bayesian Nash equilibrium. Simulations in geometric and 3GPP TR 38.901 UMi-NLOS channels reveal that authentication performance is governed by available spatial degrees of freedom, channel correlation, and operating signal-to-noise ratio. The proposed equilibrium strategies effectively balance communication rate and security, outperforming conventional benchmark policies.

papers.intro:
Authentication is the process enabling communicating entities to mutually verify their identities or allow one party to verify another. Asymmetric cryptographic primitives under computational security represent the standard solution; however, advances in cryptanalysis and quantum computing necessitate post-quantum alternatives whose complexity can constrain resource-limited devices [1].

Asymmetric cryptographic primitives under computational security represent the standard solution; however, advances in cryptanalysis and quantum computing necessitate post-quantum alternatives whose complexity can constrain resource-limited devices [1].

Physical Layer Authentication (physical layer authentication (PLA)) complements cryptography by operating outside the computational security paradigm. PLA has been investigated across diverse environments, including orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) and multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications [2, 3] and underwater acoustic channels [4]. Decision mechanisms span from classical Neyman-Pearson statistical tests [5] to modern machine learning models [6]. These schemes extract physical signal features, such as channel frequency response (CFR) and channel impulse response (CIR) [7], as well as angle-of-arrival (AoA) [8, 9], to differentiate legitimate transmitters from adversaries. Both classical statistical tools and machine learning classifiers are applied for user discrimination [10]. In standard tag-based PLA, the observed channel state during transmission is evaluated against a reference fingerprint acquired during a trusted association phase.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs)) dynamically shape propagation environments and enhance PLA effectiveness. Optimizing RIS reflections toward target locations increases channel distinctiveness and improves tag-based authentication accuracy [11], including non-line-of-sight vehicular scenarios [12]. Channel-estimating hybrid RIS architectures enable CFR-based authentication [13], whereas other approaches combine RIS spatial control with pre-shared cryptographic keys [14] or employ convolutional neural networks to withstand time-varying channels [15].

Beyond static enhancement, RIS reconfigurability enables challenge-response PLA (challenge-response PLA (CR-PLA)) [16, 17, 18, 19]. In CR-PLA, the verifier randomly selects an RIS configuration as a challenge and checks whether the resulting cascaded response matches expected legitimate propagation. Security depends heavily on attacker knowledge: when the verifier randomly perturbs the RIS configuration around its optimal communication state, an adversary forging responses via a maximum a posteriori probability (MAP) channel estimate can degrade CR-PLA into tag-based PLA if equipped with sufficient spatial degrees of freedom and perfect channel knowledge [17]. Optimizing RIS phase perturbation distributions maximizes rate bounds under misdetection constraints across single- and multi-antenna setups in Rayleigh fading [18, 19], while geometric analyses establish conditions under which a fully informed multi-antenna attacker becomes indistinguishable from a single-antenna legitimate user [20].

Although game-theoretic PLA models exist [21, 22], early formulations lacked reconfigurable environments or challenge-response dynamics. In Part I [23], CR-PLA was modeled as a finite zero-sum game under perfect channel knowledge. In this two-part work, we consider a RIS-assisted CR-PLA system in which a multi-antenna verifier, Bob, controls a RIS to authenticate a multi-antenna legitimate user, Alice, while a multi-antenna attacker, Trudy, precodes her transmission to impersonate Alice. All signals reach Bob through the RIS. In this second part of the work, we consider the scenario in which each player observes only its own channel realization and knows the statistics of the opponent’s channel, whose correlation with Alice’s channel models the spatial proximity of Trudy to Alice. Compared to the case of complete knowledge of the channel, discussed in Part I of this work, this incomplete information changes the nature of the problem in three respects. First, each player optimizes an interim utility conditioned on its private information, so that the interaction must be modeled as a Bayesian game [24], whose solution concept is the Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE), rather than as a complete-information zero-sum game with a minimax solution. Second, the players’ strategies become type-dependent: Bob’s randomization policy depends on the realization of Alice’s channel, and Trudy’s precoding strategy on the realization of her own channel. Third, Trudy can no longer compute a dedicated precoder for each RIS configuration and channel realization, and must rely on a precoder codebook designed offline from channel statistics. To the best of our knowledge, the Bayesian game arising in RIS-assisted CR-PLA under incomplete channel information has not been investigated so far.

papers.title: Epitaxial integration of GaN $\mu$-platelets and thin films on metallic TiN using a hybrid approach
papers.abstract: We demonstrate the synthesis of epitaxial, self-organized GaN $\mu$-platelets on metallic TiN thin films. To this end, we first nucleate self-assembled GaN nanowires with number densities between 0.01 to 300 $\mu m^{-2}$ by molecular beam epitaxy. Subsequent overgrowth of these seed nanowires by metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy yields GaN $\mu$-platelets with corresponding number densities. The platelets exhibit N-polarity and form an ohmic contact to the metallic TiN substrate. By adjusting the growth conditions during the metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy, particularly the carrier gas and precursor ratio, the morphology of the GaN can be controlled across a broad range. Growth under N$_{2}$ carrier gas and with a 1:1 NH$_{3}$/trimethylgallium precursor flow ratio results in platelet ensembles with broad diameter and height distributions. In contrast, employing an N$_{2}$/H$_{2}$ carrier gas mixture promotes the formation of more homogeneous ensembles with narrower size distributions around a diameter of $\approx$2 $\mu m$. Finally, N-rich growth conditions under H$_{2}$ carrier gas enhance lateral growth, leading to the formation of coalesced GaN layers. GaN grown under these latter conditions exhibits strong near-band-edge emission, accompanied by only weak deep-level luminescence at room temperature.

Group-III nitrides, particularly GaN, are the dominant semiconductor materials in solid-state lighting Pust et al. (2015); Weinold et al. (2025) and are becoming increasingly important for power electronics. Amano et al. (2018); Tu et al. (2024). Currently, common III-nitride devices such as light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and high electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) are typically based on quasi-vertical and lateral architectures, respectively. A fully vertical architecture, in contrast, uses a conductive substrate as the bottom electrode, thus enabling direct vertical current conduction through the active region of a device. This design offers several advantages over conventional lateral architectures, including superior current spreading, improved heat dissipation, reduced series resistance, and potentially higher integration density. Li and Wu (2012); Zhang et al. (2018); You et al. (2021); Shankari et al. (2026) Despite these benefits, vertical III-nitride-based devices remain relatively scarce.

The limited vertical integration of III-nitrides likely stems from two main challenges. First, bulk GaN substrates are still mainly available on a small scale and at high cost. Second, while heteroepitaxy of GaN on large and cost-effective substrates such as sapphire and Si is nowadays widely established, neither substrate offers a straightforward pathway towards vertical GaN-based devices. Due to its electrically insulating nature, sapphire prevents any vertical current transport through the substrate. Growth on Si, on the other hand, generally requires an insulating buffer layer such as AlN to suppress the reaction between Ga and Si known as meltback etching. Consequently, fabricating vertical devices from heterostructures grown on Si demands additional and complex processing steps, such as layer transfer or etching through both the Si substrate and the insulating buffer layer to establish an electrical backside contact Zhang et al. (2018).

papers.title: TotalSegmentator Aorta Report: Automated Aortic Diameter Measurement at 11 Standardized Landmarks on CT Images
papers.abstract:
Purpose: To develop and evaluate a fully automated, open-source tool that measures aortic diameters at 11 standardized landmarks from the aortic annulus to the bifurcation on any CT image, following current guideline recommendations.
  Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 239 arterial phase CT angiography examinations of 230 patients (median age, 65 years [range, 18-99 years]; 163 men) performed between April 2025 and October 2026 (209 electrocardiographically [ECG] gated). The tool locates landmarks from TotalSegmentator segmentations of aortic branches and vertebrae and measures the maximum diameter at each. A senior radiologist reviewed and, where needed, corrected the automated measurements to create the reference standard. Agreement was assessed with mean absolute error (MAE), bias, and differences greater than 2 mm.
  Results: Across all landmarks, MAE was 1.06 mm (95% CI: 0.91, 1.22), and 86.6% (95% CI: 84.4, 88.5) of differences were 2 mm or less. The tool measured slightly larger diameters (bias, 0.45 mm [95% CI: 0.34, 0.57]). The sinuses of Valsalva had the largest MAE (2.17 mm [95% CI: 1.59, 2.86]). For 1.2% of landmarks, the automatic measurement failed. Examination-level MAE did not differ significantly by pathology, atherosclerosis grade (P=.95), or ECG gating (P=.14). Examinations with mural thrombus more often had an MAE greater than 2 mm (50% [95% CI: 31, 69] vs 20%; P=.03).
  Conclusion: The tool measured aortic diameters at 11 landmarks along the entire aorta with an MAE of about 1 mm, below published interreader variability. Agreement was lower at the aortic root and with mural thrombus.
  Code availability: The tool is open source and freely available at https://github.com/wasserth/TotalSegmentator.

papers.intro:
Aortic diameter is the main measurement for the diagnosis, surveillance, and treatment planning of aortic disease. Guidelines recommend reporting diameters at defined anatomic landmarks, measured perpendicular to the vessel axis, and base the timing of follow-up and intervention on these values [1, 2, 3]. Manual measurement in double-oblique reformations is time-consuming, and its reproducibility is limited: differences between readers of 1.6–5 mm are common, which is in the same range as the growth that guidelines regard as clinically relevant [4, 5]. Aortic dilatation is also underreported when diameters are not measured systematically [6]. Automated measurement could make reporting faster and more consistent [7].

Aortic diameter is the main measurement for the diagnosis, surveillance, and treatment planning of aortic disease. Guidelines recommend reporting diameters at defined anatomic landmarks, measured perpendicular to the vessel axis, and base the timing of follow-up and intervention on these values [1, 2, 3]. Manual measurement in double-oblique reformations is time-consuming, and its reproducibility is limited: differences between readers of 1.6–5 mm are common, which is in the same range as the growth that guidelines regard as clinically relevant [4, 5]. Aortic dilatation is also underreported when diameters are not measured systematically [6]. Automated measurement could make reporting faster and more consistent [7].

Several deep learning tools measure aortic diameters at CT. The most widely studied commercial tool measures nine thoracic landmarks and agrees with readers to within 1.3–2.6 mm on average [8, 9, 10, 11]. However, its validations were mostly restricted to one scan type, such as ECG-gated CT angiography (CTA) [8] or low-dose unenhanced CT [10], it does not cover the abdominal aorta below the celiac trunk, and its errors were largest at the aortic root [11, 12]. Other tools report only the maximum diameter of a thoracic segment [13], the maximum diameter per segment of the whole aorta [14, 15], or a single maximum diameter of the abdominal aorta [16]. Openly available tools that measure diameters at standardized landmarks along the entire aorta, from the annulus to the bifurcation, remain scarce. Such landmark-based measurements are needed for structured reporting and for comparing the same location at follow-up.

TotalSegmentator is a widely used open-source model for segmenting anatomic structures at CT [17]. We extended it with an aorta report that places 11 landmarks along the aortic centerline and measures the diameter at each. The tool is designed to work on any CT image, independent of contrast phase and ECG gating. The purpose of this study was to develop this tool and to evaluate its agreement with radiologist-corrected measurements at arterial phase CTA, overall, per landmark, and in subgroups defined by aortic pathology, atherosclerosis, and ECG gating.

papers.title: TSP instances that require exponentially many subtour elimination constraints
papers.abstract: We construct pathological TSP instances that require exponentially many subtour elimination constraints (SECs) in the sense that, if a smaller collection of SECs is imposed, then the Dantzig-Fulkerson-Johnson model returns a disconnected solution costing less than an optimal tour. For asymmetric instances on $n$ vertices, we prove a growth rate of \(\Omega(\phi^n)\), where \(\phi\approx 1.618\) is the golden ratio. A node-splitting reduction gives metric instances with \(\Omega(\phi^{n/2})\) growth. We also give instances in the plane under the Euclidean, Rectilinear, and Maximum metrics that require exponentially many SECs. Concorde struggles on them, with solve times growing exponentially despite tiny integrality gaps.

papers.title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification
papers.abstract: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. Interactive theorem proving offers a complement: the theorem and its proof are written as code, and every inference is checked by a small, trusted piece of software called the kernel. This paper serves as an introduction to the Lean 4 proof assistant for a system identification and control audience, assuming no prior exposure to formal methods. We first show how a Lean proof is read using two elementary examples: the first on identifiability, the second on set invariance. We then illustrate how Lean can be used to analyse results from the literature, taking as example a classic lemma on the inversion of the noise filter in prediction-error identification (Ljung, 1999, Lemma 3.1). Since in Lean every step must be justified, the formalization brings to light a subtle point: the original claim of that lemma holds almost surely, although not for every realisation, as its statement may suggest. A simple counterexample makes this concrete. Finally, the paper discusses guidelines and perspectives on the use of Lean in system identification research.

papers.intro:
Theoretical results in system identification and control often come with intricate proofs built on, e.g., pages of matrix inequalities, probabilistic arguments, and asymptotic analyses. Delicate steps involving limits, expectations, or modes of convergence are sometimes condensed or omitted, often for readability, for lack of space, to suit a mixed audience of engineers and mathematicians, or simply by oversight. Refereeing such proofs in detail is demanding, thus, implicit assumptions, gaps, imprecisions, and occasionally outright errors still reach the published literature.

Interactive theorem provers (proof assistants) offer a complement. The authors write the proof in a formal language, and a small, trusted program, the so-called kernel, checks every step. Landmark results in mathematics have been verified this way, including the Kepler conjecture, implemented in HOL Light and Isabelle (Hales and others, 2017), and, more recently, the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture (Gowers et al., 2025), whose proof was formalized in Lean within weeks of its announcement. In September 2026, OpenAI announced an AI-generated proof, formalized in Lean, of finite-time blow-up for a forced three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes system (OpenAI, 2026), at the time of writing of this paper, the result has not been independently reviewed.

Our contributions are threefold. First, Section 2 walks the reader through a warm-up proof and two elementary examples, on identifiability under persistent excitation and on the invariance of an interval for a linear system, each shown side by side with its pen-and-paper proof. Second, Section 3 illustrates the use of Lean to analyse published results, taking as example Ljung (1999, Lemma 3.1) on the inversion of the noise filter. As is common in textbooks, Ljung’s proof condenses some routine steps, however, formalizing it in Lean requires each of them to be justified. One step in particular, the interchange of an infinite double sum, needs a technical condition that is not automatic, and we provide a counterexample showing that it cannot be dropped. The condition is satisfied for bounded noise, for which the original claim holds unchanged. For white noise with finite variance, the standing assumption of the book, the condition, and hence the claim, holds almost surely, not for all realisations; the lemma omits this detail. Third, Section 4 proposes a four-step template and guidelines for writing Lean code in system identification, illustrated on the identifiability of ARX models.

papers.title: Process Mining-Enabled Federated Anomaly Detection for the Industrial IoT
papers.abstract: While federated anomaly detection enables the integration of local data insights across diverse nodes to reduce false positives, it inherently struggles with non-IID data. In practice, industrial IoT plants often operate under varying conditions and experience diverse environmental phenomena, resulting in significant heterogeneity in the monitored time series. In such settings, standard federated learning approaches fail to perform nuanced aggregation that accounts for these cross-node differences, ultimately leading to increased false positive rates. In this paper, we propose a process mining approach to evaluate the similarity of local node data against a reference provided by a global node. The global node utilizes these similarity metrics to dynamically weight local models during aggregation, producing personalized updates distributed across the network. We evaluate our approach using industrial IoT time-series data collected from manufacturing plants operating under distinct conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our process mining-enabled federated anomaly detection pipeline achieves superior performance, yielding a 46.52% and 11.99% relative improvement in F1-score compared to isolated local training baselines and standard FedAvg, respectively, alongside a 51.24% relative reduction in false positives over standard federated aggregation.

papers.intro:
Anomaly detection for industrial IoT is an ever-popular task that allows evaluating whether the monitored plants are operating as expected and diagnosing faults that may occur due to physical disruptions or plant wear [1]. Typically, industrial IoT applications involve multiple plants working in different operating conditions that may alternate over time [2]. Notably, this makes the ability to characterize normal behavior more challenging, as modern anomaly detection approaches involve machine learning algorithms that learn normal behavior from data and may struggle with either over-generalization or overfitting [3].

Typically, industrial IoT applications involve multiple plants working in different operating conditions that may alternate over time [2]. Notably, this makes the ability to characterize normal behavior more challenging, as modern anomaly detection approaches involve machine learning algorithms that learn normal behavior from data and may struggle with either over-generalization or overfitting [3].

To account for the distributed nature of industrial IoT applications, federated anomaly detection can be used. This paradigm involves aggregating diverse knowledge from different local nodes to improve the ability to discriminate normal behavior from anomalous observations [4]. This paradigm is advantageous in distributed environments thanks to the reduction in communication overhead of local data to a centralized server and the increased privacy guarantees. However, a critical issue plagues federated anomaly detection, namely non-IID data [5]. As mentioned, this issue is frequently encountered in industrial IoT plants, where varying operating conditions make it difficult to establish a solid reference normal profile and accurately evaluate anomalous behavior.

In order to deal with non-IID data, several federated anomaly detection approaches have been proposed. They perform client clustering based on node similarity from local models’ weights [6, 7, 8] or evaluate clients’ similarity based on data distribution indices [9, 4, 10, 11, 12]. However, these approaches often incur significant computational and communication overhead during the federated rounds, or they struggle to accurately capture the complex, sequential operational variations specific to industrial processes.

To overcome these limitations, we propose a process mining-enabled federated anomaly detection approach. Process mining is a research area able to automatically extract behavioral models from event data and verify conformance of new data against such models [13]; notably, process mining has been successfully applied to time-series sensor data [14, 15, 16]. By capturing the underlying behavioral control-flow of the industrial assets, process mining allows constructing a similarity matrix that provides a weight distribution that guides the personalized aggregation of the anomaly detection models. This naturally mitigates the non-IID problem while preserving communication efficiency in federated anomaly detection.

papers.title: Large language models put existential risk from artificial intelligence at 10%
papers.abstract: How likely is it that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) will cause human extinction or a similarly permanent disempowerment of humanity? Humans, including AI experts, frequently disagree on this question. Yet one important perspective is missing from this debate: that of AI systems themselves. We put the question to 241 large language models (LLMs) at every available reasoning setting. The models converged on a median risk of 10.0%, with the middle 90% of their estimates between 3.5% and 15.8%, far narrower than the spread among human experts. More expensive, and typically more capable, models stated higher risks; newer models showed more uniform, but not higher, risks. More reasoning barely changed the models' estimates but widened their uncertainty, mostly toward higher risk. Almost all models named loss of control over AI as the most likely cause. These answers are not independent judgments; they likely echo training data, including published expert polls, and choices made in aligning the models. Still, they document the position that current AI systems state on the risks of their own technology. Whether this position reflects any genuine understanding of the systems' own capabilities remains open. Repeated measurements can show whether it shifts as AI systems advance, and how training and alignment shape it is a question for both research and public debate.

papers.title: Essential spectrum of singularly perturbed Dirac operators on bounded domains
papers.abstract: In this paper self-adjoint Dirac operators on bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ with elliptic boundary conditions perturbed by singular $\delta$-shell potentials supported on compact curves or surfaces are considered. While the unperturbed operator has purely discrete spectrum, it is shown that certain critical values of the interaction strengths lead to the appearance of essential spectrum. More precisely, each connected component of the interaction support, where the coupling constants have such critical values, produces in dimension two a point and in dimension three even a closed interval in the essential spectrum, where the size of the latter depends on the geometry and the coupling constants.

papers.title: Scalar Entropic Damage Transport: Well-posed softening with a single damage variable
papers.abstract: Entropic Damage Transport (EDT) represents material softening via a local continuum damage model while ensuring the well-posedness of the mechanical boundary value problem. It is based on a convexification of the time-incremental potential associated with a rate-limited scalar damage model. A one-dimensional distribution of damage states serves as the internal variable, and the number of these states grows with the number of time steps. We show that the emergence of the damage distribution is an artifact of the time discretization. Surprisingly, the distribution concentrates at a single damage state in the time-continuous limit, and EDT converges to a rate-limited damage model with a scalar damage variable, whose free energy is jointly convex in the strain and the reciprocal degradation. We exploit this hidden convexity by a frozen-metric discretization in terms of the reciprocal degradation, which renders every increment jointly convex. The resulting scalar update preserves damage irreversibility, the prescribed damage-rate limitation and thermomechanical consistency, reduces to a scalar equation and provides a symmetric and positive definite algorithmic tangent in closed form. Computational experiments assess the accuracy and the efficiency of both formulations from the material point to the microstructure level, and demonstrate that the scalar update permits a finite-element computation of industrial size with more than 14 million degrees of freedom.

papers.intro:
Local continuum damage mechanics describes the progressive loss of load-carrying capacity of a material by a degradation variable affecting the free energy. Its first concepts emerged from creep-rupture studies [1, 2] and were subsequently embedded into thermodynamically consistent constitutive frameworks [3, 4, 5], see the review by Krajcinovic [6] and the monograph by Murakami [7]. Various variables are in use to carry the damage, among them scalar degradations and damage tensors [8] as well as stiffness- or compliance-based variables [9, 10].

Its first concepts emerged from creep-rupture studies [1, 2] and were subsequently embedded into thermodynamically consistent constitutive frameworks [3, 4, 5], see the review by Krajcinovic [6] and the monograph by Murakami [7]. Various variables are in use to carry the damage, among them scalar degradations and damage tensors [8] as well as stiffness- or compliance-based variables [9, 10].

Softening renders such models useful for failure prediction [11], for instance of fiber-reinforced composites [12, 13, 14]. Computations which resolve the microstructure, be it of a lab-size coupon [15] or of the unit cells of a multiscale chain [16, 17, 18], typically evaluate a local constitutive law at every material point. In such a finite-element computation, however, damage tends to localize into a single band of elements whose width decreases with the element size. Thus, the material response depends on the mesh, and, without a regularization, the energy dissipated in the band typically tends to zero under refinement, as the dissipation per unit volume remains bounded whereas the volume of the band vanishes [19]. This deficiency of rate-independent softening models was recognized early [20] and motivated nonlocal remedies [21]. For a comparison of these remedies, see Jirásek [22], and for a review, see Bažant and Jirásek [23]. Mathematically, softening typically deprives the incremental potential of a local damage model of its quasiconvexity, so that minimizers of the associated boundary value problem need not exist [24, 25]. At the level of rates, localization may be accompanied by a loss of ellipticity of the boundary value problem for the displacement rate, which is detected when the acoustic tensor formed with the tangent stiffness ceases to be positive definite for some direction of propagation [26].

At the level of rates, localization may be accompanied by a loss of ellipticity of the boundary value problem for the displacement rate, which is detected when the acoustic tensor formed with the tangent stiffness ceases to be positive definite for some direction of propagation [26].

The remedies proposed in the literature fall into four classes. • Mesh adjustment. Engineering practice commonly adapts the constitutive law to the mesh. The crack-band model [27] ties the band width to a characteristic element length, which fixes the dissipated energy by a deliberate adjustment of the softening law to this length. Phenomenological approaches such as GISSMO [28], widespread in crashworthiness and sheet metal forming, reduce the mesh sensitivity by tabulating failure parameters over the element size. These parameters are tied to the discretization for which they were identified and have to be identified anew for every element size. The adjustment regularizes the dissipated energy, not the boundary value problem, whose solution still localizes into a single row of elements aligned with the mesh. • Rate limitation. This class starts from the observation that inertia bounds the speed at which a crack propagates [29] and thus how fast the stored energy may be dissipated. A quasi-static computation neglects inertia, so that nothing prevents the damage from jumping within a single time step, and the constitutive law has to supply this limit instead. Viscous models penalize a rapid damage evolution [30, 31, 32], and the delay-damage models bound the damage rate by a characteristic time [33, 34, 35]. In dynamics, this time and the elastic wave speed combine into an internal length [19], whose regularizing effect fades for slow loading and may be absent for dynamic failure out of rest [36]. Quasi-statically, the rate limitation bounds the damage increment per time step without introducing a length and is thus no spatial regularization by itself. Moreover, it generally alters the elastic domain, i.e., the range of driving forces under which the damage remains inactive, unless the threshold is adjusted accordingly. Without a term linear in the damage rate, the elastic domain is lost altogether, as the damage evolves under any positive driving force unless the free energy provides a threshold [37, 38]. Viscous regularization was also combined with relaxation [39, 40], where the required viscosity may be unphysically high and its effect depends on the loading rate [41, 42]. • Nonlocal and gradient-extended models. If the damage at a material point depends on its neighborhood, a localization band cannot become narrower than an internal length, and the dissipated energy does not vanish under mesh refinement. This class comprises nonlocal averaging [43, 44, 45], gradient-extended [46, 47, 48] and micromorphic formulations [49, 50] as well as phase-field fracture [51, 52, 53]. Mathematically, the direct method requires coercivity and weak lower semicontinuity [25], and without quasiconvexity the latter fails, so that minimizing sequences oscillate on ever finer scales. Nonlocal and gradient terms upgrade weak to strong convergence of the damage field, by a compact Sobolev embedding or by the convolution with a fixed kernel. For a coercive functional, minimizers thus exist [54], which, however, need not be unique or depend continuously on the load. In practice, the incremental energy of gradient-damage and phase-field models remains nonconvex jointly in the displacement and the damage, so that the solution of a time step may be nonunique and jump under a steady increase of the prescribed loading [55, 56]. Moreover, the internal length is typically not accessible to measurement [53], and if it approaches the size of the microstructure, first-order homogenization lacks the separation of scales it requires [57, 58, 59]. Finally, the additional global field enlarges the system solved in every increment [60, 41]. • Relaxation. A nonconvex incremental potential favors the formation of microstructures on ever finer scales [61], which a finite-element computation resolves only down to the element size. Relaxation replaces the incremental potential by a generalized convex envelope – the quasiconvex, the rank-one convex or the convex one [62]. In contrast to nonlocal and gradient terms, it does not upgrade weak to strong convergence but renders the energy compatible with weak limits, as the quasiconvex envelope is weakly lower semicontinuous [25]. Relaxation does not restore coercivity, however. As the degradation of a softening model tends to zero, the incremental energy loses its coercivity in the strain, and minimizing sequences need not be bounded. The envelope stands for a microstructure on a finer scale [63, 61, 64], which relaxed damage models carry along in the evolution [39, 65, 66]. No efficient algorithm is known for the quasiconvex envelope [67, 68], one reason being that quasiconvexity lacks a local characterization [69]. Hence, the rank-one convex envelope [67, 70] or the convex one [38, 68] is taken instead, although rank-one convexity does not imply weak lower semicontinuity. Convexity alone ensures neither existence nor uniqueness. A lower semicontinuous and strongly convex incremental energy, however, admits a unique minimizer, which depends Lipschitz-continuously on the prescribed load [71]. Relaxation was also combined with a viscous regularization [40].

papers.title: Correlating orbital order and photovoltaic effect in Layered Ruddlesden-Popper Pr0.5Ca1.5MnO4 and PrCa2Mn2O7
papers.abstract: The understanding of growth and structure-property relations of epitaxial thin films of layered Ruddlesden-Popper perovskite oxides open up new pathways to tune correlated electron properties and to fabricate new types of correlated electron junctions, such as e.g. photovoltaic devices. In particular, the layered Ruddlesden-Popper systems Pr$_0.5$Ca$_1.5$MnO$_4$ and PrCa$_2$Mn$_2$O$_7$ at half doping exhibit much higher transition temperatures for the formation of charge and orbital ordered phases of $T_c$ = 320 K and $T_c$ up to 370 K, respectively, compared to the half doped non-layered system Pr$_{1-x}$Ca$_{x}$MnO$_3$ (PCMO) with $T_c$ = 240 K. Here, we demonstrate the successful growth of epitaxial PrCa$_2$Mn$_2$O$_7$ thin films by ion beam sputtering and compare electric transport, optical absorbance, electronic bandstructure and photovoltaic response with epitaxial Pr$_0.5$Ca$_1.5$MnO$_4$, both deposited on (Nb:)SrTiO$_3$ (110) substrates. An enhanced density of Ruddlesden-Popper type of stacking faults is identified as a relaxation channel for misfit strain in PrCa$_2$Mn$_2$O$_7$ and seems to be the origin for the reduced $T_c$ = 320 K and the reduced spatial coherence of charge and orbital order in comparison to Pr$_0.5$Ca$_1.5$MnO$_4$. Since the onset of the hot polaron photovoltaic effect is correlated to the formation of charge and orbital ordering, the comparative study of temperature dependent electric transport and photovoltaic response gives insights into the different role of strain and strain relaxation related defects on photo-electric properties.
