papers.intro:
The 3D Perovskite Pr1-xCaxMnO3 (PCMO)-System as well as the layered Ruddlesden-Popper variants Pr0.5Ca1.5MnO4 and PrCa2Mn2O7 are model systems for highly correlated manganite oxides that exhibit strong correlations between spins, charges, orbitals and crystal structure. These competing mutual interactions result in rich electronic phase diagrams with charge, orbital and magnetically ordered states [23],[20],[27],[40]. In the case of Mn3+ the single Mn 3d-ege_{g} electron lifts the orbital degeneracy to drive Jahn-Teller distorted MnO6 octahedra/orbitals. The Ruddlesden-Popper crystal structures Pr0.5Ca1.5MnO4 and PrCa2Mn2O7 are made up of one / two perovskite unit cells respectively, separated by an additional Pr/Ca-O ayer with a rock salt structure. This layering gives rise to a pronounced anisotropy. Due to strong electron-phonon coupling the charge carriers in PCMO as well as in the RP variants are small polarons. In the doping range between x=0.3 and x=0.9 PCMO undergoes a phase transition from a paramagnetic polaron liquid state to a 3D polaronic charge / orbital ordered state with a maximum at the ordering temperature TC​O≈240K{}_{CO}\approx 240\,$\mathrm{K}$ around half doping [23]. For the Ruddlesden-Popper phases, the transition of the polaronic liquid to the charge / orbital ordered state of quasi-two-dimensional polarons occurs at significantly higher temperatures than in the three-dimensional PCMO. For half doping, TCO of Pr0.5Ca1.5MnO4 amounts to about TCO=320​K320\,$\mathrm{K}$ [27]. In PrCa2Mn2O7, two different charge / orbital ordering transitions are observed at about TC​O1≈370K{}_{CO_{1}}\approx 370\,$\mathrm{K}$ and TC​O2≈320K{}_{CO_{2}}\approx 320$\mathrm{K}$ [40]. Previous experiments have shown that the emergence of charge and/or orbital ordering in the manganites increases the life time of optically excited polarons up to nano seconds [33]. Due to this increase, the open circuit voltage measured in illuminated junctions composed of hole-doped PCMO and n-doped Nb:SrTiO3 (STNO) significantly increases in the ordered regime below the ordering temperature TC. A correlation between TC and onset of the photovoltaic effect was observed for the orbital ordered (x=0.1) and the charge / orbital ordered (x=0.34) PCMO as well as for the Ruddlesden-Popper variant Pr0.5Ca1.5MnO4 [23],[33],[22].

papers.title: Interpretable weight-space programming builds transparent transformers and brain encoding models
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful predictors, yet their opacity limits their usefulness in science, where the goal is explanation rather than mere prediction. In neuroscience, for example, deep encoding models accurately predict brain activity in response to natural stimuli, but struggle to reveal which stimulus features drive those predictions. Here we introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), a method in which an LLM agent iteratively builds interpretable models by explicitly programming their weights and features in code, without gradient-based training (backpropagation). Without backpropagation to tune parameters, the agent must draw on its prior knowledge and reason over previous trials to hypothesize, hand-craft, and refine human-interpretable computations mirroring the workflow of a human scientist. LLM audits confirm the interpretability of the hand-crafted models. We first validate iWSP by tasking it with constructing transformers for canonical benchmarks such as arithmetic and sentiment classification, finding that LLM agents can successfully craft compact, accurate networks directly. Next, we apply iWSP to build neural encoding models across vision, language, and audition. In the visual cortex, iWSP outpredicts existing interpretable baselines, uncovers distinct computations across early/higher visual areas, and generalizes to unseen data. In language fMRI, iWSP surfaces a confound in the data and in auditory ECoG, it systematically discovers interpretable acoustic features that predict neural activity. Together, these results establish iWSP as a general paradigm for aligning high predictive performance with human-interpretable scientific discovery.

papers.intro:
Figure 1: The iWSP loop and its interpretability audit. a, An LLM agent reads a task prompt and writes a model whose weights are set directly in code. No training is allowed. A fixed evaluator compares the model’s output with the target yy and returns a performance metric, which the agent uses to revise the code. On algorithmic/NLP tasks the model is a neural network whose weights are all set by the agent to generate the exact answer. For brain encoding, the hand-written network computes fixed features, and the evaluator fits a ridge regression from those features to recorded responses and evaluates it on visible stimuli. b, After the search, an LLM judge audits every saved model for training, rule violations and uninterpretable edits. To test interpretability, an agent (Opus 5.5) describes the best model in at most 200 words and a fresh session of the agent rebuilds it from that text alone, shown here for an addition task. c, In the algorithmic/NLP tasks for example, we find that the original and rebuilt models achieve very similar performance (2 rebuilds per task).

In the early days of artificial neural networks, McCulloch and Pitts wrote every connection of small networks by hand to make them compute logical functionsMcCulloch and Pitts, 1943. The values of these weights were interpretable, allowing one to understand how the models worked. The resulting opacity raises concerns around regulatory compliance, safety, and alignmentGoodman and Flaxman, 2017; Amodei et al., 2016; Gabriel, 2020; Singh et al., 2024. papers.title: GraphScent: Calibrating Directional Relevance Signals for Bounded-Context Code Localization
papers.abstract: Running open-weight language models locally on a single consumer GPU requires replacing expanding multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections. Stateless repository localization, however, hinges on a foundational question: when a frozen language model evaluates an unedited code entity from a compact view, which structural relationships make its relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target? Studying Gemma 4 models across 211 real-world Python issues in 86 repositories, we uncover a systematic directional relevance asymmetry: zero-temperature relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers consistently separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, whereas scores on downstream callees, peer methods, historical co-change partners, and dense node embeddings remain near chance. Zero-leakage masked-scope probes and regressions controlling for lexical similarity and snippet length confirm that this asymmetry reflects functional role (callers expose symptom entrypoints delegating to defective routines, while downstream helpers appear benign alone) rather than target leakage or surface overlap. Guided by this finding, we introduce GraphScent, a training-free search controller that propagates out-of-repository, relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over runtime Typed-AST multigraphs before resolving ties via a single listwise comparison, alongside AST Ripple, a lightweight post-edit check for missed co-edits. Likelihood calibration prevents overconfident smaller models from chasing false-positive callers while lifting exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B within a single-GPU budget.

papers.title: TSGP-2: On the Non-Linearity of Symbolic Regression Problems and How to Exploit It with Model-based Semantic Genetic Programming
papers.abstract: Model-based variation operators such as the one used in Transformer Semantic Genetic Programming (TSGP) are affected by possible biases of their training data. TSGP is trained, in particular, on programs generated by Genetic Programming (GP) runs on linear target functions, which leads to a bias toward linear offspring. This bias can hinder search performance on problems that require non-linear solutions. This work has two goals: first, it investigates the linearity of standard test problems such as the Feynman and real-world benchmark problems. While most of the structure of real-world problems can be well approximated by linear structures, the Feynman problems exhibit varying levels of non-linear structure. Thus, a proper variation operator of a search method should be able to create both types of programs, linear as well as non-linear ones. Motivated by this observation, we propose TSGP-2, which follows the functionality of TSGP but uses as training data programs from GP runs on both linear and non-linear target functions. As a result, the training data includes a lower share of programs that behave linearly (the share drops from 83% to 37%). With a higher share of non-linear structures, TSGP-2 outperforms TSGP on problems with non-linear structure, while performing similarly on linear problems. In addition, TSGP-2 is less biased toward linear offspring and is able to propose a higher number of meaningful non-linear offspring earlier during search, which coincides with better solutions. The findings underscore the importance of training data for a learned variation operator and emphasize that the biases of search operators should be aligned with the problems they are applied to.

papers.intro:
The goal of symbolic regression (SR) is to find a mathematical function whose behavior, its semantics, fits a given target behavior as closely as possible. In genetic programming (GP) these functions are evolved in an evolutionary search process through selection and variation. In particular, the variation operators have a major influence on which behavior is found and how quickly the search converges to a good solution (Vanneschi et al., 2014; Moraglio et al., 2012; Uy et al., 2011).

The goal of symbolic regression (SR) is to find a mathematical function whose behavior, its semantics, fits a given target behavior as closely as possible. In genetic programming (GP) these functions are evolved in an evolutionary search process through selection and variation. In particular, the variation operators have a major influence on which behavior is found and how quickly the search converges to a good solution (Vanneschi et al., 2014; Moraglio et al., 2012; Uy et al., 2011).

Standard operators such as subtree mutation and subtree crossover (Koza, 1992; Poli et al., 2008) randomly vary parts of the function. They thereby ignore how a variation affects a function’s semantics (Moraglio et al., 2012). Consequently, variation often produces offspring that are either semantically identical to their parents or substantially different from them, both of which harm search efficiency (McPhee et al., 2008; Beadle and Johnson, 2009; Uy et al., 2009). Semantic GP addresses this with variation operators that control the semantic similarity between offspring and parents (Vanneschi et al., 2014). Some approaches such as Geometric Semantic GP (GSGP) (Moraglio et al., 2012) and SLIM_GSGP (Vanneschi, 2024) work with pre-defined syntactic rules that define how a parent should be varied to obtain an offspring that is semantically similar.

Consequently, variation often produces offspring that are either semantically identical to their parents or substantially different from them, both of which harm search efficiency (McPhee et al., 2008; Beadle and Johnson, 2009; Uy et al., 2009). Semantic GP addresses this with variation operators that control the semantic similarity between offspring and parents (Vanneschi et al., 2014). Some approaches such as Geometric Semantic GP (GSGP) (Moraglio et al., 2012) and SLIM_GSGP (Vanneschi, 2024) work with pre-defined syntactic rules that define how a parent should be varied to obtain an offspring that is semantically similar.

Instead of relying on fixed rules, the recently proposed Transformer Semantic GP (TSGP) (Anthes et al., 2025) uses a trained machine learning model as a semantic variation operator. This model is trained using pairs of semantically similar functions to learn how a syntactic change affects the semantics of a function. TSGP is able to produce meaningful offspring, effectively guiding the search process. As a result, it finds better solutions for a wide range of SR problems compared to standard GP, SLIM_GSGP, GSGP, and other model-based approaches (Anthes et al., 2026; Anthes, 2026). An open and unsolved question is why the performance improvements of TSGP are not consistent across all problems (Anthes et al., 2026).

papers.title: SWIFT: Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning of Time-Series Foundation Models for Forecasting
papers.abstract: While current few-shot adaptation strategies for time series forecasting foundation models are predominantly dataset-centric, the necessity of obtaining an additional dataset for the finetuning process poses a significant hurdle for adoption. To address this constraint, we propose Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a novel forecasting adaptation framework that achieves fine-grained specialization by leveraging structural priors from the target instance's own history. This shift allows the fine-tuning process to be entirely transparent to the end-user, which significantly enhances the ease of adoption. To implement this framework, SWIFT synergizes Self-Retrieval for historical mining and Frequency-Aware Loss for spectral consistency, while employing Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance adaptation with general knowledge preservation. Extensive experiments across four TSFM backbones and three long-history benchmark subsets validate SWIFT, yielding average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83% across 24 combinations of four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SWIFT is the first framework to investigate sample-wise instance fine-tuning of time-series foundation models, specializing the model for an individual prediction window using only the corresponding forecasting sample's own observed history.

papers.title: SemRAG: Semantic-Guided Sentence-Level Retrieval-Augmented Sign Language Production
papers.abstract: Sign language production (SLP) aims to generate sign pose sequences that faithfully express spoken-language text while preserving the rhythm and coordination patterns of signing. Common SLP methods learn text-to-pose mappings from training data but often suffer from semantic inaccuracies in long or complex sentences. Retrieval augmentation offers a way to introduce realistic signing priors to provide more explicit guidance for text-to-pose generation. However, existing retrieval-based SLP methods typically operate at the gloss or word level, relying on gloss-pose dictionaries or isolated sign segments that require costly annotations and fail to preserve continuous sentence-level dynamics. To bridge this gap, we propose SemRAG, a semantic-guided sentence-level retrieval-augmented framework that retrieves full-sentence signing templates as priors without constructing gloss/word-level sign dictionaries. While such templates preserve local motion patterns and global rhythm, they also introduce a semantic mismatch problem: irrelevant motions in the retrieved sentence may interfere with the target semantics. To address this issue, we introduce an SLT-guided template semantic localization module that identifies target-relevant temporal regions within the retrieved template while suppressing irrelevant signing content. To adaptively incorporate the template features into the generator, we further introduce layer-specific learnable gates that regulate their contribution across generator layers. Extensive experiments show that SemRAG improves semantic consistency and motion quality over baselines under both back-translation and motion accuracy metrics.

A desirable SLP system should preserve input semantics while generating natural and temporally coherent signing sequences.

Existing text-to-pose models typically encode the input text to provide semantic conditions and then either directly regress pose sequences in the original pose space (Saunders et al. 2020b; Tang et al. 2025) or generate pose representations in a learned latent space using generative models, such as diffusion models (Xie et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2026) and Transformer-based decoders (Yin et al. 2024; Zuo et al. 2025; Ma et al. 2024). Although these models generate plausible signing poses, they rely on sequence-level supervision and lack explicit grounding between words or phrases and their corresponding pose segments. One promising direction to alleviate semantic drift is retrieval-augmented generation (Zhang et al. 2023; Yu et al. 2025; Xu et al. 2026). Existing retrieval-based SLP methods often rely on gloss-level (Saunders et al. 2022; Zuo et al. 2024; Walsh et al. 2024b) or word-level (Zuo et al. 2025) motion priors. Given an input text, these methods first predict a gloss sequence or directly match spoken-language words, retrieve the corresponding pose segments from the dictionary, and then concatenate and smooth them to produce the final pose sequence. Despite their explicit gloss/word-to-pose correspondence, such methods have two main limitations. First, existing approaches either depend on expensive human annotations (e.g., gloss labels or word-level sign dictionaries), or rely on automatically extracted segments, whose localization errors may introduce irrelevant motion priors. Second, isolated gloss- or word-level segments discard their original sentence context. Although transition modules can smooth adjacent segments, sentence-level timing and long-range coordination must still be reconstructed from independently retrieved units. papers.title: Patient-specific Modeling of the Tricuspid Valve from 3D Transesophageal Echocardiography
papers.abstract: Purpose: Image-based patient-specific simulations of the tricuspid valve (TV) could support repair planning. However, clinical images incompletely resolve the chordal anatomy and cannot directly determine tissue properties, which hinders the development of such models. We developed and evaluated a framework that simulates the TV from clinical images and addresses these limitations using measurements on explanted human valves. Methods: We reconstructed ten functionally competent human TVs from 3D transesophageal echocardiography. Following manual segmentation, we automatically built finite element models with synthetic chordae and with leaflet thickness, chordal insertion density, and tissue properties informed by ex vivo human measurements. Next, we used shape matching and force-based chordal-length adjustment to simulate valve closure. We also assessed inter-observer segmentation variability and sensitivity to chordal insertion density, leaflet stiffness, leaflet thickness, and chordal size and material properties. Results: Per-valve median geometric errors were 0.61-1.13 mm relative to the morphed references and 0.55-0.95 mm relative to the image-derived surfaces. Coaptation covered 20-42% of the leaflet area, and median leaflet stresses ranged from 7.6 to 16.9 kPa. Inter-observer variability in segmentation most strongly affected coaptation area. Of the population-based inputs, insertion density and leaflet stiffness most affected geometric error. Thickness primarily affected stress, whereas chordal size and material properties had limited effects. Conclusion: Clinical echocardiography, supplemented with ex vivo human tissue data, enabled patient-specific simulation of ten human TVs. This framework provides a foundation for investigating valve mechanics and developing repair-planning tools, while sensitivity analyses identify priorities for model refinement and uncertainty assessment.

However, TR recurs in 10-30% of patients after surgical repair Rodriguez Torres et al. (2022); Krivickienė et al. (2024), and selecting the most appropriate treatment for an individual patient remains unclear Praz et al. (2025). Further, the tricuspid valve (TV) exhibits substantial variation in leaflet number and configuration Hahn et al. (2021), making the interaction between a proposed intervention and the patient’s anatomy an important consideration in treatment planning.

Patient-specific computational models provide a controlled and repeatable means to investigate these interactions. They could complement anatomical assessment tools, such as the GLIDE score for tricuspid edge-to-edge repair Gerçek et al. (2024), by estimating how interventions alter leaflet deformation, coaptation, and tissue loading. Previous studies have built finite element (FE) models from idealized geometries Stevanella et al. (2010); Johnson et al. (2021), explanted valves Mathur et al. (2022), computed tomography Kong et al. (2018), and echocardiography of ex vivo porcine hearts Tondi et al. (2026b). These models combine valve geometry, tissue mechanical properties, and loading conditions to estimate valve mechanics in health Stevanella et al. (2010); Kong et al. (2018), disease Mathur et al. (2022); Tondi et al. (2026b), and repair Mathur et al. (2022); Haese et al. (2026a). However, their predictions depend on the data used to construct the models Kong et al. (2018); Mangine et al. (2026). Clinical imaging, and echocardiography in particular, provides only part of this information.

In this work, our objective was to develop and evaluate TV models using clinical images as the only source of patient-specific anatomical data, supplemented by population-based measurements of human tissue. To this end, we constructed FE models of 10 TVs from three-dimensional transesophageal echocardiography (3D-TEE). We prescribed leaflet thickness, leaflet and chordal material properties, chordal cross-sectional areas, and regional chordal insertion densities using ex vivo human tissue data. We then simulated valve closure and assessed agreement with the imaged end-systolic configurations. Finally, in three valves, we investigated sensitivity to modeling assumptions over ranges informed by variability in the human data. We compared these effects with the variability arising from image segmentation by three independent observers. These analyses aimed to determine how reliably the models reproduce valve closure and which inputs most influence predicted valve mechanics. This workflow provides a foundation for building patient-specific TV models from routinely acquired clinical images, which can be used to investigate the mechanical effects of repair procedures.

papers.title: Wireless Node Ranking via Fourier-Driven Maximum-Likelihood Estimation (extended version)
papers.abstract:
We apply non-abelian Fourier theory to the problem of maximum-likelihood estimation of the order of a line topology, based on signal strength measurements under shadowing only. This yields up to a 60-fold speedup over standard methods for uncorrelated shadowing.
  Moreover, for correlated Gaussian shadowing with a singular covariance (e.g. the joint path-loss model), maximum-likelihood recovery is exact and independent of the shadowing variance (an infinite Le Cam threshold), which our implementation confirms for $\sigma/\alpha$ as high as 7.0. The key object is the covariance's null space. Its dimension is fixed by the topology; its orientation depends on the correlation function only through the per-link variances.
  Although the mechanism formally requires an exact line, it is robust to small perturbations of the formation: an approximate kernel recovers as well as the exact one. We explore the dependence on the perturbation in detail for five nodes.

Wireless sensor and ad-hoc networks are frequently deployed in physically elongated, near-linear arrangements — along roads, pipelines, tunnels, building corridors, or the rows of a photovoltaic plant [19] — where the order of the nodes along the line is itself the quantity of interest (for routing, in-order data fusion, or fault localization), while GPS or anchor infrastructure is unavailable or too costly [15]. Received signal strength (RSSI), by contrast, is reported by virtually every radio at no extra cost. Wireless node ranking is the problem of recovering the order of such nodes from signal-strength measurements alone.

Even in the simple case of a line topology with uniform spacing, the problem is hard once one insists on best possible solutions — by which we mean the maximum-likelihood estimator (MLE). While there are heuristics like order derivation (AOD) [7, 6] in the wireless literature, the least-squares method (ALS) we proposed in [3] (also cf. [4]) is NP-hard in general. Its benefit is, as we will see in this work, that its solution is the MLE in the case of log-normal shadowing (LNS), i.e. uncorrelated Gaussian shadowing with fixed variance σ2\sigma^{2}. As we have pointed out in [4], AOD can dominate ALS when correlation is present. However, AOD is only a heuristic when its underlying assumption does not hold, as is the case, for instance, in the joint path loss models ([13], [4]). Thus it is natural to ask for the MLE also in the case of correlated shadowing.

What comes as a surprise is that the concept of node ranking is known as seriation in the mathematical statistics community with — to the best of our knowledge — no connection to the wireless community. In the words of Atkins et al. [9], seriation is the sequencing of elements in such a way that highly correlated pairs of elements are near each other. This can clearly be solved by finding the maximizer of the graph correlation, which is the way Kondor states the quadratic assignment problem (QAP) in his seminal work [1] — which in turn we tackle with the Fourier Framework he developed there based on the Clausen Fourier Transform [2]. Even more surprising is that the noise-free seriation case is solved by a tool the wireless community knows well — spectral graph theory, with the Fiedler eigenvector at its center [9] — which nonetheless never led it to seriation. We adopt these seriation methods (Fiedler and the minimax-optimal SABRE [22]) as polynomial-time benchmarks. Crucially, these are spectral or convex relaxations built for polynomial-time, minimax-rate recovery; none computes the maximum-likelihood estimator, even under i.i.d. Gaussian noise — where our LNS algorithm, solving the exact least-squares QAP, is the MLE and already outperforms them. The decisive gap is under correlated shadowing: there the MLE is best possible — 100%100\% recovery — which the i.i.d.-built seriation methods cannot reach.

papers.title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture
papers.abstract: Phase-field simulation of thermally driven fracture requires resolving localized crack bands whose paths are unknown in advance and thermal boundary layers whose thickness evolves during the transient. Neural energy-based computations of thermal fracture have so far started from defects placed in advance. This paper proposes a mesh-free deep energy method based on multiresolution neural representations that predicts spontaneous crack nucleation, crack spacing, and selective crack propagation and arrest under transient thermal loading. Two networks, each with its own multiresolution encoding, represent the displacement and phase fields and the transient temperature, and the mechanical energy and the incremental functional of the backward Euler heat equation are estimated on integration points redrawn at every iteration. Restricting irreversibility to the crack set, carrying the optimizer state across load steps and decaying the learning rates within each step help prevent spurious damage accumulation. On two notched plates the initiation peak loads agree closely with an independent finite element reference. On a quenched glass strip under an analytical temperature field the crack path changes from straight to oscillatory and then to branched, with an oscillation threshold close to the linear stability prediction. Under a prescribed boundary temperature a quenched ceramic slab forms a crack array of the type observed in experiment, with a spacing close to that of a published benchmark. On the slab and a quenched annulus the arrays are denser than those of a finite element computation on the same material field. No crack paths, nucleation sites or crack-adapted meshes are prescribed.

papers.intro:
Brittle solids subjected to rapid surface cooling form characteristic fracture patterns. A ceramic slab quenched into water develops a periodic array of parallel cracks along its cooled faces, a subset of which propagates into the depth while the rest arrest, so that the spacing of the array grows with the depth [1, 2, 3]. A glass strip notched at its leading edge and drawn at constant speed from a hot region into a cold bath develops a single crack, which starts at the notch and follows the immersion front. As the temperature jump or the drawing speed grows, the path changes from straight to oscillatory and then to branched [4, 5]. The same mechanism, a contraction that the surrounding material resists, produces the columnar joints of cooling lava [6], the crack networks of drying and cooling in rock, concrete and soil [7, 8, 9] and the thermal shock fracture of ceramic components [10, 11]. The classical theory of thermal shock and the experiments that tested it [12, 10, 13, 14, 8, 15] describe the initiation of fracture from flaws of given size and the propagation and selective arrest of an initial crack array assumed in advance. A computation of thermal shock has to predict the pattern itself, where the cracks nucleate, how many form, at what spacing, and which of them continue.

The sharp-crack description of linear elastic fracture mechanics represents the crack explicitly and advances it when the energy release rate [16], or the stress intensity factor [17], reaches a critical value. Remeshing [18], the extended finite element method [19] and element-free Galerkin methods [20, 21] carry such a crack with separate criteria for nucleation, for the direction of growth and for branching, and such cracks have been advanced under thermal loads [22, 23, 24]. On the thermal shock problem those criteria would have to supply the quantities the computation is meant to predict. Cohesive surfaces between all elements [25], peridynamic models [26, 27, 28] and lattice models [29] instead form cracks where bonds or cohesive surfaces fail.

Of the formulations that produce such patterns without assuming them, the one adopted here is the variational formulation of fracture of Francfort and Marigo [30] in the regularization of Bourdin et al. [31, 32]. In it the sharp crack is replaced by a phase field that localizes in a band of width proportional to a regularization length ll [33], and nucleation, propagation, branching and arrest result from minimizing one energy. The model has since been extended by energy decompositions that treat tension and compression differently [34, 35, 36], interpreted as a gradient damage model with a finite strength [37, 38, 39], and given a strength surface [40], higher-order densities [41] and penalized irreversibility [42], as reviewed in [43]. On the thermal shock problem Sicsic et al. [9] showed that the uniform damage band under the cooled surface bifurcates toward a periodic mode whose wavelength is proportional to the regularization length. The computations of Bourdin et al. [44] pass through this bifurcation to an array of short cracks whose selective propagation follows the spacing law of Bahr et al. [8] and the experiment of Shao et al. [45]. The problem tests the model both at nucleation, where the strength governs, and in propagation, where the toughness governs, and in the regularized model the two are not independent, since the strength is set by the toughness, the modulus and the regularization length together [39]. Lopez-Pamies et al. [46] argue that classical models of this class, without a strength surface, cannot describe nucleation in general, and Kamarei et al. [47] pose a set of challenge problems on which fracture models can be assessed in this respect. Zeng et al. [48] treat nucleation in thermal quenching with a model whose strength is independent of the regularization length, together with random fields of the strength.

Of the two experiments above, the glass strip is the one in which quasi-static crack propagation under a thermal load is controlled and reproducible. Yuse and Sano [4, 5] mapped its straight, oscillatory and branched regimes and reported the transition to oscillation as a supercritical Hopf bifurcation. Ronsin et al. [49] measured the temperature field and the thresholds as functions of the drawing speed, Ronsin and Perrin [50] the thresholds and the wavelength at onset, and Yang and Ravi-Chandar [51] followed the growth of the crack in real time. Linear stability analyses [52, 53, 54, 55] and an equation of motion for the tip [56] gave the threshold and, in most cases, the wavelength, and the paths were computed with lattice models, finite elements, the extended finite element method, universal meshes, peridynamics and phase-field models [29, 57, 23, 24, 27, 55, 58, 11]. The computation of Corson et al. [55] recovered the transition but not the complex paths well above the threshold, where the authors suggest that the quasi-static approximation may no longer hold.

Phase-field computations of thermo-elastic fracture have been made with finite elements in quasi-static and dynamic settings and with monolithic, explicit and staggered solvers [59, 60, 61, 62, 63], for the hot cracking of the melt pool in additive manufacturing [64], in three dimensions [65, 66], on meshes adapted around the growing cracks [67, 68, 69] and with a strength independent of the regularization length [11]. Each of them meets the resolution requirement of the model with a mesh, and a strong-form meshless method [70] meets it with a set of nodes. On the thermal shock problem the mesh has to resolve two narrow zones that change during the computation. One is the band of width proportional to ll, along a path the computation is meant to discover [34, 71]. The other is the thermal boundary layer, whose thickness after a cooling time tt is D​t\sqrt{Dt}, with DD the thermal diffusivity, and is smallest early in the transient, when the array nucleates. A refinement that anticipates either is not neutral, since nonuniform meshes can favor the nucleation of cracks in their refined zones [37]. A uniform mesh avoids this bias at the cost of the finest resolution everywhere, as in the finite element computations of this paper. In purely elastic fracture the authors’ mesh-free deep energy method [72] is built so that no mesh follows the crack.

papers.title: Turbulence at the Correlation Scale as the Driver of Magnetic Reconnection: In Situ Observations and Kinetic Simulations
papers.abstract: We study the statistical properties of magnetic reconnection using high-resolution in situ observations from the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) Mission in the terrestrial magnetosheath and kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. For the first time, using in situ observations, we find that the statistics of upstream reconnecting fields in a macroscopic turbulent plasma system are closely linked with the amplitude of turbulence at the correlation scales. These results are further confirmed with fully kinetic plasma turbulence simulations. Consequently, the average magnetic reconnection rates and associated heating rates, determined through the upstream fields, could become orders of magnitude higher than those predicted using the turbulence amplitude at the dissipation scale. We then use a simplified model of the heating of reconnection exhausts to estimate the ratio of this reconnection heating rate to the overall energy cascade rate due to turbulence. Estimates from the PIC simulations and the MMS observations yield a ratio on the order of $1/5$, indicating that direct reconnection heating is playing a substantial role in dissipating the turbulent fluctuations.

papers.title: Noncommutative Rational Positivstellens\"atze with Operator Coefficients
papers.abstract: We establish a convex Positivstellensatz for noncommutative rational functions with bounded operator coefficients. A hermitian operator-valued rational function that is positive semidefinite on a matrix convex set described by a linear pencil admits a positivity certificate consisting of rational hermitian squares and a completely positive term involving the defining linear pencil. The certificate comes with an explicit complexity bound independent of the dimension of the coefficient Hilbert space. As a consequence, we solve the operator-valued noncommutative rational analog of Hilbert's 17th problem: every positive semidefinite operator-valued noncommutative rational function is a sum of hermitian squares, and even a single hermitian square when the coefficient Hilbert space is infinite-dimensional. In contrast, the corresponding commutative statement fails for infinite-dimensional operator coefficients.

papers.intro:
Hilbert’s 17th problem asks whether every nonnegative real polynomial is a sum of squares of rational functions. Artin’s affirmative solution is a cornerstone of real algebraic geometry [BCR98, Mar08, Sce24]; matrix versions were subsequently obtained by Gondard–Ribenboim [GR74], Procesi–Schacher [PS76], and Djoković [Djo76]. The situation is more rigid when the variables are freely noncommuting and positivity is tested on matrices of all sizes. Helton [Hel02] and McCullough [McC01] proved that a noncommutative polynomial positive semidefinite on all matrix tuples is a sum of hermitian squares of polynomials; see [McC01] also for foundational operator-valued factorization results. Further approaches to noncommutative Positivstellensätze, based on separation arguments, quadratic modules and operator algebras, were developed in [Oza13, NT13, ANT19].

Noncommutative (nc) rational functions arise by applying addition, multiplication and inversion to elements of the free algebra ℂ⁡⟨x1,…,xg⟩\mathbb{C}\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{\texttt{g}}\rangle. More precisely, they are equivalence classes of rational expressions under agreement of their matrix evaluations, and form the free skew field, the universal skew field of fractions of the free algebra. The viewpoint of matrix evaluations and realizations, which connects nc rational functions to free analysis, systems theory and free real algebraic geometry, was developed in [HMV06, K-VV12]; see also [Vol18].

papers.title: Euclid DR1 Legacy Science on Ultracool Dwarfs: New URLD candidates in Euclid and SPHEREx
papers.abstract:
Unusually red L dwarfs (URLDs) probe extreme atmospheric conditions in the substellar regime, where enhanced dust opacity, cloud structure, and surface gravity effects challenge standard brown dwarf models. As free-floating analogues of young giant exoplanets, they provide key benchmarks for interpreting low-resolution infrared spectra from current and future wide-field space missions.
  The goal is to identify new red L dwarf candidates both photometrically and spectroscopically in the first data release (DR1) of the Euclid space mission. The area covered is about 1,900 and 50 square degrees in the wide and deep survey, respectively.
  We used colour cuts in multiple colour-colour diagrams combined with point-source and quality criteria to identify candidate red L dwarfs in both the Euclid wide and deep survey fields. We cross-matched photometric candidates with the SPHEREx mission and Euclid red grism spectra to confirm spectroscopic properties and evaluate bolometric magnitudes and colours.
  We identified 1202 and 38 red L dwarf candidates in the Euclid wide and deep surveys, respectively. Spectroscopic follow-up and archival cross-matching confirm a substantial new population of red L dwarfs. Distance-independent diagnostics show that these objects occupy distinct loci characterised by enhanced condensate opacity and significant redness.
  Euclid vastly expands the census of unusually red L dwarfs. While preliminary spectral classifications suggest many of these new candidates are intermediate-age (Pleiades-like) objects, a subset exhibits extremely red signatures indicative of very young, low-gravity (<=10 Myr) atmospheres, providing vital benchmarks for young exoplanet research.

papers.intro:
Ultracool dwarfs, spanning spectral types from late-M through L, T, and Y (Kirkpatrick et al., 1999; Martín et al., 1999; Burgasser et al., 2002; Kirkpatrick, 2005; Cushing et al., 2011), represent the lowest-mass products of star formation, bridging the gap between hydrogen-burning stars and giant planets (Chabrier & Baraffe, 2000; Burrows et al., 2001; Baraffe et al., 2003). These objects have effective temperatures below about 2500 K (Basri et al., 2000; Golimowski et al., 2004; Stephens et al., 2009; Filippazzo et al., 2015) and emit most of their flux in the infrared. Wide-field optical and infrared surveys have uncovered a large number of field L, T, and Y dwarfs (Delfosse et al., 1997; Kirkpatrick et al., 2000; Kirkpatrick et al., 2011), and have led to well-characterised volume-limited samples of the solar neighbourhood (Reylé et al., 2021; Kirkpatrick et al., 2021; Best et al., 2021; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2021b). Within this population, an intriguing subset known as unusually URLDs (hereafter URLDs) stands out due to their near-infrared colours that are significantly redder than typical field L dwarfs of the same spectral type (Kirkpatrick et al., 2006; Gizis et al., 2012; Marocco et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2017). These URLDs are rare but scientifically valuable because they challenge standard models of ultracool atmospheres and offer unique insights into substellar atmospheric physics and evolutionary processes.

In this context, certain extreme cases such as the L7pec object ULAS J222711−-004547 (Marocco et al., 2014) have revealed that enhanced dust opacity and non-standard cloud properties likely drive the very red photometric and spectroscopic characteristics of some URLDs. Other well-studied examples include the very young field L dwarf 2MASS J01415823−-4633574 (Kirkpatrick et al., 2006) and the unusually red, dusty L dwarf WISEP J004701.06++680352.1 (Gizis et al., 2012; Gizis et al., 2015a). Detailed spectral analysis showed that differences in cloud optical depth and sub-micron grain populations can well explain their infrared excesses relative to "normal" L dwarfs (Marocco et al., 2014; Hiranaka et al., 2016), posing challenges for traditional atmospheric models which typically include only larger cloud grains and simpler cloud prescriptions (Ackerman & Marley, 2001; Marley et al., 2002).

The first systematic search for unusually URLDs was presented by Schneider et al. (2017), who exploited combined photometry from 2MASS and AllWISE to identify 50 new late-type L dwarf candidates, 47 of which were spectroscopically confirmed. This study not only expanded the sample of known URLDs substantially but also identified likely members of young stellar associations such as Beta Pictoris, AB Doradus, Tucana-Horologium, and Argus (Zuckerman & Song, 2004; Torres et al., 2008), reinforcing the view that red colours may be linked to youth and low surface gravity in some cases. This link had already emerged from the identification of young L dwarfs in the field (Kirkpatrick et al., 2008; Cruz et al., 2009; Allers & Liu, 2013), several of which were subsequently associated with young moving groups (Schneider et al., 2014; Gagné et al., 2015; Best et al., 2017) or were shown to be free-floating planetary-mass members of nearby associations (Schneider et al., 2016). Parallax programmes have since provided distances, luminosities, and temperatures for a number of these objects (Zapatero Osorio et al., 2014a; Faherty et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016). Additional peculiar L dwarfs were identified in other public wide-field surveys (Zhang et al., 2022), and follow-up spectroscopy has confirmed a handful of ultra-red objects spanning a range of ages, gravities, and kinematic properties (Marocco et al., 2015; Scholz et al., 2020; Bickle et al., 2024).

The scientific importance of URLDs can be summarised through three key aspects. First, URLDs provide empirical constraints on the formation, composition, and vertical extent of condensate clouds in cool, low-temperature atmospheres (Stephens et al., 2009; Hiranaka et al., 2016). Traditional cloud models developed for L dwarfs often underpredict the reddening seen in these objects (Marocco et al., 2014). Models that incorporate both large and sub-micron dust grains have been shown to reproduce observed spectral energy distributions more effectively, motivating improvements in atmospheric modelling. Second, the association of some URLDs with young moving groups suggests that their spectral peculiarities could be signatures of lower gravity (Cruz et al., 2009; Allers & Liu, 2013; Liu et al., 2016). However, not all URLDs show unambiguous indicators of youth, implying that multiple physical parameters (e.g. cloud opacity, metallicity) play a role (Looper et al., 2008; Burgasser et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2013) play a role (Liu et al., 2013). Third, URLDs share photometric and spectroscopic similarities with directly imaged giant exoplanets, which also display very red near-infrared colours (Chauvin et al., 2004; Chauvin et al., 2005; Marois et al., 2008; Lagrange et al., 2009; Marois et al., 2010; Barman et al., 2011b; Macintosh et al., 2015; Chauvin et al., 2015; Gauza et al., 2015). The spectral sequence of young planetary-mass objects in star-forming regions provides a natural extension of this comparison to even lower masses and ages (Lodieu et al., 2018; Luhman et al., 2018).

papers.title: Frustrated Interlayer Coupling Creates a Higher-Order Helical Superstructure in a Twist-Bend Smectic Phase
papers.abstract: Bent liquid-crystalline dimers provide a model system for studying the spontaneous emergence of chirality from achiral molecules. Depending on terminal-chain length, these materials exhibit a competition between heliconical, synclinic, and anticlinic packing tendencies in tilted smectic phases. In short homologues, the tendency to form twist-bend phases dominates, leading to two distinct helical phases: the SmCTB-SH phase, with a helical periodicity of four molecular lengths, and at lower temperatures, a double helical structure - the SmCTB-DH phase, with progressive rotation of the four-layer unit. With increasing terminal chain length, this twist-bend tendency is gradually suppressed, favoring phases with simple synclinic and anticlinic tilt arrangement in successive layers. Remarkably, in the regime where these tendencies become comparable, a new modulated smectic phase, SmCTB-mod develops; a double helical structure in which the internal four-layer unit undergoes a periodic modulation. This additional level of structural organization provides a means of accommodating competing heliconical and synclinic/anticlinic tendencies and produces a characteristic splitting of the resonant x-ray diffraction peaks into four signals symmetrically located around a signal of four-layer periodicity. These results reveal how bent dimers resolve local-packing-mode frustration through complex spontaneous hierarchical structural organization.

papers.title: Stable projective immersions of K\"ahler metrics with some radial symmetry
papers.abstract: We combine Calabi's criterion with Pringsheim's theorem to study projective inducibility under positive rescaling. By restricting to suitable radial holomorphic curves, we obtain an obstruction to local K\"ahler immersions into finite- or infinite-dimensional complex projective space that applies uniformly to every positive rescaling. For invariant rational curves, we show that non-rationality of the moment map implies that no positive rescaling is projectively induced. We apply these criteria to the Taub-NUT, Candelas-de la Ossa, non-flat Stenzel, and Hwang-Singer scalar-flat metrics, as well as to Gibbons-Hawking metrics. Except for the Burns-Simanca metric in the Hwang-Singer family, no positive rescaling is projectively induced. For Gibbons-Hawking ALE spaces with at least two centres, the conclusion holds in every compatible complex structure. We also extend the results to complex space forms of arbitrary curvature with at least one finite signature index.

papers.title: Distributed Output-Feedback Control for Linear Multichannel Systems
papers.abstract: This paper investigates distributed output-feedback stabilization of linear multichannel systems in which agents exchange state estimates without disclosing local control inputs or feedback gains. Remote control actions are treated as unknown inputs and geometrically decoupled from stable quotient-error dynamics. The proposed framework accommodates nontrivial intersections of local loss subspaces by retaining the coupling between the plant and common estimation errors. A Hurwitz condition on the coupled dynamics, together with a sufficient consensus-gain bound, guarantees exponential closed-loop convergence for every fixed feedback selection in a compact family. For polytopic feedback families, a quotient-preserving parameterization of output injections enables joint synthesis of nominal feedback and observer gains via alternating linear matrix inequalities, followed by a convex semidefinite program certifying a common consensus gain. A numerical example demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed design.

papers.intro:
Many engineering systems are actuated and sensed by spatially distributed agents acting on a shared plant, as in cooperative multi-agent systems [1], vehicle platoons [2], and microgrids [3]. A linear multichannel model assigns each agent a local input–output channel through which it measures a partial output and applies a control input. Here, “multichannel” describes the plant structure, whereas “centralized”, “decentralized”, and “distributed” describe the information available during operation. A centralized controller processes all channels together, decentralized controllers use only their own channels, and distributed controllers additionally communicate with neighboring agents. A separate issue is which model parameters, control inputs, and feedback gains each agent must know or disclose.

A separate issue is which model parameters, control inputs, and feedback gains each agent must know or disclose.

Early work on decentralized control identified fixed modes as a fundamental obstruction. It was shown in [4] that stabilization by finite-dimensional linear time-invariant (LTI) decentralized controllers is possible if and only if all decentralized fixed modes are stable. Conditions for decentralized stabilization and spectrum assignment based on channel interactions and complementary subsystems were developed in [5]. Fixed modes can also arise from structural constraints rather than exact parameter coincidences. Their generic absence is characterized through structural completeness, including systems with dependent parameters [6]. These limitations motivate inter-agent communication.

It was shown in [4] that stabilization by finite-dimensional linear time-invariant (LTI) decentralized controllers is possible if and only if all decentralized fixed modes are stable. Conditions for decentralized stabilization and spectrum assignment based on channel interactions and complementary subsystems were developed in [5]. Fixed modes can also arise from structural constraints rather than exact parameter coincidences. Their generic absence is characterized through structural completeness, including systems with dependent parameters [6]. These limitations motivate inter-agent communication.

The question is then what the agents should communicate. The results in [7, 8] show that sharing neighboring measurements alone need not eliminate fixed modes, even when the plant is jointly controllable and observable and the communication graph is strongly connected. They also establish conditions on the dimensions of shared controller states that remove this obstruction. Exchanging control inputs or feedback gains may be undesirable when local actions and policies are not to be disclosed. A natural alternative is to exchange local state estimates, which serve as communicated controller states and support estimate-based feedback at each agent.

The main difficulty is that an agent with access only to its local input cannot directly reproduce the aggregate plant input in its observer. The input-cancellation mechanism used in centralized observer-based control is therefore generally unavailable. The observer-based constructions in [9, 8] replace remote estimates by the local estimate through the substitution rule, but retain the aggregate feedback matrix in each observer. The discrete-time weak-separation result in [10] retains this dependence. The scaled-local-input construction in [11] avoids remote feedback gains and enables decentralized gain computation and plug-and-play operation. Its fixed-gain result requires Hurwitz state-feedback and aggregate observer dynamics. Under collective strong detectability, [12] combines local unknown-input decoupling with adaptive consensus to enable separate observer and controller design.

papers.title: Where Tree Ensembles Decide: Structural Local Explanation with Decision Predicate Graphs
papers.abstract: Tree ensembles are among the most accurate models for tabular data, yet the computation behind a single prediction is spread over hundreds of decision rules. Feature attributions and counterfactuals explain such predictions through the influence of features or a change of the input, leaving open which of the thresholds applied by the trees a prediction responds to, while structural explanations compress these rules and lose the trees behind them. To address this gap, we propose a local Decision Predicate Graph (local DPG), which gathers the rules executed for a sample into a verifiable record of the computation, with a class support that reproduces every explained prediction. From these rules we select the critical predicate, the executed predicate whose crossing is estimated to move the model most strongly toward a chosen class, which offers the user a concrete threshold and the trees that share it, without an external explainer. Across 16 datasets and four ensemble families, it separates differently predicted neighbours better than random and nearest-threshold predicates. A single crossing recovers the true class in 46-69% of wrong predictions, against 29-50% when the same rule is applied to the feature ranked first by TreeSHAP, a measure close to the selection criterion, and on planted faults it finds the faulty threshold in 46-71% of the resulting errors, against 6-21% at random. Although training-free edits of these predicates did not reduce the error on unseen data, the critical predicate complements attributions and counterfactuals by naming where a prediction can be changed.

papers.intro:
Tree ensembles, such as random forests, bagging and gradient boosting, remain among the most accurate and widely deployed models for tabular data. Their predictions result from the aggregation of hundreds of decision trees, each of which routes the input through a sequence of threshold tests, so the computation behind a single prediction is distributed across the model. Local explanation methods aim to make this computation intelligible for one input at a time [1, 2, 3], and they serve different purposes, among them justifying a prediction, controlling what a model has learned, and improving it through an understanding of its behaviour [4]. Improvement is the use that practitioners report most often, since explanations are mainly employed to debug models [5, 6], and debugging begins with understanding why individual predictions fail [7, 8]. This paper addresses the first step of this purpose, the examination of individual predictions, and asks, for a trained ensemble and a given input, which of the predicates executed by the model, if crossed, would most change the prediction toward an alternative class.

A prediction of a tree ensemble can be explained from three complementary points of view. Feature attributions such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) describe the influence of each input, quantifying how much it contributed to the output [9, 1, 10]. Counterfactual explanations move instead to the input space, where they describe a change of the input that would have produced a different prediction [11, 12, 13, 14]. A third view looks at the logical structure of the model, that is, at the predicates and rules that the trees actually executed, and underlies the route-based and formal explanations of tree ensembles [15, 16, 17, 18]. These perspectives are not interchangeable, and a growing body of work shows how far they can diverge. A large attribution does not imply that a feature affects the prediction [19], the features ranked first by attribution methods are often neither necessary nor sufficient to change it [20, 21], and Shapley values may even rank irrelevant features above relevant ones [22, 23]. Counterfactuals, in turn, indicate what should change in the input, yet they do not single out a predicate of the model at which the prediction can be changed. This is the question that motivates the present work, and it is the structural view that can answer it.

papers.title: Mapping the Evolving Cosmic Web on the Lightcone with WebON: HOLI Mock Strategy
papers.abstract: Wide-area spectroscopic surveys such as DESI require large ensembles of mock catalogues that follow gravitational evolution and tracer populations across the observer's past lightcone. We present WebON (Web ON the lightcone), a fast method for mapping the evolving dark-matter cosmic web onto the lightcone without periodic-box replication or the stitching of separately evolved snapshot shells. Displacements computed at a limited set of redshifts are combined with a particle-wise Zel'dovich estimate of the emission redshift and a continuous-redshift correction, allowing lightcone positions to be generated in a single forward pass. The method supports regularised ALPT and eALPT gravity solvers, with an optional short-range ridging correction. We illustrate full-sky matter and cosmic-web evolution and find percent-level agreement between lightcone and fixed-redshift angular power spectra over the tested redshift and multipole ranges, providing an internal consistency check of the lightcone construction. Optional modules address approximate relativistic position corrections and local primordial non-Gaussianity. Finally, we show how the spectral cosmic-web hierarchy connects WebON to the HOLI (Higher Order LIghtcone) mock strategy, in which post-processing ridging and calibrated HICOBIAN bias and subgrid prescriptions can recover tracer clustering beyond the nominal resolution of the ALPT matter field. Independent comparisons of ridged LPT matter fields with Abacus N -body simulations and published percent-level tests of the hierarchical tracer-bias model complement the lightcone consistency measurements presented here.

The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) is mapping large-scale structure over an unprecedented combination of comoving volume and redshift range, providing precision baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) and redshift-space distortion (RSD) measurements from multiple tracer populations. Robust inference requires mock catalogues that capture gravitational evolution, tracer clustering, and survey selection, in numbers sufficient for covariance estimation and systematic tests.

High-resolution NN-body simulations accurately model nonlinear structure formation but face a demanding volume–resolution–cost trade-off when thousands of DESI-scale realisations are required. Fast approximate gravity solvers coupled to calibrated field-level tracer models offer a complementary approach: large-scale matter evolution is computed explicitly, while unresolved tracer physics is represented statistically.

papers.title: Deep Latents, Long Memory: Latent persistence explains temporal correlations in transformer activations
papers.abstract: The hidden layers of Large Language Models (LLMs) are believed to encode representations of the data whose abstraction increases with depth. However, in the absence of an operational notion of abstraction, this statement is hard to test quantitatively. Here, we propose an alternative view, building on the principle that the correlations of a sequence reflect the structure of the process that generated it. We define the autocorrelation function of a layer as the average dot product between its activations at two context positions separated by a lag. Latent variables encoded persistently along the context create slowly decaying tails in the autocorrelation, and we find these tails to grow across layers in both synthetic and natural data. In synthetic data with controlled hierarchical latent structure, this growth stems from the encoding of abstract latent variables, which govern long stretches of the input. Indeed, the persistence of latent codes predicts the qualitative structure of autocorrelations and accounts for most of the empirical measures. In real text, we take sparse-autoencoder features as proxies for latent variables, and find that their persistence correlates strongly with the magnitude of autocorrelations across datasets and LLMs. In particular, the persistence time increases with depth, as do autocorrelations, implying that deeper latent features persist for longer context spans. We complement this analysis by explicitly ablating the persistent sparse-autoencoder features and observing a consequent decrease in the autocorrelations.

papers.intro:
Language is structured across many temporal scales: local constructions constrain nearby tokens, while abstract concepts such as topic and discourse states can remain relevant over much longer spans. Large Language Models (LLMs) adapt to this structure over training, developing representations of syntactic (Peters et al., 2018; Tenney et al., 2019; Manning et al., 2020; Diego Simon et al., 2024) and semantic features (Engels et al., 2024; Gurnee et al., 2025; Acevedo et al., 2026a). Understanding such representations, including their content and the mechanism of their formation, remains a central challenge for a theory of LLMs and deep learning at large (Michaud, 2026).

On the empirical side, a growing collection of methods probes the content of LLMs’ representations, as well as their organisation across layers. Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features (Huben et al., 2024) change or emerge with depth Balcells et al. (2024), shifting from positional and structural signals in early layers to context-binding, semantic features in intermediate layers, and then to output-oriented signals in the final layers (Sun et al., 2025). Features shared across languages are likewise most common in the middle layers (Lindsey et al., 2025). Temporal extensions of SAEs (Lubana et al., 2026; Bhalla et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026) find that semantic features vary slowly along the context, whereas rapidly changing ones capture lexical and syntactic patterns. Geometric measures, both local (Hosseini and Fedorenko, 2023; King et al., 2026) and global (Cheng et al., 2025), also indicate that representations become more abstract with depth, as the superficial properties captured by the early layers gradually give way to high-level semantic information. Abstract representations can be identified via similarity measures between points in semantic correspondence, such as image-caption pairs (Huh et al., 2024) and translations (Acevedo et al., 2026b). However, we still lack a framework that unifies these observations and characterises the layerwise information processing in LLMs without relying on prior assumptions about the represented concepts.

papers.title: The effect of vertical mixing on oxygen sequestration by refractory elements in the atmosphere of giant planets
papers.abstract: The most widely used route to study the formation history of giant exoplanets is the C/O ratio, usually derived from H$_2$O, CO, CO$_2$ and CH$_4$. However, refractory elements can sequester a significant fraction of O, causing the observed C/O ratio to be overestimated with respect to the intrinsic one. Previous calculations of this bias relied on chemical equilibrium models. Here we quantify the impact of vertical mixing using the 1-D chemical kinetics code VULCAN, expanded with a Mg-Si-Fe network including the condensation and settling of enstatite, forsterite and metallic iron. We compute 168 models spanning equilibrium temperatures $T_{eq} \in$ [700, 1500] K, eddy diffusion coefficients $K_{zz} \in$ [$10^6$, $10^{10}$] cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$ and metallicities $Z \in$ [0.9, 7.2] $Z_\odot$, derived self-consistently from planet formation simulations. We find that vertical transport causes magnesium silicates to destabilize already at $T_{eq} \sim 900$ K regardless of metallicity, releasing oxygen to H$_2$O and to minor gas-phase carriers such as SiO and Mg(OH)$_2$. Therefore, while equilibrium models predict a nearly constant C/O overestimation up to 1100-1300 K, in disequilibrium it drops sharply between 900 and 1200 K. In this transitional range the C/O overestimation is controlled by $K_{zz}$ and is partially degenerate with metallicity, while outside it is robust against both mixing intensity and the probed atmospheric layer, ranging from 14.5-23\% at 700 K to 4.5-7\% at 1500 K. Metallic iron condensation prevents Fe from sequestering oxygen, lowering the overestimation by about one third with respect to previous estimates. Finally, CH$_4$, CO$_2$ and the CH$_4$/CO ratio are most sensitive to $K_{zz}$ in the transitional range, and can provide a constraint on vertical mixing.

papers.intro:
Thanks to the rapidly increasing number and quality of available exoplanetary spectra a transition from the detections of species to the quantitative compositional characterization of known objects is well underway. While early investigations were able to identify only especially opaque (Charbonneau et al., 2002, e.g. Na,) or abundant (Tinetti et al., 2007, e.g. H2O,) chemical species in exoplanetary atmospheres, the continuous improvements in both spectral resolution and sensitivity are now allowing to retrieve the concentrations of several molecules at once (Cabot et al., 2019; Giacobbe et al., 2021; Guilluy et al., 2022; Rustamkulov et al., 2023; Alderson et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024), even in cooler and smaller targets (Madhusudhan et al., 2023; Beatty et al., 2024). The recently announced discovery of silicate clouds in the atmosphere of the exoplanet YSES-1 c (Hoch et al., 2025) further expanded observations to the domain of condensates. These advances make possible to characterize the elemental composition of a larger and larger number of Jupiter-like objects with an unprecedented degree of precision.

The existence of the so-called Hot Jupiters in close orbits around their parent star and the difficulty in explaining how they could have formed in situ (Rafikov, 2005; Schlichting, 2014; Lee & Chiang, 2016) strongly support the idea that planets can migrate inside a planetary system. Migration can happen at several stages in a planet’s history, such as during the formation via interactions with the protoplanetary disc (Goldreich & Tremaine, 1980; Nelson et al., 2000; Alexander & Armitage, 2009; Baruteau et al., 2014), or at a later time because of planet-planet interactions (Turrini et al., 2020; Turrini et al., 2022; Zhu & Dong, 2021; Hamer & Schlaufman, 2022). While alternatives to this picture do exist (Batygin et al., 2016; Boley et al., 2016; Poon et al., 2021), migration is generally considered as the best solution to the existence of short period massive planets.

While alternatives to this picture do exist (Batygin et al., 2016; Boley et al., 2016; Poon et al., 2021), migration is generally considered as the best solution to the existence of short period massive planets.

One way to shed light on the many uncertainties related to the formation and migration processes (Dawson & Johnson, 2018; Fortney et al., 2021, see e.g. the reviews by) is to reconstruct the evolutionary history of known exoplanets by using their compositions (Öberg et al., 2011; Mordasini et al., 2016; Madhusudhan, 2019; Öberg & Bergin, 2021; Turrini et al., 2021; Turrini et al., 2022; Knierim et al., 2022; Pacetti et al., 2022; Pacetti et al., 2025; Pacetti et al., 2026). This is possible since protoplanetary discs exhibit chemical gradients, generally described in terms of snow lines, i.e. radial boundaries identifying the orbital regions where the disc temperature gradient causes the condensation of chemical species such as H2O, CO2, NH3 and CO in grains. These grains aggregate to form planetary embryos which will then grow by accretion of nearby dust and planetesimals. Once their mass reaches a certain threshold value, these objects will undergo a runaway accretion of the surrounding gas, producing Saturn- and Jupiter-like objects (Johansen & Lambrechts, 2017; Tanaka et al., 2020). Specific elemental ratios are thus imprinted on the atmospheres of these planets, that can then be observed and interpreted (Moses et al., 2013; Line et al., 2014; Pinhas et al., 2019; Spake et al., 2021; Turrini et al., 2021; Pacetti et al., 2022; Pacetti et al., 2025; Pacetti et al., 2026, e.g.). The most widely investigated in this sense is the C/O ratio, hereupon called RobsR_{\text{obs}}, since C and O are the most abundant heavy elements and thus are the easiest to observe with the current instrumentation (Madhusudhan, 2019, see e.g. the review by). The value of RobsR_{\text{obs}} is derived by estimating the volume mixing ratios (VMR) of H2O, CO2, CO and CH4 by the strength of their near- and mid-infrared absorption bands. However, O is a very reactive element that can be readily sequestered by other, more difficult to observe species. Among them, there are the oxides and hydroxides of relatively abundant refractory elements such as Si, Mg and Fe, which can be present both in gas phase and condensed in grains. At temperatures below 1100-1200 K, around 22% of O atoms in a solar-composition atmosphere can be bound to refractories, thus skewing RobsR_{\text{obs}} (Burrows & Sharp, 1999; Fegley & Schaefer, 2010; Visscher et al., 2010). This bias, known as oxygen deficit, has been investigated in the case of warm and hot Jupiters using a chemical equilibrium code for a variety of formation and migration histories by Fonte et al. (2023) (21, hereafter,) who concluded that, due to the non-solar composition of these planets’ atmospheres, it can reach values around 30-40% at temperatures below 1000 K. The same study identified a new class of transitional hot (900-1100 K) exoplanets, where oxygen deficit impacts the transition between CH4- to CO-dominated atmospheres.

Chemical disequilibrium is exoplanetary atmospheres is expected to play an important role in shaping their chemical makeup (Spiegel et al., 2009; Moses et al., 2011; Visscher & Moses, 2011; Venot et al., 2012; Line & Yung, 2013; Drummond et al., 2016; Molaverdikhani et al., 2019). Examples of observations for which it has been invoked are the presence of HCN and NH3 in Hot Jupiters (MacDonald & Madhusudhan, 2017) and the CH4 depletion in Warm Neptunes (Kreidberg et al., 2018). A variety of processes can drive this intrinsically 3D phenomenon, including dayside-nightside temperature differences, vertical mixing, highly energetic radiation and atmospheric escape. Models with varying levels of complexity have been deployed to explore these effects, from fully integrated global circulation, chemical kinetics and radiative transfer codes (Drummond et al., 2020; Zamyatina et al., 2023, e.g.) to partially parameterized or semi-analytical approaches that focus on a specific aspect, such as the atmospheric transport (Mendonça et al., 2018; Beltz et al., 2021; Baeyens et al., 2021), photochemistry (Tsai et al., 2024) or photoevaporation (Rumenskikh et al., 2022). Both self-consistent but computationally expensive coupled models and much faster single-column calculations that can be used to cover the planetary parameter space are required to disentangle this complex problem, and to interpret the increasing volume of high-quality observational data on exoplanetary atmospheres.

papers.title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
papers.abstract: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

papers.intro:
Research on the smart home, ambient assisted living (AAL), and domestic healthcare has increased considerably over the last ten years. One reason is demographic: people aged 65 or over are expected to reach 30% of the European population (Giannakouris, 2008). A smart home is expected to provide its inhabitants with services that help them live better, healthier, and safer lives in their own home. To do so, it needs a set of smart objects that cooperate to acquire, manage, communicate, and share knowledge about the domestic environment and its inhabitants. Integrating and managing such objects is not a trivial task (Jiang et al., 2004), and the health issues associated with ageing further require a consistent, shared conceptualization of the dwellers.

papers.title: Unlocking Cross-Attention in Label-Scarce Regimes: A Weakly Supervised Approach for Video Semantic Segmentation
papers.abstract: Weakly Supervised Video Semantic Segmentation (WS-VSS) aims to learn temporally consistent semantic object masks in videos using only video-level labels. While fully supervised models successfully learn temporal relationships by means of cross-attention, training these temporal weights under weak supervision is unstable and even pushes the model below its single-frame baseline. Therefore, existing WS-VSS methods exploit temporal consistency by relying on external priors, such as optical flow. Unfortunately these cues are non-semantic, computationally expensive and noisy, degrading the supervisory signal. Instead of supervising attention weights directly or using external priors, we propose MemCAM, a WS-VSS transformer framework that learns temporal cross-attention directly through feature-space self-supervision. MemCAM introduces a CAM Propagation Algorithm that synthesizes a supervisory signal by propagating past CAMs according to patch-level feature similarities in the latent space. Specifically, we constrain their induced CAMs through a consistency objective between predicted and propagated maps, stabilizing temporal attention learning. Experiments on the YouTube-Objects v2.2 and WS$^2$ datasets demonstrate that MemCAM consistently outperforms the temporal localization and segmentation performance of WS-VSS alternatives, showing that cross-attention can be effectively trained in label-scarce video settings through internal self-supervision.

papers.intro:
Video semantic segmentation (VSS) is becoming increasingly important for a wide range of computer vision applications. Recent foundation models, such as SAM 2 [30] and SAM 3 [7], have achieved remarkable performance in this domain. Their success relies on cross-attention between frames, which lets transformers learn temporal relationships much as ViTs [14] learn spatial ones via self-attention. Despite their outstanding performance on natural domains, these foundation models often struggle to generalize to highly domain-specific scenarios like waste sorting [28, 42] or industrial defect detection [6, 25]. In such contexts, the dense pixel-level masks required by fully supervised training are costly to acquire. These settings underscore the need for Weakly Supervised (WS) VSS solutions capable of simultaneously learning object semantics and masks using only video-level class or tag. Modern WS methods rely mainly on transformer-based extensions of Class Activation Maps (CAMs) [43] that refine activations by exploiting the self-attention weights learned during training on static images [37, 38, 44]. Although transitioning from self- to inter-frame cross-attention in VSS is conceptually straightforward, our experiments show that naively training these temporal cross-attention weights in a label-scarce regime fails: video-level labels provide no signal to optimize inter-frame attention, so the added temporal weights are at best left untrained and at worst drive the model below its single-frame baseline (Sec. 6.1). Extending this paradigm to WS-VSS thus remains an open problem.

To address this challenge, we propose MemCAM, a framework that trains inter-frame cross-attention within this label-scarce regime. Our key insight is that temporal supervision can emerge from feature-space similarity between nearby frames: by matching patch embeddings across frames, we construct a synthetic CAM target that provides stable supervision for temporal attention. In other words, we decouple the temporal context from its supervision, supervising not the cross-attention weights directly but their effect at the CAM level through feature-space propagation. This lets MemCAM learn temporal cross-attention entirely within a WS setting, without dense annotations or external priors such as optical flow or color consistency that existing temporal WS-VSS models rely on [27, 4, 5], and which are non-semantic, fragile to occlusions or lighting variations, noisy, and introduce a significant computational bottleneck.
