In summary, our main contributions are: (i) We show that inter-frame cross-attention can be effectively trained under video-level supervision, without relying on dense masks or external motion priors, by leveraging learned semantic consistency across frames; (ii) We propose CAMPA, a feature-space CAM propagation strategy that generates synthetic supervision from past frames to stabilize the training of temporal attention in a label-scarce regime; (iii) We introduce a transformer-based WS-VSS architecture that integrates memory-based cross-attention with minimal inference overhead over a standard single-image model. We instantiate it on the family of token-based WS classifiers that natively expose patch tokens and per-class token CAMs (e.g., [38]), and we delimit and discuss this scope explicitly in Sec. G of the Supplementary Material.

papers.title: Gravitational-wave hierarchical inference from population samples
papers.abstract: Standard approaches to gravitational-wave population inference require evaluating the probability density of the population model. While appropriate for models composed of exact functional forms, this approach is not compatible with state-of-the-art astrophysical predictions from population-synthesis codes, which simulate samples from astrophysical models whose densities are unknown. We present an approach that solely requires samples and never density evaluations of the targeted population model. Key technical ingredients include efficient surrogates for the single-event likelihoods and detection probability, together with an efficient sampling strategy. Using detections up to GWTC-5.0, we validate the method against standard inference with a parametric model, showcase its flexibility on a simulated population including hierarchical mergers, and present a realistic application to a grid of astrophysical population-synthesis simulations with five formation channels. This work paves the way toward a direct comparison of astrophysical models and gravitational-wave data.

papers.intro:
Population analyses are now among the most anticipated outcomes of gravitational-wave (GW) observing campaigns, with flagship LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA (LVK) [1, 15, 18] studies [13, 3, 6] stimulating a wealth of further analyses [32]. The distributions of black hole (BH) masses, spins, and redshifts probe the processes that assemble merging binaries, including isolated stellar evolution and dynamical encounters in dense star clusters [96, 98]. Hierarchical Bayesian inference reconstructs these distributions by combining individual event likelihoods with detector selection effects [97, 142].

Hierarchical Bayesian inference reconstructs these distributions by combining individual event likelihoods with detector selection effects [97, 142].

In standard implementations, hierarchical inference requires the density of the population model to be evaluated at arbitrary points in parameter space. This restricts those models to analytical closed-form densities, either parametric (e.g., [13, 3, 6]) or nonparametric (e.g., [49, 34, 115, 76, 119, 133]). In both cases, the connection with astrophysics is drawn after the inference, by comparing the measured features in the population-level distribution, such as peaks, breaks, and cutoffs, with the predictions of formation scenarios. This “comparison” is, at present, still performed somewhat loosely, often by simply overplotting distributions.

Population-synthesis codes (e.g., for isolated binaries [128, 31, 118, 64] and dense star clusters [121, 82]), on the other hand, directly encode the astrophysics driving binary BH mergers and represent our best attempt to predict the population from first principles. State-of-the-art codes evolve a set of initial conditions and return a finite catalog of merging binaries. The population is defined implicitly by the simulation code, and its density is not available in closed form. Such outputs cannot be used directly in the standard framework for hierarchical inference. In statistical terms, we have access to a forward model, while inference requires solving the inverse problem. In practice, astrophysical simulations provide a population model that is “easy to sample” (by running the simulation) but “hard to evaluate” (by computing its probability density at a given point). This is a central obstacle to comparing astrophysical models with GW data, leaving such comparisons at a somewhat heuristic level.

Previous studies have addressed this issue by replacing the population model with an intermediate density estimate constructed from the simulated binaries. This involves running population-synthesis simulations on a grid and interpolating the conditional probability density of the BH parameters across the population hyperparameter space. A variety of density estimation and interpolation methods have been used, including kernel density estimation [152, 38], Gaussian process regression [25, 132], neural networks [100, 117], and normalizing flows [147, 39, 107].

Employing intermediate density estimators fitted to simulations has several drawbacks, however. First, uneven coverage of the population parameter space and varying numbers of binaries across simulations can introduce systematic uncertainties into the population inference that are difficult to quantify. On the practical side, these estimators must be rebuilt and validated for each new set of simulations, whenever population-synthesis predictions are revised or the input physics is updated. Simulation-based inference offers an alternative that avoids these density evaluations [40, 84, 83], but likewise requires retraining a neural network for each new set of simulations. Another strategy separates the description of the data from their astrophysical interpretation by deriving astrophysical results from existing, ideally nonparametric GW population fits [148, 55, 120]. However, this approach assumes an ad hoc conversion from existing Bayesian fits to the population. In this paper, we instead tackle the problem the other way around, and develop a general framework to perform hierarchical inference by sampling the population model instead of evaluating it (Sec. II). Our method is tailored to the general case where the population model is only available through samples and does not require interpolations of the population density or analytical approximations of the likelihood. Specifically, we rewrite the population likelihood so that samples are drawn from the population model, while the functions to be evaluated are the single-event likelihoods and detection probability, which thus require efficient surrogates (Sec. papers.title: Wasserstein geometry of analytic cycle spaces
papers.abstract: We use optimal transport to define an intrinsic distance on connected components of the Barlet space of analytic cycles on a compact K\"ahler manifold, by associating to each cycle its normalized volume measure. We prove that any two cycles in the same connected component can be joined by a deformation of finite Wasserstein length, and that the resulting metric is complete and geodesic. On the locus of smooth reduced cycles at regular parameter points, Wasserstein lengths and energies coincide with those of the normalized Weil--Petersson metric. The construction thus gives a transport interpretation of Weil--Petersson geometry and extends beyond it to components containing no smooth reduced cycles.
papers.intro:
What is the optimal way to deform a complex projective hypersurface into another one? In [ACL25], Antonini, Cavalletti and Lerario approached this question using optimal transport. The starting point was to associate to a hypersurface its normalized volume measure, obtaining a topological embedding of the space of degree-dd hypersurfaces in ℂ​Pn\mathbb{C}\mathrm{P}^{n} into the Wasserstein space of probability measures on ℂ​Pn\mathbb{C}\mathrm{P}^{n}. Singular hypersurfaces were included by integrating over their regular parts and keeping track of multiplicities. One could then measure a deformation by the Wasserstein length of the corresponding curve of measures, and define a distance by minimizing this length among deformations through hypersurfaces of the same degree. A main result of that work was that this distance is finite, complete and geodesic. Moreover, on the open set of smooth hypersurfaces, the construction gives a natural Kähler structure.

A main result of that work was that this distance is finite, complete and geodesic. Moreover, on the open set of smooth hypersurfaces, the construction gives a natural Kähler structure.

This question is part of a more general problem: how should we measure distances in a parameter space of geometric objects? For hypersurfaces, the parameter space is itself a complex projective space, namely the projectivization of the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree dd. A first possibility is therefore to use the Fubini–Study distance associated with a Hermitian inner product on the coefficient space. This geometry is homogeneous: it does not distinguish points representing smooth hypersurfaces from points representing singular ones, and it does not directly measure the motion of their zero sets. One way to incorporate this distinction is to make motion more expensive near the discriminant. This is the principle behind condition geometry in polynomial system solving, developed from the work of Shub and Smale; see [Shu09, SS93]. For example, when the discriminant Σ\Sigma of singular hypersurfaces is nonempty, one can rescale the Fubini–Study Riemannian metric by the inverse square of the distance to Σ\Sigma. The resulting metric has locally Lipschitz coefficients, and approaching Σ\Sigma requires infinite length. (The usual condition metric is defined on a space of problem–solution pairs, with the condition number as a weight.) For the geometric deformation problem, however, we also want to include singular objects and allow paths to reach them. The Wasserstein construction from [ACL25] does this while measuring the motion of the hypersurfaces themselves.

papers.title: Strong solutions to the Cahn--Hilliard--Darcy--Forchheimer system for incompressible two-phase flows with a soluble surfactant
papers.abstract: We study a diffuse-interface model for incompressible viscous two-phase flows with a soluble surfactant in a bounded porous medium in two or three dimensions. The resulting system consists of a Darcy--Forchheimer equation for the seepage velocity $\bm{u}$ coupled with two Cahn--Hilliard equations, one for the difference in volume fractions of the two fluids denoted by $\phi$, and the other for the local concentration of the surfactant $\psi$. In the general scenario of non-constant coefficients and mobilities, we establish the existence of a local (resp. global) strong solution in three (resp. two) dimensions to the corresponding initial-boundary value problem with the no-flux boundary conditions for the phase-field variables and chemical potentials and a no-penetration condition for the velocity. In the case of constant coefficients in the Darcy--Forchheimer equation and constant mobilities in the Cahn--Hilliard equations, with a suitably large Forchheimer exponent, we establish the existence of a global strong solution in three dimensions. Furthermore, using the {\L}ojasiewicz--Simon approach, we prove the global existence of a unique strong solution when the initial data are sufficiently close to a local energy minimizer of the free energy.

papers.intro:
In [29], the authors introduced and analyzed a generalization of the Cahn–Hilliard–Hele–Shaw system proposed in [36] to describe the dynamics of incompressible two-phase flows in a Hele–Shaw cell, which itself is a simplification of the classical “Model H” that couples the Navier–Stokes equations with a convective Cahn–Hilliard equation [4, 33]. Compared with the Cahn–Hilliard–Hele–Shaw framework, the model in [29] incorporates a soluble surfactant through the additional phase-field variable ψ\psi, allows mass transfer through the source term in the ϕ\phi-equation, and includes a Darcy–Forchheimer law that describes the fluid motion in a porous medium. This law contains an additional nonlinear drag term known as the Forchheimer term [8, 46]. The existence of a global weak solution and its convergence to a single equilibrium are the known theoretical results so far (see [29]; see also [11] for a related result). In this study, we deal with the existence and uniqueness of strong solutions. This is a delicate issue, especially in three dimensions, even for the standard Cahn–Hilliard–Hele–Shaw system (see Section 1.2 below). As we shall see, the presence of the Forchheimer term makes the analysis more complicated when dealing with strong solutions, but it helps in proving the existence of a global strong solution in dimension three also for initial data that are not necessarily close to an energy minimizer, at least in the case of constant coefficients and mobilities. This is still an open question for the original Cahn–Hilliard–Hele–Shaw system. In a similar spirit, it is worth recalling the so-called Navier–Stokes–Brinkman–Forchheimer equation, a “tamed” version of the Navier–Stokes system. In this case, thanks to the additional regularity given by the Forchheimer term, it is possible to establish a number of results in dimension three which are unknown for the usual Navier–Stokes system (see, e.g., [44] and references therein, see also [6] for the Navier–Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard system).

papers.title: Evidence for a Fast, Long-Period, Hot Population of Accreting Neutron Stars
papers.abstract: Context. Accreting neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries allow us to probe the accretion histories that produce recycled millisecond pulsars. Aims. We expand the analysis of the spin distribution with an enlarged sample of 39 accreting neutron stars and investigate whether the high-frequency objects preferentially occur in binaries with longer orbital periods and have higher quiescent surface temperatures. Methods. We compare several empirical models for the spin distribution. We use stochastic drift-diffusion estimates and simple braking models to determine whether short-timescale torque fluctuations or secular spin-down can account for the observed population widths. Results. The best statistical description of the spin distribution consists of a broad low-frequency component and a narrow high-frequency concentration centred at ~566 Hz with a width of ~32 Hz. Fast rotators preferentially occupy longer orbital-period binaries, with possibly higher neutron star temperatures. Short-timescale stochastic accretion torque fluctuations cannot produce the observed spin-frequency dispersion in either the fast or the slow component, even under generous assumptions. We show that a non-linear deterministic braking mechanism can instead shift and compress a spin distribution, but the spin data alone do not identify the braking mechanism. Conclusions. The population widths appear to reflect differences in long-term torque conditions and/or evolutionary histories rather than short-timescale torque noise. If the fast systems are close to spin equilibrium, their narrow distribution requires the combination of physical parameters setting the equilibrium frequency to vary relatively little from source to source.Any model that explains the spin distribution should therefore also explain why the fast systems tend to have longer orbital periods and, possibly, higher temperatures.

papers.intro:
Accreting neutron stars (NSs) in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) allow us to study how millisecond pulsars are formed. Matter transferred from a low-mass companion can spin the neutron star up to millisecond periods (Alpar et al., 1982; Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan, 1982; Bhattacharya and van den Heuvel, 1991; Patruno and Watts, 2021). The spin frequency reached by the neutron star depends on the net amount of angular momentum transferred during this accretion phase. The final distribution of spin frequencies therefore can be used as a fingerprint to test accretion-torque models and accretion histories (Patruno et al., 2017a; Niang et al., 2026).

Accreting neutron stars (NSs) in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) allow us to study how millisecond pulsars are formed. Matter transferred from a low-mass companion can spin the neutron star up to millisecond periods (Alpar et al., 1982; Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan, 1982; Bhattacharya and van den Heuvel, 1991; Patruno and Watts, 2021). The final distribution of spin frequencies therefore can be used as a fingerprint to test accretion-torque models and accretion histories (Patruno et al., 2017a; Niang et al., 2026).

An open related question is why accreting NSs do not appear to approach their centrifugal break-up frequencies. Early studies found a possible upper cutoff at around 700 Hz (Chakrabarty et al., 2003; Patruno, 2010; Patruno et al., 2012; Papitto et al., 2014), which is, however, well below the break-up limits of any realistic NS equation of state (Cook et al., 1994; Özel and Psaltis, 2009; Lattimer and Prakash, 2007; Haskell et al., 2018). Several mechanisms could limit further spin-up, like the interaction between the accretion disc and the magnetosphere (Ghosh and Lamb, 1979; Wang, 1995; White and Zhang, 1997; Dai and Li, 2006; Ho et al., 2014). Propeller torques, a trapped disc, or the detachment of the companion from its Roche lobe can also remove angular momentum (D’Angelo and Spruit, 2010; D’Angelo and Spruit, 2012; Tauris, 2012; Patruno et al., 2016). Gravitational waves (GWs), emitted by a deformed star (quadrupolar asymmetry) or through an unstable rr-mode, offer another possibility (Bildsten, 1998; Melatos and Payne, 2005; Haskell et al., 2008; Owen et al., 1998; Andersson, 1998; Andersson et al., 1999). Patruno et al. (2017a) studied 29 accreting NSs and found evidence for a broad lower-frequency component and a much narrower component near 575 Hz. Their two-Gaussian fit gave a mean of 575 Hz and a standard deviation of 30 Hz for the fast component. They also estimated a membership-based division point near 540 Hz, defined as the frequency where the probability of belonging to the fast subpopulation Gaussian is 95%. The concentration of sources in a narrow range of ∼500−600\sim 500-600 Hz raised the question about the possible presence of a spin-down torque becoming important only at high frequencies, once the neutron star enters this narrow spin frequency window. Today we know 39 accreting NSs with a securely measured spin frequency. This larger sample, albeit still small, allows us to revisit that picture. We can also ask whether the fast systems differ from the slower ones in their binary properties, and the orbital period provides a simple way to test this. In fact, the donor and the mechanisms that remove orbital angular momentum affect, in principle, the rate and duration of mass transfer and therefore can be used as a simple framework to interpret the observations (Deloye and Bildsten, 2003; Nelemans and Jonker, 2010; Podsiadlowski et al., 2002; Knigge et al., 2011; Echeveste et al., 2024; Yang and Li, 2024). It is therefore reasonable to ask whether systems with different orbital periods have followed different evolutionary and accretion histories. The relation, however, is complicated by the presence of donor and disc irradiation, outflows, or other subtle effects that can alter the evolution (Patruno et al., 2017b; Rivera Sandoval et al., 2020). The transient behaviour of many LMXBs also changes the time-averaged torque relative to that inferred from a single accretion episode (Bhattacharyya and Chakrabarty, 2017; Gittins and Andersson, 2019). Therefore, disentangling all these effects may not currently be possible given the small number of known objects. However, we can directly test correlations between NS spin frequencies and orbital parameters.

Additional information may come from the quiescent thermal emission of the accreting NSs. Accreted matter heats the crust, while photons and neutrinos cool down the neutron star by carrying energy away. The surface temperature consequently depends on the long-term accretion rate, but also on the efficiency of cooling and the composition of the NS envelope (Brown et al., 1998; Rutledge et al., 2002; Yakovlev et al., 2004; Wijnands et al., 2013). A temperature difference between fast and slow systems could therefore suggest different accretion histories for the NSs.

In this paper, we first reassess the spin distribution of accreting neutron stars (Sect. 2.1). We then compare the orbital periods (Sect. 2.2) and temperatures (Sect. 2.3) to the spin distribution to identify potential differences between slow and fast systems. Finally, we ask whether short-lived torque fluctuations can account for the fitted spin distribution widths, and whether simple secular spin-down prescriptions can produce a narrow distribution when the NSs are not in spin equilibrium (Sect. 3). These calculations allow us to discuss what the observations imply for spin evolution (Sect. 4). This is particularly important for current and future GW searches, as ground-based detectors in the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) network (Aasi and others, 2015; Acernese and others, 2015; Akutsu and others, 2021) have reached the sensitivity where they can set constraints on the scenario in which GW torques are setting the spin equilibrium of these systems (Abac and others, 2026; Whelan and others, 2023; Haskell and Bejger, 2023; Wette, 2023; Abbott et al., 2022a; Abbott et al., 2022b; Middleton et al., 2020; Meadors et al., 2017; Messenger et al., 2015, e.g.). It is therefore crucial to understand whether GWs are expected in some of these systems and, if so, which objects are more likely to emit them.

papers.title: Deciphering multiple binding modes in large protein complexes via Enhanced Sampling and beta-VAE: the CYFIP1-eIF4E case
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) drives cap-dependent translation, regulated by 4E-binding proteins (4E-BPs) competing for its dorsal and lateral surfaces. CYFIP1, a scaffold protein, is both a WAVE Regulatory Complex component and a non-canonical 4E-BP repressing translation via a short helical motif, linked to autism spectrum disorders and cancer. Prior work modeled only this isolated motif as a peptide, leaving the full interface uncharacterized. Starting from this preliminary evidence, we modeled the full-length proteins as flexible partners: all-atom simulations fed a data-driven docking search (HADDOCK3), which guided funnel-restrained Temperature-Accelerated Molecular Dynamics of a coarse-grained Martini 3 representation. Ten replicas accumulated 100 $\mu$s of enhanced sampling. Funnel-restraint variables efficiently sample binding and unbinding but are structurally degenerate: direct clustering of the raw trajectory collapses these poses into poorly resolved groups. We instead reweighted the biased trajectories onto a contact-based latent space built by benchmarking PCA against a beta-Variational Autoencoder, then clustered minima of the equilibrium free-energy surface: only intermediate regularization resolved distinct, homogeneous modes. Three such modes recur, engaging eIF4E's canonical dorsal site, its non-canonical lateral site, and both. We find that CYFIP1 also engages eIF4E through a second surface, the same that mediates its WAVE-complex dimerization, and a basic patch. Both plausibly explain residual binding previously reported after motif mutation. This suggests its translational and cytoskeletal roles compete for the same surface. Most contacts on eIF4E fall outside this dorsal/lateral interface. This heterogeneous, plastic ensemble offers a structural basis for mutagenesis and therapeutic peptide design.

papers.intro:
Eukaryotic initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) is a cap-binding protein that plays a pivotal role in the regulation of translational initiation. By recognizing the 5′ m7GTP cap structure of mRNA, eIF4E recruits the translation machinery binding to eIF4G and promotes ribosome assembly, making it a master regulator of protein synthesis and a key node in the control of cell growth, proliferation, and survival[1]. Its activity is tightly regulated through direct protein-protein interactions with a family of translational repressors known as 4E-binding proteins (4E-BPs). These repressors compete with eIF4G for two binding sites on eIF4E: i) dorsal binding site, Fig. 1a, and ii) lateral surface, Fig. 1b, preventing the assembly of the eIF4F complex and globally suppressing cap-dependent translation [2].

CYFIP1 (Cytoplasmic FMR1-Interacting Protein 1) is a multifunctional scaffold protein that operates at the intersection of two major cellular regulatory axes. On one hand, it is a core structural component of the WAVE Regulatory Complex (WRC), a pentameric assembly comprising CYFIP1, WAVE, ABI, NCKAP, and BRK1, which controls actin cytoskeleton remodeling [3]. On the other hand, CYFIP1 was identified as a non-canonical 4E-BP: through a short helical motif located within its sequence (residues 721–734, Fig. 1c), it binds eIF4E and the Fragile X Mental Retardation Protein (FMRP)[4], suppressing cap-dependent translation.

This dual functionality, Fig. 2a, positions CYFIP1 as a molecular switch essential for neurogenesis, and synaptogenesis[5, 3]. Its dysregulation has been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders including autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia[6].

The structural basis of the CYFIP1-eIF4E interaction remains only partially understood. Mutagenesis studies have established that the helical motif of CYFIP1, spanning residues 721-734, is essential for complex formation; indeed, mutations in this region reduce binding by up to 70% [4] (Fig. 1c). Previous computational investigations provided an initial structural model of the complex but only considered the helix binding motif as an isolated peptide, without treating the entire CYFIP1 protein [1, 7]. Due to the lack of other information, the full extent of the interaction interface and the conformational heterogeneity of the complex have not yet been characterized at atomic resolution. This gap limits both the mechanistic understanding of translational regulation by CYFIP1 and the rational exploitation of this interface for therapeutic purposes.

To address these open questions, we developed and applied a multi-scale computational pipeline specifically designed to handle the conformational flexibility of a large protein-protein complex, a challenge shared with other large, flexible multidrug transport systems whose substrate binding has been characterized through molecular dynamics simulations [8]. The strategy is organized in three sequential tiers. In the first tier, extensive all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of the individual proteins were used to generate different structural ensembles, which were subsequently clustered and used for a data-driven docking protocol using HADDOCK3 [9]. The resulting ensemble complexes served for defining the geometrical parameters for a specific funnel-shaped spatial restraint potential around the known binding motif of CYFIP1 (Fig. 2b) used in the second tier. The most representative docked structures were converted to a coarse-grained representation using the Martini 3 force field [10] and subjected to Temperature-Accelerated Molecular Dynamics (TAMD)[11] in combination with a funnel restrain [12], accumulating 100 μ\mus of enhanced sampling across 10 replicas, Fig. 2c. This approach enables multiple binding and unbinding events, thereby ensuring extensive sampling of the binding free energy landscape, in line with enhanced-sampling strategies developed for resolving protein-protein binding pathways and rate constants [13]. In the third tier, the configurational ensemble generated by TAMD simulations was first reduced to binary contact matrices of the most frequently contacted residues (Fig. 2d), converted into inter-residue distance matrices (Fig. 2e), and analyzed using a combination of β\beta-Variational Autoencoder (β\beta-VAE) and free-energy reweighting, addressing the broader challenge of extracting structure from the high-dimensional, time-correlated data generated by molecular dynamics simulations through deep learning [14].

papers.title: Rational lines on pairs of quadrics and cubic hypersurfaces
papers.abstract: We study rational lines on smooth intersections of two quadrics and on smooth cubic hypersurfaces over number fields. For an intersection of two quadrics in $n$ variables, we prove the Hasse principle and weak approximation for the variety of lines when $n\geq 11$, and more generally for the variety of $r$-planes when $n\geq 3r+8$. In this range an $r$-plane exists over the ground field if and only if one exists over every real completion. For the variety of lines, we also prove the Hasse principle and weak approximation when $n\geq 8$, conditional on the finiteness of certain Tate-Shafarevich groups. For a smooth cubic hypersurface in $n$ variables, we prove that a line exists over the ground field when $n\geq 23$.

papers.title: Deep, label-free, volumetric lifetime microscopy via low-noise, single pulse sampling
papers.abstract: Fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) provides label-free metabolic contrast, but conventional time-correlated single-photon counting requires thousands of excitation pulses per pixel to avoid pile-up distortion, limiting imaging speed and increasing motion artifacts and photodamage. Here, we develop single-pulse analog sampling that combines sub-photoelectron read noise with a jitter-immune, frequency-domain estimator for accurate lifetime measurement at low photon counts. Single low-flux traces achieve a photon economy of $F < 1.5$ at 100--150 detected photons, enabling accurate lifetime estimation from a single excitation pulse in label-free, volumetric samples. In in vivo zebrafish eyes, single-shot acquisition recovered the lifetime content of 20-pulse averaging at one-twentieth the exposure, resolving endogenous lipofuscin heterogeneity. In intact mouse kidney, scattering and reduced photon throughput impaired lifetime contrast; this was mitigated by lightweight denoisers that enabled label-free lifetime imaging to 200 micron depth at one pulse per pixel. These results establish single-shot FLIM as a route to deeper, faster, motion-tolerant, low-photodamage lifetime imaging.

papers.title: Hierarchical hyperbolicity of Coxeter groups
papers.abstract:
We show that for every finite rank Coxeter system, the Coxeter group is hierarchically hyperbolic relative to its nonhyperoctahedral irreducible higher rank affine parabolic subgroups. This is sharp---the Coxeter group admits a hierarchically hyperbolic group structure if and only if it has no such parabolic subgroups, and we give a complete diagrammatic characterization of when this is true. Moreover, this condition is equivalent to the existence of a coarsely equivariant coarse median on the Coxeter group.
  We also show that the Coxeter group is virtually a colorable hierarchically hyperbolic group. This is achieved by passing to a congruence subgroup of the Tits representation.
  As consequences, the Davis complex is a hierarchically hyperbolic space and the group admits a coarse median of rank equal to its algebraic rank. Furthermore, the Coxeter group is quasimedian quasiisometric to a finite dimensional CAT(0) cube complex and is virtually coarsely injective.
  Two appendices prove results of independent interest that are not Coxeter-specific. The first promotes a relative HHS structure with HHS peripheral coordinate spaces to an HHS structure. The second shows that a virtually Abelian group admits a coarsely equivariant coarse median precisely when it is hyperoctahedral.

papers.intro:
Coxeter groups have a rich geometry arising from their wall structure and the structure of their parabolic subgroups. In a previous paper [17] we showed that hyperbolic aspects of this geometry can be understood in close analogy to those of the mapping class group of a hyperbolic surface. By coning off the nonhyperbolic regions in the Davis complex Σ=Σ⁡(W,S)\Sigma=\Sigma(W,S) of a finite rank Coxeter system (W,S)(W,S), we produced a hyperbolic space Σwidehat\widehat{\Sigma} playing the role of the curve graph of the surface: it recognizes the Morse quasigeodesics and stable subspaces of the Davis complex, and provides the largest acylindrically hyperbolic structure on the Coxeter group. However, coning off the nonhyperbolic regions collapses them to bounded diameter, effectively discarding the geometry of unbounded regions in Σ\Sigma. The purpose of this paper is to recover that missing geometry, in a way that further strengthens the mapping class group analogy.

The notion of a hierarchically hyperbolic space formalizes these hierarchical constructions.

A hierarchically hyperbolic space (HHS) is a quasigeodesic metric space described by a system of hyperbolic coordinate spaces that are indexed by hierarchically related “domains”. A set of axioms governs the interactions between domains, their coordinate spaces, and projections to the coordinate spaces, in such a way that consistent coordinate data can be coarsely realized by a point in the original space. Moreover, a distance formula recovers the original metric, up to quasiisometry, from the sum of sufficiently large coordinate distances. A hierarchically hyperbolic group (HHG) is a group with an HHS structure on its Cayley graph that has additional equivariance properties. HHSs were introduced to provide a common framework for studying the geometry of mapping class groups and cocompactly cubulated groups [5], thus providing a bridge to transfer results from one setting to the other.

papers.title: FOMOS: Feature-Oriented Meshing of SDFs
papers.abstract: We introduce FOMOS, a purely geometric method for feature-oriented meshing of signed distance functions (SDFs) that addresses various challenges of the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our algorithm improves mesh quality and runtime, enabling the SDF meshing in a matter of seconds. While existing techniques such as Marching Cubes and Neural Dual Contouring either produce dense, low-quality triangulations or sacrifice details for sparsity, often requiring carefully chosen user parameters, our single-parameter FOMOS leverages feature sized sampling to dynamically adjust mesh resolution based on local feature size (LFS), which we compute efficiently by sampling a medial scaffold. The LFS considers not only curvature but also shape thickness and captures large features through non-local structure, omitting many redundant small triangles from existing methods. Through extensive comparisons, we demonstrate the distinct strengths of FOMOS in execution time, reconstructed result accuracy, and triangle quality in the output mesh. We also introduce a lightweight variant of FOMOS targeting huge ($10k^3$) sparse inputs, which, to the best of our knowledge, no existing method can handle except Marching Cubes. To demonstrate the usefulness of our method, we show that FOMOS enables instant previews using a sub-sampled medial scaffold and can accelerate volumetric simulations by orders of magnitude.

papers.intro:
A Signed Distance Field (SDF) is a scalar function that, for any given point in space, returns the distance to the nearest point on a given boundary, with the sign indicating whether the point lies inside or outside the boundary. As a classical representation, SDFs have served as a fundamental building block for a wide range of applications in shape modeling and geometry processing. In addition to these traditional applications, recent advances in machine/deep learning have increasingly relied on SDFs for geometric deep learning, thanks to their advantages in continuous shape encoding and differentiable geometric operations. Despite the advantages of a continuous representation, which ensures resolution independence and facilitates procedural modeling and shape reconstruction (e.g., DeepSDF (Park et al., 2019)), it is often discretized into triangular meshes to support various downstream applications. This discretization is typically preferred as it can be easily parallelized, seamlessly integrated into standard rendering pipelines, and efficiently stored.

As a classical representation, SDFs have served as a fundamental building block for a wide range of applications in shape modeling and geometry processing. In addition to these traditional applications, recent advances in machine/deep learning have increasingly relied on SDFs for geometric deep learning, thanks to their advantages in continuous shape encoding and differentiable geometric operations. Despite the advantages of a continuous representation, which ensures resolution independence and facilitates procedural modeling and shape reconstruction (e.g., DeepSDF (Park et al., 2019)), it is often discretized into triangular meshes to support various downstream applications. This discretization is typically preferred as it can be easily parallelized, seamlessly integrated into standard rendering pipelines, and efficiently stored.

Mesh generation from SDFs is often performed by sampling the function at discrete points, typically using grids, octrees, or point clouds. Although these methods are simple and easy to implement and use, their reliance on uniform sampling prioritizes volumetric coverage over geometric fidelity. This often leads to the omission of important edges, corners, or surface curvature variations, as it does not explicitly preserve these features. Consequently, it introduces approximation errors in critical applications such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and finite element methods (FEM), which reduce simulation accuracy. Although it is possible to implement workarounds using a very dense grid sampling followed by feature-aware remeshing, such solutions are both computationally expensive and require significant peak memory as volumetric data grows with cubic complexity. Furthermore, such workarounds are suboptimal as they do not account for the global shape structure.

Our core idea is to adopt an ε\varepsilon-sampling framework that determines the sampling density according to the local feature size (LFS), defined as the distance from a surface point to the medial axis (Amenta et al., 1998) (please see Section 3.1 for a formal definition). This choice addresses key limitations of conventional sampling strategies: uniform-length sampling uses a fixed spatial scale regardless of local geometric complexity, whereas curvature-aware sampling relies solely on surface curvature alone, which may not fully capture the scale of thin structures or closely spaced surface regions (particularly useful for volumetric meshing). In contrast, ε\varepsilon-sampling based on LFS accounts for both local curvature and the spatial proximity of surface regions, providing a principled basis to preserve fine geometric details while avoiding unnecessary sampling in less complex regions (Amenta and Bern, 1998; Boissonnat and Oudot, 2005). To achieve this, we introduce a new technique for computing the local feature size (LFS), and subsequently incorporate an iterative refinement process to add points that meet that sampling condition, thereby preserving and capturing features of arbitrary size. We demonstrate that our method outperforms the state of the art in both quality and runtime, further enabling instant in-memory meshing of SDFs with huge grid sizes of 10240310240^{3}, and illustrate the advantages of feature-based meshing by running FEM simulations on its volumetric interior.

papers.title: BLiMP-RO: A Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for Romanian
papers.abstract: Evaluating grammatical knowledge in language models requires benchmarks that cover diverse linguistic phenomena and are validated against human judgments. We introduce BLiMP-RO, a Romanian minimal-pair benchmark covering 50 grammatical phenomena across ten domains. It comprises 493 linguist-constructed sentence pairs, evaluated by native speakers in five experiments, and 5,942 additional semi-automatically generated, human-validated pairs. We further investigate grammatical generalization under limited linguistic input by training GPT-2 and GPT-BERT models from scratch on Romanian BabyBabelLM data and a newly collected corpus of 10 million words from child-targeted video captions. Increasing caption training data yields approximately 9 percentage points of accuracy improvement per tenfold increase in corpus size. At matched data sizes, BabyBabelLM generally outperforms video captions, while GPT-BERT consistently outperforms GPT-2. Our findings highlight how training data quantity, composition, and model architecture shape grammatical generalization in Romanian.

papers.intro:
Minimal-pair benchmarks test whether a language model assigns a higher probability to a grammatical sentence than to a minimally different ungrammatical one (Marvin and Linzen, 2018; Warstadt et al., 2020). They build on acceptability judgments, a standard source of evidence in syntax (Chomsky, 1965; Schütze, 2016), and probe agreement and syntactic dependencies that overall predictive performance does not isolate (Linzen et al., 2016; Wilcox et al., 2018; Wilcox et al., 2024). Minimal pairs can be used to examine the point at which grammatical knowledge emerges when language models are trained on smaller, developmentally-motivated corpora. As such, they must have broad linguistic coverage and evidence that speakers recognize the intended contrasts.

For Romanian, existing minimal-pair evaluation is limited. MultiBLiMP (Jumelet et al., 2026b) contains 2,056 Romanian pairs derived from treebanks, but they focus on agreement involving subjects, verbs, and participles and have not been validated with native-speaker judgments. The dataset, however, does not cover typical properties of Romanian grammar such as differential object marking (DOM), clitics and clitic doubling, strict negative concord, referential null subjects, or subjunctive complements in contexts where other Romance languages prefer an infinitive (Pană Dindelegan, 2013; Dobrovie-Sorin, 1994).

We introduce BLiMP-RO, a linguist-constructed benchmark covering 50 phenomena across ten grammatical domains (see Table 1). We develop two datasets: an initial hand-crafted set of 10 pairs of sentences per phenomenon (500 items) and an extended set constructed semi-automatically consisting of 120 pairs of sentences per phenomenon (6000 items). The initial set is used for acceptability rating with at least 50 human participants for each item across five experiments. After further validation, we retain 493 pairs. Human accuracy (96%) and agreement (93.1%) are computed on this dataset. The extended set is constructed using few shot prompting using Claude Opus 5.5 and has been validated by 3 human annotators, leaving a total of 5,942 valid sentence pairs. The complete set is mainly used to compare language models.

Following the BabyLM approach of training relatively small models on developmentally motivated corpora (Warstadt et al., 2023), we train Romanian GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and GPT-BERT models from scratch using two data sources. The first is the Romanian portion of BabyBabelLM (Jumelet et al., 2026a), which combines child-directed speech and children’s books with subtitle-based fallback text. The second is a curated corpus of 10 million Romanian words from captions of child-targeted videos discovered through YouTube Kids profiles for ages 0–4 and 5–8, followed by collection from eligible channels.

papers.title: DoubleTake: Focused Verification of Visual Evidence for Long-Document Understanding
papers.abstract: In long-document question answering, a vision-language model can answer incorrectly even when the retrieved pages contain sufficient evidence. Rereading those pages with the original question gives the model little guidance about which fact to check. We introduce DoubleTake, a training-free framework for focused verification of visual evidence. An initial reading produces a candidate answer and a separate evidence record that guides retrieval for a second reading. A planner compares the two candidates and their supporting evidence to formulate a factual question. A verifier answers it from the source images without seeing either candidate or evidence record, and a reasoner uses this observation to resolve the original question. With a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone, DoubleTake achieves the highest overall accuracy among the evaluated methods on each of four benchmarks. With the same pages and number of model calls, asking a focused factual question yields higher accuracy on all four benchmarks than asking the original question again. Our code is available at https://github.com/small-code-cat/double_take.

papers.intro:
In long-document question answering, the evidence needed to answer a question may be distributed across prose, tables, and charts whose interpretation depends on their visual structure [1, 2]. A vision–language model (VLM) can read page images directly [3], but locating the relevant information in a long document can require searching across many pages [4, 5]. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) narrows this search to a set of relevant pages [6, 7]. Within that set, MDocAgent combines specialized readings of text and images, while SLEUTH extracts clues and filters pages to build a compact context for answering [8, 9].

It must determine which facts are relevant and, when the question calls for a comparison, how to compare them. This judgment can be checked against the original pages once a candidate answer is available. Asking the original question again, however, leaves the VLM to decide for itself which part of its interpretation needs checking (Fig. 1(b)). A focused check therefore requires identifying a fact on which the proposed answer depends.

papers.title: Shape of semiflexible polymer chains: L\'evy walks vs. Persistent random walks
papers.abstract: The conformational size and shape characteristics of semiflexible polymer chains, modeled via two distinct frameworks: persistent random walks (PRW) and L\'evy walks (LW), are analyzed through numerical simulations. We introduce a mapping that treats the mean jump length $\langle \ell \rangle$ of a L\'evy distribution ($\sim \ell^{-(1+\sigma)}$) as an effective persistence length of the semiflexible polymer chain, controlled by the exponent $\sigma $. While the conformational characteristics of the PRW model statistically exhibit a sharp crossover from flexible coil to the rigid-rod-like behavior in the immediate vicinity of the maximum persistence probability $p \to 1$, the LW model shows a much richer conformational behavior. We obtain the quantitative estimates for universal shape parameters, such as asphericity \(\langle A_3 \rangle\) and prolateness \(\langle S \rangle\), which gradually increase with decreasing parameter $\sigma $ (and thus with an increase of the persistence length), thus supporting previously observed findings for semiflexible polymers. Our results demonstrate the effictiveness of applying L\'evy-walk statistics to capture the universal conformational properties of semiflexible polymer structures.

papers.title: Latent resonances in oscillator networks
papers.abstract: In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's global oscillation energy decreases and its spectral properties improve. The amplified oscillation arises from a latent resonance that lies in the spectrum yet barely manifests. The added passive damping reshapes this resonance by mixing it with adjacent eigenmodes. In random power-grid networks, damping can boost weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant channels can grow to exceed the originally strongest channel. Damping thus not only suppresses oscillations but also provides a way to redistribute oscillatory energy. For any passive network, the amplified response and its upper bound follow exactly from baseline quantities, offering a principled route for network design and control.
papers.intro:
Collective dynamics emerge in networks of coupled oscillators across nature and technology, from circadian cells and neurons[57, 1] to ecological populations[5], mechanical structures[56, 7] and power grids[13]. Their function depends on how these networks withstand and respond to perturbations[18, 58, 29]. Whether a network withstands small perturbations is commonly assessed from the eigenvalues of its linearized dynamics[24]. A stable network can still respond strongly. A periodic disturbance near the frequency of a mode drives a resonant response, as in the forced oscillations that can spread across an entire power grid[15, 26, 36]. Even when every mode decays fast, non-normal interactions can amplify perturbations[52, 2, 32], as quantified by the reactivity and the pseudospectra of the system matrix[33, 51, 11]. How strongly a network responds also depends on where it is driven and where it is observed, the input-output channel[31], and on its topology[53, 60].

In power grids, oscillations manifest as oscillating power flows on transmission lines, bounded by the thermal ratings and protection schemes of these lines. The grid dynamics follow the swing equation[24] and can be described by a second-order Kuramoto model, in which these lines define the coupling between nodes[13]. The physical lines are fixed once built, but converter controls can introduce inertia and damping at selected nodes[12]. For an isolated weakly damped oscillator, added damping shifts the mode away from the imaginary axis and reduces the forced response across all frequencies. Because damping dissipates energy, it is commonly assumed to suppress oscillations across the entire network. Inertia and damping have been allocated to minimize an H2H_{2} performance measure of the grid[43], to stabilize the synchronous state[28], and, in our previous work, to suppress the worst-case oscillation[59]. Modal methods and screening indices guiding such placement rank modes, nodes, and channels according to their baseline behavior[24, 39, 53], so weakly responding channels receive low priority. This practice treats added damping as a benefit, to be placed where it helps most. The energy reasoning underlying this perspective, however, focuses on the total stored energy of the network, rather than its distribution over branches, which are the connections between nodes. Added damping can therefore improve global network behavior, as widely anticipated, without benefiting every channel, and may even amplify oscillations along some channels. It remains open how network structure and parameter allocation jointly determine which channels are amplified, and the magnitude of such amplification.

Reorganizing this oscillatory energy can open a channel on which a resonance of the network barely shows up at baseline. We call such a resonance latent on that channel, and the channel a latent channel. Figure 1 shows the simplest case. The units are coupled by springs, and we monitor the spring forces acting on the inter-unit connections. For three identical units arranged in a triangle, a disturbance at unit 3 excites a lightly damped resonance, yet the force between units 1 and 2 vanishes at all frequencies, because the two units are interchangeable[46, 55]. Increasing the damping of unit 1 brings this resonance into the force signal, even as the total network damping rises. We say that the damping opens the channel. Any mismatch between units 1 and 2, in damping, inertia, or coupling, opens the channel, whereas identical parameter changes do not. More generally, identically positioned nodes with the same inertia and damping move together when the disturbance enters elsewhere, so latent channels of this kind are set by the structure of the network[38, 47]. Unlike resonant and non-normal amplification, which are properties of a given network, this amplification is caused by a change of the network itself.

Here we derive exactly the response of any channel to a local change of damping from the frequency response of the network before the change. For any passive network, both the resulting channel response and its upper bound can be predicted prior to modifying damping. A modal expansion reveals that inter-node damping heterogeneity mixes adjacent eigenmodes, increasing the spectral weight of a latent resonance on the corresponding channel. In random power-grid networks, local damping can amplify oscillations on weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant branches may develop responses exceeding the network’s largest baseline oscillation. This latent-channel mechanism also operates in eight oscillator models (Fig. 2), the pan-European transmission grid (section S6), and under local reductions of node inertia or line coupling (section S12). Our theory yields an important implication for collective dynamics in coupled oscillator networks: a more stable network is not necessarily a safer one. Stability is governed by the spectrum, whereas safety depends on how network structure and parameters jointly distribute the response across its connections.

papers.title: On the Limits of Sufficient Explanations
papers.abstract: We formally characterize the conditions under which sufficient explanations exist for classifiers on structured data such as graphs and strings. We focus on post-hoc explainers that select parts of the input as sufficient explanations. An explanation is sufficient if the selected part alone ensures the predicted label. Sufficient explanations have been widely adopted across data modalities, including graphs, strings, and images. However, a unified formal analysis of sufficient explanations remains missing. We bridge this gap with four main contributions: (i) We define a general explanation formalism consisting of an instance space, a classifier, and a select relation. The select relation specifies which potential sub-instances or feature subsets can be selected as explanations from each instance; (ii) We show that the existence of sufficient explainers is fully characterized by the interplay between the classifier and the select relation; (iii) We extend this analysis to practically relevant variants of sufficiency, including probabilistic sufficiency and deletion sufficiency; (iv) Based on the formal analysis, we devise statistics that bound the maximum achievable sufficiency for a given task. We evaluate these statistics on language, protein, and molecular classification datasets and find that full sufficiency is unattainable on most of them. Since these bounds hold for every explainer, they provide a task-level reference against which any explainer's sufficiency can be judged in absolute terms.

papers.intro:
We investigate the fundamental limits of post-hoc sufficient explanations on structured data. We characterize when such explanations exist, when achieving exact sufficiency is impossible, and how much sufficiency can still be achieved. Given a classifier’s prediction on an input, sufficient explanations identify a subset of the input features that ensures that the prediction remains unchanged (Dasgupta et al., 2022). Sufficiency is a widely studied notion of explanation, appearing in sufficient reasons (Darwiche and Hirth, 2020; Barceló et al., 2020; Marques-Silva et al., 2021; Bassan et al., 2024; Bassan et al., 2025; Bassan et al., 2026), prime-implicant explanations (Shih et al., 2018; de Colnet and Marquis, 2022), Anchors (Ribeiro et al., 2018; Dasgupta et al., 2022), and sufficient input subsets (Carter et al., 2019; Dasgupta et al., 2022). Although sufficient explanations have been adopted as a strong notion of faithful explanations for graphs, strings, and vector data, most formal analyses have focused on fixed-dimensional feature spaces (like ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and {0,1}d\{0,1\}^{d}) (Barceló et al., 2020; Darwiche and Hirth, 2020; Marques-Silva et al., 2021) and logical reasoning systems (Eiter and Gottlob, 1995; Bylander et al., 1991; Bienvenu, 2008). These analyses do not characterize when sufficient explanations exist in general.

We uniformly formalize the space of explanations that can be expressed by different explanation methods for graphs, strings, or vector spaces in terms of a select relation on the instance space. Intuitively, the select relation formalizes whether a set of features corresponding to an instance xx can be selected by an explainer as an explanation for a prediction on an instance yy. Our key insight is that the select relation and the classifier jointly characterize co-bounds, i.e., an instance that can be selected from a differently labeled instance (e.g., see Figure 1). This results in a simple characterization: a sufficient explainer exists iff there are no co-bounds. Although simple, this characterization separates what an explainer can achieve from what the task permits. A task which admits instances that can be selected from differently labeled instances is fundamentally not amenable to sufficient explanations. This obstruction differs from the out-of-distribution problems discussed in the post-hoc explainability literature (Hase et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2024). Crucially, existence of co-bounds is an in-distribution barrier to sufficiency that can be checked directly on a dataset. Even the trivial explainer, which selects the whole instance as an explanation, is not sufficient for a task that admits co-bounds.

We extend our analysis to two relaxed notions of sufficiency, probabilistic sufficiency (Dasgupta et al., 2022) and deletion sufficiency. Probabilistic sufficiency is the probability that the prediction remains unchanged under perturbations to features outside the explanation. We show that this probability can be intrinsically bounded away from one, i.e., for some instance- and task-dependent constant c>0c>0, every explainer has probabilistic sufficiency at most 1−c1-c. Deletion sufficiency underlies several perturbation-based evaluations of post-hoc explanations (Carter et al., 2019; Amara et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2024). It requires that the prediction remains unchanged when features outside the explanation are removed. Because it considers only deletions from the original instance, rather than arbitrary extensions, it is strictly weaker than sufficiency. Although deletion sufficiency is always achievable, we identify tasks where deletion-sufficient explanations are vacuous, i.e., provide no information about the classifier.

These statistics are computed from the dataset alone, independently of a specific classifier or explainer. We evaluate them on molecular, protein, peptide, and sentiment classification datasets. Nine of the ten datasets contain co-bounds, so no classifier that fits their labels admits a sufficient explainer. The statistics also show that the co-bound count alone can understate their effect. ENZYMES (Borgwardt et al., 2005) has only 2.2% of the instances as co-bounds, yet removing them requires relabeling 82% of its instances.

papers.title: Detection and Classification in Latent Spaces: High-Dimensional Analysis and Validation
papers.abstract: Foundation models produce high-dimensional latent representations in which suitably designed statistical decision rules can be effective yet analytically tractable. We study such detectors in the high-dimensional regime, where latent dimension and training sample size grow proportionally. For linear and quadratic statistics, we derive explicit large-deviation characterizations of false-alarm and miss-detection performance under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm, and show how the binary analysis extends to multi-class classification. The resulting error probabilities and corresponding decay rates exhibit non-monotonic dependence on the shape parameter, including double-descent and, in some regimes, multiple-descent. Experiments on vision, text, and audio datasets using modern foundation models show close agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical performance. In particular, the proposed framework allows us to set a prescribed false-alarm level and accurately predict the corresponding miss-detection probability. Overall, our results provide a theoretically grounded and interpretable framework with competitive empirical performance across different modalities.

Our focus on foundation models is motivated by recent insights from Balestriero and LeCun [5]. papers.title: Local Stochastic Volatility Iterations
papers.abstract: We propose a calibration method for local stochastic volatility models that determines the leverage factor by a fixed-point iteration. Each iteration simulates the model with the current leverage factor and approximates the conditional expectation of the stochastic variance given the spot by a single regression in time and state, with a quasi-likelihood loss for positive responses. The resulting leverage factor is a smooth function of time and spot with relatively few parameters, which can in addition be refined directly against option quotes. We recalibrate the leverage factor to S&P 500 index options on the day of an interest rate announcement, keeping the parameters of a two-factor Bergomi model calibrated four weeks earlier. After five iterations, leverage factors with 63 and 143 coefficients reproduce the implied volatility surface fitted to the quotes within a few basis points over the quoted strikes, the smaller one except in the left wing, and further iterations change them little. A few regularized Gauss-Newton steps against the quotes then bring 87% and 95% of the liquid quotes inside their bid-ask intervals.

Local stochastic volatility (LSV) models combine a stochastic volatility model with a local volatility factor, the leverage factor, so that the stochastic volatility governs the dynamics of the smile while the model reproduces the observed prices of vanilla options [29, 26, 42]. An Euler-type time discretization of the equation is well defined, and weak error estimates for it were recently obtained in [17].

papers.title: Go under Chinese Rules with a Succinct Game History is Complete for Exponential Space
papers.abstract:
The complexity of games is a central topic in combinatorics, algorithms, and computational complexity theory. It asks how difficult it is to determine the winner of a combinatorial game under optimal play. Many games, such as Hex or Othello, are PSPACE-complete: the game tree has polynomial depth, so the game can be decided in PSPACE. However, some games allow exponentially long plays, for instance Chess (without a generalized 50-move rule) or Go under Japanese rules; these are complete for exponential time. To prevent infinite games, some games employ a no-repetition rule (super-ko rule), for instance Go under Chinese rules. Robson (1984) proved that Chess and Checkers with a no-repetition rule are even harder: deciding whether the first player has a winning strategy is EXPSPACE-complete. Since then, it has been an open problem whether Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete, too.
  The complexity of a game under a no-repetition rule is typically interpreted as follows: given a board position, decide whether the first player has a winning strategy such that no repetition occurs from that position on. We introduce the concept of a succinct game history: a Boolean circuit that, given a board position, outputs 1 if the position is in the game history and 0 otherwise. It serves as a "judge" that tells the players whether a move is illegal because it creates a repetition. We prove that deciding whether Black has a winning strategy in Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete when the game history is given succinctly. Moreover, the starting position in our hardness proof is reachable by legal gameplay, which has not always been the case in prior proofs.

Classical board games such as Checkers, Chess, and Go have been extensively studied in combinatorial game theory and computational complexity theory. To study the complexity of such games, we must allow for arbitrary board sizes. Classical board games such as Checkers, Chess, and Go have been extensively studied in combinatorial game theory and computational complexity theory. To study the complexity of such games, we must allow for arbitrary board sizes. For Checkers and Go, this generalizes rather naturally and in fact, Go is even played on different board sizes in reality (typically 9×99\times 9, 13×1313\times 13, and 19×1919\times 19). For Chess one typically has one king but increases the number of the other pieces proportionally to the board size. In each case, we study the following decision problem: given a particular board configuration, determine whether the player whose turn it is has a winning strategy.

While TQBF\mathrm{TQBF} (if interpreted as a game) and Generalized Geography allow an exponential number of distinct playthroughs, each game ends after a polynomial number of moves. For games like Checkers, Chess, or Go this is not true, in principle a game could last forever by creating a cycle in the gameplay. This is not desirable in real gameplay and typically prevented by the rules. The exact way in which this is prevented can have a huge impact on the complexity of the game. For instance, Checkers requires that some progress must be made after 40 moves or the game is a draw. Fraenkel et al. [4] generalize this rule to arbitrary board sizes: A game is drawn whenever there occurs a sequence of n3n^{3} moves for both players, with none of these moves being a capture or the advance of a non-king. Under this rule, Fraenkel et al. show that Checkers is 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-complete. Without such a rule, Checkers becomes 𝖤𝖷𝖯\mathsf{EXP}-complete. The same is true for Chess. Storer [16] shows that generalized chess with a polynomial draw rule like in Checkers is 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-complete. Without this rule, Fraenkel and Lichtenstein [5] prove that Chess is 𝖤𝖷𝖯\mathsf{EXP}-complete. To stop potentially infinite gameplay, one can also add a no-repetition rule (also called super-ko rule, as it is used in Go under Chinese rules). The impact of no-repetition rules on the complexity is the main subject of this work. Such a rule states that no board position may repeat during gameplay and a player loses if all of their moves create a repeated board position. Such games end after at most an exponential number of moves, assuming that each board configuration has polynomial description size, which is true for Checkers, Chess, and Go. While such a rule makes games finite, deciding whether a player has a winning strategy often becomes harder! This may seem counterintuitive at first glance, but it is due to the fact that one has to keep track of the whole game history. In particular, Robson [12] created a general method that proves that games that allow a certain reduction from a combinatorial game by Stockmeyer and Chandra [15] become 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{EXPSPACE}-complete with a no-repetition rule added. Specifically, Checkers as well as Chess are 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{EXPSPACE}-complete with a no-repetition rule. However, Robson [12] notes that this does not apply to Go. In fact, the complexity of Go under Chinese rules has been an open question since the work of Robson [12], see for instance [7, Section 6.3] or [17]. (Go with a no-repetition rule is often called Go under Chinese rules, as the Chinese rules of Go include such a no-repetition rule as opposed to Japanese rules. There are other rule sets of Go that include the no-repetition rule, the interested reader is referred to [18]. Note that our hardness proofs work for other rule sets that include a positional no-repetition rule.)

papers.title: Query Processing with eBPF-Offload on Computational Storage
papers.abstract: The idea of pushing computation to storage devices has been explored for decades. In recent years, research has focused on computational storage, i.e., devices that allow a host to execute functions as I/O commands on local data. Today, the NVMe and SNIA computational storage standards share an execution model in which the host invokes functions on the device, on data that the host has moved into device memory. Both standards single out eBPF as a format for functions offloaded by the host. In this paper, we study whether this form of computational storage is a good match for query processing. We present the design and implementation of Delilah, a prototype based on an open-hardware device that implements the standard execution model on an actual device and runs eBPF programs calling device-resident functions. As an initial step, we hand-coded a portion of SSB Q3.3 for execution on the device, aiming to integrate computational storage with a database system's storage manager. The series of experiments that we ran showed that offloading gains little over host execution, execution degenerates into column-at-a-time processing, and time is spent staging and moving data in device memory. Because these roadblocks stem from the execution model rather than from the query, we did not pursue integration further. We detail these limitations and lay the groundwork for a different computational storage model better aligned with data-intensive workloads.

To avoid the data-access bottleneck [36], data-centric architectures place processing capability near where the data resides. For data management, this idea goes back to active disks [42] and has resurfaced with each generation of storage hardware [1]. Its current incarnation is computational storage, a form of near-data processing that enables hosts to invoke functions on device data via I/O commands [29]. After a first generation of prototypes and products based on proprietary interfaces, computational storage is now standardized through SNIA11 1 Storage Networking Industry Association, the trade association representing storage companies. The SNIA programming model is broad [49]. In its direct usage model, the host invokes a function on data in device memory. In its indirect usage model, the storage controller moves data from storage into device memory and triggers a function as a side effect of a storage request. Aggregator functions invoke sequences of functions on the device, possibly in parallel and possibly repeatedly, so as to operate on data with minimal host involvement.

The SNIA programming model is broad [49]. In its direct usage model, the host invokes a function on data in device memory. In its indirect usage model, the storage controller moves data from storage into device memory and triggers a function as a side effect of a storage request. Aggregator functions invoke sequences of functions on the device, possibly in parallel and possibly repeatedly, so as to operate on data with minimal host involvement.

The SNIA and NVMe interfaces that realize this model are much narrower [48, 38]. They are both explicitly tailored for a host-orchestrated interface. In NVMe, a computational program operates only on data in the device memory, denoted subsystem local memory [39]. The host copies data into that memory and executes the program with separate commands. The SNIA API [48] softens this model with batch requests, which chain storage, copy and compute requests into an acyclic graph that the device executes without interacting with the application. A batch is fixed when it is submitted, so it cannot contain loops, and its structure cannot depend on the data it processes. In short, computational storage, as exposed through standard interfaces, is based on host-invoked functions and host-managed data movement. The device performs the computation; the host orchestrates it.

It is also attractive from a standardization standpoint: it adds a few operations to the storage interface while leaving the storage stack semantics untouched. The question we address in this paper is whether it is a good match for query processing.

There are reasons to doubt. First, computational storage relies on computation that accesses SSDs through their external interface [29]. As a result, computational storage has no bandwidth or latency advantage over the host CPU when accessing stored data [28]. Since computational storage increases the cost of the storage subsystem, it must pay off in other ways: by reducing the amount of data transferred to the host, by freeing host cores and memory, or by executing hardware-accelerated functions [9, 26].

Query processing stresses exactly these constraints. We cannot assume that base tables fit in device memory, so columns must be processed in chunks. Operators maintain state across chunks (e.g., selection vectors), and the amount of data flowing between them depends on selectivities that are only known at run-time. Both SNIA and NVMe single out extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) as a favoured format for representing functions downloaded at run-time: SNIA lists eBPF among its execution environments, and its API defines eBPF programs as a type of downloadable function [48]; NVMe proposes eBPF as the representation of downloadable programs [38]. eBPF originates in the BSD Packet Filter, designed to evaluate boolean-valued functions without copying packets inside a UNIX kernel [33]. Modern eBPF [47] executes user-defined functions inside the Linux kernel for performance monitoring [14], security monitoring [11] and storage management [56], and serves as an intermediate representation for hardware-accelerated packet processing [5]. It would be tempting to judge eBPF for computational storage by the standards of packet filtering, as a sandboxed language in which stateless functions of a few instructions are executed on data streaming through a device, or to compare it with other bytecodes as a general-purpose data processing language [24]. We argue that this is not its role in computational storage.

In computational storage, eBPF is best understood as a relocatable binary format. eBPF is a vendor-neutral instruction set [19], generated from C by both gcc and clang. An eBPF program refers to external functions by name; the program resolves these references when it is linked against the functions registered with the run-time environment on the device. Device-defined functions, possibly hardware accelerated, can thus be registered with the eBPF run-time environment and called from a program generated on the host, without extending the host-device interface with a new operation for each function (Section 3.1). In this role, eBPF programs act as glue: they massage the inputs and outputs of registered functions and orchestrate their execution. At the same time, native or hardware-accelerated code performs most of the processing. eBPF’s limitations as a programming language (no floating point, no indirect calls, and the difficulty of verifying programs with loops) matter less in this role. However, safely executing downloaded code remains an open problem.

papers.title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
papers.abstract: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.

papers.title: Transforming local positivity: from minimal valuations to irrational Seshadri constants
papers.abstract:
We explain how a valuative Nagata type statement proposed by Dumnicki, Harbourne, K\"uronya, Ro\'e and Szemberg on a polarised surface $(S, H)$ implies maximality (and hence often irrationality) of Seshadri constants on simple cyclic covers.
  As sample applications we show that very general degree two K3 surfaces and very general hypersurfaces in $\mathbb P^3$ of degree $6$, $8$ or $d\geq 10$ have irrational Seshadri constant at a very general point, unless $d$ is a square.

papers.title: The Dirichlet Problem for Quaternionic $k$-Hessian Equations
papers.abstract: We study the Dirichlet problem for quaternionic $k$-Hessian equations on smooth bounded domains. For a smooth positive density $f(q,z)$ satisfying $f_z\ge0$, we prove existence and uniqueness of a smooth admissible solution whenever a smooth admissible subsolution with the prescribed boundary values exists. The proof extends the quaternionic Monge--Amp\`ere subsolution method to $2\le k<n$ through boundary second derivative estimates. We also construct subsolutions on strictly quaternionic $(k-1)$-convex domains and characterize smooth solvability for constant boundary values.

Hessian equations form a basic class of fully nonlinear elliptic equations in analysis and geometry. The Monge–Ampère equation arises in the Minkowski problem and the Calabi conjecture [14, 30, 34], while the kk-Hessian equations interpolate between the Laplace and Monge–Ampère equations. Caffarelli, Nirenberg and Spruck developed the classical Dirichlet theory for real Hessian equations [11, 13]. The complex theory was developed by Caffarelli, Kohn, Nirenberg and Spruck [12] and, for complex Hessian equations, by Li [27]. Further results, including degenerate equations, were obtained by Trudinger and Ivochkina–Trudinger–Wang [32, 26].
