papers.title: A Realizability-Based Kinetic-Fluid Domain Decomposition Method for Single-Temperature Gas Mixtures
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a domain-adaptive numerical method for multi-species kinetic models that relax toward a single-temperature and single-velocity hydrodynamic limit. To this end, we derive moment realizability matrices for this regime. In this way the ideas of Levermore, Morokoff, and Nadiga are extended to non-equilibrium mixtures in which inter-species and intra-species collisions occur at comparable rates, so that all species relax to a common velocity and a common temperature. The realizability conditions are used as an indicator to divide the computational domain, at each time step, into macroscopic and kinetic regions. In the kinetic regions, where the continuum description fails (e.g., across strong shocks, non-equilibrium interfaces, or kinetic boundary layers), the method solves the multi-species kinetic equations. Close to local thermodynamic equilibrium, the Euler equations of the mixture are solved instead. Confining the kinetic computations to the non-equilibrium regions reduces the simulation time, while the results remain close to those of the full kinetic solver. The method is discretized on Cartesian grids with high-order schemes in space and time. The kinetic equations are integrated with an Asymptotic-Preserving Implicit-Explicit (IMEX) scheme, so that a consistent discretization of the single-velocity, single-temperature Euler system of the mixture is recovered when the Knudsen number goes to zero. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first realizability-based adaptive spatial domain decomposition method for gas mixtures in this single-velocity, single-temperature setting.

Gas mixtures appear in many problems, from aerospace engineering to evaporation–condensation [35] and plasma physics [10]. In transitional regimes, as in the re-entry of spacecraft at high altitude [25] or in micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS), the continuum hypothesis is no longer valid. In these conditions macroscopic models such as the Navier–Stokes equations do not correctly describe localized structures like shock profiles and kinetic boundary layers, and kinetic models, such as the multi-species Boltzmann equation, are needed.

In these conditions macroscopic models such as the Navier–Stokes equations do not correctly describe localized structures like shock profiles and kinetic boundary layers, and kinetic models, such as the multi-species Boltzmann equation, are needed.

The theory of multi-species kinetic models is well developed [12, 11], and more recent works also consider granular mixtures and their long-time behaviour [48]. These equations couple a linear transport operator with nonlinear collision terms, which become stiff in the fluid regime. Their numerical solution is expensive, because the distribution functions depend on up to seven variables [26]. When the mean free path goes to zero, the solution of the kinetic system approaches that of the Euler equations of the mixture, which are much cheaper to solve. For this reason, using a kinetic solver in the whole domain is wasteful when the flow is close to equilibrium in most of it.

In both domain decomposition methods the kinetic and fluid regions are fixed before the computation and do not change in time. Here, instead, the partition is dynamic: it is updated at every time step with a realizability-based indicator, so that the kinetic and fluid regions evolve in time with the flow.

The main objective of this paper is the design of a spatially adaptive, automated numerical method for gas mixtures operating within a single-temperature, single-velocity hydrodynamic limit. At the microscopic level, this physical regime is characterized by intra- and inter-species collisions acting on the same asymptotic time scale. Thanks to these interactions, the distinct components of the mixture rapidly converge toward a common macroscopic velocity and temperature. Since all species of the mixture converge toward a single local equilibrium state, our domain decomposition algorithm treats the whole mixture as a single entity (i.e. all species switch together between the macroscopic solver and the kinetic solver).

At the microscopic level, this physical regime is characterized by intra- and inter-species collisions acting on the same asymptotic time scale. Thanks to these interactions, the distinct components of the mixture rapidly converge toward a common macroscopic velocity and temperature. Since all species of the mixture converge toward a single local equilibrium state, our domain decomposition algorithm treats the whole mixture as a single entity (i.e. all species switch together between the macroscopic solver and the kinetic solver).

From a mathematical point of view, the main new contribution of this work is the derivation of a moment realizability matrix for this single-velocity and single-temperature limit. This matrix is used to detect the regions out of local equilibrium, and therefore to decompose the domain. In this paper the criterion is derived and tested for a multi-species BGK operator. The collision model enters the indicator only through the Chapman–Enskog corrections, so the same construction can be used for the multi-species Boltzmann operator once these corrections are known. The coupling between the two solvers does not depend on the collision operator, so the proposed strategy can be extended to the full multi-species Boltzmann collision integral.

papers.title: Marimba: A System One Model for Speech
papers.abstract: Speech applications require decisions about term presence, turn completion, and language within an audio window. We present Marimba, an interface for typed speech decisions built on frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B features. Lexical questions use zero-shot scoring of ASR transcripts; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head and a separate layer-18 turn-end readout. Language identification uses the ASR model's own language scores. On private conversational test sets, decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92; on public read speech it is 0.92-0.97. Speech Commands four-way accuracy is 0.93; binary lexical ECE is at most 0.08. Personal-information detection, which passes the greedy transcript to a private, curated PII pipeline, reaches item-level F1 0.904 on synthetic Brazilian Portuguese speech (1.000 on reference transcripts). Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on AMI and VoxConverse, above an ECAPA baseline, and count speakers (0, 1, 2, or 3+) more accurately than pyannote 3.1. The turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set. On a subset of ICSI meetings labeled by next speaker, AUROC is 0.716 versus 0.712; the paired confidence interval includes zero.
papers.intro:
Speech applications require distinct decisions about the same short window. These include turn-end detection for voice agents, term spotting, voice activity detection, and language identification. Term spotting tests whether a queried word was spoken; voice activity detection separates speech from silence and noise. Constrained answers with calibrated uncertainty can inform acceptance or deferral for review, but calibration alone does not validate an automated acceptance policy.

Audio language models, including Qwen2-Audio, SALMONN, and Qwen3-Omni, accept audio and answer through text generation without a separate speech-recognition step [13, 19, 14]. They typically require a separate prompt and generation for each question, and their token log probabilities are not calibrated probabilities over a typed decision space. Passing a single 1-best transcript to a text model discards the recognizer’s uncertainty; a rare name or term lost in decoding cannot be recovered or calibrated downstream. Single-task tools do not provide a shared request-time interface across terms, turns, voice activity, and language identification.

papers.title: S1Pert: Scalable Target-Specific Gene Response Prediction with System-One Intelligence
papers.abstract: Predicting transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations is essential for extending CRISPR screens across vast target--gene combinations. However, models can achieve strong aggregate predictive performance by reproducing historical gene-level response frequencies without adequately distinguishing the effects of different perturbations. Reliable prediction at the transcriptome scale is further challenged by uncertain response labels and redundant computation across millions of target--gene pairs. We present S1Pert, a System-One framework for target-specific gene response prediction with non-autoregressive online inference. S1Pert combines directional Welch tests and equivalence testing to distinguish statistically supported responses from inconclusive observations. A frozen System-One encoder extracts reusable semantic representations of perturbation targets, query genes, and historical evidence. Compact pair-specific interactions are then computed and cached offline. A lightweight hierarchical cross-attention decoder integrates these representations with cross-target pairwise ranking and synchronized historical-evidence dropout to reduce reliance on gene-level response frequencies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that S1Pert improves target-specific response discrimination while maintaining reliable prediction and efficient inference across diverse cellular contexts. These findings highlight the potential of System-One decision learning for scalable perturbation-response prediction beyond historical gene-level response tendencies. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/liujiawen-jpg/S1Pert.

papers.title: Pressure and Magnetic Field Control of Topology in Antiferromagnetic Bilayers
papers.abstract: Controlling band topology in magnetic semiconductors requires strategies that couple electronic structure to experimentally accessible degrees of freedom. Here we propose a cooperative approach based on pressure and magnetic reorientation in A-type antiferromagnetic bilayers. Antiparallel layer magnetizations suppress hybridization between exchange-polarized band-edge states, limiting their response to interlayer compression. A magnetic field that aligns the layer moments removes this spin mismatch, enabling pressure-enhanced hybridization to drive a band inversion. The magnetization direction then controls the symmetries of the inverted bands and whether spin--orbit coupling produces a Chern-insulating gap or symmetry-protected nodal crossings. First-principles calculations for bilayer CrSBr illustrate this mechanism within a compressed orthorhombic structural model. Out-of-plane magnetization yields a Chern insulator with a chiral edge state, whereas in-plane magnetization supports a two-dimensional Weyl semimetal with node-connecting edge states. Continuous spin canting further demonstrates how magnetic reorientation can drive the transition and stabilize the Chern phase before full magnetic saturation. Although material-specific transition conditions depend on electronic correlations and structural stability under compression, the underlying strategy identifies interlayer hybridization as a link between magnetic order and band topology. These results provide a design principle for externally tunable topological phases in layered antiferromagnetic semiconductors.

papers.title: Sampling recovery for intersections of Lipschitz classes in the low-smoothness regime
papers.abstract: We study sampling recovery in $L_p(\mathbb T^d)$ for intersections of Lipschitz classes defined by smoothness conditions in two different metrics $L_p$ and $L_q$, where $1\le p<q\le\infty$. Our focus is on the low-smoothness range, where the $L_p$-smoothness does not exceed the classical continuity threshold $d/p$. We determine the exact orders of the sampling numbers for both linear and general recovery algorithms, including critical smoothness cases in which logarithmic factors appear or uniform convergence fails. To analyze sampling approximation in the low-smoothness range, we establish new inequalities for averaged moduli of smoothness with different integrability parameters and derive sharp estimates for these moduli and the corresponding semi-discrete measures of smoothness. These estimates provide error bounds for linear sampling operators acting on functions whose smoothness may lie below the classical continuity threshold. Finally, we determine the Kolmogorov widths of the intersection classes and quantify the gap between optimal sampling recovery and approximation by finite-dimensional subspaces.

This raises the question of which smoothness assumptions allow one to obtain meaningful and sharp LpL_{p}-error estimates for recovery from function values.

papers.title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
papers.abstract: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.

papers.intro:
Global trade has relied on maritime transport for centuries. Today, an estimated 90%90\% of all international goods, ranging from raw materials to everyday products such as fruit and clothing, are transported by sea [1]. Maritime transport is attractive because vessels can carry large volumes of cargo over long distances at relatively low cost. However, the growing reliance on this mode of transportation, combined with other maritime traffic, has led to increased congestion at sea [2]. This is particularly evident near ports and in narrow waterways, where dense traffic heightens the risk of accidents. In addition to congestion, the vast and largely unregulated nature of the oceans facilitates illicit activities such as smuggling, unreported fishing, and sanctions evasion.

Although initially designed as a collision-avoidance tool, authorities rely heavily on the Automatic Identification System (AIS) [3, 4] for continuous vessel tracking. AIS transponders broadcast information such as a vessel’s Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number, type, position, and course to nearby ships and coastal authorities. Despite its essential role, AIS is widely recognized to have significant limitations, including incomplete coverage and vulnerabilities to deliberate manipulation [5]. Spoofing AIS messages to falsify identity or location, as well as intentionally deactivating transmissions, referred to as “dark vessels”, are well-known tactics of manipulation. For example, in July 2023, a Malaysian-flagged oil tanker was found to have spoofed its AIS signals to mask its true location, a tactic used for loading and transferring Iranian oil in violation of US sanctions [6]. Similarly, in late 2024, the Finnish Coast Guard reported that tankers had spoofed their location data to conceal visits to Russian ports [7].

papers.title: Zeeman-Doppler imaging of V889 Her: Surface spots and magnetic field topology 2017 - 2023
papers.abstract: The surface magnetic field of the young solar analogue V889 Her is studied using Zeeman-Doppler imaging (ZDI). This well-studied star has previously been reported to have an exceptionally high differential rotation and show abrupt changes in the surface magnetic field and spot configuration. Our aim is to study the evolution of the magnetic field topology in V889 Her. This will contribute to understanding dynamo action in young solar-type stars. We also want to constrain the surface differential rotation curve of the target star.Methods. We employ the ZDI method on observations collected with the SOFIN spectropolarimeter mounted at the Nordic Optical Telescope. We test differential rotation parameters previously reported in studies of the star. We observe significant changes in the radial field near the rotational pole throughout the whole span of the observations. Specifically, the polarity of the radial field is reversed around 2021. The large-scale magnetic field also contains a persistent strong azimuthal component at high latitudes. We detect abrupt changes in the spot configuration in June 2018 on the time scale of a week. The observations favour a solar type differential rotation. The different rotation parameters influence the brightness map more than the magnetic field topology. We cannot link the observed changes in the magnetic field topology with the evolution of the long-term spot activity. The abrupt changes observed in 2018 confirm previous reports that the surface magnetic field and spot configuration may undergo rapid evolution on short time scales. This complicates the estimation of the surface differential rotation.

The solar analogue V889 Her (HD 171488) is an extremely active BY Dra star of spectral type G2V with an estimated age of 30-50 Myr (Kazarovets & Samus, 1997; Strassmeier et al., 2003). It has been the target of several extended studies that have reported strong differential rotation and rapid changes in its spot activity (Willamo et al., 2019; Willamo et al., 2022a; Brown et al., 2024, see, e.g.,). Attempts to identify regularities in its magnetic activity have so far been inconclusive. Furthermore, its surface differential rotation has been a major problem to determine, as it may even be significantly varying (Brown et al., 2024, see, e.g., Fig. 2 in) and could be non-monotonic (Tuomi et al., 2024). This makes V889 Her a challenging but interesting target for monitoring.

papers.title: Additive cubes are avoidable over $\{0,1,2,3\}$, $\{0,1,4\}$ and $\{0,2,5\}$
papers.abstract: We prove that additive cubes are avoidable over the alphabet $\{0,1,2,3\}$, thereby solving a long-standing question initiated by Pirillo and Varricchio in 1994. By extending the reduction and spectral machinery of Cassaigne, Currie, Schaeffer, and Shallit (2014), we prove that the search for additive cubes in such morphic images reduces to a finite graph traversal. We exhibit eight explicit morphisms from $\{0,1,3,4\}^*$ to $\{0,1,2,3\}^*$ of length 3 whose images on the Cassaigne \textit{et al.} infinite word contain no additive cubes.

papers.title: On Borwein polynomials with multiple roots outside the unit disk
papers.abstract:
A Borwein polynomial has coefficients in ${-1,0,1}$ and nonzero constant and leading coefficients. We seek Borwein polynomials having a multiple root outside the unit disk. To this end, we consider the powers $L^2$ and $L^3$ of Lehmer's polynomial $L$, which has a real root $\tau>1$.
  Since $L$ has exceptionally small Mahler measure, the theorem of Bombieri and Vaaler guarantees the existence of Borwein multiples of these powers. Such multiples have $\tau$ as a root of multiplicity at least 2 and 3, respectively. Mossinghoff (2003, Algorithm 3, p. 323) constructed examples that, under the substitution $x\mapsto -x$, yield such multiples.
  The main contribution of this paper is to determine the least possible degrees of Borwein multiples of $L^2$ and $L^3$, with and without symmetry restrictions on their coefficients, and to describe their degree spectra. For $L^2$, the minimum degree is 34 without symmetry restrictions, 38 among self-reciprocal multiples, and 41 among antireciprocal multiples. For $L^3$, the corresponding minimum degrees are 115, 115, and 117.
  We determine the complete degree spectra for $L^2$ and, for $L^3$, classify the degrees from 115 to 150 for which self-reciprocal or antireciprocal Borwein multiples exist, giving an explicit example for each admissible degree in each symmetry class. Further constructions yield Borwein multiples of $L^3$ in every degree $D\geq 215$, with both symmetry types for every $D\geq 231$.

papers.title: Lens: Training-Free Semantic Search for Cross-Tile Object and Scene Retrieval in Satellite Imagery
papers.abstract: We developed Lens, a training-free system for semantic object and scene search across large satellite mosaics that requires no detector trained for the class of interest. Lens represents each tile with a frozen, self-supervised vision transformer (DINOv3), removes the positional bias in its dense features by projecting them onto the subspace orthogonal to a positional basis estimated once from a constant image, and centers the debiased features on the mean feature computed across the whole area before comparison. Lens forms a query by averaging the centered features of a small neighborhood of patches around a chosen point, or of an entire tile for scene-level search, and matches it against the index by cosine similarity. It stores the centered patch features in a byte-quantized similarity index that supports real-time range search over a mosaic of thousands of patches, and a coarser whole-tile embedding index for scene-level retrieval. A guided upsampling network (AnyUp) runs once per tile to recover pixel-accurate boundaries beyond the native feature grid, and the result is cached so later queries reuse it. We evaluated Lens on the 5,128-tile DFC2020 test set and ran it as an interactive tool on five Sentinel-2 areas spanning agricultural, industrial, and desert terrain; the pipeline is not tied to a specific sensor. On DFC2020 a single click reaches 0.09 to 0.80 pixel F1 across eight land-cover classes at the per-class best threshold, with a mean F1 of 0.39, and it beats a pairwise INSID3 baseline on six of the eight classes at roughly four hundred times lower query cost. Indexing 1.31 million patches takes 169 s on one CPU thread, and a click returns a rendered overlay in 6 to 10 ms.
papers.intro:
Satellite archives have grown faster than our ability to ask questions of them. Copernicus alone delivers global Sentinel-2 coverage every five days at 10 m (Drusch et al., 2012). The bottleneck is no longer acquisition. It is that almost every question an analyst wants to ask has to be converted into a supervised learning problem first. An analyst who wants to know how many center-pivot irrigation fields are active this summer in the Wadi As-Sirhan basin has to collect training examples, annotate them, train a detector, tune it, and run it over the area: weeks of work, most of it annotation, and none of it transferring if the next question is about solar arrays in Rajasthan. Detectors get built for the few classes that justify the investment, and the long tail goes unexamined.

Satellite archives have grown faster than our ability to ask questions of them. Copernicus alone delivers global Sentinel-2 coverage every five days at 10 m (Drusch et al., 2012). The bottleneck is no longer acquisition. It is that almost every question an analyst wants to ask has to be converted into a supervised learning problem first. An analyst who wants to know how many center-pivot irrigation fields are active this summer in the Wadi As-Sirhan basin has to collect training examples, annotate them, train a detector, tune it, and run it over the area: weeks of work, most of it annotation, and none of it transferring if the next question is about solar arrays in Rajasthan. Detectors get built for the few classes that justify the investment, and the long tail goes unexamined.

Lens changes the economics of that first query. It is a retrieval system rather than a detector: the analyst points at one example and the system returns everything in the area that resembles it. No labels are collected, no model is trained, and the class is whatever the analyst just clicked on. Retrieval by example is an old idea with a substantial remote sensing literature behind it (Sumbul et al., 2020), and what makes it newly practical is the quality of self-supervised features. DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) produces dense patch descriptors that are semantically meaningful without task supervision and holds up on aerial imagery, so in principle one can index those descriptors and search them directly.

Lens changes the economics of that first query. It is a retrieval system rather than a detector: the analyst points at one example and the system returns everything in the area that resembles it. No labels are collected, no model is trained, and the class is whatever the analyst just clicked on. In practice this does not work, and understanding why is the substance of this paper. Two distortions sit on top of the semantic signal. Dense DINOv3 features carry a component that depends on where a patch sits in the image rather than what it contains (Cuttano et al., 2026). Separately, when every tile in an area shows the same terrain, the descriptors cluster so tightly that cosine similarity loses its range. Both are removable with linear operations that cost nothing at query time, but they are not equally important: the positional projection carries most of the benefit, and area centering adds to it only when the target occupies a small fraction of the area. We report that asymmetry rather than the cleaner story we expected. The system is measured on the DFC2020 test set and exercised as a deployed tool on five Sentinel-2 areas.

papers.title: Learning Recommendations under Imperfect Human Compliance with Record-Level Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: This paper investigates human-in-the-loop recommendation systems, where effectiveness relies on human compliance and privacy concerns restrict the use of historical response data. The pro posed framework models the implemented action as a random response to the recommendation and formulates the recommendation mechanism as a decision-dependent optimisation problem under an unknown compliance distribution. A batched Gaussian process upper confidence bound algorithm is then adapted to learn from locally perturbed historical actions, providing privacy for individual raw records. The analysis establishes record-level differential privacy and derives high-probability simple regret bounds when the compliance distribution is unknown. These bounds characterise how privacy noise, batch size, and behavioural information affect the guaranteed quality of the learned recommendation. In particular, a known upper bound on the non-compliance rate enables the rec ommendation space to be screened before any private data are queried. Simulations of a fixed-state car-following problem with synthetic historical driver responses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm and verify the theoretical findings.

papers.title: DART ejecta reveal the recoil momentum budget of a kinetic impact
papers.abstract: Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) demonstrated that ejecta recoil enhances asteroid deflection, but the ejecta processes generating and distributing this recoil remained unclear. We reconstruct three-dimensional ejecta evolution from time-resolved morphology and brightness observations, recovering previously missing constraints on momentum transfer and material transport. Integrating reconstructed momentum yields momentum enhancement factors $\beta_\mathrm{D}=2.13 \pm 0.19 (1{\sigma})$ for Dimorphos and $\beta_\mathrm{sys}=2.04 \pm 0.19 (1{\sigma})$ for the Didymos system. Combined with the measured deflection, the reconstructed recoil constrains Dimorphos's bulk density to $1435.18_{-153.71}^{+112.59} \mathrm{kg m^{-3}}$ without assuming its mass. By linking observed orbital deflection to the released material, this reconstruction provides ejecta-based constraints for assessing kinetic-impact effectiveness and investigating how natural collisions drive mass loss and debris transport among small Solar System bodies.

papers.title: LaMe: a Joint Latent Mediation Framework for High-Dimensional Systems
papers.abstract: Mediation analysis seeks to understand how an exposure influences an outcome through intermediate variables. However, as increasingly rich datasets become available, hundreds to thousands of potential mediators make these systems difficult to model and hard to interpret. Latent-variable approaches offer a natural way to accommodate these high-dimensional settings. However, existing latent mediation methods face limitations, including overparameterization, biased inference, or limited scalability. We develop LaMe, a joint linear-Gaussian framework that summarizes a high-dimensional exposure-mediator-outcome system through a small number of latent variables. We identify natural direct and indirect effects under an explicit assumption that the manifest measurements fully capture the latent mediators, and characterize conditions under which the latent representation effectively restricts the observed cross-covariance structure. Simulations assess recovery of observed association parameters, natural effects, and manifest features associated with latent mediation pathways across a range of challenging settings. Four real-world applications demonstrate competitive predictive performance with compact latent representations, including single-dimensional representations of biomarker and proteomic measurements. Together, these results establish LaMe as a practical framework for estimating and summarizing multivariate mediation systems under explicit structural and measurement assumptions.

papers.intro:
Deciphering how complex exposures exert their effects through intermediary processes is a cornerstone of modern epidemiology. In the NHANES data considered here, for example, lifestyle characteristics may directly influence glycohemoglobin levels, but might also affect blood biomarkers which in turn cause these variations. However, the continued emergence of large-scale, high-dimensional datasets poses new challenges to established mediation analysis methods. Analyses conducted on biological data are particularly affected, as molecular profiling can yield hundreds or thousands of correlated molecular measurements, only a subset of which may be relevant to the mediating process linking an exposure to an outcome. Latent variable models have been introduced to extend classical mediation models to these settings (Derkach et al., 2019; Albert et al., 2016; Nath et al., 2023; Chén et al., 2017). This approach brings a number of improvements over non-latent mediation techniques (Zeng et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2024) (e.g. based on OLS, LASSO or ElasticNet): noise decomposition, information compression, interpretability and robustness of the estimates.

This approach brings a number of improvements over non-latent mediation techniques (Zeng et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2024) (e.g. based on OLS, LASSO or ElasticNet): noise decomposition, information compression, interpretability and robustness of the estimates.

However, existing latent mediation approaches face several limitations. Stepwise methods estimate latent scores separately from subsets of the observed data and use the resulting scores in subsequent regressions on remaining observed variables, potentially inferring latent variables that are irrelevant to mediation systems (Nath et al., 2023; Chén et al., 2017). Joint approaches avoid this issue by estimating latent variables along with their relation to observed variables, but may be overparameterized, prone to overfitting, limited in scalability, and typically assume univariate exposures, univariate outcomes, and the conditional independence among manifest variables given the latent mediators whereas biological measurement are generally correlated (Derkach et al., 2019; Albert et al., 2016). To address these limitations, we introduce the Latent Mediation (LaMe) framework, which jointly models multivariate exposures, outcomes and high-dimensional manifest variables through a small number of latent mediators without assuming diagonality of noise covariances, while explicitly accounting for direct exposure-outcome effects.

To address these limitations, we introduce the Latent Mediation (LaMe) framework, which jointly models multivariate exposures, outcomes and high-dimensional manifest variables through a small number of latent mediators without assuming diagonality of noise covariances, while explicitly accounting for direct exposure-outcome effects.

This approach makes three main methodological contributions. First, LaMe is novel in that it infers latent mediators from a joint probabilistic model with multivariate exposures and outcomes, high-dimensional manifest variables, and non-diagonal residual covariance matrices. As a result, it avoids biases associated with estimating latent scores separately from the rest of the system as in stepwise procedures and estimates all its parameters based on all available information rather than subsets of observed variables. We characterize when the representation imposes a genuine restriction on cross-block relationships, distinguishing dimension reduction from a reparameterization of unrestricted regression. Second, LaMe connects joint probabilistic estimation methods (Derkach et al., 2019; Albert et al., 2016) with representations in which latent mediators are exactly recoverable from the manifest measurements (Nath et al., 2023; Chén et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2020). Under this explicit restriction and suitable rank conditions, the aggregate natural direct and indirect effects are statistically identified from the observed data. Throughout this article, identifiability refers to statistical identification from the observed-data distribution, rather than causal identification of natural effects. We also introduce a score to assess which manifest variables are associated with exposures and informative about outcomes through the latent mediators, independently of how the latent variables are represented. Third, we derive closed-form EM updates for two equivalent likelihood factorizations, allowing computational efficiency to be improved when manifest measurements and exposures have substantially different dimensions. Simulations assess parameter recovery, effect recovery under the exact recoverability assumption, and feature ranking; real-world applications assess predictive performance and the compactness of the learned representations. These results position LaMe as a useful methodological option.

papers.title: Distinguishing cosmologies with topological analysis of 21-cm hydrogen 2D brightness fields at Cosmic Dawn
papers.abstract: The 21-cm hydrogen line brightness field is a potentially valuable source of information about astrophysical parameters during the cosmological Dark Ages and the Epoch of Reionization. However, it can also be a source of observational data for cosmologists seeking to constrain cosmological parameters. While much of the effort has been focused on constraining parameters using information across a broad frequency range, most often with the power spectrum of inhomogeneities, we investigate whether a single frequency channel, corresponding to a single redshift slice, can distinguish between cosmological models. We utilize topological data analysis to evaluate the possibility of such constraints. In particular, we use cubical complexes to perform persistent homology analysis of the 21-cm line brightness field. We generate 21-cm brightness fields of different cosmologies with the 21cmFAST package and then select snapshots at several redshifts corresponding to the Epoch of Reionization. Our goal is to find the redshift that is most suitable for highlighting the diversity between scenarios within a certain range of cosmological parameters. To compare persistent pictures built on simulations of the brightness field, we use Wasserstein distance, computed between any two persistent diagrams. We find that observations of the 21-cm field near $z=10$ have the potential to distinguish between cosmological models with different values of the normalized Hubble parameter $h_0$, the spectral index of scalar matter perturbations $n_s$, the matter density parameter $\Omega_m$, and the matter fluctuation amplitude $\sigma_8$, even in the presence of instrumental thermal noise. We perform the PERMANOVA statistical test on the matrices of Wasserstein distances to confirm this hypothesis for all considered cosmological parameters.

The redshifted 21-cm line of neutral hydrogen is the most direct probe of the Cosmic Dawn and the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), the era in which the first luminous sources heated and ionized the intergalactic medium (Furlanetto et al., 2006; Pritchard and Loeb, 2012). Current and forthcoming low-frequency interferometers—LOFAR, MWA, HERA, and ultimately the Square Kilometer Array (SKA)—aim to measure the spatial fluctuations of the 21-cm brightness temperature across this epoch (Koopmans and others, 2015; DeBoer and others, 2017; Mertens and others, 2020). The standard summary statistic for these measurements is the power spectrum, which is statistically sufficient for a Gaussian random field but discards the substantial non-Gaussian information encoded in the morphology of the ionized regions.

The standard summary statistic for these measurements is the power spectrum, which is statistically sufficient for a Gaussian random field but discards the substantial non-Gaussian information encoded in the morphology of the ionized regions.

This motivates exploring summary statistics that are explicitly sensitive to the geometry and topology of the field. Morphological descriptors have a long history in cosmology, beginning with the genus of isodensity contours (Gott et al., 1986) and the Minkowski functionals (Mecke et al., 1994), and extending to the Betti numbers (Park and others, 2013; Pranav and others, 2017; Tymchyshyn et al., 2024), and, finally, to persistent homology (Pranav and others, 2019; Tsizh et al., 2023; Bermejo et al., 2024). Topological data analysis (TDA), and persistent homology in particular, characterizes a manifold through the birth and death, across a filtration process, of its topological features, such as connected components, loops, and enclosed voids, providing a scale-free, parameter-less description of a complex structure of a given manifold. A persistence image of a field or pointcloud, with intermediary to a manifold, allows one to effectively reduce the amount of data, keeping the important connection and morphological information present that the power spectrum would probably omit.

In the broader cosmological context, TDA has emerged as a competitive and complementary summary statistic. Persistent homology of the large-scale structure constrains primordial non-Gaussianity and the standard cosmological parameters, in several cases outperforming the combined power spectrum and bispectrum and breaking parameter degeneracies (Biagetti et al., 2021; Biagetti et al., 2022; Yip et al., 2024). Parameter inference directly from persistence images combined with machine learning has further improved these constraints while retaining interpretability, since each pixel of such an image corresponds to a definite region of the birth–persistence plane (Calles and others, 2024). Their way of separating model differences from cosmic variance is similar to ours: they simulated several 21-cm lightcones of each model from different random initial conditions and compared the two groups with a permutation test, using the mean squared Wasserstein distance between persistence diagrams as the test statistic.

They found that tunnels (β1\beta_{1} features) dominate the topology during reionization, and that their number is the easiest to observe and the most sensitive to the source properties. Their way of separating model differences from cosmic variance is similar to ours: they simulated several 21-cm lightcones of each model from different random initial conditions and compared the two groups with a permutation test, using the mean squared Wasserstein distance between persistence diagrams as the test statistic.

Betti numbers can track the characteristic percolation history of the ionized regions, as shown in (Giri and Mellema, 2021). Related morphological analyses based on shapefinders and percolation were performed in (Bag et al., 2018; Bag et al., 2019). Three-dimensional Minkowski functionals were used in (Diao and others, 2024) for reionization parameter inference. Minkowski functionals shapefinders were also utilized in (Ghara et al., 2024) to study the morphology of the binarized 21-cm field in heating-dominated Cosmic Dawn. In (Shimabukuro and others, 2025), the authors analyzed a 1-dimensional continuous field of 21-cm forest, which is formed by X-ray heating from matter clusters, by counting 0-dimensional homologies obtained in a filtration process. However, all of the studies mentioned above vary astrophysical or small-scale dark-matter properties while keeping fixed the cosmological parameters that govern large-scale structure and the expansion history.

papers.title: Dimensionalities on monoids
papers.abstract: We study equivalence relations on monoids in $\Rel$ that are lax morphisms. We call them \emph{dimensionalities}. We prove that the quotient of a monoid in $\Rel$ by a dimensionality is again a monoid. We prove that polygroupoids (and hence hypergroups) are exactly the symmetric $\dag$-Frobenius structures in $\Rel$. We use this characterization to prove that the quotient of a polygroupoid by a dimensionality that preserves the inverse is a polygroupoid.

papers.title: Sample complexity and scalability of adaptive-sampling trust-region methods for zeroth-order stochastic optimization --- Part~II: a new pathwise analysis with randomized subspaces
papers.abstract: Stochastic trust-region methods are usually analyzed in expectation or with high probability: the guarantee is about the law of the algorithm, not about the run in hand. This paper analyzes the adaptive sampling stochastic trust-region method ASTRO-DF (which is the reuse variant ASTRA-R in Part I) in random subspaces along almost every sample path. The route has one probabilistic ingredient, the accuracy of the common-random-number estimates at the adaptive sample size, uniformly over the trust region; Part~I established it by chaining, here it is obtained at the stopping time by optional stopping and converted, by the first Borel--Cantelli lemma, into an accuracy that holds from a random index on, after which the deterministic trust-region argument applies. We prove almost sure convergence and almost sure iteration and sample complexity of orders $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\epsilon^{-2})$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^2\epsilon^{-4})$, with a subspace dimension growing logarithmically; we show that at a fixed subspace dimension the eventual-accuracy argument yields $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2-\mathcal{O}(1/p)})$ iterations and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-4-\mathcal{O}(1/p)})$ samples; we show that the random index after which the rates hold cannot be too large and has an explicit, rapidly decaying tail. Compared with the supermartingale route, the pathwise route needs no lower bound on the per-iteration probability of a good iteration, no coupling between the trust-region expansion factor and the sketch, and no moment condition on the summed squared radii.

papers.title: RSSA: Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner for Collaborative Perception
papers.abstract: V2X collaborative perception improves single-vehicle perception by aggregating multi-view features from collaborative agents. However, existing methods typically rely on simple spatial warping to align the collaborative features, which can cause semantic misalignment during fusion. Meanwhile, these deterministic warping-based methods are highly sensitive to the positional noises. In this paper, we propose a plug-in module called Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner (RSSA), which performs semantic and probabilistic spatial transformations for robust feature alignment. Specifically, a Semantic Transformation (SemT) block modulates feature channels based on the observed relative pose to correct semantic inconsistencies. Subsequently, a Probabilistic Spatial Transformation (P-SpaT) block performs probabilistic warping by sampling from the Gaussian-modeled relative pose space. A Relative Transformation Augmentation (RT-Aug) strategy is further introduced to augment the relative poses and facilitate the training of the RSSA. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that RSSA improves the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin under the configuration of both clean and noisy positions.

V2X collaborative perception effectively addresses these limitations by aggregating information from multiple collaborative agents. Most collaborative perception methods follow a broadcast-based paradigm [13, 3, 16, 15]. In this paradigm, each collaborative agent extracts local BEV features, packages them with its pose, and then broadcasts them to the ego vehicle. Upon receiving the message, the ego vehicle spatially warps the collaborative features to its own coordinate system for subsequent feature fusion.

Although efficient, this paradigm suffers from two critical limitations. First, it overlooks the semantic misalignment caused by the spatial warping. papers.title: Model Choice or Model Bias? How stellar spectral libraries and activity modelling choices influence Ariel spectra- I. Forward model
papers.abstract: The Ariel mission will conduct a population-level survey of approximately 1000 exoplanet atmospheres across its nominal lifetime, requiring unprecedented consistency in the treatment of stellar contamination of transmission spectra. We present a systematic comparison of stellar spectral libraries and modelling approaches for computing facular and spot contamination spectra across the full Ariel wavelength range (0.5-7.8 microns) for six stellar spectral types spanning F3 to M2. Using a surface resolved forward model with approximately 200 randomly generated active region configurations per spectral type, we compute contamination spectra at Ariel Tier 3 resolution and compare three 1D spectral libraries against 3D MHD stellar atmosphere spectra as a physical ground truth. We find that library-dependent differences in the facular treatment introduce systematic biases exceeding the Ariel Tier 3 sensitivity threshold of approximately 20 ppm across most of the wavelength range, for most spectral types and activity levels considered. These biases align with the absorption bands of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methane, rendering them indistinguishable from genuine atmospheric signals at Ariel's precision. Our results demonstrate hat the choice of stellar spectral library, in particular the faculae treatment is a critical and currently underappreciated source of systematic error for Ariel atmospheric characterisation. The impact on atmospheric retrievals is quantified in a companion paper.

papers.intro:
Since the discovery of the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star in the mid-1990s, the field has advanced from detection to detailed atmospheric characterization. Out of over 6,000 known exoplanets, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has already probed the atmospheres of roughly 100 targets using transmission spectroscopy (Seager and Sasselov, 2000; Charbonneau et al., 2002; Tinetti et al., 2007; Yan et al., 2019; Rustamkulov et al., 2023). As a planet transits its host star, wavelength-dependent variations in atmospheric opacity alter the observed transit depth, encoding information about atmospheric composition. However, disentangling planetary signatures from stellar spectra remains challenging due to stellar surface heterogenieties, brought about by stellar magnetism. Occulted features crossed by the planet leave distinct imprints in transit light curves (Petit dit de la Roche et al., 2024; Ahrer et al., 2025; Fournier-Tondreau et al., 2025; Radica et al., 2025, e.g.,), whereas unocculted active regions drive the Transit Light Source Effect (Rackham et al., 2018, TLSE;). Standard corrections rely on disc-averaged representations of active regions (Rackham et al., 2018; Rackham et al., 2019) or joint atmospheric retrievals (Pinhas et al., 2018; Iyer and Line, 2020; Thompson et al., 2024). Additional stellar biases, such as fixing limb-darkening coefficients or adopting inadequate limb-darkening laws, can introduce errors of ∼\sim3% in inferred planetary radii (Espinoza and Jordán, 2015; Espinoza and Jordán, 2016) and wavelength-dependent biases exceeding 100 ppm (Coulombe et al., 2024; Keers et al., 2024). The Ariel mission (Tinetti et al., 2018; Tinetti et al., 2022), launching in the early 2030s, will conduct a population-level survey of ∼\sim1000 transiting exoplanets. Ariel’s tiered observing strategy involves repeated visits to high-priority targets, making epoch-to-epoch consistency essential. Drawing lessons from JWST is vital to fully leverage these multi-visit observations. Recently, Thompson et al. (2026) demonstrated that uncorrected inter-visit stellar variability introduces significant biases in retrieved atmospheric parameters. To balance computational efficiency, scalability, and interpretability, they adopt a simplified 1D stellar activity model that is widely used in the retrieval context. Spots and faculae are treated as separate, distinct components, with each active region represented by a spectral energy distribution (SED) from the PHOENIX BT-Settl library (Allard, 2014) characterised by its temperature contrast. However, such models neglect center-to-limb variations (CLV) and cannot reproduce the more complex temperature and spectral structure of faculae. As shown by Nèmec et al. (2026) in the solar context, disc-averaged models fail to reproduce true contamination signals, underscoring the need for physically motivated facular models incorporating CLV. Recent 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations combining MURaM (Vögler et al., 2005; Rempel, 2014) and MPS-ATLAS (Witzke et al., 2021) offer first-principles models of stellar atmospheres that account for interactions among convection, magnetic fields, and radiation (Kostogryz et al., 2026, hereafter K26). Applying magnetic fields above 100 G (associated with faculae) reveals that faculae brighten hot F-type stars but weaken toward cooler stars, even appearing dark in the coolest models (21). Furthermore, standard 1D and 3D CLV coefficients in forward models can produce transit depth discrepancies up to 3% in common photometric bands (Nèmec et al., submitted). In this work, we investigate how different treatments of faculae and choices of stellar atmosphere models propagate into transmission spectra. We compare simple TLSE prescriptions against surface-resolved active region modeling using StarSim (Herrero et al., 2016; Rosich et al., 2020) across publicly available spectral libraries, focusing on Ariel’s full spectral range (0.5–7.8 μ\mum) at Tier 3 resolution. Section 2 describes the spectral libraries, Section 3 details the spatial modeling of active regions, and Section 4 presents the model comparison.

papers.title: Who Counts as Exposed? Measurement Choices in an Open, Re-estimable Index of Occupational AI Exposure
papers.abstract: Occupational AI exposure indices are used as inputs to economic analysis, workforce planning, and policy, and the choices built into them decide which workers are described as exposed. We build an open, re-estimable task-level index and vary its two main design decisions, context and calibration, to show how much the answer depends on them. For each of the 18,796 occupation--task pairs in \onet, seven open-weight reasoning models rate exposure under a common rubric. Each model rates with or without a context of retrieved news and research passages, workplace descriptors, and a bottleneck-based reasoning protocol, and the ensemble is combined with or without simplex-constrained calibration to observed Claude usage. The largest difference from the dominant 2023 benchmark is not a disagreement about what AI can do but about how much credit to give exposure that depends on software integrations not yet built, a choice that no data can settle. At the benchmark's own weight, the calibrated index counts fewer exposed workers than the benchmark, and when only direct exposure counts it counts more. At full score resolution, the ensemble ranks tasks better than the benchmark against observed usage and an independent physical-task classification. Adding context mainly shifts the level of exposure rather than improving the ranking. Context and calibration both relocate exposure toward higher-wage occupations, and calibration, which anchors the index to one platform's users, does more of it, so we also release the uncalibrated arm. Exposure indices used as policy inputs should state such choices, report their numbers under the alternatives, and be re-estimated as systems change.

papers.intro:
Generative AI can change the speed and quality of specific knowledge-work tasks (Noy and Zhang, 2023; Brynjolfsson et al., 2025b), and current systems can use browsers and software tools to carry out multi-step workflows under human direction. Because a technology may strongly affect one activity while leaving the rest of a job intact, research on AI and work has moved from the job level (Frey and Osborne, 2017; Brandes and Wattenhofer, 2016) to the task level (Brynjolfsson and Mitchell, 2017; Webb, 2019; Acemoglu et al., 2022; Eloundou et al., 2024), following the task-based view of technological change (Autor et al., 2003). The central question is then occupational exposure: which tasks can be done much faster, at comparable quality, with help from an AI system. Exposure is not displacement, realized adoption, or a forecast of wages. It is a forward-looking signal of where an evolving technology is plausibly applicable.

The central question is then occupational exposure: which tasks can be done much faster, at comparable quality, with help from an AI system. Exposure is not displacement, realized adoption, or a forecast of wages. It is a forward-looking signal of where an evolving technology is plausibly applicable.

Exposure estimates now inform international discussion of worker protection, reskilling, and the distributional consequences of AI. The OECD, the ILO, the IMF, and the World Economic Forum all rely on task-based exposure frameworks to describe which workers and sectors may be affected (OECD, 2023; Gmyrek et al., 2025; Cazzaniga et al., 2024; World Economic Forum, 2025). The dominant benchmark is Eloundou et al. (2024), which classified O*NET tasks into four exposure classes (E0–E3) using zero-shot judgments from GPT-4 in 2023. It established task-level exposure as a common empirical object. Yet its labels come from the internal prior of a single proprietary model, not from evidence about the task, the work setting, or demonstrated capability. The procedure did not require any inspectable reasoning, and the 2023 scores are still used in 2026 employment analysis (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025a; Massenkoff and McCrory, 2026), in part because re-running the measurement was never part of the design. When a model-generated label is reused as a policy input, it becomes a measurement claim about the world, and the choices built into it decide whose work is described as at risk. Such a claim should be reproducible, externally grounded, inspectable, and renewed over time (Mouchel et al., 2026), and its validity should be argued rather than assumed (Jacobs and Wallach, 2021).

Existing measures fall into two families. Theoretical capability measures ask whether an AI system could in principle help complete a task much faster (Eloundou et al., 2024). They identify where AI may become relevant before adoption is widespread, but they can overstate present exposure when they rely on model judgments that are not tied to evidence about current systems or working conditions. Observed usage measures track which tasks are actually performed on a deployed platform, as in recent measures built from Claude and Bing interaction data (Massenkoff and McCrory, 2026; Tomlinson et al., 2025). They reflect real behavior, but low Claude usage does not mean that AI cannot help with a task done through another model, a specialized product, or an enterprise workflow that the platform cannot see.

This paper builds a third construct: a measure of present-day capability, grounded in a context a reader can inspect and released in a usage-free and a usage-anchored version. We use it to measure how much the answer to “who is exposed” depends on the choices inside the measure. For each of the 18,796 occupation–task pairs in O*NET 30.2 (National Center for O*NET Development, 2026), seven open-weight reasoning models assess the task under a common rubric written for an up-to-date agentic system. Each model receives a context with three parts: time-stamped news and research passages retrieved for the task, six O*NET work-context descriptors for the occupation, and a protocol that asks it to decompose the task and label its time bottleneck. We calibrate the task scores against observed Claude usage with inspectable, simplex-constrained weights and aggregate them to occupations with survey-based task time shares (Bouquet and Sheffi, 2026). A two-by-two design compares the Eloundou et al. benchmark with every combination of context (with or without) and calibration (with or without). Because every output is stored, we recompute every headline number under the alternatives without new inference.

papers.title: Causal and conditional tail coefficients: asymptotics, inference and graph recovery
papers.abstract: The causal tail coefficient (CTC) measures the influence of an extreme value of one variable on another variable and has been proposed as a tool for causal discovery in heavy-tailed models. Despite its popularity, the asymptotic behavior of its empirical counterpart has not been well understood. We develop an asymptotic theory for the rank-based CTC estimator with an intermediate threshold under nonparametric conditions that are satisfied by all standard copula models. A key observation is that the CTC is determined by the mean of a conditional tail limit distribution, which clarifies its interpretation and determines the asymptotic variance of the estimator. We establish joint asymptotic normality for the entire CTC matrix and prove consistency of a multiplier bootstrap for simultaneous inference. For heavy-tailed linear and recursive max-linear structural equation models, we show that the CTC equals one if and only if the first variable is an ancestor of the second, which leads to confidence graphs for the ancestral graph with asymptotic coverage guarantees. All results extend to general conditional tail coefficients, defined as further functionals of the conditional tail limit distribution. A simulation study and an application to dietary intake data illustrate the methods.

papers.intro:
Extreme events seldom occur in isolation. Floods arise from the conjunction of heavy precipitation and saturated soils, financial crises are triggered by the propagation of losses across markets, and, in nutrition, extreme intake of one nutrient tends to accompany extreme intake of others. In each case, the joint occurrence of the events often reflects an underlying causal mechanism. Learning this mechanism faces two main obstacles: the relevant information is limited to the few observations that fall in the tail, and controlled interventions are often costly, unethical or impossible. The mechanism must therefore be inferred from scarce observational data, with substantial uncertainty.

In each case, the joint occurrence of the events often reflects an underlying causal mechanism. Learning this mechanism faces two main obstacles: the relevant information is limited to the few observations that fall in the tail, and controlled interventions are often costly, unethical or impossible. The mechanism must therefore be inferred from scarce observational data, with substantial uncertainty.

Extreme value theory provides the probabilistic and statistical foundations for the analysis of such events (Resnick, 1987; Resnick, 2007; Beirlant et al., 2004; de Haan and Ferreira, 2006), and a growing literature combines it with graphical modelling and causal inference (Pearl, 2009). Two classes of models along a directed acyclic graph (DAG) have received particular attention: recursive max-linear models (RMLMs), introduced by Gissibl and Klüppelberg (2018), in which each variable is the maximum of scaled parent variables and an independent innovation, and heavy-tailed linear structural equation models (linear SEMs), in which the maximum is replaced by a sum (Gnecco et al., 2021). Learning the graph from data is an active area of research. For RMLMs, Gissibl et al. (2021) propose the minimum ratio estimator, which exploits the exact parametric form of the model, Buck and Klüppelberg (2021) extend it to propagating noise, and Klüppelberg and Krali (2021) learn the structure from the angular measure of the multivariate extreme value distribution. For heavy-tailed linear models, Gnecco et al. (2021) estimate a causal ordering by means of the causal tail coefficient (CTC), and Krali (2026) adapts the angular-measure approach to non-negative coefficients. Alternative approaches are considered in Mhalla et al. (2020); Tran et al. (2024); Mhalla et al. (2025); Jiang et al. (2025). More recently, Engelke et al. (2025) and Fang et al. (2025) proposed more general extremal structural causal models, in which causal relations and interventions are defined at the extreme scale. Undirected graphical models for extremes, building on the notion of conditional independence of Engelke and Hitz (2020), lack a notion of direction and therefore lie outside the scope of the present work.

papers.title: High-harmonic generation along a structural phase transition in silicon
papers.abstract: We explore high-harmonic generation (HHG) in silicon treated by a variable dose from a Ga focused ion beam (Ga$^+$ FIB). We identify four qualitatively different dose regimes as the sample transitions from a crystalline to amorphous phase. The phase transition manifests as a giant enhancement in yield of low-order harmonics, which is strongly correlated with surface swelling as measured by atomic force microscopy. Below the critical dose, we observe a mixed phase regime where the HHG spectra display elements of both crystalline and amorphous silicon. We show how the samples can be laser-annealed with intense non-resonant pulses, where energy is deposited preferentially into amorphous regions, allowing us to disentangle the relative importance of chemical and structural modifications to the strong-field dynamics. At very high dose, we observe an increased sensitivity to laser-induced damage, which is correlated with FIB-induced etching. Energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy reveals that laser damage leads to the formation of Ga-rich nanoparticles and porosity at the surface.

papers.intro:
In solid-state high-harmonic generation (HHG), an intense non-resonant laser field drives tunnel ionization of electron-hole pairs followed by free acceleration through the continuum. As in gases, the electron-hole pairs can recombine to emit high-energy photons at harmonics of the driving laser frequency [57, 59], however, in contrast to atoms and molecules, the continuum is not the vacuum but the conduction and valence bands of the solids as dictated by the electronic structure [68]. The electronic structure inherently modifies electron-hole trajectories, thus, it is imprinted into the spectrum of harmonic radiation. Today, HHG in crystals is a powerful spectroscopic tool sensitive to symmetry, topology, electronic structure, and crystal dynamics [58, 65, 31, 64, 25, 7, 41, 53, 70, 20, 69]. Furthermore, a variety of techniques from both attoscience and nanophotonics exist to control HHG in solids [13, 29, 45, 47].

Furthermore, a variety of techniques from both attoscience and nanophotonics exist to control HHG in solids [13, 29, 45, 47].

However, while HHG has been observed in virtually all classes of materials [32, 66, 2, 3, 37, 53, 48], relatively little is known about the role of morphology and chemical composition in solid-state strong-field processes. Theoretical studies have suggested that HHG can be dramatically enhanced by doping [23, 67], where mid-gap states are predicted to enhance the rate of tunnel ionization. However, experimental studies have revealed only minor enhancements in yield due to doping [49, 39]. Furthermore, HHG spectroscopy in solids has focused primarily on crystalline materials, with the exception of a select few studies. One prominent example is the pioneering demonstration of HHG in amorphous silica [66]. More recent studies have begun to explore new directions bridging materials science and HHG, for example demonstrating switchable HHG in phase-change materials and liquid crystals [30, 4], or exploring how nanoscale morphology alters HHG spectra [27]. More generally, liquids, which bear close resemblence to amorphous solids, have recently been of interest in the attosecond science community [3, 37, 34, 38, 36, 55].

Recently, we reported a detailed study of HHG in silicon samples amorphized by a Ga+ focused ion beam (Ga+ FIB) [44]. FIB-driven amorphization of the Si surface leads to a giant enhancement in tunnel ionization rate due to the reduction in band gap, enhancing low-order HHG yield by orders of magnitude. Simultaneously, disorder leads to a decoherence that quenches higher-order harmonics, lending new insight into the nature of dephasing in the solid state [1, 17, 42, 21, 9, 10, 35]. Furthermore, the HHG spectra reveal hidden order inherited from the original crystalline phase and unseen by conventional spectroscopic probes. While ref. 44 focuses on the extremes (crystalline vs amorphous Si, a-Si vs c-Si, respectively), FIB enables continuous control over the Ga+ dose. Measurements of Sivis et al. on low-order harmonics from FIB-patterned zone plates suggest a weak enhancement of h3 in the low-dose regime (Fig. S7 ref. 49). However, a broad range of conditions remain unexplored, leaving interesting questions, for example, into the nature of non-perturbative HHG and tunnel ionization in the mixed-phase regime or at very high dose.

The morphology of ion-implanted Si varies dramatically with dose and, due to its technological importance, has been the subject of extensive study for many decades [22, 54, 14, 26, 11, 6, 5, 43, 16, 15, 63, 19]. For the purposes of the present work, we categorize the dose scale into 4 qualitatively different regimes. (1) Well below the critical dose, isolated collision cascades can create point defects and nm-scale amorphous pockets [22, 26, 11]. With room temperature implantation, as in the present study, self-annealing during implantation tends to heal the small amorphous regions [16], leaving vacancies and point and extended defects [6]. (2) Increasing the dose, stable amorphous pockets begin to form slightly beneath the surface as collision cascades begin to overlap, leaving the sample in a mixed phase [14, 15]. (3) Above the critical dose, the amorphous pockets percolate and form a continuous a-Si layer, such that the structure has completed the phase transition between crystalline and amorphous silicon (c-Si to a-Si) [15]. This regime is associated with swelling of the surface [5, 24]. (4) Finally, at very high doses the Ga concentration becomes very large (percent scale) and the surface begins to etch away.

Here, we explore HHG through each of these regimes with an emphasis on the range over which the structural phase transition occurs. At the lowest dose, ion implantation weakly enhances perturbative nonlinearities of low-order harmonics. As the dose increases, the HHG spectra reveal a mixed-phase of a-Si and c-Si. Crucially, annealing measurements allows us to isolate the relative importance of chemical vs structural modifications governing HHG in this system. Above the critical dose, where a continous amorphous layer is formed, the lower-order harmonic yield saturates. This saturation in HHG yield is strongly correlated with surface swelling as measured by atomic-force microscopy (AFM). At still higher dose, the FIB starts etching the surface, which is accompanied by a greatly reduced laser-induced damage threshold (LIDT). Finally, elemental maps of a lamella extracted from the laser-damaged surface in the high-dose regime hint at the formation of Ga-rich nanoparticles and enhanced surface porosity.

papers.title: Asymptotic properties for weak Markov-switching AR(p) models
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the asymptotic properties of an autoregressive model of order p (AR for short), possibly non-centered, whose parameters switch according to an unobserved Markov chain. Departing from the conventional assumption of independent innovations, we merely require the errors to be uncorrelated but not necessarily independent, thereby widening substantially the range of potential applications of Markov-switching AR models. We establish sufficient conditions for the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed moment estimators. We also propose a consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance matrix of the moment estimators. The finite-sample performance of the proposed procedures is illustrated through Monte Carlo experiments and an empirical study based on hourly meteorological data, which together provide strong support for the theoretical findings.

papers.title: The Klein-Gordon equation in projective geometry
papers.abstract: We discuss a geometric method by which H\"ormander's result on the asymptotics of a Klein-Gordon field, on an asymptotically flat spacetime, can be related to some partial peeling, \`a la Penrose, along an extended projective boundary, embedded in a spacetime with one dimension higher.

papers.title: Grid-Compliance Testing of Wind Turbines through Virtualized Component Tests: Testing Concept and Test Bench
papers.abstract: As the proportion of inverter-connected wind turbines increases, test methods for evaluating their grid behavior are becoming increasingly important. This paper presents a Power Hardware-in-the-Loop (PHiL)-based method for grid connection testing of wind turbines. For the first time, geographically distributed simulations of aerodynamics via the Internet and of the grid model via a fiber-optic connection are integrated into certification-relevant tests. The concept expands upon the methods described in IEC TS 61400-21-4. Initial experimental results confirm high emulation quality and sufficiently low latencies, and meet the requirements for a standards-compliant grid emulation.

papers.intro:
Grid compliance testing of Wind Turbines (WT) constitutes a mandatory prerequisite before connecting them to the public power grid. It ensures that the plant operates in a grid-supportive manner, does not destabilize the grid, and, in certain cases, such as grid faults, actively contributes to grid stability and restoration. The testing covers several categories, ranging from evaluation of active and reactive power feed-in, through assessment of grid interaction effects, to testing under fault conditions, including two-phase and three-phase voltage dips and swells.

It ensures that the plant operates in a grid-supportive manner, does not destabilize the grid, and, in certain cases, such as grid faults, actively contributes to grid stability and restoration. The testing covers several categories, ranging from evaluation of active and reactive power feed-in, through assessment of grid interaction effects, to testing under fault conditions, including two-phase and three-phase voltage dips and swells.

The legal framework is based on a series of national and international regulations: First, the minimum requirements for grid connection of generating units are harmonized at the EU level through the Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/631 [1] and further specified at the German national level by the Verordnung zum Nachweis von elektrotechnischen Eigenschaften von Energieanlagen (NELEV) [2]. For the German power grid, this leads to the application of VDE-AR-N 4110 [3] for WT intended for connection to medium-voltage grids, where the standard form of verification consists of a plant certificate based on unit certificates and simulation models. To this end, the certification procedure according to FGW TR8 [4] applies, which references the guideline FGW TR3 [5] for measurement-based verification.

This led to a classification of test-bench types in the technical specification IEC TS 61400-21-4:2025 [6], which specifies the required test-bench type for each test case. Table I summarizes this classification.

Notably, some relevant test categories require at least Class 1 or Class 2 test benches, which necessitate a physically present generator, the converter, and the WT control unit (with the exception of Class 2b). However, for Type-IV WT, i.e., turbines equipped with a full-scale converter, the converter predominantly determines the electrical characteristics at the Point-of-connection (POC), thereby enabling component testing. The idea is to test the full-scale converter along the WT control unit with a PHiL system, where all other components, e.g., generator and grid, are emulated in a real-time system, and load application is achieved purely by power electronics. Additionally, given the large share of simulated components, the question arises of whether some can be simulated in a geographically distributed manner while being coupled to the on-site test bench via a suitable communication infrastructure, which would considerably improve the accessibility of cost-intensive testing infrastructure for manufacturers.

For the wind energy industry, further establishing PHiL test benches for component testing would be highly advantageous during the development phase and for carrying out grid-compliance measurements. First, the mechanical setup requires less complexity, space, and time compared to MHiL-based nacelle test benches. Second, the Device-Under-Test (DUT), i.e., the converter and WT controller, can be examined in isolation, which considerably simplifies fault diagnosis when tests fail. The geographic distribution also opens the prospect of treating test benches as ‘Infrastructure-as-a-Service‘ in the future, thereby protecting manufacturers’ intellectual property, since remotely connected models need not be disclosed while their use in testing remains possible. These aspects can therefore pave the way for time- and cost-efficient testing of WT with respect to system integration and electrical properties.

The objective of the proposed testing concept and test bench is to experimentally investigate their suitability for grid-compliance testing of WT.

A concept for PHiL testing of WT converters based on the Class 3a test-bench classification was presented previously, cf. [7]. Our proposed testing concept differentiates itself in two aspects: First, the PHiL system can operate both as a voltage source and as a current source. This is particularly advantageous for generator emulation, since no transformer between the PHiL converter and the DUT is required, thereby entirely avoiding parasitic effects such as saturation. Emulating the generator with a current source is also more dynamically accurate, as it avoids approximating current derivatives when calculating voltage setpoints. Second, geographically distributed simulation for grid compliance testing of WT has not been considered to date, yet it would substantially enhance the flexibility of future test infrastructure. Together, these aspects establish the testbench as a modular, geographically distributed platform for comprehensive PHiL-based type testing of wind turbine converters, thereby enabling flexible and cost-effective grid-compliance validation.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section II provides a conceptual overview of the test bench and introduces the employed models. Section III then details the hardware setup of the test bench, and Section IV presents preliminary results derived from experimental measurements, and a discussion. Finally, Section V draws conclusions and provides an outlook for future work.

papers.title: Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining
papers.abstract: A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends yet reduce it at the final training budget. We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal.

Nevertheless, the treated run gradually recovers, overtakes the no-decay baseline only after 73%\% of training, and finishes 0.02750.0275 nats better. Performance at the endpoint of an intervention can therefore be a poor predictor of its eventual effect.
