papers.title: Safety Certificates for Systems under Attack via Stackelberg Set Games
papers.abstract: We study a Stackelberg set selection game for linear systems subject to bounded disturbances and additive attacks. The defender selects the vector parameter of a polytopic safe set template; the attacker, after observing this choice, selects the vector parameter of an admissible attack set. The payoff is a signed, facet-normalised invariance margin that tests invariance exactly and quantifies either the available contraction or the facet inflation needed when invariance fails. Both controlled and robust controlled invariance are treated, corresponding to different information patterns for the control input. Exploiting the structure of parameterised polyhedra, we show that within each validity region the margin is concave in the attack parameter, which reduces the follower minimisation to finitely many extreme parameters. The complete max--min game is then solved by a finite family of LPs, one per defender validity region, each enforcing all attacker regions under a common defender decision and guaranteed margin. The framework handles hard state constraints and additional costs related to the safe set size, and recovers optimal set parameters together with state and attack realisations that activate the certificate. A load frequency control example under false data injection illustrates the construction, the validity decomposition, and the two information patterns.

papers.title: How Robust are Pinching-Antenna Systems to Practical Deployment Imperfections?
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the robustness of pinching-antenna systems (PASSs) to three practical deployment imperfections: pinching-antenna (PA) positioning errors, imperfect channel state information (CSI), and line-of-sight (LoS) blockages. We develop analytical frameworks to quantify the performance degradation caused by each imperfection. For PA positioning errors, we employ a Brownian meander model to characterize the distribution and mean of the resulting signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) loss. The results show that positioning errors can diminish the gains from long-term position selection, with the loss becoming more pronounced under stronger shadow fading. For imperfect CSI, we characterize the distribution and moments of the true scattered channel power at the position selected using noisy channel estimates. The resulting selection penalty is governed by the ratio of noise variance to the number of channel measurements, while the upper tail of the selected channel power retains the same behavior as under perfect CSI. Finally, we develop a spatially consistent blockage model and derive the distribution of the optimum long-term SNR for arbitrary blockage configurations, together with a numerically tractable expression for a single blockage. Simulation results validate the analyses and highlight a fundamental property of PASSs: although positioning errors and imperfect CSI can reduce the gains from position selection, good performance can still be achieved provided that an LoS link is available. In particular, even when a large proportion of the waveguide is blocked, PA repositioning can establish LoS links and enable performance close to that of a fully unblocked system for the considered configurations.

papers.title: Compiling Specialized GPU-Initiated Networking
papers.abstract: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication remains in generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are not visible to high-level compilers. We present Obaleth, a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it alongside computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code. Obaleth plans completions around buffer lifetimes and optimizes memory ordering, synchronization, and batching across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs, Obaleth sends small messages up to 3.3$\times$ faster, and on 256 GPUs runs all-to-all 1.25$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ faster than NVSHMEM and NCCL GIN, with much smaller memory and register use. In vLLM, it serves Qwen3-235B on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29$\times$ faster than with DeepEP.

papers.title: Correlation distribution for a class of Niho exponents via self-conjugate-reciprocal polynomials and Kloosterman sums
papers.abstract: Let $q=2^m$ for an even $m\geq 6$ and let $d=s(q-1)+1$ with $4s\equiv5\pmod{q+1}$. In this paper, the correlation distribution between a binary m-sequence of period $q^2-1$ and its $d$-decimation is considered. The cross-correlation function takes seven values $q(i-1)-1$ for $0\leq i\leq 6$, and we determine their frequencies based on the study of low-degree self-conjugate-reciprocal polynomials and three mixed Kloosterman sums, which are finally expressed in terms of $K_m(1)$ and $K_m(\omega)$, where $K_m(\cdot)$ is the Kloomsterman sum on the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $\omega$ is a primitive element of $\mathbb{F}_4$.

authors.name: Chunlei Li
authors.institution: Research Institute of Petroleum Exploration and Development

papers.title: Thresholds of the Polya Szego inequality for the fractional logarithmic p-Laplacian
papers.abstract: We establish three surprising features of the Polya Szego principle for the full signed energy of the fractional logarithmic p-Laplacian. First, the energy doesn't not decrease under rearrangement for all admissible functions. Second, the sharp threshold for Polarization and Schwarz rearrangements are different. Third, for Steiner rearrangement, the threshold in 1 dimension and N dimensions is not the same. Additionally the dimension doesn't appear in the formula.

papers.title: Arithmetical and set-theoretic semantics of the logic of problems and propositions
papers.abstract: Kolmogorov interpreted intuitionistic logic as a calculus of problems and later remarked that a complete treatment should deal with problems and propositions together. Melikhov's logic HC is such a joint two-sorted system: it combines classical propositions with intuitionistic problems by means of two modalities, the problem !A (``find a proof of the proposition A'') and the proposition phi (``the problem phi has a solution''). We give the language of HC a formal semantics in which the modalities are read literally: solutions of !A are proofs of A in a fixed formal theory, ?phi states that phi has a solution, and the connectives on problems are interpreted as in Kleene realizability. Three variants are studied: the arithmetical semantics I (provability in PA), its external version E (truth in the standard model), and the set-theoretic semantics B over ZF, where problem variables are ``black boxes'' and a quantifier Pi over them is available. Validity is defined as the existence of a computable uniform solution. We determine which schemes are valid, build calculi HCI, HCE, HCB sound with respect to the three semantics, and derive Lob's scheme from the fixed-point lemma inside the common core of our calculi and HC. The propositional fragments of HCI and HCE are exactly the provability logics GL and GLS; the positive modality-free fragment of valid problems is intuitionistic logic, while the full modality-free fragment lies strictly above it (Rose's formula is valid, Scott's principle is not). We compare the calculi with HC, which turns out to be incompatible with fixed points, prove independence results and list open questions.

authors.name: Nikolay Vereshchagin
authors.institution: National Research University Higher School of Economics

papers.title: High-order IMEX local discontinuous Galerkin methods with sparse grids for high-dimensional nonlinear parabolic PDEs
papers.abstract: In this work, we develop a high-order IMEX-LDG scheme on sparse grids for solving nonlinear parabolic PDEs in moderate to high dimensions. The method combines the advantages of LDG methods for convection--diffusion problems, IMEX-RK time integrators for stiff systems, and sparse-grid techniques to mitigate the curse of dimensionality. The resulting scheme is fully parallelized in MPI, is robust, efficient, and scalable, making it suitable for a wide range of applications involving high-dimensional nonlinear parabolic PDEs.

papers.title: Experimental characterization of magnetic multipole fields up to octupole order using smartphone magnetometry
papers.abstract: The multipole expansion is one of the organising ideas of electromagnetism: far from a localised source the field is dominated by its lowest non-vanishing moment, and each successive order decays one power of the distance faster. Although the dipole field is routinely measured in introductory laboratories, higher orders are seldom explored experimentally, because the fields are weak, decay very rapidly and require careful positioning. Here we show that with four identical neodymium cube magnets, a sheet of graph paper and the magnetometer of a smartphone, first-year students can build and characterise not one but three distinct magnetic octupoles (linear, planar and `square' arrangements), together with the dipole and the two quadrupoles that serve as reference. A simple notation and a compact set of formulae, based on the spatial Cartesian moments $M_{pq}=\sum_k m_k x_k^p z_k^q$ of the array, predict which field component survives at each measuring position and how it decays. The measured exponents are $n\simeq 3$, $4$ and $5$ for dipole, quadrupole and octupole arrangements, and the measured prefactors show fair quantitative consistency with the independently determined dipole moment of the magnets once nominal geometry and spacer effects are taken into account. We discuss the systematic effects that limit the octupole measurements (higher-order terms at short distance, residual lower-order moments at long distance, the location of the sensor inside the phone) and the ways in which the activity can be extended. The experiment generalises and unifies previous smartphone-based measurements of dipoles, linear quadrupoles and a linear octupole.

authors.name: Cecilia Stari
authors.institution: Universidad de la República de Uruguay

authors.name: Arturo C. Marti
authors.institution: Universidad de la República de Uruguay

papers.title: A New Galactic Close Binary Supersoft Source Candidate
papers.abstract: The identification of a new galactic Close Binary Supersoft Source (CBSS) candidate, whose main ID is ZTF J043609.49+364057.7, is presented on the basis of the analysis of its optical spectrum, light curve and Spectral Energy Distribution (SED). During a survey designed to find candidates to the aforementioned class independently of X-ray emissions, this object's optical spectrum was found to exhibit the typical emission features expected for a CBSS. The available photometric data show a quasi-sinusoidal modulation, with a period of 5.42 h, compatible with the orbital modulation of the system. Although there is no current identification of X-ray emission from this source, its SED displays a highly absorbed bright FUV component, given the estimated E(B - V) ~ 0.7 mag.

authors.name: Francisco Jablonski
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte

papers.title: Hydr\'oDex: gotta match 'em all!
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive hydrodynamic classification of stationary fluid profiles in first-order phase transitions within the constant-sound-speed model, a physically motivated extension of the standard bag model that allows the sound speeds in front of and behind the wall, $c_+$ and $c_-$, to differ. Solving the matching conditions at the bubble wall and evolving the profile in the surrounding plasma, we systematically identify and classify all the possible stationary solutions. The classification recovers all previously known direct and inverse detonation, deflagration, and hybrid solutions, while revealing a new class of stationary configurations, termed mixed hybrids, featuring rarefaction waves on both sides of the wall and oppositely directed fluid flows. For a sufficiently pronounced hierarchy $c_+ > c_-$, the classification in terms of the wall velocity $\xi_w$ and the asymptotic strength parameter $\alpha_N$ further exhibits degenerate regions in parameter space, where multiple distinct stationary profiles correspond to the same physical inputs $(\xi_w,\alpha_N)$. This non-uniqueness arises as the parametrization discards thermodynamic information and is resolved once the underlying microphysics is specified. We also compute the kinetic-energy budget and the associated acoustic gravitational-wave spectra within the sound-shell model, finding that mixed-hybrid solutions, despite their oppositely directed flows, introduce no additional spectral feature, and their spectra can be closely mimicked by ordinary direct or inverse hybrids with very different fluid profiles. Finally, we release Hydr\'oDex, a public code that implements the complete hydrodynamic classification, fluid-profile construction, kinetic-energy budget, and gravitational-wave calculation.

papers.title: Classical weak antilocalization in electron hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: Weak localization is strongly suppressed in electron hydrodynamics, where frequent electron--electron collisions rapidly dephase the Cooperon. Nevertheless, disorder can still produce a logarithmic correction to the bare hydrodynamic resistivity. We show that spatial fluctuations of the momentum-relaxation rate generate a classical memory kernel through the diffusive return of transverse momentum. In two dimensions, this return is logarithmic, as in weak localization, but involves a single shear propagator rather than quantum interference. Conservation laws and positivity of dissipation fix its antilocalizing sign: the return reduces momentum relaxation and hence the bulk resistivity. Unlike quantum weak localization, the logarithm is cut off by momentum relaxation and has a viscosity-dependent amplitude. For temperature-independent impurity friction, the resistivity correction scales as $-T^2\ln(T_\xi/T)$ in a Fermi liquid and $-T\ln(T_\xi/T)$ in a Planckian metal. In channels, the return competes with viscosity renormalization, and a width scan separates the two effects.

authors.name: Alberto Cortijo
authors.institution: Instituto de Ciencia de Materiales de Madrid

papers.title: Quantifying Dependence Effects on $k$-out-of-$n$ Reliability Relative to the Independent Benchmark
papers.abstract: Understanding how dependence among component lifetimes affects the reliability of redundant systems is a central problem in reliability engineering. In this paper, we develop a framework for quantifying the impact of multivariate dependence on $k$-out-of-$n$ system reliability relative to the independent benchmark. Using an orthogonal Legendre expansion of the copula density, we derive an exact decomposition that separates the dependence structure from the system architecture. This representation identifies how individual dependence contributions are transmitted to system reliability through explicit structural weights. An application to multivariate Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern copulas demonstrates that higher-order dependence can produce distinct reliability effects even when all bivariate copulas remain unchanged. Our findings provide a systematic approach to quantifying and interpreting the effects of multivariate dependence on the reliability of redundant systems.

papers.title: Stability of crystalline measures under random perturbations
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study random perturbations and the diffraction properties of translation-bounded crystalline measures. Under a non-vanishing assumption on the known perturbation factor, we prove that, almost surely, any realization of the perturbed measure preserves sufficient structural information to allow the full recovery of the original measure. Previous works have only considered crystalline measures with uniformly discrete supports and equal-mass atoms. Our general setting includes many important crystalline measures that were excluded until now. To treat this broader setting, we adopt a different framework. In this work, we model the perturbation as a random measure rather than as a random set. In particular, this leads us to consider not only perturbations of the support, but also perturbations of the atoms' masses. On the other hand, using elementary techniques of Fourier analysis, we prove that any translation-bounded crystalline measure has a diffraction measure, and we explicitly compute its diffraction.

papers.title: Admissible Yang--Baxter equation for Nijenhuis perm superalgebras
papers.abstract: We develop a superization of the theory of admissible Yang--Baxter equations for Nijenhuis perm algebras initiated by Ma and Song. We introduce Nijenhuis perm superalgebras, their representations, and the dual representation, with Koszul signs chosen so that the contraction of the Yang--Baxter tensor matches the $\mathcal O$-operator equation exactly. We define Nijenhuis perm superbialgebras and characterise them by matched pairs. In the coboundary case, we show that every even supersymmetric solution of the $S$-admissible perm Yang--Baxter equation gives rise to a Nijenhuis perm superbialgebra, and we give sufficient conditions for a perm superalgebra to admit a Nijenhuis operator constructed from such a solution. Examples with purely odd components illustrate the role of the grading.

papers.title: Learning Latent Goal Costs for Visual World-Model Planning with an Expanding Curriculum
papers.abstract: Image-goal planning with a frozen visual world model depends on how predicted observations are scored against the goal. Mean-squared error (MSE) between embeddings from a pretrained visual encoder can provide a useful signal near a goal, yet favor states across an obstacle that are visually similar to the goal and difficult to reach. We fit a small residual adapter on top of frozen I-JEPA embeddings to improve this latent goal cost. Starting near each goal, a planner collects trajectories from progressively wider regions of initial states. The adapter learns from the order of observations along successful trajectories, with additional comparisons inferred from failed rollouts. No task-specific progress labels are used for fitting, so the procedure can be applied to other goal-reaching tasks. DotWall and PointMaze are used in this work. In paired 50-case evaluations with identical starts, goals, world models, and planner settings, success increases from 54% to 98% in DotWall and from 82% to 96% in PointMaze. On 16 unseen DotWall layout-goal cases, the adapter fitted on one fixed layout improves agreement between latent-cost ordering and shortest legal-path ordering from 71.9% to 85.8%. The results indicate that planning experience can improve a frozen visual representation's goal cost without retraining the encoder or the world model.

authors.name: Konstantinos Mylonas
authors.institution: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

papers.title: Frequency-Security-Aware Real-Time Economic Dispatch with Data Center UPS Flexibility for Inertia and Primary Frequency Response Services
papers.abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy and the rapid growth of AI data centers are introducing significant challenges to power system frequency security. There is an urgent need to identify grid-compatible resources capable of providing fast frequency support. This paper proposes a frequency-security-aware real-time economic dispatch (RTED) model that enables data center (DC) uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems to provide steady-state power balancing, inertia response, and primary frequency response (PFR) services. Specifically, tractable analytical frequency-security constraints are derived and incorporated into the RTED framework through second-order cone programming (SOCP) formulation. The proposed model jointly optimizes energy, reserve, and inertia to minimize system operation cost while preventing under-frequency load shedding (UFLS). Numerical validation on a modified IEEE 39-bus system demonstrates that the proposed RTED model with UPS flexibility can economically support system operation and significantly improve frequency security under active-power deficit disturbances.

papers.title: Chiral or unidirectional? Multiterminal current partition in the quantum Hall regime from self-consistent screening theory
papers.abstract: Multiterminal current measurements on a six-terminal Hall bar were recently used to argue that the current flow is chiral on the quantized Hall plateaus and non-chiral between them, and, in a companion analysis, that the imposed current flows along one edge only. We examine these conclusions with the self-consistent screening theory of the quantum Hall effect. The plateau values of the current partition follow from a vanishing longitudinal conductivity and a quantized Hall conductivity alone: every two-dimensional conductor with $\sigma_\ell=0$ and $\sigma_{\rm H}=\nu e^2/h$ has the conductance matrix of the "coherent and chiral" model, whatever the spatial distribution of the current. Terminal currents fix the current density only up to circulating currents, made explicit here with a stream function, and the chirality of the current density is a property of exactly this part. A two-dimensional local transport calculation for the measured device, including its two interior contacts, reproduces the plateau partition for all contact configurations and the ordering of the suppression between the plateaus without edge channels. The self-consistent current density separates into a chiral equilibrium (magnetization) current, which carries no net current, and a transport current that flows in the same direction in both edge strips; the "one-edge" imposed current is a bookkeeping choice of the reference chemical potential. The floating potentials of the two interior contacts are predicted to be equal when the bulk around them is quantized and to differ by up to half the Hall voltage when the current flows in edge strips. Multiterminal current partition measures the sign of the Hall conductivity and the absence of dissipation, not the location or the chirality of the transport current; the edge channels are the premise of the interpretation, not a result of the measurement.

papers.title: Polynomial integrals and Poisson structures of the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator
papers.abstract: We classify the autonomous polynomial integrals of the nondegenerate fourth-order Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator. For a rational frequency ratio $m:n$ in lowest terms, the two sector energies together with the real and imaginary parts of a single ladder product generate all polynomial integrals, subject to one defining relation. The smallest total degree of an integral not expressible through the sector energies is $m+n$, and this bound is attained. For an irrational ratio only polynomials in the sector energies are conserved. In normal-mode variables the commensurate case is the negative oscillator resonance, and the classification realizes its invariant theory in the original higher-derivative variables. Two compatible Poisson structures generate the same dynamics with an indefinite and a positive-definite Hamiltonian. They induce different brackets on the same physical generators. We show that diagonal rescalings of the generators identifying the two abstract Poisson algebras exist only when $m$ or $n$ is even, and that none of them preserves the physical domain of nonnegative sector energies. Finally, we express the generators in terms of the original coordinate and its first three derivatives. The classical multiplier identity gives their variational characteristics in closed form and shows that the additional resonant integrals cannot arise from point variational symmetries.

papers.title: Phase-resolved spin-orbit exciton transfer with dressed quantum encodings
papers.abstract: A quantum simulation of a material runs on a register much smaller than the electronic problem behind it, and the map between the two decides what a measured correlation means. We study this map for spin--orbit exciton transfer across an Ir--Ir bond of a LiIrF$_6$-derived model. Exact references show that a bare product-state encoding has an amplitude floor above a 0.02 state tolerance at sampled times, whereas a polar-dressed encoding lowers the ten-window projected error from 0.320 to $3.54\times10^{-4}$. Three-CZ axial and two-CZ transverse circuits, run on IBM Kingston in eight acquisitions with 1.6 million shots, resolve population transfer together with both quadratures of the intersite coherence. Raw half-transfer Bell-projector scores reach 0.935 in two independent acquisitions, and on a second bond a coherent arm with lower bound 0.871 is separated from a matched dephased control. Across 2,520 model points, adaptive spectral encodings meet fixed accuracy targets with explicit dimension costs.

papers.title: Testing correlated spin--orbit multiplets beyond excitation centroids
papers.abstract: Matching an excitation centroid does not establish the resolved structure of a correlated spin--orbit multiplet. Across eight embedded iridium and osmium compounds, ligand-active XMS-CASPT2 places the K$_2$OsCl$_6$ centroid within 0.5~meV of a RIXS maximum while splitting its nearly degenerate reference triplet by 2.54~meV, and matched OpenMolcas 26.10 controls retain the bare-anion sensitivities. Independent BAGEL calculations isolate contraction dependence in a three-state spin-free model: on the same reference, replacing SS--SR with MS--MR reduces the symmetry-defined E-block splitting from 0.448~meV to $4.67\times10^{-5}$~meV. Native reconstruction, reference symmetry, representation invariance, sensitivity controls and comparison with fitted spectral features or magnetic response provide an ordered validation procedure whose tests constrain different properties of the Hamiltonian.

papers.title: Policy-Conditioned Koopman Representations for Parameterized Closed-Loop Systems
papers.abstract: Predicting the response of a nonlinear system across different feedback controllers requires a model that captures how the closed-loop dynamics change with the controller parameters. In a finite-dimensional Koopman model, these changes may affect both the latent dynamics and the observable coordinates used to represent them. In this paper, we propose a policy-conditioned Koopman representation framework to address this problem. This framework allows a single learned model to predict a family of closed-loop trajectories without retraining for each controller. We test the framework on four nonlinear prediction benchmarks, where the model stays below a 15% error threshold on every system, while each baseline exceeds it on at least one. As an example application, the resulting surrogate supports one-shot feedback-parameter selection: an optimization at the initial state selects a controller that then operates with fixed parameters and ongoing state feedback. On nonlinear control benchmarks including MuJoCo, the selected controllers stabilize every system with 3 to 97 times less online computation than nonlinear model predictive control. These results demonstrate how policy-dependent coordinates can support both prediction across closed-loop systems and controller selection without repeated online trajectory optimization.

papers.title: Topological Hybridization Gaps from Molecular Orbitals Coupled to Dirac Fermions
papers.abstract: A magnetically gapped topological-insulator surface carries a half-quantized Hall response. We show that hybridizing the surface Dirac fermions with a flat band of chiral orbitals adds an integer to it: spin-momentum locking forces the hybridization to wind around the band-crossing ring, opening a topological gap. For orbitals with total angular momentum $j$, rotational symmetry fixes the surface Hall conductivity to $je^2/h$, with the sign set by the Dirac branch crossed and independent of the sign of the Dirac mass. The result survives crystal-field quenching of the orbital moment, with the winding then set by interference between hybridization pathways. First-principles calculations for a monolayer of nitric oxide adsorbed on Bi$_2$Se$_3$ predict a $\sim 20$ meV hybridization gap and an intrinsic surface Hall conductivity of $\frac{3}{2}e^2/h$, identifying molecular orbital angular momentum as a handle on surface topology.

authors.name: Jorge I. Facio
authors.institution: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

authors.name: Veronica Vildosola
authors.institution: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

papers.title: Agent-written heuristics versus commercial solvers on unsolved job-shop benchmark instances
papers.abstract: Commercial solvers are the standard tool for difficult scheduling problems. We study whether a frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with open-source tools only, can match them in quality and speed. We report every run, and independent checkers verify every schedule. On the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer. Unchanged, it improved all ten instances of the family and closed two. With equal budgets on the same workstation, it ended 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound, against 2.6-5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4-4.4% for Hexaly. On the Behnke-Geiger flexible job shops, an agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. New lower bounds show that four published MKT values cannot be attained on the distributed instance files. Agent-run improvement campaigns closed eight further instances.

authors.name: Bruno Vieira
authors.institution: Centro de Ciências e Tecnologias Nucleares

papers.title: Physical Prior Mismatch in Variational Dual-Polarization Quantum SATCOM Channel Estimation
papers.abstract: Dual-polarization quantum satellite communications require accurate estimation of complex polarization channels. We investigate physical latent-prior mismatch in variational estimation of a $2\times 2$ complex channel, using eight Cartesian latent coordinates and a fixed latent-to-channel mapping. Gaussian, matched and sharpened Rician, Laplace, and Cauchy priors are compared under a fixed neural architecture and forward Kullback-Leibler objective. Models are trained for 300,000 updates with $\zeta=1/(2N_{\mathrm{est}})$ and evaluated using three training seeds and 10,000 shared held-out blocks per operating point. The Gaussian and Rician priors coincide at the Rayleigh limit. At higher Rician factors, the matched prior improves estimation accuracy, especially with fewer pilots. At $K=100$ and $N_{\mathrm{est}}=32$, the matched Rician variational estimator reduces mean squared Frobenius error by 2.50% relative to linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE). We also derive a joint Rician Bayesian posterior-mean estimator that incorporates the complete least-squares noise covariance and reduces posterior integration to one-dimensional quadrature. It improves on LMMSE by 3.33% at the same operating point and achieves lower observed error than the scalar Rician and both neural estimators at all 12 operating points. Additional Rician prior sharpening increases error, while Laplace and Cauchy controls remain near the Gaussian baseline.

authors.name: Anders M. Buvarp
authors.institution: Norwegian University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Stefan Werner
authors.institution: Norwegian University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Mean-field theory of neural networks: from spikes to firing rates
papers.abstract: Connecting microscopic neuronal spiking to macroscopic brain function is a central challenge in computational neuroscience. Firing-rate models provide a framework for addressing this problem by describing neuronal activity at an intermediate level between individual spikes and large-scale population dynamics. Here, we introduce the foundations of firing-rate descriptions, formalizing their definitions through temporal, population, and trial averaging. We discuss experimental evidence for firing rates, from the input-output transfer functions of individual neurons to the tuning curves of different neuronal populations. We then establish the connection between spikes and firing rates in single neurons and recurrently connected excitatory-inhibitory populations using mean-field approximation. We illustrate how collective dynamics emerge from neuronal interactions, including population stimulus-response curves and bistability induced by recurrent coupling, and brain rhythms arising from synaptic depression. We briefly review extensions and applications of firing-rate models to learning, seizure-like oscillatory activity, visual selectivity, phase-amplitude coupling in neural oscillations, and whole-brain modeling. Together, these examples illustrate how firing-rate models provide effective descriptions of neural activity, linking the dynamics of individual neurons to collective computations across scales.

papers.title: Small Open-Weight Language Models for Crowd Decision-Making: Capabilities and Limits of Output-Level Fusion and Linguistic Aggregation
papers.abstract: Small open-weight language models can run crowd decision-making (CDM) on an institution's own infrastructure, which keeps the checkpoint, the inference settings and the opinions under its control. Their judgements vary across repeated queries; whether repeating and aggregating them, often through the 2-tuple linguistic representation, settles the decision rather than the labels is untested. Five open-weight models of 8-36B total parameters on one consumer GPU and a hosted reference classify 474 TripAdvisor reviews of four London restaurants ten times each; three open-weight models repeat the protocol on 600 reviews of twelve Madrid restaurants. Continuous evaluations preserve resolution: snapping each review leaves 5 distinct values against 21-65, and snapping at every level at most two collective values. Sensitivity to the participants persists once run-to-run variability is reduced: in London, redrawing the reviewers keeps the winner on 47-81% of replicas against 86-100% for redrawing the runs. With simultaneous intervals over every pair of alternatives under crowd resampling, no system on either corpus names a single winner: in London every system keeps all four restaurants as candidates, and in Madrid the candidate sets hold five to eight of the twelve. Extra runs and output-level fusion stabilize the winner but do not remove that sensitivity, and the fusion does not beat its best member. The three larger open-weight models name the hosted reference's London winner and at least match its per-review correlation with the reviewers' stars, so small open-weight models can support local CDM, reported as candidate sets with margins rather than forced rankings.

papers.title: Weak Generators in Stable Module Categories
papers.abstract: The aim of this note is to show that the existence of weak generators in the stable module category of a ring, or equivalently, of $p$-indigent modules in the terminology of Holston et al., depends on the underlying model of set theory.

papers.title: Valid Inequalities for Bilevel 0-1 Shortest-Path Problems
papers.abstract: We characterize valid inequalities for bilevel programs in which the leader makes binary decisions, and the follower solves a shortest-path problem. We exploit a dualize-and-combine reformulation and show that even with ideal formulations for the leader and the follower primal solution sets, fractional solutions may still appear in the continuous relaxation. From that reformulation, we identify that the interaction between the leader variables and the follower dual variables, which we capture through a leader-potential set, is the key structure to be convexified to guarantee that a continuous relaxation recovers the optimal value of the original problem, closing the objective gap. Furthermore, we characterize the valid inequalities for the leader-potential set through network flows, and identify a family of inequalities we name root cuts that suffice to recover the optimal value. Complementary to the structural results, we prove that the cut generation problem is NP-hard even with partially fixed coefficients and a network with two nodes and two parallel arcs. Motivated by the complexity result, we propose a constructive method to fix coefficients in the valid inequalities while preserving separation guarantees, by exploiting the network structure.

authors.name: Bruno M. Pacheco
authors.institution: Centre interuniversitaire de recherche sur les réseaux d'entreprise, la logistique et le transport

papers.title: Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy
papers.abstract: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts.

papers.title: Calculation of Stiefel fractions via Riemann thetas
papers.abstract: Stiefel fraction is a deformation of Zolotarev one which allows to solve certain three band extentions of Zolotarev approximation problem. We propose an efficient computational approach for Stiefel's solution based on genus two Riemann theta functions. This allows us to visualise the domain in the space of three band problems corresponding to Stiefel's solutions.

authors.name: Andrei Bogatyrev
authors.institution: National Research University Higher School of Economics

authors.name: Timur Garaev
authors.institution: Federal Almazov North-West Medical Research Centre

papers.title: Fano-Enriques threefolds of Fano index $>1$
papers.abstract: We study $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds of Fano index greater than $1$ whose Weil divisor class group has nontrivial torsion. We give a complete list of their possible numerical types: there are $176$ of them, which refine to $182$ possible graded Hilbert series. At least $40$ numerical types are realised: $27$ by quotients of weighted complete intersections by cyclic groups, twelve by quotients of threefolds of codimension $4$ or $5$ and one by a quotient of the del Pezzo threefold of degree $5$. Seventy-two numerical types are shown not to occur. In particular the torsion subgroup need not have prime order, and the Weil and $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano indices can be $(1,2)$, $(1,3)$ or $(1,4)$.

papers.title: MarathonTS: a benchmark of long synthetic time series from window assembly and long-series generators
papers.abstract: Many applications of synthetic time series require a series that is much longer than the windows on which a generative model is trained. Such a series can be assembled from a pool of short generated windows, which requires deciding which windows are taken, in what order, and how their seams are processed, or it can be produced directly by a long-series generator. This study presents MarathonTS, to our knowledge the first open benchmark that compares both families under one protocol. Every method produces a series of the same length on 9 open hourly datasets with 10 seeds. The series is evaluated by its fidelity to the real data (83 metrics in 12 groups, against three real references: train, validation and an out-of-time split), by its utility (models are trained on the synthetic series only and tested on real data, TSTR against TRTR, in 14 classification and regression tasks), by its memorisation of the training data and by its computational cost. The statistical analysis is carried out as a separate stage that reads the published tables and gives the rankings of every method in every slice, the answers to the research questions with tests and uncertainty, and the results of a pre-specified confirmatory family. In the main run, the methods differ in both confirmatory cells; the choice of windows matters more than the processing of their seams, which does not improve the series, and no method trains the downstream models as well as the real series. The top tier of the leaderboard is reproduced on other hardware, whereas the exact places within it are not. For the reproducibility of the study, the code, the data hashes and all results are publicly available (links below).
papers.intro:
Synthetic time series are used to train and test forecasting and classification models when real data are scarce, sensitive or cannot be shared. Many of these applications require a long series: a forecaster learns weekly and monthly patterns only from a series that contains them, a model of rare events needs a sufficient number of such events, and a stress test needs regimes that last longer than a few days. At the same time, generative models for time series are trained on windows of a fixed and short length (Yoon et al., 2019; Yuan and Qiao, 2024). A window of one week at an hourly step contains 168 points, while the training series of a dataset covers months or years. This raises the question of how to obtain a synthetic series that is many windows long and remains realistic.

Synthetic time series are used to train and test forecasting and classification models when real data are scarce, sensitive or cannot be shared. Many of these applications require a long series: a forecaster learns weekly and monthly patterns only from a series that contains them, a model of rare events needs a sufficient number of such events, and a stress test needs regimes that last longer than a few days. At the same time, generative models for time series are trained on windows of a fixed and short length (Yoon et al., 2019; Yuan and Qiao, 2024). A window of one week at an hourly step contains 168 points, while the training series of a dataset covers months or years. This raises the question of how to obtain a synthetic series that is many windows long and remains realistic.

Two approaches to this problem can be distinguished. In the first approach, the series is assembled from a pool of short generated windows. Assembly involves three decisions: which windows are taken, in what order, and how the seams between neighbouring windows are processed. Each of these decisions has a long history outside time series, in concatenative speech synthesis (Hunt and Black, 1996), video textures (Schödl et al., 2000) and image quilting (Efros and Freeman, 2001), and the window pool can be produced by any generator. In the second approach, a long-series generator produces the whole series directly: a diffusion model extends the series window by window (Yuan and Qiao, 2024), or a pretrained forecasting foundation model (Ansari et al., 2024; Das et al., 2024; Petralia et al., 2026) continues the training series for as long as needed. The two families make different trade-offs. Assembly keeps the quality of individual windows, but it can create seams and lose structure longer than a window. A long-series generator does not select from a fixed window pool, but chunked generation can introduce boundaries; it may also drift, smooth the series, or reproduce data seen in pretraining. Both families therefore require evaluation of local transitions and longer-scale structure.

Assembly involves three decisions: which windows are taken, in what order, and how the seams between neighbouring windows are processed. Each of these decisions has a long history outside time series, in concatenative speech synthesis (Hunt and Black, 1996), video textures (Schödl et al., 2000) and image quilting (Efros and Freeman, 2001), and the window pool can be produced by any generator. In the second approach, a long-series generator produces the whole series directly: a diffusion model extends the series window by window (Yuan and Qiao, 2024), or a pretrained forecasting foundation model (Ansari et al., 2024; Das et al., 2024; Petralia et al., 2026) continues the training series for as long as needed. The two families make different trade-offs. Assembly keeps the quality of individual windows, but it can create seams and lose structure longer than a window. A long-series generator does not select from a fixed window pool, but chunked generation can introduce boundaries; it may also drift, smooth the series, or reproduce data seen in pretraining. Both families therefore require evaluation of local transitions and longer-scale structure.

These families have not been compared under one protocol. A recent study varies how overlapping windows are blended into a long series (Long et al., 2026), but it does not vary which windows are taken and in what order, and it does not compare assembly with long-series generators. Evaluations of synthetic time series score sets of independent windows of the training length (Ang et al., 2023; Nikitin et al., 2024); therefore, they cannot capture the seams, the structure longer than a window, or the distance of the series to data from a later period. The real reference in such evaluations is usually the training data or a random split of the same windows. Without a common protocol, it remains unclear when assembly from windows is sufficient, which of its decisions matter, and whether a pretrained forecaster is a good source of long synthetic series.

This study presents MarathonTS, a benchmark of long synthetic time series. To our knowledge, it is the first open benchmark that compares assembly from a pool of generated windows with long-series generators, including pretrained forecasting foundation models, under one protocol, and the first to evaluate whole long series against a real reference from a later period (section 2). The contributions of the study are as follows: • A common task and protocol (sections 3 and 4). Every method receives only the training part of a series and returns one series of length KK times the training window, the same for every method and approximately as long as the training part, in the same channels. The main run compares 30 methods on nine open hourly datasets with ten seeds: nine assemblers and three seam joiners on each of two window pools, and six long-series generators (Diffusion-TS, Chronos, TimesFM 3.0, Timestral and two sampling modes of zEDGE_TS). Within one pool, all assemblers read the same windows, so they differ only in selection, order and seam processing. • Evaluation of the whole series (section 5). Fidelity is measured by 83 metrics in 12 groups, including groups for the seams, for structure longer than a window and for tail events, against three real references: train, a validation split and an out-of-time split. Utility is measured by training downstream models on the synthetic series only and testing them on real data (TSTR against TRTR) in 14 classification and regression tasks. Memorisation and cost are measured separately. • A pre-specified statistical analysis (section 6). The analysis consists of rankings with uncertainty and robustness checks, research questions with an empirical noise level as the smallest effect of interest and tests of both difference and equivalence, and a small confirmatory family that carries the main conclusion. The analysis was frozen before the main run was carried out. • Open, reproducible and extensible software (section 7). Every component is registered by name, so a new dataset, generator, assembler, metric or test enters the comparison through a plugin. Incremental recomputation and run profiles make it possible to run the benchmark on a single GPU.

papers.title: Neural Classifiers as Error-Correcting Codes
papers.abstract: A unified framework is proposed that characterizes supervised deep classification as the decoding of error-correcting codes in the Shannon sense. Cross-entropy optimization is shown to align softmax classifiers with maximum-likelihood decoding, where logits map to Hamming distances to class-specific codewords. This correspondence explains the emergence of standard divergence objectives (e.g., Kullback-Leibler, Jeffreys) and provides a geometric basis for the stability of decision boundaries. Furthermore, the geometries of Neural Collapse and LeJEPA are identified as optimal constellations for decoding under isotropic noise. Unlike classical Error-Correcting Output Codes, deep networks are shown to learn effective codebooks in the feature space implicitly. This insight is leveraged to derive novel criteria for lossless quantization, improved knowledge distillation, and architectural regularization based on code redundancy. Finally, this perspective is extended to self-supervised encoders, offering a cohesive explanation for the geometry of latent representations in modern neural models.

authors.name: Anton Makarov
authors.institution: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Efficient and Practical Clustering of Variables in Causal Graphs
papers.abstract: Clustering variables in a graph may improve visual clarity and simplify causal inference. Harnessing the full potential of clustering requires an automated method to detect useful clusters in a graph. We introduce a novel class of clusters called conduits, and present a sound, complete and efficient algorithm for detecting all conduits in the graph. In addition to algorithmic detectability, conduits appear naturally in causal graphs stemming from real-world applications, enabling substantial size reduction. Furthermore, the structure of conduits enables the application of known identifiability results regarding clustering. We demonstrate these properties in a simulation study with real-world graphs.

papers.title: Contractions of realizations and differential invariants of the algebra sl(2,C)
papers.abstract: In this paper, we formalize a method for constructing limit transitions between local realizations of Lie algebras based on contractions of the corresponding algebras. In the complex holomorphic category, contractions of faithful realizations of the special linear algebra sl(2, C) to the complex three-dimensional Poincar\'e algebra and the Weyl-Heisenberg algebra are explicitly constructed. For the contraction of a generating realization of the algebra sl(2,C) to the algebra g_{3.4}^{-1}, differential invariants are constructed and a limit system of Newtonian type is found.

authors.name: M. Nesterenko
authors.institution: V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University

papers.title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
papers.abstract:
A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs.
  In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better.
  These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.

papers.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
papers.abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.

authors.name: Alexander Golubev
authors.institution: Troitsk Institute for Innovation and Fusion Research

papers.title: Horizontal component of the ion drag force in a plasma sheath
papers.abstract: The ion drag force is responsible for the underlying physics behind many important phenomena in complex (dusty) plasma, such as void formation, particle alignment in an ion flow, shadow-like attraction between the particles, dust clouds rotation in the presence of a magnetic field etc. In this paper, we investigate the ion drag force acting on particles levitating near the sheath edge of a capacitively coupled discharge in xenon. In particular, we calculate the radial (horizontal) component of the ion drag force directed parallel to the lower electrode above which the particles levitate. The calculation is based on the actual information about the ion flow, which is directly obtained using Laser Induced Fluorescence. The calculated horizontal component is comparable in magnitude to the vertical one, which pushes the particles toward the electrode surface, and is higher than previously expected. This unexpected finding must be taken into account in future research. The very possibility of the measurements we report opens the door for detailed studies of dusty plasma phenomena governed by ions and their flows.

papers.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
papers.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

papers.title: On the Existence of a Third Planet and an Apsidal Resonance Chain in the Kepler-396 System through TESS Data
papers.abstract: The possible existence of a third planet in the Kepler-396 system has been previously proposed. Given that the planetary mass is poorly constrained and the orbit could be either interior or exterior to planet Kepler-396 c, that proposal is not clearly known in the community. In order to address this and further investigate Kepler-396 system's configuration, new TESS data are employed to form a long baseline of transit timing. Using the pixel-level decorrelation technique, the mid-transit times are determined. Through long baseline transit-timing-variation technique, we perform a comprehensive exploration of the parameter space of the third planet. Two best-fit solutions, derived from different priors of orbital inclinations, have led to the reduced chi-square values as 2.24 and 2.34 respectively, compared to 12.97 for the two-planet model. This result strongly suggests the existence of the third planet, i.e. Kepler-396 d. Based on these two best-fit solutions, the masses of Kepler-396 b, c, d are updated to be around 9, 4, 4 Earth Mass, and the corresponding orbital periods are 43, 89, 144 days, respectively. With these updated masses, Kepler-396 b is on the border between rocky or volatile-rich, Kepler-396 c is confirmed to be a volatile-rich super-puff planet, and both planets lie in the Neptune savanna. Dynamical simulations with three planets are performed, showing that they are stable for a timescale of $10^6$ years. The examination on resonant angles leads to the conclusion that planets Kepler-396 b, c, d form a three-body apsidal resonance chain.

papers.title: Periodic orbits of quadratic polynomials of periods six and seven
papers.abstract: The dynamics of quadratic polynomials is commonly studied by using the family of maps f_{c}(x) = x^{2} + c, where c include C. In this paper we form equations of periodic orbits of periods six and seven on a new (u,v)-plane and consider also the corresponding equations on the (x,y)-plane. The new (u,v)-model produces equations for the periods six and seven with significantly lower degree than the ones obtained by the previous models which enables us to find their solutions.

papers.title: QCAP-VQA: Question-Conditioned Capped Prior-Mass Supervision for Medical Visual Question Answering
papers.abstract: Medical visual question answering models can answer correctly without attending to the anatomy that the question names. Automatic region priors allow spatial supervision without expert masks, but they are noisy, and it is unclear how strongly they should shape attention and how their effect should be verified. We present QCAP-VQA, which supervises a subset of cross-attention heads with a question-conditioned prior built from ranked segmentation proposals. Its capped prior-mass objective penalizes insufficient attention inside the prior only below a threshold. We evaluate attention against SLAKE structure boxes that play no role in training, separating attention on the named anatomy from how attention shifts between questions about the same image. QCAP-VQA matches the accuracy of a baseline without spatial supervision (84.26% vs. 84.23%), and every evaluated prior-supervised model places more attention on the annotated structures. Over a 64-fold range of regularization strength, the capped objective keeps prior mass between 0.67 and 0.77, whereas a pooled region-mass objective drives it to 0.97 and loses accuracy. The cost lies in question conditioning: as the constraint widens or strengthens, attention shifts agree less with the expert-defined contrast. Across 13 configurations, prior-referenced and expert-referenced evaluation rank the models in largely opposite order (Spearman correlation of -0.87), and the capped models it favors track the prior's own errors. Because clinical use of medical visual question answering requires answers grounded in the queried anatomy, supervision from automatic priors should be judged against independent anatomical references.

authors.name: Yining Zhao
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Multi-GPU Tridiagonal Partition Algorithm
papers.abstract: This paper presents a multi-GPU version and a multi-GPU recursive version of the parallel partition method for systems of linear algebraic equations with tridiagonal coefficient matrices and their implementations in CUDA. Computational experiments on one and two GPU cards, for different system sizes and with different number of recursive steps are conducted. The results are analyzed and discussed.

papers.title: Improved Regret via Variance-Aware Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs
papers.abstract: We study episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards and achieve regret with leading term $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$. Here $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the total number of states across decision layers, $A$ the number of actions, and $K$ the number of episodes. This improves the two incomparable prior leading terms by factors $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$, leaving a factor $\sqrt H$ to the lower-bound scale. We give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for \emph{downstream-dependent} algorithms, whose policy at step $h$ is computed only from information at steps $h+1$ and onward. This reduces the remaining leading-order gap to finding a downstream-dependent known-dynamics algorithm with $\widetilde O(H\sqrt K)$ regret, which would yield the tight $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ leading term for unknown dynamics. We instantiate the reduction with VOPO, a policy optimization (PO) algorithm. Its improved guarantees follow from a variance-aware analysis enabled by a novel bonus, which we call the Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB). VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ regret under known dynamics with full information; its $\sqrt H$ gap to the target $H\sqrt K$ rate is inherited by our unknown-dynamics guarantee. We also show that with known dynamics and trajectory bandit feedback, VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ regret. Both known-dynamics guarantees improve the corresponding state-of-the-art PO bounds by a factor $\sqrt H$. A matching lower bound establishes that the full-information rate is tight in one parameter regime.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for k-Median++ and Improved Bounds for k-Means++
papers.abstract:
The popular $k$-means++ algorithm, or $D^\ell$-sampling, is a fundamental primitive in both the theory and practice of clustering. In the bi-criteria setting, the algorithm samples $k+\Delta$ centers ($\Delta\ge0$), and its cost is compared with the optimum using $k$ centers. Despite extensive study over the past two decades, its exact approximation ratio and tight bi-criteria guarantees remain unknown.
  We give a unified analysis for every distance exponent $\ell>0$, every $k\ge1$, and every $\Delta\ge0$. For metric $k$-median, our bounds are tight for all $k$ and $\Delta$. Without extra centers, the exact approximation ratio is $2(1+H_{k-1})$ (also in Euclidean space), improving the previous upper bound by a factor of $2$ ($H_j$ denotes the $j$th harmonic number). This tight analysis reveals that even one extra center improves the approximation ratio by an additive $\Theta(\log\log k)$, whereas previous bounds show no improvement.
  For every $\ell>0$, our analysis gives upper bounds with the same dependence on $k$ and $\Delta$ as our tight bound for metric $k$-median, with leading constants depending only on $\ell$ and whether the metric is Euclidean. Beyond the improved dependence on $\Delta$, our leading constants are smaller than those in previous analyses. In particular, for the widely used Euclidean $k$-means objective, our upper bound without extra centers is $(1+\varphi)(1+H_{k-1})$, where $\varphi\approx1.618$ is the golden ratio, improving upon the previous constant of $5$. With oversampling, a constant fraction of extra centers is known to provide a constant-factor approximation. For example, with $10\%$ extra centers, our guarantee is $5.7$, compared with the best previous guarantee of $25.9$.

papers.title: Extrinsic Representation of the Partial Ricci Flow
papers.abstract: The partial Ricci flow (PRF) modifies the Riemannian metric on a foliation on a distribution orthogonal to the leaves. In this work we develop extrinsic representations of PRF on geodesic foliations (twisted/warped products, weak K-contact and weak \b{eta}-Kenmotsu manifolds) and analyze model cases where PRF admits closed-form solutions. Using the convergence of PRF on model cases, we construct its extrinsic representations initialized by rotational hypersurfaces in Euclidean space as well as parallel curved surfaces and ellipsoids. The extrinsic viewpoint for PRF provides new tools for studying curvature-driven dynamics on foliations, with potential applications to calculus of moving surfaces and mathematical physics.

papers.title: LightTAR: Light and Fast Target-Aware Representations for Multimodal Tabular Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce LightTAR, a simple, inexpensive method that adapts dimensionality reduction to the prediction task. LightTAR augments the standard PCA representation with a few target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS). We evaluate LightTAR with 21 tabular models, including tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models. LightTAR improves average predictive performance for all models and, averaged across models, improves prediction on almost every MulTaBench dataset. These gains come with a small increase in total runtime relative to PCA representations. LightTAR integrates directly into existing encoding pipelines, improving tabular learners' predictive performance without modifying the encoder or the learner.

papers.title: Separability defects in artificial satellite theory: intermediaries, zonal harmonics and secular separatrices
papers.abstract: A five-input Poisson-bracket operator, which reproduces the Levi-Civita separability expressions and is cubic in the Hamiltonian, is used as a diagnostic of artificial satellite theory, in a modified polar-nodal chart regular at prograde equatorial orbits. For the general intermediary proposed by the author in 2020, covering those of Sterne, Garfinkel, Brouwer, Aksnes, Cid and Lahulla and Deprit, the linearised defects vanish if and only if the integrability ansatz holds, the condition for additive first-order Hamilton-Jacobi separation in polar-nodal variables. Second-order defects follow in closed form, and the coupling with the nodal pair comes from the dependence on the physical latitude, shared by the zonal term, Aksnes's intermediary and the originals of Sterne and Garfinkel. For every axisymmetric field the radial defect is linear, with a torque form, and the first-order zonal defect is the operator response to the first-order Lie generator, which also gives the second-order mean radial defect per revolution. In its gauge the long-period second-order average is common to intermediaries without latitude terms. Oblate structures with a displaced centre separate the zonal field exactly if and only if its coefficients satisfy the recurrence of Vinti's translated spheroidal potential, and along orbits propagated over 300 periods in the field truncated at $J_4$ they conserve the approximate third integral better than the centred structure, by median factors of 23 to 77. On secular separatrices the integrated defect is the derivative of the Melnikov function, tested in the eccentric Kozai-Lidov problem, and transverse zero sets of the operator define event surfaces.

papers.title: Small Is Not Dead: Distance-Aware Cluster Revival for e-means
papers.abstract: e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) is a recent mini-batch k-means algorithm, now part of the FAISS library, that reaches the error of Lloyd's algorithm about an order of magnitude faster on large embedding datasets. Every five mini-batches, it removes every cluster whose running point count falls below a tenth of the average and reuses its centre to split a large cluster. In the authors' ablation, removing this mechanism, called dead-cluster revival, raises the error more than removing any other component added to the moving-average update. The rule, however, considers only cluster size: it cannot distinguish a cluster that is small because it is redundant from one that covers a rare, isolated group of points, and on data with such groups it repeatedly removes centres whose removal is costly. We add a second condition, based on the distance between centres: a small cluster is removed only if its centre is close to another centre, relative to a running estimate of the mean squared error. When a centre equals the mean of its points, this squared distance is an upper bound on the average increase in squared error, per point of the cluster, caused by removing the centre. The condition costs one nearest-centre search for the small clusters every five mini-batches and adds no measurable running time. On the e-means paper's embedding benchmarks, it never prevents a removal, so the results are identical to those of FAISS. On datasets with small isolated groups not used during development, it reduces the test error after two epochs by roughly 10% to 80% relative to count-based revival, and it preserves the advantage of k-means++ initialization; on the other evaluation datasets, it stays within about 1% of the better of revival enabled and disabled. We also report two failure modes that the analysis predicts. This is a CPU proof of concept; GPU implementations are left to future work.

papers.title: Performance and Stability Studies of GEM Detectors for High Energy Physics Applications
papers.abstract: R\&D on different gas-filled detectors such as Gas Electron Multipliers (GEMs), Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) and straw tubes has been carried out in the detector laboratory of Bose Institute for more than a decade, keeping in mind present and future high-energy physics experiments. In this article, performance studies of a single-mask triple-GEM detector using a $^{55}$Fe X-ray source with an Ar/CO$_2$ (70/30) gas mixture are described. The study focuses mainly on the gain, energy resolution, count rate, and stability of the chamber under long-term irradiation. The experimental setup, methodology, and analysis results are presented.

authors.name: S. Mandal
authors.institution: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Mohali

papers.title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.

papers.title: LECAT: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data
papers.abstract: Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM's Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of "knowledge expression". We first assess open-source pretrained models using 199 curated category-feature pairs and analyze their training data. Our findings suggest that strengthening context and category-feature co-occurrence likelihood (PMI) improve learning for larger models and verbatim rule-like statements diminish flexible category learning. To systematically isolate these effects, we then train a 68M model from scratch with precise control over the categorical information each sees in their training data, confirming that verbatim repetition reduces flexible learning but mixture of diverse knowledge expressions lead to more robust category learning. Together, our findings highlight that while contextual flexibility is persistently difficult for models, how category knowledge is expressed in pretraining greatly impacts models' acquisition of robust category knowledge.

papers.title: Quantum melting and Pomeranchuk effect of zero-field Wigner solids
papers.abstract: Wigner solids and crystals are many-body phases of matter in which repulsive interactions between the charge carriers cause them to freeze into a solid. How Wigner solids compete or cooperate with integer and fractional quantum Hall liquids has been a long-standing open question. Here, we investigate this question for zero-field, electron and hole Wigner solids in cadmium arsenide quantum wells. In the low temperature limit, our results are consistent with a recent theoretical model [A. P. Reddy and L. Fu, Phys. Rev. B 113, L161403 (2026)] that proposes that the quantum Hall liquid can become energetically favored over the solid at low integer filling factors. Going beyond the low-temperature limit, we observe a re-entrant solid that emerges from the quantum Hall liquid. We explain this observation by considering the role of spin entropy, in close analogy with the zero-field Pomeranchuk effect, but appearing here at finite fields. The competition between quantum Hall liquids and Wigner solids is thus governed by both energy and entropy terms, giving rise to rich phase stability diagrams that result from the interplay between topology and correlations.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning for 2D XRD Interpretation Using Simulated and Experimental Data
papers.abstract: Autonomous experimentation systems require characterization models that can interpret heterogeneous measurements and maintain predictive performance as data accumulate. Developing such models involves addressing domain mismatch between data sources, overconfident predictions on unfamiliar inputs, and catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates. In this work, we present a proof-of-concept framework for uncertainty-aware continual interpretation of two-dimensional X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. The framework integrates established components: maximum mean discrepancy-based domain adaptation to reduce simulation-to-experiment discrepancies, a convolutional neural network with a spectral-normalized neural Gaussian process (CNN--SNGP) for predictive uncertainty estimation, and replay with knowledge distillation for sequential model updating. We evaluate the framework using simulated and previously-collected experimental data for crystal structure classification of single-phase body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed patterns. Data are organized into predefined sequential blocks to assess adaptation and retention of previously learned knowledge. Within this setting, the results show accurate classification across simulated and experimental data, improved alignment between the two domains, and reduced forgetting compared with na\"ive fine-tuning. Predictive uncertainty is also evaluated on unfamiliar and noisy inputs. The contribution is the integration and evaluation of these capabilities for sequential XRD interpretation. The framework provides a basis for future integration into autonomous experimentation systems, with experimental planning, instrument control, and closed-loop deployment remaining areas for future development.
