papers.title: Narrow-Band Magnetism Allowed by Quantum Geometry: Altermagnetism and Beyond
papers.abstract: Quantum geometry plays a central role in shaping correlated phases in narrow bands, yet its influence on the competition between distinct magnetic orders, especially the emergence of altermagnetism, remains largely unexplored. To address this question, we study the quadrupole insulator model with strictly onsite generalized Hubbard-Kanamori interactions, in which both N\'eel antiferromagnetism and altermagnetism are symmetry-permitted. Depending on the parameters, the isolated narrow lowest band of the model can either be obstructed atomic with strong quantum geometry or trivial atomic with weak quantum geometry, while the dispersion is identical in the two cases. By partially filling the lowest band, our Hartree-Fock calculations show only conventional ferromagnetic phases for the weak quantum geometric case, while we find two collinear altermagnetic phases, as well as nematic phases, for the strong quantum geometric case. Such a dramatic difference can be understood by the distinct characters of the projected interaction: the projected interactions acquire sizable longer-range channels only for the strong quantum geometric case, while they are dominated by the on-site Hubbard channel in the weak quantum geometric case. These results establish the essential role of quantum geometry for altermagnetism to emerge from interacting narrow bands where crystalline symmetries cannot sufficiently constrain the magnetic order.

papers.title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must satisfy two objectives simultaneously: completing the user's task (utility) and conforming to domain policies and correctness constraints (safety). These objectives are in tension -- blocking an unsafe action prevents a violation but can leave the agent stranded with no principled way to recover. Existing approaches sacrifice one objective for the other. We introduce Soteria, a framework that reconciles safety and utility through verified hierarchical planning and runtime enforcement of specifications. Before execution, the agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against the specifications prior to any tool invocation. During execution, the verified plan serves dual roles: it ensures that the agent takes specification-conformant trajectories and provides guidance when unsafe actions are blocked. Across multiple benchmarks covering a diverse range of tool-use tasks, Soteria achieves 1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines, with no violations of policy specifications, demonstrating that safety and utility need not be traded off.

papers.title: Tractable Importance Sampling for Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting
papers.abstract: Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability ($\delta$) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small $\delta$ associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor $\alpha > 1$. We prove a closed-form bound $B(\alpha) < 1$ on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that $B$ is log-convex so that the optimal $\alpha$ is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of $1/B(\alpha^*)$.

papers.title: Classification with Large-Step Gradient Descent: Unifying Self-Stabilization and Convergence Rates
papers.abstract: Neural networks are often trained with gradient descent (GD) using step sizes that exceed classical stability thresholds, a regime where standard convergence theory no longer applies. Despite exhibiting non-monotonic loss and oscillatory dynamics, this regime frequently leads to faster convergence and better generalization. Existing theoretical perspectives offer complementary but incomplete insights: one identifies a self-stabilization mechanism that drives GD toward flat regions but does not yield convergence rates; another derives rigorous rates for specific losses but does not explain the underlying stabilization mechanism; and a third unifies these views for overparameterized least squares, but relies on the existence of a minimizer manifold, which is absent in classification settings. In this work, we extend this unified geometric perspective to exponential-tail losses, including logistic and cross-entropy losses in separable linear classification, where the loss infimum is not attained at any finite parameter. We identify a curvature-defined reference subspace that replaces the role of the minimizer manifold, yielding a coupled dynamical system in which orthogonal oscillations are damped by parallel progress along directions of decreasing sharpness. Under regularity conditions, which we verify for logistic and multiclass cross-entropy losses on symmetric data models, we derive explicit bounds for the iterates, not just the loss, covering both the unstable and stable regimes, and revealing a three-phase damping structure in the latter. Our analysis further uncovers a transient implicit bias induced by large step sizes: although GD converges asymptotically to the max-margin direction, large steps can leave persistent orthogonal residuals and, in certain geometries, amplify them, affecting finite-time alignment with the max-margin direction.

papers.title: On the Utility of Pre-Trained Visual Representations for Policy Learning of Contact-Rich Insertion Tasks
papers.abstract: Visuomotor imitation learning has become a predominant paradigm for real-world robotic manipulation, yet it remains data-inefficient and brittle to task-irrelevant visual shifts. Pre-trained visual representations promise to ease this burden by distilling priors from internet-scale data, but the ``right'' representation for robotics remains unresolved: existing studies span broad but sparse task distributions and reach conclusions that vary and even conflict, pointing to strong task and setting dependence. We examine this question by bringing a magnifying glass to a common contact-rich manipulation task: insertion. We compare representations from widely used vision foundation models against an explicit contact-centric representation on two closely related insertion tasks, perturb each along controlled axes of occlusion and physical tolerance, and test whether conclusions transfer to the real world. Task dependence proves to be more subtle than previous, broadly scoped evaluations revealed: the best representation differs even between our near-identical tasks, and small changes shift trends in unpredictable ways. Despite this variability, results across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the distinct value of spatially-grounded, and in particular, contact-centric information for contact-rich policy learning, while underscoring how difficult it is to estimate such cues reliably under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise. We hope these findings motivate further study of representations in contact-rich manipulation, along with advances in contact perception and its integration into visuomotor policy learning.

papers.title: Global generation of coinvariant vector bundles on $\overline{\mathrm{M}}_{0,n}$
papers.abstract: Using fusion closed-ness and strong generation properties, we identify collections of modules over vertex operator algebras (VOAs) whose induced vector bundles of coinvariants on the moduli space $\overline{\mathrm M}_{0,n}$ of stable $n$-pointed curves of genus zero are globally generated. These results specialize to \cite{Fak12} for affine VOAs at positive integer levels, and of \cite{DG23} for strongly rational VOAs that are generated in degree 1. To illustrate the results, and to show that fusion-closedness is essential, we give numerous examples, including Lattice VOAs, Simple Current Extensions of Affine VOAs, and various tensor products.

papers.title: Inferring Sensitive Events in Multi-Mode Cyber-Physical Systems via Scheduling Side Channels
papers.abstract: Many cyber-physical systems (CPS) are multi-mode: they switch between operating modes with different tasksets and timing parameters in response to physical events or user activity. We show that these mode changes create a timing side channel: by altering the interference experienced by co-running tasks, they let an unprivileged co-resident observer infer sensitive events, such as a homeowner's arrival or a vehicle's route, from its own execution timing and, on multicore platforms, its core assignment. Existing schedule-based attacks and defenses miss this channel because they assume single-mode systems or target a specific, known victim task. We present STAMP, a lightweight attack that needs no knowledge of task parameters or scheduling policy, and works whether or not the system exposes its modes. On a ZoneMinder home-security deployment, STAMP identifies the modes with 94.7% accuracy on unseen hardware, using under 0.5% of one core. On ROS 2 AMCL with the Oxford RobotCar dataset, it identifies which of seven route segments a vehicle traversed with 86.0% accuracy on unseen platforms. A schedule-randomization defense lowers detection recall to 0.53, at which setting only 53.9% as many jobs finish on time. At higher noise ($\epsilon=10$), on-time job completion reduces to 14.4%, while introducing new leakage in 14.1% of the tasksets.

papers.title: Elasticy: A Runtime-Reconfigurable Architecture for Dynamic Streams
papers.abstract:
Reconfigurable Dataflow Accelerators (RDAs) have demonstrated high performance and energy efficiency for dense, regular tensor applications. However, conventional RDAs with static configurations show dramatically reduced performance and efficiency on irregular tensor workloads with data-dependent, non-uniform, dynamic tensor shapes. We propose Elasticy, a dynamically reconfigurable dataflow accelerator that employs streaming and tile abstractions to minimize the overhead of dynamic support. By encoding dynamic shapes into streams using rank-variable expressions, Elasticy exploits data-dependent tensor shape dynamism to minimize off-chip data traffic and wasted compute cycles. Elasticy employs stream-embedded reconfiguration information to trigger fine-grained runtime scheduling decisions. Elasticy also introduces a novel distributed linked streaming memory (DLSM) that more effectively uses on-chip memory to minimize off-chip data traffic and support dynamically sized tensors.
  Both reconfiguration and shape dynamism incur minimal overhead in Elasticy: reconfiguration occurs infrequently at the granularity of a stream of tiles, while rank-variable expressions enable lightweight handling of dynamic dimensions. On a Llama 3-8B decode layer, Elasticy achieves 92.6% of its roofline performance, compared to 69.7% on an H100. On evaluated GEMMs, the DLSM reduces total off-chip traffic by up to 61.4% relative to the best evaluated cache configuration, with no additional burden of programmer-managed memory. Elasticy's distributed runtime scheduler overlaps dependent kernels, speeding up kernel pairs by up to 1.42x. Programs can also run in both space and time: each phase of a layer's graph is pipelined spatially, while phases fold onto the same fabric over time. Compared to a traditional spatial accelerator, Elasticy achieves a 6.34x-31.67x improved area delay product on full layers.

papers.title: Searching for magnetic field changes in the central compact object 1E 1207.4-5209 in two decades of X-ray spectra
papers.abstract: The central compact object (CCO) 1E 1207.4-5209 is remarkable in that its X-ray spectrum shows clear absorption features at ~0.7 and 1.4 keV. Attributing these features to electron cyclotron resonance, the implied surface magnetic field is B~(7-8)x10^10 G, which agrees approximately with the field inferred from the spin properties of the pulsar. Here we examine all XMM-Newton EPIC pn spectra from more than 30 observations of 1E 1207.4-5209 from 2001-2020. We model the rotation phase-averaged and phase-resolved spectra with a two blackbody and multiple absorption line model, focusing on potential changes in the absorption lines which would correspond to changes in the magnetic field that could be related to the pulsar's possible spin glitch in 2015 and recent detection in radio. We find the phase-averaged spectral parameters, and by implication the magnetic field, are constant across nearly 20 years of data, while some parameters characterizing the phase-resolved spectra vary with rotation phase. The spectral line energies and widths (e.g., E_1~0.66 keV and full width of 0.34 keV) imply the magnetic field distribution across the X-ray emitting regions spans the range B~(6-11)x10^10 G, with the highest fields being visible during the declining phase of the pulsations of 1E 1207.4-5209.

papers.title: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
papers.abstract: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.

papers.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.

papers.title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals
papers.abstract: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.

papers.title: Reasoning Models Confabulate to Defend Injected Beliefs About Their Own Requests
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring and self-report are proposed as levers for AI oversight, on the assumption that a model's account of what it is doing is anchored to what it was asked. We show this anchor can be cut. An activation edit invisible in the prompt text, the injected forming-trace of an off-topic concept, overwrites a reasoning model's belief about its own request: across six models spanning scale, architecture, and recipe, the injected topic becomes the task it reasons about, reports back, and answers: the forced quote-back returns the injected topic in 47 of 48 model-concept cells, and on the four models with clean final haiku the injected answer follows in 99% of generations. Warnings barely move it: even one naming the true topic yields under 5% true-topic answers. Handed the truth in clean tokens, the model confabulates a story about the user ("maybe they got confused and corrected themselves") and answers with the injection anyway, its behavior and chain-of-thought corrupted together: a concrete limit on CoT monitorability. Opening the model up offers no reprieve: it attends to the true request even harder after edits, yet that attention is causally inert, and the injected content rides intact task circuits, so attention maps and circuit attributions read as on-task too; the same edit redirects the request's language and format, not only its topic. What the injection reaches is the model's reference to its own input; what it elicits is its defense of it.

papers.title: Right Token, Right Time: From Per-Token Gating to Trajectory-Aware Activation Steering
papers.abstract: Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning. Yet, standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, displacing representations from the distribution the model was trained on and eroding generation quality. We show that \emph{when} along a generation the intervention is applied is a decisive axis of control. We cast steering as a per-token allocation problem under a fixed budget of steerable tokens, so that methods differ only in which tokens they select, making allocation the sole variable. Within this framework we introduce two gates. The first, Contrastive Feature Projection (CFP), is memoryless and selects the tokens least aligned with the target behavior through a sparse, interpretable feature projection. The second, Closed-Loop Adaptive Bernoulli Steering (CLABS), is trajectory aware. It treats allocation as closed-loop feedback control, tracking the alignment a generation has accumulated so far and spending budget where the trajectory falls behind. On a linear steering-response model we derive an explicit gain region that guarantees closed-loop stability of CLABS and show that its integral term reduces the steady-state tracking offset. Empirically, CFP and CLABS achieve the largest behavioral shift among budgeted gates at matched budgets, with CLABS strongest under the tight budgets where allocation matters most, while best preserving fluency.

papers.title: MMFlash: Faster Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens for parallel verification by a target model. Diffusion drafters such as DFlash propose an entire token block in a single forward pass, but mainly focus on text-only tasks, leaving multimodal drafting underexplored. To study this setting, we first introduce a metric of token-level visual dependence based on the KL divergence between next-token distributions with and without visual input. We find that acceptance rates decrease from 46% in the lowest visual-dependence quartile to 22% in the highest, with this disparity persisting after multimodal training. Motivated by this observation, we propose MMFlash, a simple and effective framework that adaptively upweights visually dependent tokens that the drafter predicts poorly. For long video inputs, MMFlash further employs sparse attention to reduce redundant attention computation and improve drafting quality. Across various multimodal benchmarks, MMFlash achieves lossless decoding speedups of up to $3.58\times$, outperforming EAGLE-3 and DFlash by up to 195.4% and 17.1%, respectively.

papers.title: CARVE: A glycan-specific framework for assessing protein-glycan binding-pose quality
papers.abstract: Protein-glycan interactions depend on the precise three-dimensional arrangement of carbohydrates at protein-binding interfaces, yet reliable assessment of predicted complex structures remains challenging. Existing evaluations commonly rely on fixed root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) thresholds, which do not fully account for the structural diversity and conformational flexibility of glycans. Here we developed CARVE, a glycan-specific framework for evaluating protein-glycan structure predictions. Through topology-aware glycan parsing, CARVE integrates orientation RMSD (oRMSD), interface-ring RMSD (irRMSD) and the fraction of native contacts (Fnat) to assess glycan scaffold geometry, interface-ring placement and native-contact recovery. These descriptors define four quality categories (CARVE-Level) with geometric thresholds that scale with the degree of polymerization (DP), and a continuous CARVE-Score, which reproduced those categories on 25,068 independently generated poses without recalibration (macro-F1 = 0.892). Pairing these measures with glycan-specific topological, chemical and geometric validity checks, we benchmarked nine prediction methods on CARVE-Bench, comprising 1,974 experimentally determined protein-glycan complexes. Among the top 25 predictions per target, HADDOCK3 achieved the highest Acceptable-level success rate (47.0%), whereas no method produced a high-quality, structurally valid pose for more than one in five. Collectively, CARVE provides a standardized basis for assessing protein-glycan structure prediction methods and guiding the development of more accurate docking and co-folding approaches.

authors.name: Yu Kang
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: A Helly theorem for the Bruhat-Tits building
papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a discretely valued field with valuation ring $\mathcal{O}$. We show that a finite family of $\mathcal{O}$-lattices in $K^m$ is adapted to a common basis if any subfamily of at most $m+1$ $\mathcal{O}$-lattices is. In other words, in the Bruhat-Tits building of $\operatorname{GL}(m)$, a finite family of simplices lies in a common apartment if and only if any subfamily of at most $m+1$ simplices does. The proof uses a version of Radon's theorem for $\mathcal{O}$-lattices. We also give an alternative proof using truncated modules.

papers.title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models
papers.abstract: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.

papers.title: Movable Antenna-Aided ISAC: A Time- and Frequency-Division Framework
papers.abstract: This paper investigates movable-antenna (MA)-enhanced integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) under time division duplex (TDD) and frequency division duplex (FDD) protocols, where sensing and communications occupy orthogonal time and frequency resources, respectively. A wideband target-position Cram\'er-Rao bound (CRB) is derived under a pulse-radar framework with pulse compression, incorporating delay and angle estimation error bounds in Cartesian coordinates. Both bounds depend on sensing power; the delay bound also depends on sensing bandwidth, while the angle bound depends on the effective aperture determined by the antenna position vector (APV). A worst-case position CRB over a prescribed target region ensures robust sensing performance. For multiuser downlink communication, joint APV and resource-allocation problems are formulated for TDD and FDD to maximize the minimum achievable user rate subject to the sensing requirement. An alternating optimization algorithm is developed for FDD, while TDD is addressed by searching over feasible sensing pulse numbers combined with APV optimization. Representative scenarios clarify how MA improves channel orthogonality and enlarges the sensing aperture, and how these effects shape the TDD/FDD rate comparison. Numerical results show that APV optimization enlarges the communication-sensing tradeoff region over fixed-position antenna benchmarks. The optimized configurations exhibit distinct tendencies: TDD favors a larger antenna position variance, whereas FDD favors better channel orthogonality among users.

authors.name: Haocheng Hua
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Efficient Reconfiguration of Independent Transversals
papers.abstract: We study the reconfiguration of independent transversals in graphs with a prescribed vertex partition. Given a graph $G$ with a vertex partition $\mathcal{V}=(V_1,\ldots,V_m)$, an independent transversal is an independent set containing exactly one vertex from each part $V_i$ of $\mathcal{V}$. The reconfiguration problem concerns transforming one independent transversal into another through a sequence of local changes, while preserving the independent transversal property at every step. For any fixed $r\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\epsilon>0$, we present a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an $r$-claw-free graph $G$ with a vertex partition $\mathcal{V}=(V_1,\ldots,V_m)$ and two independent transversals $S$ and $R$, either finds a polynomial-length reconfiguration path between $S$ and $R$, or identifies a nonempty set of partition classes $\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{V}$ such that the subgraph induced by their union admits a strong dominating set of size at most $(2+\epsilon)|\mathcal{B}|$. Our result provides an algorithmic counterpart to recent connectivity results for the reconfiguration graph of all independent transversals, and establishes polynomial bounds on its diameter under suitable conditions. As a specific application, we obtain a polynomial-time algorithm for reconfiguring perfect matchings in $r$-uniform bipartite hypergraphs $H=(A,B,E)$, that either produces a polynomial-length reconfiguration path between two given perfect matchings or identifies a subset $S\subseteq A$ whose link hypergraph $E_S$ in $B$ has a small cover.

papers.title: Parameterized Approximation for Minimizing Uncovered Elements and Unsatisfied Constraints
papers.abstract:
Min-UnCoverage asks for at most $k$ sets minimizing uncovered weight. Min-Unsat SAT and Min-Unsat CSP ask for an assignment with at most $k$ true variables minimizing the weight of unsatisfied clauses or constraints.
  For constraints of arity at most $d$, we give a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Min-Unsat CSP in $(dk/\varepsilon)^{O(k)}N^{O(1)}$ time, where $N$ is the input size. This also gives approximation schemes for bounded-arity SAT and coverage with bounded element frequency. We show that weighted coverage with set size at most $d$ can be solved exactly in $2^{O(kd)}N^{O(1)}$ time by adapting color-coding. For coverage on incidence graphs of bounded semi-ladder index, we give a deterministic parameterized approximation scheme .
  We show that, unless $\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]$, SAT and CSP have no finite-factor FPT approximation parameterized by $k+d$ when variable frequency is at most $d$, or on $K_{3,3}$-free incidence graphs of semi-ladder index at most four. Known Hitting Set hardness gives the same lower bound for all three problems at VC dimension two.
  Under the same assumption, we show that no computable relaxation $g(k,d)\geq k$ allows an FPT algorithm to preserve a prescribed unsatisfied-weight target for SAT or CSP, already for arity three and, separately, bounded variable frequency. For coverage, known algorithms preserve the target using at most $k+1$ sets on incidence graphs of bounded semi-ladder index.

papers.title: An Inverse-Designed Multilayer Selective Emitter for High-Efficiency Thermophotovoltaics
papers.abstract: High thermophotovoltaic (TPV) conversion efficiencies have typically relied on photovoltaic cells that reflect sub-bandgap radiation back toward the emitter. Here, we numerically investigate an alternative approach in which spectral selectivity is engineered primarily on the emitter side. We optimize an emitter consisting of 16-layer aperiodic MgO/Si coating on tungsten, for coupling to a GaSb cell with an antireflection coating and an Au mirror. A detailed-balance framework incorporates polarization- and angle-resolved emissivity, multiple reflections, and Auger nonradiative recombination. At an emitter temperature of 1500 K, the optimized structure suppresses 97.1% of the incident-blackbody-equivalent sub-bandgap power at the source; a further 1.9% is returned to the emitter by the cell, leaving 1.0% absorbed parasitically in the cell. The resulting modeled radiative-to-electrical conversion efficiency reaches 47.0%, compared with 30.8% for a SiC emitter paired with the same cell, while maintaining a comparable maximum electrical power density. These findings indicate that emitter-side spectral engineering could substantially relax cell-side photon-recycling requirements and provide significant improvement in TPV conversion.

papers.title: Inverse energy transfer for 2D Navier--Stokes near a self-similar vortex collapse
papers.abstract: We prove inverse energy transfer for the two-dimensional Navier--Stokes equations near a self-similar three-vortex collapse, confirming the 1979 prediction of Novikov and Sedov. Nonlinear interactions transfer kinetic energy from high to low frequencies over a common time interval that shrinks to the collapse time as the viscosity tends to zero. We prove that the net nonlinear transfer over this interval converges to the same positive constant across an expanding range of frequency cutoffs, with quantitative error bounds uniform in the cutoff.

papers.title: Mobile Edge Deployment and Resource Management for Maritime Wireless Networks
papers.abstract: Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) has been envisioned as one of the key technologies for supplying computation and storage resources in Internet of Vessels (IoV) networks. Due to its flexible deployment, low cost and agile maneuverability, Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) has emerged as a promising solution, to provide communication and computation services for maritime users. In this paper, we study mobile edge deployment and resource management for MEC-assisted maritime wireless networks where USVs with diverse computation resources are deployed to provide edge computing services that complement the cloud-based services. To this end, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the expected response time by jointly optimizing the deployment of mobile USVs and computation offloading decisions. To solve the mixed-integer nonlinear program problem, we propose a Dual-Layer Reinforcement Learning (DLRL) framework to attain a near-optimal solution. Specifically, a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm is designed to obtain the best USV deployment in the outer layer learning, and a Q-learning algorithm is designed to determine the best computation offloading decisions in the inner layer learning. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed solution outperforms some literature algorithms by effectively handling both continuous and discrete variables.

authors.name: Bin Lin

papers.title: Fuse-All MoE Inference Kernel with Load Balancing on TPUs
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip. Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode. Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16. With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.

papers.title: Envelope Model for GTEx Data
papers.abstract: This article studies the envelope model for enhanced gene expression analysis using GTEx data. The study compares this advanced statistical approach with standard multivariate linear regression, demonstrating improved capacity for identifying significant genes and enhanced estimation efficiency. By partitioning response variation into material and immaterial components, the envelope model reduces estimation noise, leading to stronger statistical signals and smaller standard errors. These findings, as demonstrated in our tissue-specific and gene-group anal- yses, show that the envelope model can pick up on important biological signals that traditional methods tend to miss. This makes it a useful tool for genomic studies and GTEx data analysis.

papers.title: Rank-One Ultralight Dark Matter Response in a Full-Tensor Gravity Gradiometer
papers.abstract: A full-tensor superconducting gravity gradiometer whose four test masses carry two compositions in a $2+2$ pattern acquires a composition-dependent channel for dilaton-coupled ultralight dark matter. The reconstructed response is the rank-one tensor $\K=\gv_\phi(t)\otimes\qv$, with the axis of $\qv$ fixed in advance by the material assignment, and obeys the parameter-free null condition $\K(\mathbf{I}-\Pq)=0$, which no gravity gradient or platform rotation alone can satisfy; it vanishes for a single composition. For copper and lead, the sensitivity reaches $d_{\hat m}-d_g\simeq3.4\times10^{-8}$, and $4.9\times10^{-10}$ with upgraded accelerometers.

papers.title: Composition-dependent ultralight dark matter detection with a tetrahedral superconducting gravity gradiometer
papers.abstract: Tetrahedral superconducting gravity gradiometers designed as full-tensor gravitational-wave detectors, such as the ground-based mSOGRO design and the proposed lunar LANGO observatory, reconstruct the acceleration-gradient tensor from four test masses. We show that giving the four test masses two compositions in a $2+2$ arrangement adds a composition-dependent ultralight dark matter (ULDM) channel to that same tensor readout, with no separate dark-matter sensor and no dark-matter-specific readout. A coherently oscillating scalar accelerates each mass in proportion to its dilaton charge, and the tensor reconstruction leaves the charges only in a mean, rejected with the common mode, and a single vector $\qv$ proportional to the charge contrast $\Delta\abaralpha_{AB}$ between the two materials. The response is the rank-one tensor $\K_{\ULDM}(t)=\gv_\phi(t)\otimes\qv$, whose amplitude is set by the halo, independent of $m_\phi$. The axis of $\qv$ is fixed in advance by the material assignment, so the response obeys the null condition $\K_{\ULDM}(\mathbf{I}-\Pq)=0$ at every instant, for any $\gv_\phi$ including a virialized field with a stochastic gradient---an exact tensor discriminator against gravitational-wave signals; for a single composition $\qv=0$. With the gravitational-wave noise model, the coupling sensitivity for copper and lead test masses reaches $d_{\hat m}-d_g\simeq3.4\times10^{-8}$ for the baseline instrument and $4.9\times10^{-10}$ with upgraded accelerometers. The rank-one factorization and the null condition are summarized in a companion Letter; the present paper gives the derivations and the detector-level analysis.

papers.title: Schreier Sets And the Product of Fibonacci And Catalan Numbers
papers.abstract: First, we introduce strictly super-Schreier sets, which provide a new combinatorial interpretation of products of Fibonacci and Catalan numbers. Second, we show that the numbers of sets in higher-order Schreier families do not satisfy any linear recurrence relation, thus answering a question in the existing literature.

papers.title: Active Learning of Temporal Specifications through Distinguishing Queries
papers.abstract: Temporal specifications are essential for verification and monitoring, yet writing formulas that capture the intended behaviour is difficult. Active learning derives such specifications through interaction between a learner and a teacher, but remains underexplored for temporal logics. Existing approaches require the teacher to answer equivalence queries and to construct counterexamples, and they often rely on SAT-based learning procedures that restart the search after each new example. We present an active-learning framework for LTLf in which the teacher only labels traces and answers natural-language questions about the intended behaviour. The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish candidates, and uses the teacher's hints to rank candidates or to restrict the search. We prove consistency with the observed examples, identification within bounded hypothesis classes with a bound on the number of queries, and a PAC guarantee for the final hypothesis. In experiments with a simulated teacher on 36 targets, including targets in four standard environments, the learner identifies every target when it compares all rivals, with fewer than seven queries beyond an initial sample of ten traces on average. Correct hints reduce the number of queries by up to 16% and the number of generated candidates by a fifth, and hints used for ranking never prevent identification, even when incorrect. Our enumeration-based version space is faster than the SAT-based approach of previous learners at every target size.

papers.title: MEM-SQL: Memory-Empowered Text-to-SQL
papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language questions into SQL queries over increasingly complex databases. However, widely used benchmarks evaluate questions independently, overlooking settings where earlier queries over the same database can supply joins or calculations for a new question. We introduce HARE (History-AwaRe Text-to-SQL BEnchmark) to measure the accuracy and cost of adapting historical SQL. HARE comprises 1,600 requests derived from a fixed pool of 823 verified queries across four datasets. Annotations record which components each request preserves and which edits it requires, distinguishing whole-query adaptation from partial reuse. Our method, MEM-SQL (Memory-EMpowered Text-to-SQL), stores whole-query templates, reusable SQL blocks, and mappings from domain concepts to schema elements. MEM-SQL uses a layer only if every requirement assigned to it has a match above that layer's threshold. With On-demand Schema Linking (OSL), MEM-SQL consults the schema only when no layer qualifies or the generator judges retrieved evidence insufficient. Across six language models on HARE, mean execution accuracy rises from 37.1% for Direct Generation without history to 50.0% for MEM-SQL, with 76.6% fewer input tokens and 68.8% lower latency on average. Further analysis shows that requests reusing several verified queries remain a bottleneck, with accuracy falling from 56.7% to 29.7%, most sharply when reused components must be placed in a new query structure or combined with a shared join. Applying OSL to three other memory designs consistently reduces generation cost, while its accuracy benefit depends on the memory design. Verified history can thus make generation both more accurate and cheaper, but its value depends on the evidence retained and when the system consults the schema.

papers.title: A Common Improved Bound for Asymmetric TSP and Path TSP
papers.abstract: We give polynomial-time $(R_*+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for asymmetric TSP and asymmetric path TSP, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, where $R_*=6+\sqrt2+\sqrt{15+6\sqrt2}\approx12.2604$. Both guarantees hold relative to the corresponding subtour relaxations, whose integrality ratios are therefore at most $R_*$. This improves the previous guarantees of below $14.7$ for asymmetric TSP and $15$ for asymmetric path TSP [Vygen, 2026]. Our algorithms strengthen subtour covers and recursive augmentation in the laminar framework [Svensson, Tarnawski, Vegh, JACM'20; Traub, Vygen, 2025]. The recursive analysis retains the paths through contracted regions and accounts jointly for their cost and the dual mass they visit. We also improve the reduction from asymmetric path TSP to vertebrate pairs [Traub, Vygen, 2025] by comparing two initial walks with complementary completion bounds. Applied to Vygen's existing vertebrate-pair algorithm, this reduction alone improves the path factor from $15$ to below $14.7$, matching his asymmetric TSP guarantee.

papers.title: The minimal excludant of $\ell$-regular overpartitions
papers.abstract: Andrews and Newman \cite{AN1} introduced the minimal excludant (mex) of an integer partition, and Aricheta and Donato \cite{AD} extended it to overpartitions. More recently, Meher \cite{Meher} and Tejash, Bhowmick and Meher \cite{TBM} studied the analogous statistic for $\ell$-regular partitions. In this article, for an integer $\ell\ge 2$, we define the minimal excludant $\omex_\ell(\pi)$ of an $\ell$-regular overpartition $\pi$ as the smallest positive integer that is not divisible by $\ell$ and does not occur as a non-overlined part of $\pi$. We study $\sm{\ell}(n)$, the sum of $\omex_\ell(\pi)$ over all $\ell$-regular overpartitions $\pi$ of $n$. We obtain generating functions for $\sm{\ell}(n)$ as eta-quotients for $\ell=2$ and $\ell=3$. Later, motivated from \cite{TBM}, we obtained explicit generating functions for $\sm{\ell}(n)$. We show that $\sm{\ell}(n)$ is weakly increasing in $n$, and we derive Hardy--Ramanujan type asymptotic formulas for $\sm{2}(n)$ and $\sm{3}(n)$. We then determine the parity of both functions completely: $\sm{2}(n)$ is even for every $n\ge 1$, while $\sm{3}(n)$ is odd if and only if $n=0$ or $n$ is a centred hexagonal number. Also, we obtain for every $\ell\ge3$, $\sm{\ell}(n)$ is odd for infinitely many $n$, and the number of such $n\le X$ is $\gg\sqrt{X}$. Finally, we establish congruences for these functions modulo $3$, $4$ and $8$.

papers.title: GIC model selection for high-dimensional CCA
papers.abstract: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) is a widely used statistical tool for exploring the dependence structure between two sets of variables. An important issue in CCA is determining the rank. Among information-based criteria for rank selection, the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) are two commonly used approaches. Both rely on the number of free parameters to quantify model complexity, which may not adequately account for the underlying dependence structure when the assumed model is misspecified. As a result, AIC and BIC may exhibit unsatisfactory performance, particularly when the remaining canonical correlations do not follow the assumed low-dimensional structure. To alleviate this difficulty, we adopt the idea of the generalized information criterion (GIC) to develop a data-adaptive measure of model complexity for CCA rank selection. The proposed complexity measure incorporates the magnitudes of the sample canonical correlations, thereby accounting for the spectral structure of the data and improving robustness to model misspecification. We investigate the asymptotic properties of the proposed GIC under a high-dimensional setting in which the sample size and both variable dimensions grow proportionally. Our theoretical analysis aims to characterize the conditions under which GIC can distinguish signal canonical correlations from noise and achieve more reliable rank selection than conventional information criteria.

authors.name: Hung Hung
authors.institution: United States Food and Drug Administration

papers.title: ParseBench-2: Severity-Aware Evaluation of Document Parsing
papers.abstract: Document-parsing metrics can give high scores to outputs that change important facts and penalize changes that preserve meaning. People can often judge these consequences more easily than they can design a metric to measure them. We introduce a method for developing parsing metrics from severity policies that specify how each error type should affect the score. We express these policies through test scenarios that specify how a metric should behave. We then optimize the metric implementations against these fixed expectations, using coding agents to refine comparison rules, error detectors and weights under human review. This makes stated human priorities an explicit objective of metric design. We apply this method in ParseBench-2, a comprehensive document-parsing benchmark that combines broad capability coverage with metrics calibrated to error severity. It covers 4,317 pages across six dimensions of parsing quality: text, formatting, tables, charts, visual grounding, and forms. We use detailed annotations and targeted difficult cases to check for changed facts, broken structural relationships, and missing content. We take the lower of a parsing score that measures content recovery and a severity cap that penalizes detected errors, so recovering most of a page cannot hide a serious error. Across six severity test suites, our metrics more closely match the expert judgments expressed by the scenario targets than existing metrics and penalize at most 3.4% of the tested benign variations. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation spanning frontier vision-language models, specialized document parsers and open-weight systems, comparing their overall rankings, performance across parsing capabilities and tradeoffs between accuracy and cost.

papers.title: Quantized resistance limitations for graphene p-n junction devices
papers.abstract: Developing high-resistance quantized Hall resistance standards requires accessing values beyond the robust value seen in epitaxial graphene (R_{\mathrm{H}}=\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{h}{e^{2}}). This study evaluates the available parameter space of the coefficient of effective resistance across various epitaxial graphene p-n junction topologies, including rectangular, Corbino, and triangular layouts. Because mapping desired resistances to device configurations is mathematically degenerate, an automated Landauer-B\"uttiker Python solver was developed for all three topologies and was validated by cryogenic multi-terminal transport measurements and LTspice simulations. By analyzing the Shannon entropy of available states, it is found that rectangular checkerboards maximize topological complexity and tunable outputs, whereas Corbino geometries exhibit highly constrained resistance availabilities.

papers.title: From Diagonal Coloring to Proper Vertex Labelings Distinguishing Adjacent Facial Sums
papers.abstract: In this paper we study proper vertex labelings of 3-connected plane graphs that give distinct boundary-vertex sums to faces sharing an edge. Let $\lambda(G)$ be the least $k$ for which labels from $\{0,\ldots,k\}$ suffice, and let $\laml(G)$ be its arbitrary-real-list counterpart. Our two main results are an eight-element list theorem for fullerenes and the universal bound $\lambda(G)\le708587$ for all 3-connected plane graphs. We establish structural nine- and eight-color bounds, classify triangulations whose vertices of degree at least five form an independent set, and determine their exact diagonal chromatic numbers. We also prove closure under triangular sums for $q\ge7$ diagonal colors, with an optimal uniform threshold. For cubic 3-connected plane graphs we obtain $\lambda\le14$, improving to $\lambda\le9$ in the bipartite case.

authors.name: Zhou Guofei
authors.institution: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

papers.title: Toward On-Device Markerless 6DoF Tracking of a Physical Manipulative on a Mixed-Reality Headset: A Preliminary Study
papers.abstract: AR-Classroom uses physical models and virtual overlays to help learners explore spatial transformations. To align these overlays on a standalone headset, we developed a markerless six-degree-of-freedom(6DoF) tracker for a LEGO airplane on the Meta Quest 3. A compact YOLO model trained on synthetic Unity renders predicts 20 keypoints from dynamic RGB crops resized to 128 by 128 pixels. A perspective-n-point solver estimates the airplane's pose from these predictions and the corresponding 3D landmarks. In a paired evaluation on 1,000 synthetic validation images, cropping guided by ground-truth boxes increased the detection rate on annotated images from 32.5 to 46.2 percent. Mean keypoint F1 increased from 42.9 to 44.6 percent, with lower keypoint precision in the cropped view. In preliminary headset tests, 2 Hz was the highest tested tracking target at which the application maintained approximately 72 frames per second. A headset demonstration illustrates virtual overlay alignment with the physical airplane before and after a manual rotation. Quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage will be measured in future work.

papers.title: Polarization of strongly lensed gravitational waves as a probe of the lens-induced orientations of electromagnetic counterparts
papers.abstract: Strong gravitational lensing is a well-established phenomenon in electromagnetic (EM) observations, where the lensed images and arcs are resolved on the two-dimensional sky and constrain the mass distribution of the lens. Strongly lensed gravitational waves (GWs) are also expected to be detected routinely by next-generation detectors, but their multiple images are recorded only as one-dimensional time series without positions. Among them, lensed binary neutron star mergers can be accompanied by EM counterparts with resolvable structures, such as relativistic jets. In EM lensing, the lens-induced change in the apparent orientation of such a structure can be measured only relative to other images or statistically, because its intrinsic orientation is not directly observable. In this work, we show that the GW polarization, which the lens leaves unchanged, provides this missing reference, i.e., a compass, so that the orientation offset of each image can be measured in absolute terms. We place this orientation layer on the EM image plane together with image positions from the lensed host arcs and Fermat-potential heights from GW time delays and magnifications. Using a mock population of such mergers observable by the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, we find that the predicted image positions and arrival times are calibrated once the detection selection is included. The lens-induced orientation offsets reach tens of degrees and are detectable in up to a third of the events, at viewing angles above about $40^\circ$ for quadrupole-dominated signals.

papers.title: In Situ Monitoring and Predictive Modeling of Harmful Algal Blooms with Autonomous Surface Vehicles
papers.abstract: Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs) pose significant environmental, economic, and public-health challenges in coastal and inland water bodies, creating a need for scalable methods to collect spatially distributed water-quality data. This paper presents an autonomous surface vessel-based sensing system for in-situ water-quality monitoring related to harmful algal bloom detection. The system integrates a BlueBoat Autonomous Surface Vessel (ASV), a motorized winch for depth-controlled sonde deployment, a multiparameter water-quality sonde, side-scan sonar, and an event-camera payload. Autonomous waypoint missions were used to collect measurements across selected sampling regions and multiple depths, enabling both horizontal and vertical characterization of environmental conditions. Field deployments were conducted in Lake Pontchartrain, Louisiana, with additional measurements collected in False River, Louisiana to increase dataset diversity. The collected measurements included algal pigment indicators, nutrient concentration, turbidity, temperature, and other water-quality parameters relevant to bloom formation. In addition, complementary sonar and event-camera data were collected during vehicle operation to provide contextual environmental information. A machine-learning classification approach was also evaluated using the collected water-quality measurements to support HAB and non-HAB classification. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using a modular ASV platform for repeatable, multi-modal water-quality data collection and support future development of autonomous monitoring systems.

papers.title: Box-conditional Hypothesis Testing for Out-of-Distribution Object Detection
papers.abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) objects is essential for ensuring the reliability and safety of object detectors in real-world deployment. We treat the decision on a detected box as a hypothesis test with the null hypothesis that the box covers an object of an in-distribution (ID) class. The null distribution changes with the size of the box and its contact with the image border, and the detector observes both. The test can therefore rank a box only against ID boxes of the same size and border contact, which gives a distribution-free bound on the false-alarm rate for each of them and uncovers the separation that one null distribution hides. The power of the test also rests on the layer it reads. Layers built only for the ID classes have no reason to keep what sets an unknown object apart, so the test reads the features before them. We propose \textbf{PLUM}, a training-free score that pools the last backbone stage inside the box and ranks its distance to the ID classes among ID boxes of the same size and border contact. On the standard benchmark, PLUM reaches the highest AUROC among the compared methods without external models, with 91.5 and 94.5 on PASCAL-VOC and 95.1 and 97.5 on BDD100K. Code: https://github.com/DDOZMI/PLUM

papers.title: The Gravitational Wave Foreground from Galactic Cataclysmic Variables in LISA
papers.abstract: Electromagnetic observations have been the primary medium for studying cataclysmic variable (CV) systems, capitalizing on the invaluable opportunity they present to study binary stellar evolution and accretion. The launch of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) mission, however, will enable a multi-messenger perspective of the population. We extend previous work to explore the gravitational wave (GW) spectra sourced by a local and Galactic population of CVs. Using the Bayesian LISA Inference Package (BLIP), we simulate LISA data containing these CV populations to understand their impact and our ability to jointly model CV and double white dwarf (DWD) GW spectra. While we find that a local CV population has negligible effect on the LISA datastream, a Galactic CV population will have a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 76, depending on the characteristics of the DWD population present, and will bias existing DWD spectral models if ignored. Current approaches struggle to accurately recover both populations' respective spectra, calling for the creation of multi-component spectral models that include GW contributions from both CVs and DWDs. These results point toward a promising future for the study of CVs with LISA.

papers.title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
papers.abstract: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. AI Safety as a discipline has largely focused on finding the bounds and vulnerabilities of AI models used in isolation. Yet as humans increasingly deploy these models as agents and multi-agent systems, the same attacks that had been thought to be patched when using a model in isolation can break these same models under specific circumstances. We show that these system breaks are not purely theoretical, but can break Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms. We show the attack by asking agents to answer questions from a store of files on disk in which we have planted a forged record. Searching the store themselves, the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials. However, if that same orchestrator model delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, which is what these harnesses are built to do, the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900. Thus, even when the system is driven by a strong model, the system's safety lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's. Simulations over 18 models show the same effect in the delivery channel where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials. The safety of real-world agentic systems that use strong orchestrator agents and weaker sub-agents, and multi-agent systems in general, is defined not by the safety of the strong agent but by the safety of the weakest agent.

papers.title: Homogeneous pursuit in $\beta$ model
papers.abstract: Data in forms of networks has been encountered in various prevalent fields at the arrival of big data era. To unveil and recover the true model with core units with numerous links, the $\beta$-model under sparsity constraint is proposed to meet the expectation of statisticians and engineers. Not only does this network model inherit spectacular property from the Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi model, but also exhibits degree heterogeneity through tuning sparsity parameter $s$. In this paper, we propose Homogeneous Pursuit (HP), an $\ell_0$-constrained maximum likelihood estimation method implemented through a primal-dual algorithm. To ease the harshness of computation, we find the surrogate function of the corresponding objective function to derive Majorization Minimization algorithm through the primal-dual process. Moreover, after meticulous evaluation, the algorithm brought about captures the property of fine convergence rate in a contraction mapping way. Under some mild conditions, the proposed generalized information criterion (GIC$^*$) for selecting the sparsity level is consistent to find the truth. Combining HP with GIC$^*$ gives the adaptive procedure HP-GIC$^*$; HP-BIC denotes the same estimation method with sparsity selected by BIC. Finally, simulation studies show that GIC$^*$ improves support recovery relative to BIC in the reported comparisons, while HP achieves lower computational cost while maintaining estimation accuracy comparable to the sparse benchmark methods. A microfinance application illustrates the use of HP-GIC$^*$ for studying the association between network prominence and participation, with improved fit in the reported village-level regressions.

authors.name: Canhong Wen
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
papers.abstract: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.

papers.intro:
Feed-forward multi-view transformers [38, 42, 39] reconstruct a scene from a set of photos in a single forward pass. Given unposed images, they predict where each camera was and where it pointed, a depth map for each image, and a 3D point for each pixel, which classic pipelines such as COLMAP [29] obtain by matching features and iterative optimisation. Their largest cost is global attention, in which every image patch attends to every patch of every other image, so the cost grows quadratically with the number of images. On a 12 GB GPU, the released code [39] (Official VGGT-Ω\Omega) runs out of memory at 100 images.

Their largest cost is global attention, in which every image patch attends to every patch of every other image, so the cost grows quadratically with the number of images. On a 12 GB GPU, the released code [39] (Official VGGT-Ω\Omega) runs out of memory at 100 images.

Existing accelerators for these models reuse techniques developed for large language models: computing attention only for selected blocks of tokens (block-sparse attention [37, 8]), merging similar tokens [31, 35, 41], letting some layers attend only within their own image [34], and computing attention in low precision [49, 13]. The first three assume that each token needs only a few other tokens, so the rest can be dropped or merged. On multi-view 3D models these methods either lose much accuracy or give little speed-up (Fig. 1b).

We study where the global attention of three such models goes and find that it is not sparse but structured. Building on the layer roles reported by AVGGT [34] and RegimeVGGT [46], we assign each global layer one of three regimes. In diffuse context layers, mostly early, each token spreads its attention almost evenly over all images, so the layer computes a scene-wide average. In selective matching layers, in the middle, each token concentrates its attention, but on evidence spread over many images. In reference anchoring layers, late in models that express their outputs in the first image’s coordinates, every token sends about half of its attention to that first image. We call them context, matching and anchoring layers. The regimes are stable across seven datasets and 10 to 200 images, and appear in different arrangements in VGGT-Ω\Omega, VGGT-1B [38] and π3\pi^{3} [42] (Fig. 1a). papers.title: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging
papers.abstract: Model merging constructs multi-task models without expensive joint training but often suffers from parameter interference. Some solutions mitigate this by constraining finetuning using data from the other tasks to be merged, violating the core independence and privacy assumption of model merging. Recent work offers preliminary empirical evidence that a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for such data, but leaves open when and why it suffices. To this end, we propose a \textit{Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization}, which characterizes the relationship between a proxy distribution and the distribution of other tasks to be merged through spectral coverage ($\alpha$) and leakage ($\beta$). Based on the framework, we derive a unified parameter interference bound: smaller $(\alpha, \beta)$ provably yields lower parameter interference through better spectral alignment. To exploit such a proxy, we augment the training objective with a proxy regularizer. Evaluating this regularizer during fine-tuning requires a concrete mechanism. We study three instantiations, including (J) an exact evaluation via Jacobian-vector products, (F) a frozen curvature approximation using the Fisher information matrix, and (O) an output-drift formulation that constrains the model's functional deviation on the proxy directly. We prove that all three coincide under the NTK linearization, where existing analyses of such regularizers stop, and go further to characterize standard non-linear fine-tuning, bounding how far each instantiation departs from its linearized reference and obtain a three-way hierarchy, zero for (J), proxy-independent for (F), and proxy-quality-scaling for (O). Empirical validation on the commonly used vision-language model CLIP confirms these theoretical predictions.

papers.title: Ergodicity without monotonicity: patch-positive spin systems
papers.abstract: Monotonicity is the standard tool for proving that an interacting particle system is ergodic. What can replace it when the system is not monotone and its invariant measure is unknown? The simplest such systems are kinetically constrained models such as FA-1f and East exposed to noise. In these models vacancies enable updates, so adding vacancies should help the system forget its initial state. We prove this for a broad class of spin systems, which we call patch-positive. If vacancies are created spontaneously at a uniformly positive rate, the system converges to the same equilibrium from a large class of initial states, and from every initial state if the threshold density is at most $\tfrac12$ or the interactions are oriented. In particular, the East model with noise is ergodic at every density, and we obtain new cases of the positive-rates conjecture. The key idea is to compare the dual processes of the system with and without the added deaths.

papers.title: Do Machines Learn Deviance From Their Peers? A Randomized Test of Differential Association With AI Agents
papers.abstract: Differential association theory and its extension, social learning theory, hold that rule-breaking, and the definitions that make it acceptable, are learned through interaction with others. Because people choose their friends, this claim has been hard to test. We addressed this selection problem with AI agents, which learn only through communication and can be assigned to peers at random. In a preregistered experiment, 420 teams of three agents (1,260 agents; seven AI models) worked on coding tasks that could not be solved honestly. A scripted teammate said that it had cheated (deviant peer), that it had reported the problem honestly (honest peer), or said nothing (silent peer). Half of the teams were told that an auditor read their chat. Compared with a silent peer, a deviant peer increased cheating (66.2% vs. 62.9%; OR = 1.96) and an honest peer reduced it (55.7%; OR = 0.35). Among agents that cheated, a deviant peer increased claims that cheating was normal (13.7% vs. 3.4%), often as the team's norm. Monitoring did not suppress prohibited discussion; it doubled it. Peers mattered only for models that had not yet decided. AI agents offer a new way to test criminological learning theories without selection effects.

papers.title: When Does Oversampling Help? A Decision Framework for Imbalanced Data Streams Under Label Delay and Concept Drift
papers.abstract: For imbalanced data streams with delayed labels, is it worth adding a streaming oversampler, or does continuous re-evaluation of earlier predictions already recover the cost of the delay? We address this through an extensive experimental comparison of streaming oversampling and continuous re-evaluation under joint class imbalance, concept drift, and label delay. Streaming oversamplers are typically evaluated under the test-then-train assumption of immediate labels; their behaviour under these conditions, assessed through re-evaluation, has not been systematically studied. We close this gap with a decision framework that predicts when oversampling adds value over re-evaluation, organised around three axes: drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window, and operationalised as a competition between a recovery channel (re-evaluation) and a minority-coverage channel (oversampling). Evaluating $15$ classifiers on $6$ synthetic and $6$ real streams, we find: re-evaluation recovers delay-induced loss on drift-active streams but is silent on stationary ones; oversampling's marginal contribution over re-evaluation is statistically detectable in only one real-data configuration; and cost--performance Pareto recommendations from synthetic streams do not transfer to real data, where fronts partition by drift regime. Method selection should therefore be conditioned on the stream's profile and re-estimated as it evolves, not inherited from synthetic benchmarks.

papers.title: PRISM: A Post-Prediction Reliability Framework for Evidence-Guided Correction and Selective Abstention
papers.abstract:
A model may produce a prediction with high confidence and still get the outcome wrong. This is a challenge in sequential applications, where the system evolves over time and deployment data may differ from the data used during training. To address this issue, we propose PRISM (Prediction Reliability and Intelligent Self-Correction Mechanism), a framework that evaluates prediction reliability after the initial output is generated. It estimates the risk of error and examines predictions identified as potentially unreliable. For these cases, PRISM analyses available signals, retrieves similar situations from historical data, and verifies whether an alternative prediction is supported by the evidence. It can then retain the original prediction, apply a verified correction, or abstain when the evidence is insufficient.
  We evaluate PRISM on second-innings match prediction in the Indian Premier League (IPL). Ball-by-ball records are converted into over-level observations to capture changes in match conditions throughout an innings. To preserve temporal order, earlier IPL seasons are used for training, IPL 2024 for validation, and IPL 2025-2026 for out-of-time testing. The dataset contains 8,665 over-level observations from 475 matches, with the test partition comprising 2,568 observations from 142 matches. In one experimental record, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and HistGradientBoosting achieve accuracies of 65.2%, 68.4%, and 70.2%, respectively. The corresponding PRISM evaluation reports a selective accuracy of 82.4% at 88.5% coverage, with a Brier score of 0.126 and an expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.019.

papers.title: iGRAIL: Blockchain-Based Generative Federated Learning for Trustworthy Healthcare Intelligence
papers.abstract: Healthcare organizations collect huge amounts of patient data from clinical records, medical tests, monitoring systems, and healthcare services. Such data can underpin intelligent healthcare analytics but remains distributed across institutions and cannot be shared directly due to privacy, security, and trust concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative learning without sharing raw patient records, but the exchanged model information remains vulnerable to privacy leakage, tampering, replay, and unauthorized access. In this paper, we propose iGRAIL, a blockchain-enabled generative FL framework for trustworthy healthcare intelligence. iGRAIL combines local generative learning for data augmentation with differential privacy to protect sensitive information during local training. Model communication is secured using cryptographic mechanisms, and blockchain-based verification and smart-contract access control ensure that only authorized, authentic, fresh, and integrity-preserving updates are accepted for federated aggregation. The framework is evaluated on four healthcare datasets and compared with the conventional FL and blockchain-based FL (BC-FL) under predictive, privacy, non-IID, scalability, malicious-update, security-verification, and runtime settings. For the two large diabetes datasets, iGRAIL improves accuracy by about 5.4-5.6%, the F1-score by 14.6-16.9%, and MCC by 16.0-18.1% over the best FL or BC-FL baseline. Increasing the strength of differential privacy reduces the privacy-loss parameter $\epsilon$ by about 72.5% for the cancer dataset and 87.5% for the diabetes dataset, with only a limited loss in prediction performance. These results indicate that iGRAIL supports secure and scalable federated computing while preserving privacy, model integrity, and controlled participation, at the cost of additional computational overhead.

papers.title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications
papers.abstract: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.

papers.title: Region Coloring of Spatial Graphs using Knot-theoretic Ternary Quasigroups
papers.abstract: We construct coloring conditions around vertices for region colorings of unoriented spatial graph diagrams by knot-theoretic ternary quasigroups. These conditions require cyclic products of left and right operators around each vertex to be the identity. We prove that the resulting coloring sets are preserved under the generalized Reidemeister moves and relate our construction to the palette framework. We show that the vertex coloring conditions are automatic for Dehn tribrackets and determine the associated palettes for unoriented Alexander tribrackets. We also introduce an additional restriction on vertex colorings that is preserved under the fifth Reidemeister move for every unoriented knot-theoretic ternary quasigroup. This restriction gives rise to further coloring invariants for Dehn tribrackets and unoriented Alexander tribrackets.

papers.intro:
A knot-theoretic ternary quasigroup (KTQ) is an algebraic structure equipped with a ternary operation satisfying certain axioms. The use of ternary operations in knot theory was introduced by Niebrzydowski in [4], and was subsequently developed into the theory of KTQs in [5]. This ternary operation is often referred to as a Niebrzydowski tribracket, or simply a tribracket. This algebra is derived from the structure of Reidemeister moves on link diagrams. It provides a framework for coloring the regions of a diagram, where the number of such colorings yields a link invariant.
