papers.title: AI-guided robotic in situ fabrication of curvature- and tissue-adaptive wireless bioelectronics
papers.abstract: Personalized bioelectronic devices for wound therapy require not only conformal fabrication on complex body surfaces but also functional adaptation of their electrical characteristics to individual wound geometries. Here, we present an AI-guided robotic in situ printing platform for fabricating wireless wound electrotherapy devices directly on transparent wound dressings. The system integrates a 3D vision camera, a six-degree-of-freedom robotic arm, direct-ink-writing, and geometry-aware RF design optimization. AI-based wound segmentation is used to determine wound dimensions and local surface curvature, while the reconstructed three-dimensional geometry is incorporated into the electromagnetic design of the receiving coil and interdigitated electrodes. In contrast to conventional approaches that use surface geometry only for trajectory generation, the proposed method accounts for both anatomical curvature and tissue dielectric loading to compensate for geometry-induced shifts in resonant behavior. A printable silver ink was characterized in terms of rheology, dimensional reproducibility, electrical resistance, and electromechanical stability, and was used to fabricate multilayer wireless devices directly on curved polyurethane dressings. Wireless power transfer, impedance characteristics, and electric-field delivery were evaluated experimentally and numerically. Finally, robotic in situ fabrication was demonstrated on an anthropomorphic tissue-equivalent forearm phantom, where the measured dielectric properties of the phantom were incorporated into the RF optimization, enabling resonant operation near the target frequency of 25 MHz. This work establishes a perception-to-design-to-fabrication framework for geometry-adaptive wireless bioelectronics and provides a technological foundation for future physical-AI-enabled manufacturing of personalized on-body electrotherapy devices.

papers.title: Disturbance-Aware Informative Planning in Spatiotemporal Environments
papers.abstract: Autonomous robots are widely used for persistent monitoring of spatiotemporal environments, where quantities of interest (QoI) change across space and time and require repeated measurements. In practice, robot motion can be affected by external disturbances that vary across the environment. When such external disturbances are not considered in trajectory optimization, it can lead to inaccurate predictions of robot motion and, consequently, the information acquired about the QoI during execution. However, estimating disturbances throughout the environment can be inefficient, as disturbances in regions with little overlap with monitoring trajectories have limited impact on monitoring performance. We therefore propose a two-stage informative planning framework for unknown, spatially varying but time-invariant disturbances, combining informed disturbance sampling with disturbance-aware trajectory optimization. First, we identify where QoI measurements are needed and generate alternative paths to these locations using the environment geometry. We then prioritize disturbance measurements based on their expected reduction of disturbance uncertainty along these paths. Second, rather than optimizing information acquisition based on nominal robot motion, we incorporate the learned disturbance belief into trajectory optimization to account for its effects on robot motion and information acquisition. Across four simulation scenarios, the proposed method reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.0--52.3 percent compared with environment-wide estimation and identifies paths that appear costly under nominal dynamics but become preferable when disturbances are considered.

papers.title: Mutable Inference: Architecting LLM Accelerators for Inference-Time Learning
papers.abstract:
Long-context LLMs must retain growing histories, but full attention makes each new token increasingly expensive. Inference-time learning (ITL) offers another approach. The model keeps training on the context during inference, retaining what it learns in its weights. Recent work shows that ITL can match full-context attention quality while attending only to a recent fixed-size window. This bounds attention costs but adds Learning (backward computation and weight updates) alongside Prediction (the forward pass) costs. Inference accelerators assume fixed weights, while training accelerators target complete training steps.
  This work identifies two opportunities. Attention's non-matrix operations leave enough idle matrix capacity for Learning, while selected layers can tolerate delayed weight updates with little quality loss. We exploit both with Learning While Serving (LWS), an inference accelerator architecture that shares compute hardware between latency-critical Prediction and deadline-flexible Learning. Hardware-managed per-layer weight versioning allows Learning to publish updates while in-flight computations read older versions. Resumable reduction blocks let Learning kernels span fragmented idle windows and yield to Prediction, while dedicated softmax-gradient units relieve vector contention. On modeled datacenter and edge NPUs, LWS hides Learning within Prediction, sustaining Prediction-only throughput while preserving 99.3% of fully fresh Learning's quality benefit for TTT-E2E 3B at 128K tokens. Across nine models, LWS achieves 1.6x the throughput of serial execution and 1.3x that of the best prior co-execution architecture. RTL synthesis shows that LWS adds 1.5% to NPU core area without another MAC array. By efficiently turning idle inference capacity into learning capacity, LWS establishes inference-time learning as a first-class workload for future LLM accelerators.

papers.title: An Algebraic Perspective on Operational Semantics
papers.abstract:
Languages with effects are typically given two independently specified semantic accounts: a denotational semantics based on (free) models, and an operational semantics defined by effect-specific reduction rules. This separation leads to two independently constructed semantic structures whose relationship must then be established a posteriori. We present a unified construction in which both denotational interpretation and operational reduction are constructed from an algebraic theory specifying the effects.
  We work with call-by-push-value extended by the operations of an algebraic theory. We prove equational canonicity and give a tree-based operational semantics that reduces every closed computation to a tree of operations. When the free model monad is a monadic container, we derive from it a configuration-based small-step semantics. Configurations are elements of the free model. Every step preserves the denotation. Under a condition we call affinity, every reduction terminates and at ground types computes the denotation. We instantiate the framework with state, errors, writer, and weighted and pre-convex probabilistic choice. For errors, writer and weighted choice we recover the familiar rules. For state we get a machine that runs the program from every initial state at once.

papers.title: Scattering for cubic and Yukawa--Hartree Dirac equations wiith polynomially decaying spacetime metrics
papers.abstract: We study massive Dirac equations in three space dimensions with small, time-dependent perturbations of the principal coefficients and decaying zeroth-order matrix terms. The principal perturbation and its spatial derivatives decay polynomially at rate $\rho>7/2$, and its first time derivative has one additional inverse spatial power. We prove small-data global well-posedness and scattering for local cubic nonlinearities in $H^s$, $s>1+5/(2(\rho-1))$, and for Yukawa--Hartree nonlinearities in $H^s$, $s>1/2+5/(2(\rho-1))$. The argument retains the coupling between the metric-adapted positive and negative branches. Its main ingredients are a time-independent modified energy, a weighted estimate controlling the full massive low-frequency component, and frequency-dependent spatial cutoffs. The operator class contains the geometric Dirac Hamiltonian of a synchronous spacetime metric with its full spin connection. No second time derivative, temporal integrability, or asymptotic stationarity is assumed. Scattering is formulated relative to the exact nonautonomous linear evolution.

papers.title: The retarded interaction and non-scattering for 3D Maxwell--Dirac system
papers.abstract: We prove an a priori obstruction to linear scattering for the massive Maxwell--Dirac system in three space dimensions. A global solution with nonzero charge cannot scatter linearly in $L^2$ if its full and homogeneous potentials are $O(t^{-1})$, and the homogeneous potential is $o(t^{-1})$ in compact timelike cones. No nonlinear asymptotic expansion is assumed in this non-scattering theorem. We also identify the exact leading interaction when the nonlinear current approaches a free Dirac current in $L^1$. Its coefficient is a positive quadratic form in the velocity density and is bounded below by the square of the charge divided by $4\pi$. The proof uses free Dirac asymptotics and an estimate for retarded source errors after pairing with a smooth free current. The main arguments, including the oscillatory retarded interaction, are proved here. Global existence and the required nonlinear decay remain separate inputs; a small-data application to existing theory is stated explicitly as such.

papers.title: Interpretable confidence regions for causal discovery
papers.abstract: Most work in causal discovery focuses on point estimation of the underlying causal graph, while uncertainty in the learned structure has received substantially less attention. We develop confidence regions for the completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG) identified from observational data. Our approach builds on perturbed PC (Chang et al., 2026), which generates plausible CPDAGs by perturbing the conditional independence tests underlying the widely used PC algorithm. The threshold used in these tests controls how perturbations translate into variation across the resulting CPDAGs. We propose a new thresholding strategy that suppresses spurious variation across runs while preserving asymptotic coverage, producing a substantially tighter collection of plausible CPDAGs. This collection is summarized through confidence balls and model confidence intervals constructed from the partially ordered set of CPDAGs under model inclusion. We also develop new theory and algorithms for the exact computation of these regions. Simulations show that our confidence regions attain good coverage while being substantially smaller and more interpretable than the original perturbed PC collections.

papers.title: Beyond Bot Labels: Retrospective Consequence-Grounded Ranking of Attributed Cache Harm in E-Commerce Logs
papers.abstract: Web caches reduce origin load and latency, but automated traffic can either warm them or evict objects shoppers reuse, lowering the cache hit ratio (CHR). Existing bot defenses generally infer automation from User-Agent (UA) strings or behavior rather than identify sessions that impose cross-session cache harm. We instead formulate the task as ranking sessions by eviction damage and propose consequence-grounded session ranking. A single chronological replay attributes each eviction-induced miss by a protected shopping session (a victim) to the session whose insertion last evicted the object. A behavioral model predicts the target from session behavior alone. Selected sessions bypass the cache but remain origin-served. In a controlled check of 539 non-victim sessions selected across harm levels, attribution order tracks victim-hit changes after removal (Spearman correlation 0.80). On a 12.7-million-request real trace, the top 1% of sessions carry 48.8% of attributed harm. Sessions without bot tags contribute 49.1% of this tier's harm. At the 20% request-volume target, the default conditional CHR difference reaches 93% of the UA baseline, which selects 47 times as many sessions. Six training seeds show little variation. This comparison conditions on the victims that remain, so we also report victim bypass. Local replay and retraining on a second store reproduce harm concentration and a top tier dominated by sessions without bot tags. These results establish attributed cross-session harm as an outcome-based target for retrospective cache audits and selective intervention design.

papers.title: Fourier Harmonics and Pentagonal Rigidity in the Planar Ulam Floating Body Problem
papers.abstract: We give a new proof that the disk is the only strictly convex planar body floating in equilibrium in every orientation at perimetral densities $\sigma=1/5$ and $\sigma=2/5$. The proof uses the Fourier harmonics of the chord-angle function and the closure relations of the associated pentagonal carousel. Their combination gives inequalities that force the body to be a disk.

papers.title: Hidden Markov Models for Dynamic Co-Clustering
papers.abstract: To jointly identify temporal regimes and row-column structure in matrix-valued time series, we propose a hidden Markov model (HMM) with Gaussian co-clustering distributions. A single latent regime governs each matrix. Conditional on the regime, row and column memberships define Gaussian blocks, each with its own mean and variance. Membership probabilities and block parameters are shared across occurrences of a regime, while individual memberships may vary between time points.

authors.name: Jing Li
authors.institution: Beijing University of Civil Engineering and Architecture

papers.title: Upper bounds for the number of spanning forests of a graph
papers.abstract:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on $n$ vertices, and let $F(G)$ denote the number of spanning forests of $G$. Bencs and Csikv\'ari proved that every $r$-regular graph $G$ with $r\ge 2$ satisfies $F(G)\le r^n$. Motivated by this result, they conjectured that if $G$ has minimum degree at least $3$, then $F(G)\leq \prod_{i=1}^n d_i$, where $(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n)$ is the degree sequence of $G$. In this paper, we prove that graphs with minimum degree at least $n/3$ $(n\geq7)$
  satisfy $F(G)\leq \prod_{i=1}^n d_i$. We also construct a counterexample to the conjecture. We therefore further study the enumeration of spanning forests in general graphs, proving an upper bound in terms of the degree sequence
  and characterizing the extremal graphs attaining this bound. In addition, using the matrix-forest theorem, we obtain an upper bound for the number of spanning forests of a connected graph in terms of its algebraic connectivity,
  and characterize the extremal graphs attaining this bound.

papers.title: TradeGauntlet: Evaluating Compliance Controls for Autonomous Trading Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.

authors.name: Soovadeep Bakshi
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: What Do Multilingual Self-Supervised Speech Encoders Know About Sentence Meaning?
papers.abstract: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) have been scaled up to thousands of languages and millions of hours of audio, yet little is known about how these models structure semantic knowledge across languages. In this work, we probe sentence-level semantics in massively multilingual S3Ms across 76 languages, using linear maps from frozen speech representations into a frozen text embedding space, evaluated by cross-modal retrieval. Sentence meaning is linearly accessible but highly uneven across languages and resource tiers. Cross-lingual probes can match language-specific probes on languages never seen in probe training, but per-model monolingual decodability does not predict transfer. Within the OmniASR wav2vec family, scaling from 300M--7B disproportionately benefits high-resource languages, and ASR tuning sharply improves semantic decodability while making representations more language-specific. However, semantic content is entangled with acoustics, inflating apparent performance on single-speaker corpora.

papers.title: Towards High-Performance Multimodal Discovery: Evaluating Retrieval Efficacy and Operational Scalability in Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: Large-scale digital repositories with million plus digitized volumes serve as vital engines for scientific and scholarly discovery. However, as collections grow, finding specific research or educational material remains a significant challenge. This difficulty is compounded by the multimodal nature of texts, that is, texts which combine dense narrative content with essential illustrative charts, annotated diagrams, and complex layouts. Historically, discovery has been supported by full-text search indexes implemented as inverted indexes (e.g., Lucene or Solr). While these systems scale well for textual strings, they are fundamentally "blind" to the semantic nuance of visual information. We explore the benefit of discovery through texts that have been converted to numerical vectors. By representing page images as numerical vectors rather than OCR-extracted text, and doing so for both text and images on a page, we capture both textual and visual semantics while mitigating reverse engineering and copyright infringement concerns. The primary contribution of this research is an evaluation of the multimodal retrieval landscape, encompassing both semantic precision and architectural scalability. Our findings demonstrate that integrating visual and textual features significantly enhances the discovery of relevant material, particularly in domains where diagrammatic content is essential for conceptual understanding. We assess retrieval efficacy, demonstrating that the system achieves sub-linear scalability. Our findings suggest that an optimized vector database configuration is the critical factor in transforming VLM-based embeddings into a production-ready, library-scale discovery solution.

authors.name: Krishna Priya
authors.institution: PSG Institute of Medical Sciences & Research

papers.title: AI Reviews Are Biased Towards the Appendix
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by reviewers to highlight weaknesses during the reviewing process, and their outputs often shape the reviews that humans submit. Prior work studies how LLM reviews align with human ones, yet we know little about which parts of a paper these models actually criticize. In this work, we investigate 2,000 papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR, and show that the latest GPT and Claude models draw about 50% or more of their review weaknesses from the appendix. This behavior holds across the API, coding-agent, and web access methods for using LLMs to review a paper. In contrast, we find that humans draw only 8.4% of their weaknesses from the appendix, and these weaknesses primarily revolve around a paper's presentation and content related to its core idea. Meanwhile, LLMs draw weaknesses from deep in the appendix that concern fine-grained technical details not central to the paper's contributions. We anticipate that our analysis will contribute to the scholarly discourse on AI reviews. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/cincynlp/review_appendix.

papers.title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Measured Neutron Flux Profiles of the SAFARI-1 Research Reactor
papers.abstract: Knowledge of the neutron flux distribution is essential for safe and effective reactor utilisation. In the SAFARI-1 research reactor, a set of axial flux profiles are periodically measured by activating natural copper wires inserted along the height of the fuel or control assemblies and subsequently measuring their activity using a sodium iodide detector. Improper wire insertion can, however, result in profiles that do not accurately represent the actual neutron flux distribution. Building on previously identified potential indicators of improper wire insertion, an automated approach based on unsupervised learning was developed to detect anomalous axial flux measurements. The measured data were preprocessed using missing-value imputation, decay correction, and normalisation. High-order polynomial fitting was then applied to characterise the axial flux profiles and derive features describing their shape. The Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) algorithm was employed to group flux profiles into regular and abnormal clusters based on these features with results matching the known groups. In addition, Convolutional Autoencoders were developed and trained on flux profiles from central and peripheral core positions to identify deviations from the regular profiles through reconstruction error, achieving better performance in central assemblies than in peripheral assemblies. The developed framework is intended to provide feedback to reactor operation by identifying potential wire-insertion problems in the manual technique used for axial flux monitoring at SAFARI-1.

authors.name: Pavel M. Bokov
authors.institution: South African Nuclear Energy Corporation (South Africa)

papers.title: Offline KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Transitions
papers.abstract: KL-regularized reinforcement learning is the objective behind RL fine-tuning of language models, and its data are often collected by the reference policy itself. However, beyond bandits and deterministic transitions, little is known about how much offline data it needs. In this work, we study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown stochastic transitions, $K$ state-action pairs and effective horizon $H$. For data that cover the regularized optimum with concentrability $C\geq 4$, every estimator needs $\Omega(KCH^3/(\epsilon\max\{\epsilon,\beta\}))$ samples on some instances when $\epsilon$ is small, where $\beta$ is the temperature. Under a fixed design, pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty attains this rate with high probability, up to logarithmic factors, when $\beta\geq 1.4H$. When the data come from the reference policy itself, we show that it covers the optimum up to a power law whose exponent grows as $H/\beta$; in the same temperature range, this power law alone gives the estimator a sample complexity polynomial in $1/\epsilon$, with no coverage assumption. For $\beta\geq H$ the power can also increase the sample size needed by a factor polynomial in $1/\epsilon$. Finally, the plug-in estimator, which is minimax optimal with a generative model, can fail on reference data at small temperatures when many actions are rarely seen, while the pessimistic estimator does not.

papers.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
papers.abstract: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.

papers.title: Brunn-Minkowski inequality for Riesz capacity in one dimension
papers.abstract: The Brunn-Minkowski inequality for Riesz $p$-capacity is proved on the line for every $p<1$ and all compact sets, including disconnected sets. For $-1<p<1$, equality holds exactly for a singleton summand or else two intervals, provided at least one capacity is positive. The proof couples equilibrium measures in increasing order.

papers.title: Sub-Synchronous Control Interaction Risk of Large Data Center Loads: A Frequency-Scan Assessment with Cross-Model Validation
papers.abstract: Data centers are now one of the fastest-growing loads on the bulk power system, and most of their demand reaches the grid through power converters inside uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). Whether these loads can take part in sub-synchronous control interaction (SSCI), as wind and HVDC converters do, has not been studied extensively. We examine this question with impedance-based frequency scans at the point of common coupling (PCC). Using a detailed proprietary model (INS-ISU), we scan the motor, variable-frequency-drive (VFD), lighting, and UPS-fed information-technology (IT) branches of a representative facility separately. Only the UPS in double-conversion mode shows negative resistance; it covers the whole sub-synchronous band and continues up to about 170 Hz. The other branches, and the UPS in bypass mode, stay passive. We then repeat the scans on three public models from PNNL, TAMU, and NLR. None of them shows negative resistance in bypass mode, while three of the four models do in double-conversion mode. Lowering the load from rated to light load makes the negative resistance deeper, as expected for a constant-power load, so a lightly loaded facility in double-conversion mode is the worst case. Raising the UPS DC-link capacitance pushes the negative resistance into a narrow band around the fundamental. These findings give a basis for screening data centers for SSCI during interconnection studies.

authors.name: Min Lwin
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: VellSSLH: Sound Type-Guided Selective Speculative Load Hardening for LLVM IR
papers.abstract:
Constant-time cryptographic programs written in C can still leak secrets during speculative execution. Mispredicted branches may allow instructions to access secret data and expose it through observable behavior. Speculative load hardening (SLH) addresses these leaks, but protecting values unnecessarily can introduce significant runtime overhead. We present VellSSLH, which selectively inserts speculative load hardening at LLVM IR. Programmers specify Public and Secret inputs in annotated C programs, and our analysis infers which values may become secret during speculation. The transformation then inserts misspeculation-flag operations and protections only where needed. VellSCT, our extracted checker, validates the resulting LLVM IR.
  We formalize speculative constant-time (SCT) security by extending Vellvm's LLVM semantics with speculative execution, attacker directives, and leakage observations. Our security type system reasons about SSA joins, symbolic values, poison, pointer provenance, and observable faults, and supports declared declassifications and trusted external services. In Rocq, we prove that programs accepted by the checker satisfy SCT, and that a reference hardening transformation preserves architectural behavior. Evaluated optimized variants are rechecked for SCT but are not covered by this preservation proof. Our mechanized guarantees apply at LLVM IR; security of the generated binary additionally depends on backend and hardware assumptions.
  We evaluate VellSSLH on 24 cryptographic entries on a bare-metal Intel processor. VellSSLH achieves 4.03% lower geometric-mean runtime than LLVM SLH, with 13 comparisons favoring VellSSLH, eight favoring LLVM SLH, and three inconclusive. For X25519, VellSSLH improves runtime by 22.69% over LLVM SLH with only 1.86% overhead over unprotected code. Compared with Ultimate SLH, VellSSLH achieves 19.65% lower runtime.

papers.title: On the Construction of New Families of Distance Equienergetic Graphs
papers.abstract: For a graph $G$ with vertex set $V(G)=\{v_{i}:1\leq i \leq p\}$ and edge set $E(G)=\{e_{j}:1\leq j \leq q\},$ its subdivision graph $S_G$ is generalized to $S_{G}(n,m),$ by replacing each vertex $v_{i}$ with $n$ vertices and each edge-vertex $e_{j}$ with $m$ vertices, with each copy having the same neighbors as the vertex it replaces. Building on this construction, we define the generalized subdivision vertex join $S_{G_{1}}(n,m)\dot{\vee} G_{2}$ and the generalized subdivision edge join $S_{G}(n,m)\veebar G_{2},$ which extend the known subdivision vertex and subdivision edge join of graphs. In this paper, we determine the distance spectrum of $S_{G_{1}}(n,n)\dot{\vee} G_{2}$ and $S_{G}(n,n)\veebar G_{2},$ when $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ are regular graphs. As an application, we construct new families of $D$-cospectral graphs and $D$-equienergetic graphs of diameter $4.$

papers.title: An Obstruction to Realizing Aspherical $3$-Manifold Groups via Torus Surgery
papers.abstract: Let $Y$ be a closed, connected, oriented, aspherical $3$-manifold with fundamental group $\pi = \pi_1(Y)$ and positive first Betti number $\beta_1(Y) > 0$, and let $X_0 = Y \times S^1$. We prove that no torus surgery on $X_0$ along a torus-fibered $T^2$-knot $T \subseteq X_0$ can yield a $4$-manifold $X = X_{0; T, f}$ with fundamental group $\pi$. The obstruction combines the vanishing of the Euler characteristic of $X$ with a classifying-map argument showing that the unimodular intersection form on $H^2(X; \mathbb{Z})$ must admit an isotropic subgroup of rank $\beta_1(\pi)$, forcing $\chi(X) \geq 2$. Along the way, we also present an independent geometric proof via covering space theory, the Sphere Theorem, and Scott's Core Theorem that the fundamental group of a closed aspherical $3$-manifold is torsion-free.

papers.title: Counterexamples to the clamped-plate eigenvalue ratio conjecture
papers.abstract: Ashbaugh in 1999 conjectures that the ball maximizes the ratio of the second to the first eigenvalue for the vibrating clamped-plate problem. We disprove this conjecture by constructing smooth connected domains in every dimension $d\ge2$. The construction starts with an interior sphere on which the displacement is required to vanish. The first two eigenvalues have the same relative increase at first order, but the second increases more at second order. This gives a strict increase of their ratio, which survives approximation of the sphere by finitely many codimension-two supports and their replacement by smooth holes. We identify the limiting Sobolev spaces through trace estimates and logarithmic cutoffs, and use the geometric construction for the buckling problem to obtain connected perforated domains.

papers.title: Cohen Macaulayness and Buchsbaumness of Cartesian Products of Paths and Cycles
papers.abstract: We study the independence complexes of Cartesian products of paths and cycles. Let G(m,n) denote the Cartesian product of the path P_m and the cycle C_n, and let Delta(m,n) denote its independence complex. We determine the well-covered graphs in this family and use reduced homology to study their Cohen-Macaulay and Buchsbaum properties. Using these results, we completely classify the Cohen-Macaulay members. We then study the Buchsbaum property of Delta(m,n) through vertex links. For the remaining family P_m x C_3, we introduce an auxiliary family of graphs and use an inductive link argument together with Reisner's criterion to determine precisely when the independence complex of P_m x C_3 is Buchsbaum. Combining this with the remaining well-covered cases yields the complete Buchsbaum classification.

papers.title: Understanding Contextual Bias in Agricultural CNNs Through Hidden-Neuron Concept Induction
papers.abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can classify images using background-dominated patches that contain little or none of the target object, showing that they exploit contextual information. Previous studies detected this behavior through classification accuracy but say little about what CNN hidden layers represent. We investigate whether Concept Induction can reveal interpretable visual properties associated with hidden-neuron activations on contextual image patches. Using five agricultural datasets with high, moderate, and low contextual bias, we analyze four CNN architectures at three network depths and five patch locations. Quantitative image descriptors of each patch are encoded in a knowledge graph and used as background knowledge for Concept Induction, which derives logical expressions characterizing neuron activation. These expressions are tested on held-out images using the Mann-Whitney U test and Cliff's delta. Of 48,013 tested neuron-feature pairs, 13,164 (27.4%) were validated. Validation was most frequent at intermediate depths (mean 40.2% at mid layers versus 12.0% at deep layers), and no patch location dominated across datasets. Among the tested descriptors, edge, Gabor, and Tamura texture features had the highest validation rates. Stronger contextual bias did not correspond to higher neuron-feature validation rates: moderately biased Sugarcane had the highest rate (40.5%) and highly biased Cassava the lowest (19.2%). These results suggest that behavioral context dependence and the semantic interpretability of hidden neurons capture different aspects of CNN behavior, and that Concept Induction can complement patch-based bias detection.

papers.title: Certificates of Immortality for Gliders on the Hat and Spectre Tilings
papers.abstract: Cellular automata on the hat and spectre monotilings support gliders: localized patterns that travel at constant speed and heading on a tiling that has no translational symmetry. An earlier paper found them by search and left open whether they travel forever; here it is settled by finite computation. A certificate is a finite set of local situations, a pattern with a collar of terrain, closed under the rule on every environment the tiling can present, the environments enumerated by the tilings' substitution transducer. Seven closed sets, covering the earlier paper's gliders, prove that each never dies on any tiling of its hull and holds its heading inside a rigorous interval. Three further gliders, from a rule hand-designed in 2023, one found independently in 2026, and the author's spectre rule moved to the hat, certify on the lane the hat gliders share, with the same cocycle. An independent program re-derives each certificate.

authors.name: James Edmond
authors.institution: United States Air Force Research Laboratory

papers.title: End-line Fourier restriction for hyperbolic surfaces in three dimensions
papers.abstract: We prove new bilinear adjoint Fourier restriction estimates for pairs of separated rectangles associated to a hyperbolic surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$. We then employ these bilinear estimates to prove Fourier extension inequalities along the (sharp) parabolic scaling line for any smooth hyperbolic 2-surface that is either the graph of a polynomial or that obeys a mild finite type condition.

papers.title: What a Memory Preview Cannot Tell You: Ambiguity in AI Memory Permissions
papers.abstract: A memory rule states when an assistant may reuse a remembered event, and an editor can confirm a rule by previewing one use it allows and one it blocks. We ask what such a preview lets a person infer about the rule they saved. For an editor with six or twelve valid rules, we enumerate every rule compatible with a preview. Splitting the rules most evenly does not target the question a user cares about. For an explicit preference, two adaptive tests leave all three recommendation scopes open (for a one-off choice the outcome turns on a tie), while one test of transfer to another task settles the question. Weak previews are also the default. Under the intended rule, 36 of 39 possible allowed/blocked pairs contain a blocked example that no rule allows, and no pair identifies the rule. Three or four tests suffice here; when permissions depend on each other, a fixed checklist grows to six or nine and adaptive questioning needs at most five or seven. These counts use a specified rule vocabulary and fictional events. In a small pilot, 10 of 20 people who saw such a weak preview of a rule they had just chosen mispredicted, or were unsure about, at least one of two uses, and none of those 10 said the outcomes matched what they wanted. Whether better previews help people is untested.

papers.title: Effectively nuclear C*-algebras
papers.abstract:
We study the computable content of nuclearity for $C^*$-algebras. We show that nuclearity effectivizes automatically: a presentation of a $C^*$-algebra is effectively nuclear, in the sense that the completely positive approximations witnessing nuclearity can be computed uniformly from the data they approximate, if and only if it is a computable presentation of a nuclear $C^*$-algebra, and likewise for the effectivization of the Choi--Effros form of nuclearity. The main tool is an effective version of the Arveson extension theorem: we prove that the $n$-th matrix numerical range of a tuple from a computable presentation is computably compact, uniformly in all of its data, and deduce an algorithm which converts an approximately attainable tuple of matrices into a computable unital completely positive map attaining it. A byproduct is that the computable states of any computable presentation of a unital $C^*$-algebra are weak$^*$-dense in its state space.
  We also prove that the Cuntz algebras $\mathcal{O}_n$ are computably categorical and obtain an effective form of Kirchberg--Phillips absorption. By contrast with the conditions above, we do not know whether every computable presentation of a nuclear $C^*$-algebra admits a computable embedding into $\mathcal{O}_2$ with a computable conditional expectation; we answer this affirmatively for commutative $C^*$-algebras, for AF algebras, and, by a dynamical argument using invariant states, for the group $C^*$-algebras of a class of amenable groups including all finitely presented residually finite ones. Finally, we show that the set of indices of computable presentations of nuclear $C^*$-algebras is $\Pi^0_2$, and that the corresponding set for c.e. presentations is $\Pi^0_2$-hard; the latter rests on a result of independent interest, namely that amenability of computable groups is $\Pi^0_2$-complete within the class of computable groups.

papers.title: Minimaxity in Robust Nonparametric Regression: from Heavy-Tailed to Sub-Gaussian Assumptions

authors.name: Yikun Li
authors.institution: Changchun University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Exponential Double and Multiple Riordan Arrays as Fiber Products
papers.abstract: A double Riordan array has nonzero entries only in positions $(n,k)$ with $n+k$ even, and its even and odd parts are Riordan arrays with the same multiplier function. We develop this observation systematically, with the emphasis on exponential double and exponential multiple Riordan arrays. Using generalized Riordan arrays with respect to a sequence $(c_n)$, we show that the double Riordan group, the exponential double Riordan group, the multiple Riordan group, and the exponential multiple Riordan group are fiber products of (generalized) Riordan groups over the Lagrange group. For exponential double and exponential multiple Riordan arrays this yields product and inverse formulas without square or $\ell$th roots, valid over any field of characteristic zero; an abelian normal subgroup with quotient the Lagrange group and a corresponding splitting; subgroups isomorphic to the Riordan group; an iterated split-extension description of the multiple groups; and a characterization of elements of finite order, including the fact that over ${\mathbb R}$ every element of finite order is an involution. We show that the $\ell$th power of the production matrix is the direct sum of the production matrices of the compressions, give an explicit formula for it in terms of partial Bell polynomials, and characterize these arrays by a shared $A$-sequence. Finally, we reverse the construction. Two Riordan arrays with a common multiplier can always be interleaved into a unique double Riordan array, and into an ordinary Riordan array exactly when their first functions satisfy one more condition. Examples include Pascal-, Catalan-, Morgan--Voyce-, and ballot-type arrays.

papers.title: Online Allocation with Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: We study private online allocation problems, where allocation decisions must satisfy differential privacy (DP) to protect sensitive user information while optimizing performance under limited resources. We first formalize differential privacy notions suited to different privacy requirements in online allocation and establish the fundamental performance limits of any algorithm under these definitions. Based on these insights, we propose PPOA, a privacy-preserving meta algorithm for online allocation, and establish sufficient conditions under which PPOA preserves Joint DP (JDP) or Local DP (LDP) while achieving asymptotically near-optimal performance. Building on these conditions, PPOA can be instantiated into a variety of concrete algorithms. In particular, we present the specific designs, which include PPOA-DMD that preserves JDP and LDP and PPOA-FTRL that preserves JDP. We analyze their performance under both adversarial and stochastic settings and characterize the fundamental trade-offs between DP and allocation performance. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed algorithms via numerical experiments on AI model routing in battery-powered edge systems.

authors.name: Jianyi Yang
authors.institution: Nanjing University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Xingyu Zhou
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Zoom In, Scale Out: Metric Depth Models Mistake Digital Zoom for Moving Closer
papers.abstract: Many new AI models estimate how far away things are, in metres, from a single photo. To do this they must also work out what camera took the photo. We check whether they really do with a simple test: digital zoom, that is, cropping a photo and enlarging the crop back to full size. Zooming moves nothing in the scene, so a correct model should give the same distance for every point still in the picture. The test is free, exact and needs no labels. Two numbers describe a model's reaction: its depth changes like $s^{-\alpha}$ (ideal $\alpha=0$) and its focal-length estimate like $s^{\beta}$ (ideal $\beta=1$), for zoom factor $s$. On 800 images from KITTI, NYUv2 and DIODE, the widely used Depth Anything V2 has $\alpha=0.95$: it treats a zoomed photo almost as if the camera had moved closer, because it judges distance mainly from how large things look. Models that also predict the camera remove only part of this error ($\alpha\approx0.31$-$0.36$), because their focal estimate grows too little. Given the true camera, Depth Pro and DA3-Nested keep their depth ($\alpha\approx0$), so the error lies in their camera estimate. The reason: a zoomed photo is, pixel for pixel, a normal photo of a scene squashed in depth, so size alone cannot tell the two apart, and a focal estimator trained by regression stays close to the cameras it saw in training. Undoing this needs no labels or training and makes Depth Pro pass the test ($\alpha=0.04$) at almost no cost on normal photos. Controls, including a real optical zoom lens, rule out blur and resizing artefacts. Finally, label-free fine-tuning for self-consistency lowers $\alpha$ to 0.05 on KITTI and 0.07 on NYUv2 once a "blurry means zoomed" shortcut is removed; we report what this costs on normal and unseen photos.

papers.title: Probing the Activity History of Repeating Fast Radio Bursts with Cluster Lensing
papers.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond duration coherent radio transients, some of whose sources repeat, but the nature and active lifetimes of their engines remain uncertain. Strong lensing by galaxy clusters provides a physical lever on this lifetime problem: a short campaign can sample emission epochs of a repeating FRB separated by years, and distinct bursts in different lensed images, given a known relative lens delay, set a lower bound on its active lifetime, whereas delayed copies of a single burst only encode the lens delay. Based on the cluster-lens model of MACS J0717.5+3745, we quantify the accessible range of emission epochs for finite activity episodes, observing windows, and discovery selection. For a source-frame episode of duration \(100~{\rm yr}\) at \(z_s=2\) and a source-frame rate of \(0.1\,{\rm h}_{\rm src}^{-1}\), a five year campaign conditional on discovery yields a \(95\%\) gain threshold of \(m_{95}\simeq25.6\), corresponding to a source-frame span of \(L_{95}\simeq42.6~{\rm yr}\). At the population level, combining distinct burst associations with same burst echoes provides a way to test specified activity durations with a finite lens catalogue, e.g., activity durations differing by an order of magnitude can be distinguished with expected Bayes factor above $20$. More broadly, these lensed source frame epochs enable applications beyond activity-duration tests, e.g., linking burst activity to the evolution of the engine and its environment. Galaxy-cluster lensing therefore provides a promising future probe for accessing otherwise unobserved source history and for distinguishing between different activity duration models.

papers.title: Sharp Finite-Time Blow-Up for Unforced Axisymmetric Euler Without Swirl via Multiscale Data
papers.abstract:
For the unforced Euler equations, we construct a compactly supported initial vorticity within the class of axisymmetric flows without swirl, whose solution blows up in finite time. The initial vorticity belongs simultaneously to every H\"older space $C^\alpha$, $\alpha<1/3$. This is sharp given that global regularity is known when $\alpha=1/3$ in the case of axisymmetric flows without swirl.
  Previous constructions by Shkoller \cite{Shk26}, Chen \cite{Chen26I,Chen26II}, and Shao--Wei--Zhang--Zhang \cite{SWZZ26} establish blow-up for each prescribed exponent $\alpha$ in the same sharp range. Our construction achieves simultaneous membership in all these spaces. In addition, our construction is short.
  Our proof uses multiscale initial data, in the spirit of Kim--Jeong~\cite{KJ22}, C\'ordoba--Mart\'inez-Zoroa--Zheng~\cite{CMZZ25}, and Bang--Cheskidov~\cite{BC26}. The blow-up mechanism is a forward cascade through successively smaller scales. A main difficulty in approaching the critical exponent $1/3$ is caused by large self-deformation. Our main idea to overcome this difficulty is to obtain a lower bound for strain at the stationary non-smooth point by using angular redistribution.
  A related outstanding open problem is to establish an unforced Euler blow-up from smooth data in the case of axisymmetric flows with swirl. A recent multiscale construction by OpenAI for the unforced Euler equations is, however, non-axisymmetric. Although we work in the no-swirl class, the axisymmetric multiscale mechanism developed here may offer a possible route toward the still-open problem of axisymmetric smooth blow-up.

papers.title: Potential Flow, Stress, and Straightness in Flow Matching: Euler Error on Gaussian-Mixture Targets
papers.abstract: In linear flow matching, coupling straightness measures conditional displacement variance. The conditional covariance gives a kinetic stress in the Jeans balance. The virial identity relates the mean trace of the covariance to a radial moment of acceleration. Euler error also depends on how the flow propagates acceleration. On constructed Gaussian-mixture targets, closed-form couplings with matched straightness yield different median Euler errors. Learned fields from fresh minibatch assignments also yield different Euler errors from their partners at matched estimated straightness. The leading Euler coefficient accounts for more of the error variation than straightness in these experiments. We relate the additive-noise characterization of isotropic Gaussian sources to potential flow. A gradient constraint reduces velocity error on the independent isotropic Gaussian example and increases it on two examples with rotational exact fields.

papers.title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
papers.abstract: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.

papers.title: Internal diameter bounds for DLA on random planar maps under invariance principles
papers.abstract: We establish sublinear bounds for the internal diameter of External Diffusion Limited Aggregation (DLA) clusters on random planar maps. We develop two conditional DLA growth results for deterministic planar maps: the weaker condition yielding sublinear growth for DLA, and the stronger yielding polynomially sublinear growth for DLA. We then verify the strong assumption a.s. for the $\gamma$-mated CRT maps, and the weak condition a.s. for ergodic scale-free random environments, establishing the corresponding a.s bounds.

papers.title: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation
papers.abstract: Complete game generation requires agents to coordinate rules, interactions, states, and presentation over a long development process. A single aggregate score obscures which capabilities are implemented and which requirements remain unmet. We present OCTAVE, a benchmark for complete HTML5 game generation organized around eight Capability Dimensions, with 180 tasks and 1,800 Evaluation Requirements drawn from real player requests, commercial-mechanics reconstruction, and human expert design. It covers PC Web, Mobile Web, 2D, and 3D. Requirements distinguish Completeness, assessing publicly specified core implementation, from Richness, assessing hidden, deeper system relationships. Static source-code judgments provide requirement-level diagnosis across capabilities and task conditions. Evaluation of 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness; 19.9% of generation records are static gate failures or missing artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, even the best combination remains below 50% on both public and hidden requirements. Richness is not harder than Completeness under every task condition. Systems perform relatively better on Core Rules and Numerical Design, while AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel show more prominent gaps. Requirement difficulty offers coarse stratification but is only weakly negatively correlated with pass rates. A limited human cross-check finds that requirements judged satisfied by humans but failed by the automated evaluator are the main direction of disagreement. OCTAVE extends evaluation beyond aggregate scores to diagnosis localized by requirement, capability, and task condition.

papers.title: Periodic Modulation of Linear Polarization Fraction in Repeating FRB 20240114A
papers.abstract: Long-term polarization changes in repeating fast radio bursts (FRBs) can probe their emission geometry and propagation environment. We searched for periodic variation in the degree of linear polarization (DOL) of FRB~20240114A using the polarization catalog from the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope. The sample contains 6,099 bursts detected on 95 observing days over $\sim 488$ days. The daily mean DOL series was analyzed using phase distance correlation and Lomb--Scargle periodograms over trial periods of 10--240 days. The strongest peaks occur at $119.91^{+2.67}_{-2.04}$ and $122.31^{+2.63}_{-2.82}$ days, respectively. The quoted ranges correspond to the period intervals above the global $3\sigma$ thresholds. Global false-alarm probabilities were estimated from \(10^7\) random permutations of the daily values among the fixed observing dates, with the full period search repeated for each permutation. The resulting probabilities are \(9.98\times10^{-4}\) and \(8.95\times10^{-4}\), corresponding to equivalent Gaussian significances of \(3.09\sigma\) and \(3.12\sigma\), respectively. As a supplementary check, the same analysis using daily median DOL yielded similar peaks near 120 days. A descriptive sinusoidal fit to all 95 daily mean DOL measurements at a fixed period of 119.91 days has a semi-amplitude of 3.23\%. Possible explanations include precession-driven changes in viewing geometry and variations in propagation conditions within a binary system.

papers.title: ESI: An Embodied Self-Improvement Flywheel for LLM-VLA Agents
papers.abstract: Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.

papers.title: Atlas-DeePC: Learning Behavioral Atlases for Predictive Control
papers.abstract: Data-enabled Predictive Control (DeePC) uses linear combinations of recorded input-output trajectories to compute control actions without a parametric model. For nonlinear systems, these linear combinations may not satisfy the system dynamics, and the computational cost grows with dataset size. We propose Atlas-DeePC, which approximates the behavior of a dynamical system using a collection of low-dimensional subspaces, termed a behavioral atlas, to enable computationally efficient prediction and control. The atlas is constructed offline by clustering the data and fitting a subspace to each cluster. Online, the controller selects the subspace that best matches recent measurements and solves a predictive control problem parameterized by its orthonormal basis. A graph-based reference planner complements the controller by providing intermediate references across operating regions. We illustrate Atlas-DeePC on a planar robotic manipulator, where it achieves higher success rates and substantially lower online computation times than the compared controllers based on online data selection. An additional benchmark of an autonomous racing task is also included. The project website provides code and demonstrations https://dianjin-frederick.github.io/Atlas-DeePC/

papers.title: 1.56 THz Full-Field Rydberg-Atom Imaging with 0.3 mm-scale Spatial Response
papers.abstract: THz imaging via Rydberg-atom up-conversion offers a powerful full-field modality with high sensitivity and rapid acquisition. However sub-millimeter imaging above 1 THz is still constrained by source power and beam-delivery loss. In this paper, we demonstrate a \(50~\mathrm{mm} \times 50~\mathrm{mm}\) full-field imaging at 1.56~THz by implementing the \(11P_{3/2} \rightarrow 10D_{5/2}\) transition of a cesium Rydberg-atom vapor. The measured spatial response FWHMs are \(0.314~\mathrm{mm}\) in horizontal and \(0.354~\mathrm{mm}\) in vertical for a \(0.5~\mathrm{mm}\) pinhole, alongside a sensitivity of \(31.7~\mathrm{fW}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}/(6.5 \times 6.5)~\mu\mathrm{m}^{2}\), and a frame rate up to \(300~\mathrm{fps}\). Under matched illumination, relay, and image-processing conditions, mask imaging at 1.56 THz reproduces finer features and edges with substantially higher edge contrast, deeper intensity-trough separation in line profiles, and recovered detail that remains blurred or unresolved at 0.55 THz. Furthermore, preliminary imaging of a \(200~\mu\mathrm{m}\) tissue slice suggests morphological correspondence with H\&E histology histology, offered as a proof-of-concept for label-free tissue characterization. By validating the wavelength-dependent resolution scaling in Rydberg THz imaging, this work establishes frequency scaling as a general design principle for sub-millimeter Rydberg-THz imaging.

papers.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

papers.title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Experimental optimization of perovskite solar cells is constrained by combinatorial diversity in absorber compositions, device layers, and processing, which makes virtual screening attractive for prioritizing recipes before fabrication. We develop a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework that casts recipe generation as virtual screening, enriching candidate shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors. A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides recipe generation, while a reference pool of 890 measured devices enables neighborhood-based assessment. Five-fold evaluation on 1,846 devices shows top-ten selection raises mean power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 19.68\% to 23.74\%. Three learned policies are compared with six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run. In top-100 shortlists, Proximal policy optimization (PPO) and recurrent PPO (RPPO) achieve neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23\% and 24\% (7.9- and 8.3-fold Pure Random's 2.9\%), versus 10\% (3.4-fold) for the baselines with the highest supported hit rate (L-SHADE and Ax BO, tied) at $K = 100$. Gains coexist with weak-support fractions. Of 9,000 recipes, 65.4\% match a composition family at similarity 0.80, falling to 11.7\% at 0.90. Results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or matched-budget advantage.

papers.title: On the spectrality of non-homogeneous self-similar measures
papers.abstract: We develop a finite-cylinder difference-set obstruction to the existence of an exponential orthonormal basis for a compactly supported probability measure. This obstruction uses the equal-scale and equal-mass structure of finitely many disjoint affine copies of the measure, together with Parseval's identity and an elementary atom bound for positive measures. We apply it to prove that the golden-mean self-similar measure generated by $x/2$ and $(x+2)/4$ is non-spectral. Together with a weight-rigidity argument, this excludes spectrality for every positive choice of weights in this iterated function system. We also analyze a logarithmically incommensurable example generated by $x/2$ and $(x+2)/3$, proving non-spectrality for all first-branch weights $p\in[1/3,5/6]$, including the natural weights. The latter proof reduces to two finite, exactly checkable integer difference-set conditions; an independent verification program is included in the paper.

papers.title: The Capillary Orlicz--Christoffel--Minkowski Flows
papers.abstract: We study a capillary Orlicz--Christoffel--Minkowski flow on a non-obtuse spherical cap for $1\le k\le n-1$: \[ \partial_t h= \frac{h^2\varphi(\ell/h)}{f}\, \bar{\sigma}_k(\nabla^2h+h\sigma)-h, \qquad \nabla_\mu h=\cot\theta\,h. \] In the supercritical regime \[ a_\varphi(s)=\frac{s\varphi'(s)}{\varphi(s)} \ge k+1+\delta, \qquad s a_\varphi'(s)\ge0, \] we obtain time-uniform $C^0$ and $C^1$ estimates and a closed scalar equation for the speed ratio. A dynamic Orlicz square-completion identity, combined with inverse-concavity, yields a viscosity estimate for the minimum principal radius. Under a strict dynamic Orlicz-convexity condition and \[ \frac{f_\mu}{f}\ge\frac{n-k}{n}\cot\theta, \] we prove time-uniform two-sided principal-radius bounds on every smooth existence interval for $0<\theta\le\pi/2$ and deduce long-time existence and smooth convergence to a stationary solution. The boundary regularity step uses a quantitative interior concave estimate through Neumann reflection and a concave uniformly elliptic extension. Under the weaker condition $(f\ell^{k-1})_\mu\ge0$, strict convexity is preserved on every smooth existence interval. For $k=1$, the transformed scalar equation is uniformly parabolic for every $0<\theta<\pi$. Classical parabolic estimates then give an all-angle scalar flow theorem, without asserting geometric convexity preservation in the obtuse range.

papers.title: The Capillary Dual Orlicz--Christoffel--Minkowski Problem
papers.abstract:
We study a capillary dual Orlicz--Christoffel--Minkowski problem on a spherical cap. For $2\le k\le n$, $1<p<k+1$, and $0<\theta<\pi/2$, we consider \[
  \sigma_k(\nabla^2h+h\sigma)
  =
  f(\xi)h^{p-1}\frac{\rho^{k+1}}{\varphi(\rho)},
  \qquad
  \rho=(h^2+|\nabla h|^2)^{1/2}, \] with the capillary Robin condition $\nabla_\mu h=\cot\theta\,h$. Assuming that $f$ is positive, smooth and horizontally even, $g=f^{-1/(p+k-1)}$ satisfies the capillary spherical-convexity and boundary compatibility conditions, and $H(r)=\varphi(r)/r^p$ is strictly increasing and proper with $Q_\varphi(r)\le k+1$, we prove the existence of a smooth, positive, horizontally even solution that is strictly capillary convex. The proof uses an Orlicz homotopy, uniform a priori estimates, a viscosity constant-rank argument when $k<n$, global oblique regularity, and degree theory.
