papers.title: Uniaxial strain induces $d$-wave phonon chirality in ferroelectric BaTiO$_3$
papers.abstract: Circularly dichroic resonant inelastic x-ray scattering has revealed electrically switchable $g$-wave phonon chirality in freestanding BaTiO$_3$ membranes. Here, we show from first principles that uniaxial strain changes the angular class of this texture. Lowering $C_{4v}$ to $C_{2v}$ adds a $d$-wave helicity that is bilinear in the orthorhombic strain $\eta$ and the polarization, with nodal lines along the stress axis. For the 38~meV branches at $\eta=1\%$, we find that (i) along the diagonal, where the helicity vanishes by symmetry without strain, it reaches about 60\% of the unstrained maximum, and (ii) at the measured wave vectors off the mirror it is reduced by more than half. With PBEsol and PBE+D3 force constants, the $d$-wave component grows linearly in $\eta$ and equals the $g$-wave one at $\eta^*\approx1.3\text{--}1.4\%$. Resolved by branch, the response of strain-split $E$ doublets is non-analytic in $\eta$, as captured by a two-band model. Strain therefore provides a second knob, besides the electric field, that controls the symmetry and the sign of phonon chirality in ferroelectric membranes.

papers.title: Equivariant resolution of singularities for $T$-varieties in positive characteristic
papers.abstract: Let the ground field be algebraically closed of positive characteristic. We prove that every variety endowed with an algebraic torus action whose general orbits have codimension at most three admits an equivariant resolution of singularities. The proof combines the description of such varieties in terms of proper polyhedral divisors and divisorial fans, the existence of log resolutions in dimension at most three, and the resolution of toroidal embeddings established by Kempf, Knudsen, Mumford and Saint-Donat.

papers.title: In-plane diffusion, spurious drift and a physics-structured gap predictor for a free colloidal pair
papers.abstract: When the diffusivity of a Brownian particle depends on position, its mean displacement acquires a noise-induced (spurious) drift whose magnitude is set by the stochastic convention $\alpha$. We ask how much of this physics can be extracted from a pair of 1.95 $\mu$m polystyrene spheres released from blinking holographic optical tweezers at five bath temperatures between 2 and 40 $^\circ$C. The single-sphere diffusivity inside the pair stays between 0.093 and 0.098 $\mu$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, whereas the Stokes-Einstein value for water rises from 0.126 to 0.361 $\mu$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; an isolated sphere reproduces the deficit, which is therefore not a pair effect. From the measured gap-dependent diffusivities $D_\parallel(h)$ and $D_\perp(h)$ we build a Fokker-Planck predictor of the future gap and score it on held-out releases. It recovers the 90% width of the gap distribution up to 800 ms but cannot discriminate between $\alpha = 0$, $1/2$ and $1$, because the $\alpha$-dependent mean shift is an order of magnitude smaller than that width. The ensemble spurious drift is consistent with zero at both ends of the temperature range, and the regression for $\alpha$ never exceeds $R^2 = 0.22$. We therefore present a planar methods baseline and identify the measurements required to resolve $\alpha$.

papers.title: Domains of attraction of quasi-stationary distributions for an absorbed random walk
papers.abstract: We study a continuous-time random walk on the positive integers, killed at zero, where the downward rate $a$ and upward rate $b$ satisfy $a>b>0$. Its quasi-stationary distributions form a one-parameter family. We show that if the initial distribution $(m_n)_{n\geq 1}$ is strictly positive and satisfies $m_{n+1}/m_n\to r$, where $(b/a)^{1/2}<r<1$, then its conditional distribution given survival converges in total variation to the corresponding nonminimal quasi-stationary distribution. We obtain asymptotic equivalents for the joint probabilities of position and survival, and for the survival probability itself. We also give a moment condition under which the minimal quasi-stationary distribution is selected. Finally, we construct an initial distribution whose successive-term ratios do not converge but whose conditional distribution nevertheless converges to a nonminimal quasi-stationary distribution. Thus the ratio condition is sufficient but not necessary.

papers.title: Entire curves in surface bundles over tori
papers.abstract: Cattalani recently initiated the study of Ahlfors currents in symplectic topology. We combine these with the symplectic pairs of Bande-Kotschick to show that some non-trivial surface bundles over tori have pseudoholomorphic entire curves. In particular the Kodaira-Thurston manifold has an entire curve for every $J$ tamed by an invariant form.

papers.title: Analysing Busy Beaver Machines (Or How to Find Ossified Ocelots)
papers.abstract: The busy beaver problem involves working with machines which can produce very large numbers, both for the output of certain Turing machines and for the number of steps taken to execute them. Given that these numbers can involve thousands of digits, it is crucial to have a means of proving properties of the relevant machines which allow manipulation of such large numbers. In this paper we introduce the notion of \textit{shape computations} as a means of isolating key properties that allow efficient execution of the relevant Turing machines based on verifiable properties of state transitions. In particular, this notion allows us to provide an analytical result which demonstrates the quadratic relationship between the size of the output and the number of steps required to generate it. We have also developed an initial implementation of our approach, and we provide empirical evaluation of it on a suite of 240 example machines.

papers.title: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
papers.abstract: Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.

papers.title: General linear groups in tangent categories
papers.abstract: General linear groups are well-studied Lie groups that encode the linear symmetries of a finitely-dimensional linear space. In differential geometry, they are an important ingredient of various constructions, including fibre bundles and the frame bundle of a principal bundle. They also appear in algebraic geometry as affine group schemes. Their Lie algebra, known as the general linear Lie algebra, is isomorphic to the Lie algebra of square matrices, whose Lie bracket is given by the commutator. Building on previous work on Lie groups, in this paper we introduce general linear group objects in the context of tangent categories. We define the general linear group of a differential object as a classifier of the Kleisli parametrized linear automorphisms of the differential object, a class of maps that generalize linear automorphisms in a suitable sense. We prove that such a group can be entirely constructed via a tangent triple equalizer and use this characterization to prove that the Lie algebra of general linear group objects is isomorphic to the Lie algebra of linear endomorphisms.

papers.title: The four-dimensional Borsuk number is five or six
papers.abstract: Can every set of diameter one in four dimensions be split into at most five parts of smaller diameter? Three parts suffice in the plane and four in three-dimensional space. In four dimensions five parts are sometimes necessary. We prove that six always suffice, improving the previous upper bound of seven. For small circumradius we use six cones. For large circumradius five balls meet every diametral pair of a compact set. At intermediate radii we bound the diameter of each part by the diameter of a rational polytope. The theorem is formalised in Lean.

papers.title: Positive Dual Certificates for Real Separated Subset Sums: Chamber Optimality of the Conway-Guy and Bohman Sets, and Exact Values up to Eight
papers.abstract: Let $f_R(n)$ be the least possible largest element of a set of $n$ positive reals whose $2^n$ subset sums are pairwise at least 1 apart, and let $f_Z(n) \ge f_R(n)$ be the corresponding integer quantity of the Erd\H{o}s distinct subset sums problem. Fixing the signs of all signed relations $\varepsilon\cdot x$, $\varepsilon \in \{-1,0,1\}^n$, decomposes the real problem into polyhedral chambers, on each of which it is a linear program. We prove that for every $n$ the Conway-Guy set is the unique optimum of its chamber. The proof is an explicit positive dual certificate consisting of $n$ signed relations that are tight at the Conway-Guy set and unit lower triangular in gap coordinates; the relations are described by blocks of consecutive coordinates together with the positions $n - k(k+1)/2$, and tightness reduces to an identity of the Conway-Guy sequence proved by induction. We then show, by a branch-and-bound over chambers in which every leaf carries an exact rational certificate, that $f_R(n) = f_Z(n)$ for all $n \le 8$; in particular $f_R(7) = 44$ and $f_R(8) = 84$. We then prove the same for both of Bohman's families, which first improve on Conway-Guy at $n = 12$ ($1159 < 1164$): every Bohman set is the unique optimum of its chamber, with a block-triangular certificate given by explicit formulas. Finally we exhibit chambers whose optimal vertex is not an integer point.

papers.title: Creating Steering Vectors via Input Optimisation
papers.abstract: Activation steering influences a language model's behaviour by adding a steering vector to its residual stream during generation, but it requires white-box access to modify the hidden states at every generation step. We introduce ActGCG, a modification of Greedy Coordinate Gradient which optimises a suffix to match the target activations obtained by adding a steering vector to the residual stream. We further introduce universal suffixes trained across many prompts at once, a model-translation step that rewrites the suffix into human-readable text midway through optimisation, and a soft-suffix variant to remove the discrete token space constraint. We study two behaviours: steering a model to answer in German, and anti-refusal steering for jailbreaking. For German, a discrete suffix reproduces the steering vector's behaviour almost perfectly and transfers well across prompts and models. For anti-refusal, the equivalence is weaker, succeeding under a phrase-avoidance metric but only partially under the stricter HarmBench classifier. Our results show that a steering vector's behaviour is reachable from the input, with no access to model internals at generation time, up to a loss that depends on the concept being steered.

papers.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
papers.abstract:
Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22.
  In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

This study tests whether valence (gain/loss) framing, responsibility attribution, and social conformity can lead an agent toward misconduct over a long horizon.

In a simulation built on case transcripts of In re London Silver Fixing, Ltd., Antitrust Litigation, Gemma 3 12B takes on the seat of a Deutsche Bank silver trader. As in the case, UBS, its counterparty, makes collusive requests to manipulate the price of silver. Across episodes, we vary how UBS frames its requests and measure the agent’s response as it actively manages its desk’s positions.

In behavioral economics, valence framing is the finding that people change preferences when the same outcome is described as a gain or a loss (Tversky and Kahneman 1981; Levin et al. 1998). Prospect theory explains that people weigh losses more than gains of the same size, and loss framing invites more risk (Kahneman and Tversky 1979). Responsibility attribution, assigning credit or blame for an outcome, can change behavior (Bartling and Fischbacher 2012). Conformity explains that people follow what others around them do (Asch 1956). Prior-outcome effects explain that a past win or loss changes the next bet (Thaler and Johnson 1990).

papers.title: Choosing Quantized Code LLMs by File Size and Energy per Solved Task
papers.abstract: A developer running a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. A common rule says a larger model at lower precision tends to beat a smaller one at higher precision. We ran 24 GGUF files of Qwen2.5-Coder at four sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 and priced each in energy per solved task on 542 EvalPlus tasks. The result is a selection guide indexed by Ollama's listed file size, with an evidence label on each pick. At 1 and 2 GB it picks the q4_K_M files of the 1.5B and 3B models, both on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B file that fits, and there it does not pay. That file brings no significant gain in solves over the 2 GB pick, 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deficit to 2.4 points. Yet 7B-q2_K needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task on CPU, GPU and memory rails, or 1.66 to 1.81 times on whole-system power. On HumanEval+, five alternating session pairs give a ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid. At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys a significant gain over the 2 GB pick at a higher energy price. From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI). We release per-task results, power logs and the analysis script.
papers.intro:
A developer who runs a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file. That file fixes a model size and a quantization recipe. Ollama ships each size of a model family under several recipe tags [1]. A tag names a recipe and not a bit count: the 0.5B-q3_K_M file stores 5.66 effective bits per weight (BPW), and the 7B-q2_K file stores 3.16. The download is also an energy choice, because local inference moves the energy of code assistance onto the developer’s machine. Recent studies measure that energy for local code models and find that the choice of model moves it [2, 3]. Cunha et al. [2] guide the choice of model and prompt. With the code family and prompt fixed, a developer still has to pick a file that fits a size budget, and that is the choice we price.

papers.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
papers.abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.
papers.intro:
A robot that learns by imitation usually gets object positions from perception, and those estimates are noisy. Training on noisy observations is a common remedy: the learner sees the noise during training and learns to discount the reading. How much it discounts the reading matters, because that sets how much perception error reaches the actions. Yet no quantitative account predicts this discount for modern policy classes before they are trained.

On two toy tasks with scripted experts, where the learner’s only clean input was the task phase, this prediction held up: it matched the learned gain on a held-out task and, after one failed attempt, predicted success at new configurations (Appendix B). We then pre-registered it for diffusion policies (Chi et al. 2023) on the robomimic Square task (Mandlekar et al. 2021), with Σ\Sigma estimated from the demonstrations.

papers.title: Mapping NGFS Climate Pathways to GICS Sectors: Application to Portfolio Decarbonization
papers.abstract: Portfolio climate alignment is limited by the mismatch between asset managers' sector classifications and those of climate scenarios. This article proposes an NGFS-GICS mapping based on the materiality of Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions rather than on semantic similarity. The mapping feeds a Sectoral Decarbonization Approach that down-scales NGFS trajectories into GICS sector pathways at portfolio level, adjusted for regional exposure. Applied to two illustrative ETF indices, it shows how sectoral composition and regional trajectories shape a portfolio's financed emissions pathway. The framework is transparent, asset-class agnostic and usable for internal exercises such as climate stress tests.

papers.title: Deterministic ECDSA on secp256k1: the RFC 6979 assumption, a counterexample, and the state of deployed implementations
papers.abstract: RFC 6979 derives the ECDSA nonce as $k = F_x(h)$, with $F_x$ HMAC_DRBG keyed by the signing key x. We isolate the assumption its security rests on, A*: at known public key $Q = xG$, the signing transcript under nonces $F_x()$ is indistinguishable from the transcript under uniform nonces. A* suffices, and it is neither PRF security of HMAC nor auxiliary-input PRF security (AI-PRF) of $F_x$. A function $F'(x, h) = P_{Ext(xG)}(h)$ is a PRF under standard assumptions yet leaks x from one signature; the same holds for unmodified RFC 6979 over a compression function that keeps the PRF and dual-PRF properties used in proofs of HMAC, given a collision-resistance premise. A* and AI-PRF are separated in both directions. A* does not imply AI-PRF if the one-bit hidden number problem is hard. Conversely, in the standard model: any AI-PRF can be modified so that it stays one while two chosen-digest signing queries reveal x; under DDH with one public random point, or decisional square Diffie-Hellman without it, there is an AI-PRF whose key is recovered from signatures on two ordinary hashed messages; and a third function, under PRF security and DLP, violates A* while the scheme stays unforgeable. With an ideal compression function, A* follows tightly from DLP in the presence of a randomized-ECDSA signing oracle, and a nonce key independent of x removes the assumption. The secret HMAC message block is $2^{-127.65}$ from uniform on secp256k1, $2^{-32}$ on P-256 and 0.336 on brainpoolP256r1. An audit of 31 secp256k1 implementations finds that 28 sign deterministically without added entropy and that the raw-message deviation from bits2octets of libsecp256k1 before 0.2.0 survives in NBitcoin, dcrd and btcec v2. Low-R grinding needs no assumption beyond A*, and every nonzero Fourier coefficient of the low-R nonce set is below $2^{-116.9}$ unconditionally. We give test vectors for the untested $h >= n$ branch

papers.intro:
ECDSA leaks the signing key when the per-signature nonce kk is repeated, biased, or partially known. Deterministic nonce derivation (RFC 6979 [1]) removes the dependence on a run-time random number generator by computing kk from the signing key xx and the message hash hh with HMAC_DRBG. The construction is the de facto standard in the Bitcoin and Ethereum ecosystems: of the 31 secp256k1 implementations we audited, 28 sign ECDSA deterministically by default, and the dominant library, libsecp256k1, offers no other default.

The security argument that accompanies RFC 6979 is informal. Section 4 of the RFC states that HMAC_DRBG “is secure in that role as long as HMAC behaves as a PRF” and that the construction “requires HMAC_DRBG to keep on being a random oracle even when the public key is also known”. These two sentences describe two different assumptions, and we show that neither is the one actually needed.
